TO GOD, THE BEST,
THE GREATEST, THE INCOMPREHENSIBLE
CREATOR OF MAN, FOR HIS IMMENSE
BENEVOLENCE AND MERCY TOWARDS HIM.

PRAYER OF THANKSGIVING.

[Decorative initial O]MNIPOTENT founder of all things, my incomparable creator, who, from your remarkable kindness towards man, created him with such excellence and sublimity, $^a$ that you in a certain way established him as the end of all things: $^b$ indeed, by granting him reason, you made him akin to Angels; by attributing sensitive powers, you made him equal to beasts; by providing natural forces, you made him similar to plants; by bestowing a body, you made him agree with inanimate things: $^c$ indeed, you wished to create him, this very animal, provident, sagacious, acute, mindful, full of reason and counsel, in an admirable condition, $^d$ and you so tempered his exalted nature, that you made it known to the very celestial beings, and as close as possible to the Angels: $^e$ whose whole being you formed from soul and body, that is, from an eternal and mortal disposition, so that an animal thus affected by your creation could satisfy both its origins, both to marvel at celestial things and adore you (eternal Elohim), and to inhabit and govern earthly things, so that he might love and care for what is below, and he himself might be loved and cared for by you and your superior ministers, namely, the Angels: $^f$ similarly, that he might cultivate the earth, be mingled with the elements by swiftness, descend into the depths of the sea with sharpness of mind, and that all things might shine openly and clearly for him, inasmuch as no darkness of the air might confuse his mind's intention, or density of the earth impede his works, or deep height of the water remove his view: I, your man, your creature, glorified and exalted by the immense dignity and nobility of its creator, cry out through fire, through air, and through earth, through heaven, through the universal spirit, through the abyss, and through the created things of the world:
                                                                                A 3                You

$^a$ Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book 2.
$^b$ Theological Resolutions, Vol. 2, Part 2, Page 3, Question 1.
$^c$ Aristotle, Politics, Book 3.
$^d$ Hermes Trismegistus, Asclepius, Chapter 4.
$^e$ Hermes Trismegistus, Asclepius, Chapter 4.
$^f$ Hermes Trismegistus, Poimandres, Chapter 4, and Asclepius, Chapter 3.

^h Psalm 111. 10. which makes offspring mighty in the earth, and has blessing, wealth, and riches in its house, makes righteousness perpetual, and causes light to shine in darkness; it is gracious, merciful, just, liberal, and courageous. ^i Job 11. 6. O that, most wise God, you would kindly speak with me, and open my lips for me, that you might show me the secrets of wisdom, and teach me the manifoldness of your law, so that I might truly be instructed in your schools, and become wise before you! What also can I say in praise of your will, ^k Wisdom 12. 12. who do whatever you wish, and no one is going to ask you, what or why you do so? Therefore, to you, O Jehovah, be praise, honor, and glory forever and ever.

Behold, indeed, good God, and most full of mercy, I, your human, blessed by the enjoyment of a portion of your inexplicable essence, humbly offer my mind (the sublime and most noble part of my inner being) to you, in the place of due tribute, as to my Emperor; likewise my middle soul, the effect of your excellent secondary act of nature, that it may adhere to your ways and the institutions of its mind; and my lowest soul, or ^n 1 Cor. 2. 14. my animal man, the product of your third act, that it may persist in your laws; and finally my whole body, the work of your hands, that it may be moved here and there according to your holy will, I humbly subject to you from my soul and heart. For the divine and most excellent fruit of your kindness, which, from my birth, in a honey-flowing manner, both invisibly and visibly, my soul as well as my body has tasted, I long to give immense and most grateful thanks to you, my creator, by humbly praying to you, and by earnestly entreating you with constant prayers, that you would pour out upon me the abundance of your faith, mercy, and grace through the inspiration of your spirit from the holy heavens, or the eternal mountains of Zion, so that your external power, sent from heaven and recently inspired, uniting and joining itself to that breath of life of yours comprehended within me, may strongly, vividly, and cheerfully raise my spirit by a living and true regeneration to the place of the blessed, and by joyful contemplation in this life, and by certain and infallible vision, through a true resurrection in the second life, may lead to your super-celestial throne. Therefore, into your hands (after the course of this first life has first been completed and finished by divine contemplation of divine things) I may breathe out my
soul.

--- Page 17 ---
G R A T E F U L.                                     15

I implore you, that you permit my soul, carried on golden wings in its crystalline spirit, and in the fullness of balsamic grace in Christ, and by your true word, to die, so that finally, by the alacrity of your most holy spirit, I may rise again with a complete resurrection to you, the first and sole unity of created number – that is, the principle from which my soul was first infused from simplicity into the multitude of matter – to the ineffable unity and simplicity of your glory. Be to me, O GOD, I pray, a rock in power and strength, a shield, and a fortress, so that my enemies may feel that I am covered, preserved, and happily breathing under the shadow of your wings. Grant that I may be snatched away by the inexplicable ray of your majesty to true meditation on higher things, and that lower things may be held as most vile by my soul. Grant, I say, that the memory of your glory may be perpetually retained by my spirit in deserved honor, and just reverence and fear, and be inscribed upon it with living characters. May your ineffable and most holy name be venerable and laudable to me forever; Be gracious and propitious to me by your justice: May your providence direct and govern me in my ways, while I adore counsel with admiration, preach eternity to the world, extol the incomprehensible riches of glory, and declare the perfection of truth to the entire world. Make me capable of your knowledge and doctrine, so that I, illuminated by your most holy light, well known to myself, may reverently worship you in a manner acceptable and pleasing to you and properly, admire your height, most diligently explore the beauty of the nobility and sublimity of your place and seat with fitting meditation, meditate on the mystery of infinity in ecstasy, proclaim the inscrutable depth of wisdom to all people as if with the sound of a trumpet, acknowledge the permanent will of your omnipotence, and finally, be able to sing your eternal praise and honor, which no age can end, with a unison voice to the world, relate it with the harmony of a lyre, elevate it with triumphant glory, and confidently commit it to immortal fame and perpetual writings, monuments never to be erased by any age. Nor will I, son of man, ever cease to cry out with open mouth through the most holy rays of my mind, through the subtle and empyrean spirits of intellect and reason, through the lucid substance of the vital soul and its ethereal fluid, and through the air, the receptacle of every part of my inner man, through fire, through water, and through earth, from which the composition of my earthy body is tempered, through my inner, through my outer, and through my whole being—I cry out, I say, and with an exerted voice I proclaim: YOU ALONE, THE GREATEST PROTECTOR, O JEHOVAH, ARE GOD, who made heaven and earth, and benevolently fashioned the world and man in your own image, whose name be blessed forever.

*Your creature, most happy in the goodness of your light.*

I, THE SON OF MAN.

# Contents

TREATISE I.

This treatise
on the microcosm
according to nature
is divided into two
sections, in
which
*   The first narrates the metaphysical & physical
    history of the Microcosm, in which three things
    are explained, namely its
    *   Internal or soul, whose
        essence is of a threefold
        disposition, inasmuch
        as it participates
        in the nature of heaven
        *   Empyrean, whence
            it is called
            *   Mind.
            *   Intellect.
            *   Reason.
        *   Ethereal, whence
            it is called
            *   Vegetative.
            *   Vital.
        *   Elementary,
            and for this
            reason it is called
            *   Animal.
            *   Sensitive.
            *   Idol.
    *   External or
        body, in
        which two things
        are explained,
        namely its
        *   Principle of Constitution.
        *   Harmony, by which its rebellious parts are bound together in concordant peace.
    *   The Internal in
        the External, that
        is, the operation
        of the soul in the
        body, both in
        *   Creation.
        *   Generation.
*   The second proposes the
    technical history of the
    microcosm, both
    internal and external
    nature, distributed
    into seven portions,
    namely in
    *   Divination or Prophecy, which is the science of the mind.
    *   Geometry, which is the elucidation of the intentions of the intellectual & rational soul.
    *   The Art of Memory, which is the operation of the memorative & imaginative soul.
    *   Genethlialogy or the inquiry into genius & nativity, which is the science pertaining to the vital soul.
    *   Physiognomy or the investigation of the vital & natural soul through the mere inspection & observation of the lines of the face & other parts of the body.
    *   Chiromancy, by which we explore present, past & future accidents, both of the mind and of the body, through due observation.
    *   Pyramidal Contemplation, by which the symmetry and symphonic proportions of man's internal & external parts are observed.

[Decorative woodcut ornament]

Of Light

TO THE READERS ILLUMINATED BY THE SPLENDOR
OF UNCREATED LIGHT, STIRRED BY SACRED
MENTAL ARDOR. F. R. C. THAT IS,
adorned with faith, religion, charity, [I offer] the incomprehensible life-giving strength in this life from the mountain
and rock of JEHOVAH in His word JESUS CHRIST,
the dissolution of this composition, and at last the glorious and
triumphant resurrection from the Holy Spirit through the word.

[Large decorative initial E containing a figure]
N behold, Readers adorned with the beauty of eternal light (for
scoffers, mockers, and men who have never, or at least too sparingly,
sown seed in the divine field of more abstruse Philosophy,
since their thick ears and obstinate heart reject those things
which are very often held to be true, we keep them away from this
our Philosophical feast by the magical whispers of truth itself,
and hide them in the perpetual oblivion of pious
men.) Behold, I say, and behold the figure and image, as in the preceding treatise of the Macrocosm itself, so in
this of the Microcosm, as it were deformed by uncertain human opinions, and transformed into
various fictitious and deceptive images, like Proteus, I undertake to restore it again in itself by mutual
effort: provided that you will not disdain to inspect this our treatise, otherwise perhaps rough
and ill-cultivated, written by the subtlety of a rude and unpolished pen. May glorious GOD
grant that I may soothe your eyes, perhaps desirous of novelty, with the benevolent aspect of this
not common Philosophy, your thirsty ears with the calm whisper of this wisdom now proclaimed by us, and finally your
soul desiring divine things with its pleasant contemplation. Therefore, I beseech you to be
favorable and propitious in this my Microcosmic work, so that by bringing the rest to a climax and happy
conclusion, I may consecrate them to you, filled with no common joy, willingly and gladly,
and that you cease not to favor him who will always commend obedience to your commands, while I
commend you and my cause to the providence of almighty Jehovah, who is accustomed to clothe
those worthy of His wisdom abundantly with its reward and to treat them mercifully and liberally.
Farewell.

R. F.

OF TREATISE I,
SECTION I.

let us carefully ascend, on the spiritual wings of St. Paul (relying on the virtue of the most holy spirit) let us rise to the life and immortal light of the third heaven, and if we cannot perceive the mysteries of supersubstantial numbers according to the essence of the Godhead with intellectual eyes, let us at least contemplate in them the idea, image, or example of the glory of the Trinity, and let us compare its divine and formal numbers with material ones (preceded by the highest reverence and adoration of the most holy divinity), let us mix the divine with the mundane, let us compare the mundane with the human: for thus was the world made, thus was man propagated by creation. Therefore, from the harmony of man let us ascend to the mundane symphony, and finally (transcending that mundane [symphony] with the wings of reason) to the divine: And in this way, by knowledge *a posteriori*, we can elicit those things which it will be impossible for human understanding to comprehend by knowledge *a priori*. But we, following the order of knowledge *a priori*, as from a principle to that which is principled (these things having been understood first *a posteriori*), for the sake of a more excellent method, shall begin from divine and simple numbers, and the most simple harmony formed from them, so that by their guidance, gradually and step by step, we may arrive at composite or material numbers, both mundane and human, with the symphony derived from them, and thus finally immerse ourselves more deeply in material things.

C A P. II.
*Of the monad, or the highest and mystical unity.*

[Large drop cap O]With the eyes of the divine mind illuminated by keen sight, let the metaphysician look around everywhere; with the most luminous lens of nature, let the physicist explore the angles of elements and things composed from them with the deepest inspection of his intellect (occupied with concrete things); with the sharpness of his fancy or imagination (relying on the support of demonstration, and propped up as if by Atlantean shoulders), let the mathematician examine Arithmetic, Music, Geometry, Optics, Astronomy, Astrology, and Geomancy with his prospective intuition (engaged with abstract things); with the most subtle keenness of reason, let the logician speculate on the series and orders of predicables descending from transcendent being to genera, and from genera to their subordinate species, and from those to individuals, similarly, the derivations, origins, predications, relations of predicaments, and especially the transition of the predicament of substance from the most general genus into the multitude of particulars; finally, with the confidence of memory (not without candid contemplation of the mind), let the grammarian recall the order and origin of elementary letters, the propagation of syllables derived from them, the origin of words from the union of syllables, and then afterwards, the flowing forth of sentences or speech emanating from the due connection and concatenation of words with one another: and all these [scholars] will finally perceive and discern with manifest countenance and most open eyes that the origins and existences of all things benignly spring from that one and sole mystical root, and are derived in an ineffable (but most certain) manner, which is called the monad of monads, and the highest and most divine monad, which is that one God, three times greatest, from whose fount all things, both created and uncreated (and poured forth into multitude), are observed to flow and emanate by the keen sight of the divine mind. For if we turn our contemplation to Metaphysical things, in them this unity is found to exist as the root of roots, since it is the God of Gods, the summit of summits, the good of goods, the fount of wisdom and the origin of all roots, the intelligence of intelligences, more powerful than omnipotence, unbegotten by another, of infinite benignity and a mystical mind; Indeed, in the trinity of persons—

--- Page 23 ---
DE DIVINE NUMBERS. 21

...of persons' supersubstantial essence holds the first place, since it is that most
holy unity, from which divine number proceeds, and into which it returns. Finally,
looking forth beyond its essence into material and created things in a manner surpassing imagina-
tion, from its brilliant root it produced the choir of Angels, the host of Demons,
and the assembly of souls in immense multitude, and by its ineffable wisdom,
it disposed each of them, their company and retinue, into shining and fire-gleaming orbs.
Similarly, considering the physical creatures of the world, and regarding
them in the proper manner, we shall find this mystical monad to hold the first
place among them, since this same unity is no less the root of the number ten
than of a hundred and a thousand, from which numbers we shall declare below
that the fabric of the world was constituted in the beginning, and now endures.
Hence, among physicists, it is called the divine principle, infinite nature, and nature
naturing, the principle of principles, the star of stars, the light of lights, or the light of creatures shining everywhere,
the spirit of spirits, and the maker and effector of spirits, the world of worlds,
the leader, governor, and director of all, the exalter and depressor.
No Philosopher will deny that Time also had its origin from this root,
inasmuch as this monad, in its eternal nature and unbegotten by another, exists as the
beginning and end, or α and ω, of all created things. Wherefore also from the
said mystical root it received its beginning (the Now), without which no time would ever
exist; since the Now is its terminus, from which it is deduced and moved, no differently
than a line from a point. Without this root, there would also be no logical relation, since
we speak of the Son for no reason unless it is with respect to the Father, neither in supersubstantial
things, where the Father is called of Himself, or a principle arisen from Himself, nor in inferior
things, since there this root is the hidden seed of beings, the parent of ages, and life
producing all things, filling and satisfying all things with its own goodness and bounty.
Furthermore, this root, also considered according to Mathematics, in Geometry, is the
point of the primordial line, and the center of the circle, from whose multiplication all
lines, all surfaces, and all bodies, both mathematical and physical,
proceed, and again, by preceding resolution, they finally return to it, as to the
principle from which they came. In Music, it is the origin of concord and harmony,
namely that primordial unison, from whose supersubstantial tone empyrean
or spiritual melody, whether mundane, or human, and also instrumental,
arises, inasmuch as from the terminus of its radical voice or sound (producing the word),
the compound consonances Diatessaron, Diapente, Diapason, Diapason with Diapente, and Dis-
diapason are derived. In Arithmetic, this monad
also exists as the root, from which digits, articuli (tens and hundreds), numbers, hundreds, thousands, and so
on to infinity are observed to arise and emanate. Whence it is manifest that
this root or monad and unity is one and all, one of all, one
before all, and one in itself, the root and center of present, past, and
future things, which are, prior to material unity, because it is most simple, the number
of numbers, unity and number, and a unity which penetrates every number by its simplicity;
for in the Trinity, the Father is ineffable, looking towards the empyrean heaven,
is the mind of mind, and the soul of souls, and looking further downwards into the material
world, is the nature of natures. O, therefore, admirable disposition of the monad
or unity, which, though it is the cause and origin of the existence of things, yet what
it is, cannot be discerned by the acuteness of intellect, indeed, not even of the mind (which immediately
flows from it), nor expressed by any reason. Yet, the wonderful
nature of this essence is clearly explained to our reason in the contemplation
of arithmetical unity: For arithmetical unity is the common
measure, fount, and origin of all numbers, containing within itself every number, however
great, and yet innocent of all multitude, always the same, immutable, indi-
                                                                                                C 3             visible

--- Page 24 ---
22 TRACT. I. SECT. I. LIB. I.

indivisible and devoid of equals: And hence it is, that this unity multiplied by itself produces nothing but itself. For 1. multiplied by itself produces only 1. and internally, from that 1. multiplied by itself, nothing but a single unity will arise: Whence it is clear, that unity is its own root, square, cube, etc. and yet it is always the same thing. For however it is multiplied into unities, none of the produced unities is greater or less than the radical unity, nor is it a part smaller than its whole, because it is not multiplied into parts but into itself. Finally, it is the beginning and end of all things, while it itself has neither beginning nor end by which it exists, because nothing is prior to one, and nothing is posterior to one. One, therefore, is the principle of all things, and all things exist up to one, and beyond it nothing exists. Furthermore, all things that exist desire one itself, as their root, because from it they first proceeded, and of that one they necessarily partake: Hence it is, therefore, that all things strive to return to that one, inasmuch as they radically flowed from it; which regression, and return to the first principle, would never be perfected unless plurality and multitude were gradually and step-by-step stripped away from them. Such, therefore, is that mystical monad of monads, unity of unities, the prior summit of simplicity, the seed and center of all things, devoid of all substance, the principle, root, and origin of all, a principle, I say, containing every number yet contained by none, generating every number yet generated by no number, father of all, father of itself, father of the only-begotten son: Indeed, such and beyond what the human mind can imagine, is that unity, one and monad, the holy of holies, the summit of exaltation, and God of gods, who, above the peaks of heaven, and beyond all material existence, sits constantly joyful and replete in his throne and seat, resplendent with immortal glory, intoning to the world that most sacred, mystical, ineffable, and original tone, by whose pulsation, act, and uniform and harmonious breath, the world and its creatures are imbued with various concordances of forms, by which they exist and live, and the most elegant and active harmonies of things (soothing the thirsty ears of the mind) are heard, and are conceived and hidden in the innermost parts of human reason, by whose ineffable melody, and effective voice and word (with the divine Spirit breathing everywhere), the structure of the macrocosm is observed to leap with a certain joy, to dance proportionally, and as it were, to spring forth into life, and the stars, both fixed and wandering (as if suffused with supernatural joy), are perceived to lead eternal dances, and the proportions and consonances of the microcosm, in mind, intellect, reason, soul, motion, life, and the elemental construction of the body (performing beautiful and admirable functions), are perceived to be supported as if by divine buttressing. This unity, I say, is the pulsator of the Monochord and the very form and soul of all macrocosmic and microcosmic harmony, whose string or instrumental matter is that universal spirit, which it, by its ineffable act, liberated from the depths of chaos, and made from nothing, so that something might actually exist, and in place of being passive, might serve its stupendous actions, to whom, as King of Kings, all things of all nature are to be offered, and as a tribute due to it, are to be attributed and conferred (namely, the life, essence, souls, and bodies of things, inasmuch as they are dependent on it), and above all, with the utmost effort and final endeavor of the mind, anyone of sound mind and adorned with a modest gift of reason ought to acknowledge and confess it.

Some examples by which the Unity of the most holy Trinity (comparing it to inferior things) is demonstrated for human capacity.

The supersubstantial Unity of essence is explained in Arithmetic by 1. For from this unity in Arithmetic, all numbers, progressing to infinity, are derived as from their source and fundamental origin, such as 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. &c. In Mathematics and the art of Geometry, it is demonstrated by a point, from which a line is derived, by which it is continued, and in which it is terminated (whence a line is most correctly defined as the flux of points connected to each other.) But because every surface is composed of lines and every body of surfaces, it follows thence by necessity that both lines, as well as surfaces, and consequently the body itself, originate from a single point; In a similar manner, from unity and its flux, the denary number is formed, in which unity joins itself to composition, namely, a superexcellently substantial nature with created matter, as 1. with 0. without which the cipher will be no more than prime matter deprived of essential and luminous form: Whence simple unity relates to the denary number as a point to a line, and the denary number to the centenarian (hundred), as a line to a surface, in which also GOD, unity or the point, always precedes, and the centenarian number to that millenarian (thousand), as a surface to a body, as we shall indicate more broadly below. From which it is clearly evident that unless God is placed before all things, things will be no more in actual existence than arithmetical ciphers, which, however much they may express multitude by themselves, yet without unity, or any of the digits flowing from it, will signify absolutely nothing, as 0. 00. 000. 0000. 00000. denote nothing, but 10. 100. &c. denote something. By a point also, GOD is wonderfully explained in physical reality, since that is motion in generation and corruption, the principle, and as it were this (*now*) from which, as from the paternal foundation of its origin, or the terminus a quo (point of departure), time proceeded, and into which it again returns.

CAP. III.
*Concerning the Dyad or mystical and supersubstantial duality.*

THE first monad of monads, and the holy supersubstantial unity of unities, poured forth in an ineffable manner by the birth of the simplicities of the summits, gave birth and produced, indeed, that which, proceeding through its primordial form, obtained a threefold power: For where the depth of the Father is, there shines forth the illustrious splendor of the Son, and the conciliatory splendor of the Holy Spirit, and thus that supersubstantial fount is crowned by the beauty of its offspring, which flowed from its center, and revolves around the center, and the Son was begotten, who is the glorious wisdom of the Father, and the maker of all things: For through the outpouring of the one into the Son, an ineffable middle nature was born, which was before all natures, indeed a sacred birth and an inexpressible offspring of the ineffable Father, whose hidden and mystical origin no time indeed has known, because he appeared together with the Father, always born, who was to be born, and remains in him, although begotten from him, so that he may govern all things with a wise spirit: The Son, I say, proceeding from the Father, remains in the Father eternally, and again, rules over what is outside of the Father. This is the Father's vocalizing Word and the most active and first discourse, begotten from the first root: He is the root of all; for all things were created through his glorious origin, since he is the seed of all things. Therefore, Unity is the fount of Duality of the same essence: and Duality or the Son is the form and image of Unity or the Father: Unity or the Father is the power of Duality or the Son; but Duality or the Son is the beauty of the Father. And although the duality of matter is an inauspicious number: because it is the fount and origin of strife, discord, impurity, and confusion, for this number, by assuming matter to itself, is separated from unity, because it enters into the limits of contention, and by multiplying itself downwards into multitude, fleeing from the presence of unity, and tending towards the center and depth of dark matter, it flows forth, therefore this number in matter is called the most imperfect of all, because it can never be resolved except by resolution, and reduced to the apex of essential and supersubstantial unity, nevertheless, this divine number of form, the binary, not receding beyond the limits of the essence of unity, is the most formal and most blessed number; because in the same essence, by virtue of unity (with the Holy Spirit mediating and connecting, proceeding from the center of unity or the Father, and of duality or the Son) it is reflected to unity, and renewed with unity, according to that saying of *M. Trismeg. The Monad generates the Monad, and has reflected its ardor into itself.* And this essence is God-like, uniform and threefold, because although there is a triple here of persons and numbers, in respect to

--- Page 27 ---
DE DIVINIS NUMERIS. 25
the difference of distinct offices and virtues attributed to each, there is
always, however, a unity of essence and identity of Deity; which unity indeed, by the power
of spiritual glue, will be inviolably preserved forever. And in this way
we have the Dyad from the Monad, which, by the reconciling power of the Triad,
is again reduced to unity with the Monad. Therefore, the duality of numbers is unity, because it is trinity,
and it is trinity, because it is unity; namely, a trinity of persons, and a unity of the
Deiform essence.

C A P. IV.
*Of the supersubstantial origin of the Triad or the ternary number.*

For indeed GOD, Mind most full of the fecundity of both sexes (now I speak
with the mouth of *Mercurius Trismegistus*), life and light, with His word begot another
creative mind; which God indeed is called fire and a divine spirit, whom
*Synesius* called the Holy Spirit, a mediating principle proceeding from the center of the begetter and from the
center of the son, whose shining light is called conciliatory, because
its ternary number is the truest and most sincere love, which joins the Father with the
Son in an inviolable bond, inasmuch as duality (which is a multitude
progressing from unity) is reduced to harmonious unity by the bond of the ternary number.
Such, therefore, was the origin of the world, a progression, I say, from unity into multitude,
and such its period, namely, the reduction of multitude to unity.
Therefore, according to the progression of these divine numbers always contained in unity,
the order, harmony, proportion, measure, or intervals of material duality,
or spiritual, or aqueous, or humid nature are arranged: for hence the division
of the entire world into three regions, of which the second received its essences from the first and third and from both:
hence the three harmonies of every symphony, Dia-
pason, Diapente, & Diatessaron, of which Diapente [is] from Diapason as if from unity,
and Diatessaron from both: hence the double, sesquialteral, and sesquitertial
proportions of all things and of the world itself, derived from the varied disposition of divine light in the universal
spirit in hyle (matter): hence the intervals of things, namely line, su-
rface & body, or length, width, & depth; namely, line from a point,
& surface from a line, & body from both: hence the three kinds of souls, in-
tellectual, sensitive & vegetative: hence the disposition of the world by three, namely,
number, measure & weight: hence finally three Princes of the world are proclaimed by Philosophers;
GOD, Mind, & Spirit. And this was the reason why the Pythagoreans called unity
Apollo, the dyad matter, but the triad form and justice, which is the highest perfection.
Therefore, the Poet says that God delights in an odd number, because the first and simplest odd number in the supercelestial
essence is that love which joins the father with the son, whence (*says Synesius*) *Hail, O pu-*
*rest Spirit, center of the son and the father.* And elsewhere: *He called it the companion of the son and the medium between the root and the shoot.*
And elsewhere: *Conciliatory light*, because derived from the two first persons
and united with them, it formed the Trinity: therefore, this ternary number
is called; a sacred number, a number of perfection, & a most powerful number, because it is un-
compounded and the first odd number, by whose bond Duality becomes Trinity and Trinity
is made Unity. And hence it is, that the one has acquired a threefold power, by which it is brought
about that GOD is one and all things, one in Himself and through all things, & that Unity
is, when it is Trinity, & that Trinity is, when it is Unity: according to *Synesius' hymn 2.*
*I sing of you, Unity, I sing of you, Trinity: You are One, though you are Trinity; You are Trinity, though you are Unity.*

For Unity is and is the sole act in itself; Trinity is in its perfection, emanating from itself, by which all things are said to be created, perfect, and good. Therefore we conclude that unity is the starting point and duality the first-born of unity, as a number intermediate between unity and the ternary, by whose perfection, in the divine essence, duality, or the middle, is joined to the two extremes by an indissoluble bond, which again cohere to themselves in a wonderful way by a circular progression. From this it follows that all three persons, distinct in property, are nothing but one in essence, namely, the one highest and sole essence, which exists as nothing apart from the three persons, that is, three properties, of which one is not another, nor are any two the third, nor is any third the two; that is, two are what the third is, and the third is what the two are. What is this? One Godhead, one essence, finally one. How is this, if three? How are three, if this? Therefore, incomprehensibly, wonderfully: Faith alone knows, but as if the whole, by the divine Spirit, instituting the formula of baptism under this ternary number and relation: "*Baptize*," he says, "*in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit*," which three relatives indeed receive a declaration, as we will show more fully below.

From one essence, namely A, three distinct properties proceed, which in themselves are one and the same, namely, as it were, the supersubstantial essence A. But in the fabric of the world there are various and diverse properties of the Deity: For God, constantly seated at the summit of the heavens, sent forth from Himself His son or wisdom for the creation of the spherical world, no differently than the mobile leg of a compass advances by expansion from the leg of the same, fixed and firmly remaining in the center, for the production of a circle or periphery, by whose operation the circle is delineated, and yet they agree in essence, namely in unity or a point. "By the word of Jehovah (says the Psalmist) were the heavens established," etc.: And elsewhere; "the machine is completed by the wisdom of God": Therefore, the Unity and Father, constantly and invariably remaining, ordained the duality or son, so that he might execute His will, and the son, obedient to his father, and regularly governed by the Spirit (proceeding from the father and himself), did not advance beyond his circle and limits equidistant from the center; because through the Spirit

--- Page 31 ---
DE DIVINE NUMBERS. 29

By the Spirit, both extremes are joined into this one same thing, so that the whole is nothing but one unique GOD, and one divine essence, superexcellent and surpassing all understanding, to whom be eternal praise, excellence, and dignity. Thus one and the same compass is distributed into various offices, one of which is to stand firmly, and to govern the twofold actions of the other properties according to justice, and to dispose according to its own disposition, without which it is impossible to describe a circular figure: Another is, to operate externally in space and spacious matter, and to delineate a circular and orbicular figure: A third, to connect the virtue of both by the bond of love, and to proportion exactly and according to justice the harmony and conformity flowing from the embrace of both. The offices also of the one Deity are explained in a similar manner, but also further than the human mind can conceive. For the Father, constantly sitting in the sublime citadel (with flashing fire), by ordering, said, and by the word FIAT fabricated the orbicular world and the spherical heavens; and the intermediate Spirit, embracing the virtue of both by the bond of love, infused power and efficacy, both of the speaker and of the word, into the world and its creatures, and poured it forth abundantly, according to that royal Psalmist previously quoted: "By the word of the Lord were the heavens established, and by the spirit from His mouth all their power."

C H A P. V.
That each person of the holy and individual Trinity has a distinct property in the fabric of the world and the production of its creatures;
And concerning the universal property of unity, and its agreement with the number ten.

The admirable principle of the mystical creation of the world lies hidden in the arcane disposition of the Trinity and the bosom of the Deity, so that there exists no "finger" in the Trinity, whether it be one, or two, or three, which does not possess its own proper and peculiar mystery within itself, and does not produce a varied effect in the world (according to the immense and admirable efficacy of its function). For in unity (insofar as it cannot be multiplied in itself, or reduced or divided from its nature into a multitude), as in a unique universal, ideal, and purely formal world, the effigy of the material world is delineated in an abstruse manner: For one, beyond doubt, was the principal exemplar of things to be founded in the mind of the creator. Therefore, as the Monad was first in the production of the Trinity (which is the first root of things both uncreated and created), so also, secondly, after the birth of that simple square, unity occupied the first place in the number ten for the composition of the world, since it is bound by a strong connection with the number ten: For unity is the supersubstantial father of generation, and the number ten is the substantial father of generation, which two progenitors indeed do not differ from each other, since both are one God, but nevertheless differ in the property of action: because the former unity was simple, and in an inexplicable way dwells in the supersubstantial world, but the latter, in the denary (that is, joined with a cipher), acts upon the material world. Hence Mercurius Trismegistus says: "GOD is the father of the cosmos, and the cosmos is the son of God," etc. Therefore GOD is unity in the formal world and has the place of the number ten in the material world: For as the number ten is the end of simple numbers, so also it is the beginning of composite numbers, and the middle or center between unity and the number one hundred. Therefore unity begins the number ten in simple numbers, and again, the same unity is observed to terminate any denary numbers.

that it regards the entire nature of things and the universal spirit of the world, reduces from
potentiality to act, sustains with its fiery breath of life, and finally props up the entire
machine with its immense strength.

This duality indeed does not behave in the same way as that formal one, which we demonstrated above to be most complete and most perfect in its nature, and the preserver of things; but conversely, the material spirit does not exist in the nature of things by itself any more without divine rays and assistance than a cipher without a digit among arithmeticians, as was shown before. Moreover, this material number is in itself the number of sedition and the origin of discord, and consequently most imperfect, inasmuch as it does not have an actual principle consubstantial to itself, since its consubstantial principle was something one in potential, but after its production into act, it abandoned that denomination and assumed the form of plurality, losing its unity, and rightly attributing it to formal unity. And hence it is that it possesses least of all a unity actually suitable to its nature, wherefore it has neither beginning nor middle nor end, whence it happens that matter itself is the worst thing without the presence of the divine number and the assistance of the source, namely, of all goodness, because unless the supersubstantial trinity were to infuse something of its perfection and goodness into this worldly matter, there would be nothing but a heap of evils, a gathering of envy, an accumulation of discord, an abyss of deformity, and an inclination towards multitude: Nor would all these things even be, unless it were mere potentiality, inasmuch as every act (as has been said) and all goodness is from the luminous source. Hence therefore this material binary number has been called *the number of discord, confusion, misfortune, and impurity*. Therefore, by progression from this inauspicious material number, which tends downwards, the divine soul is more and more incarcerated, and is enveloped in the densest snares of darkness, and is rendered most unhappy, vexed by passions and deceived by the deceptions and illusions of the world; Whence it happens that the more light descends from the sight of the luminous source towards the base of the material pyramid, the more it is endangered and submerged in darkness: Thus this duality, drawn into itself, produces 4 elements, which first, by their viscosity, encircle the soul in their spirit, and again, immersing itself still deeper into its profound depths, the soul, captivated by the snares of the spirit, is reduced to a cube, and is introduced into an opaque body, or three dimensions, or the element of elements, or a composition of 4 elements constituting the cube of a square, by the flatteries of the spirit, which is on the side of matter. C A P. VIII.
*On the property of the ternary number in the Trinity, or of the third person*
*in the fabric of the world.*

**T**his odd, supersubstantial number is most holy, in which G O D is said to rejoice, inasmuch as it is an uncompounded, sacred, most powerful, and most perfect number; to that extent it comprehends many mysteries of the Godhead and has produced many secrets in the composition of the world. For in the first place, since G O D is referred to by the ternary number, it is therefore argued and indicated that this number is most perfect, inasmuch as it is the beauty perfecting the beginning, middle, and end, and absolutely possessing equality. But other numbers, which have those three degrees of perfection, do not have them absolutely and simply, but relatively and compositely. Therefore, this ternary number reveals God as the beginning, cause, and form from the principal form; it reveals the most perfect from the beginning, middle, and end, so that, through whom all things are, and in whom all things are. From which it is evident that this number is the most abstruse and admirable communion and indissoluble bond of the third person in the Trinity with the first and second, clearly explaining, and connecting all three together by an ineffable knot of unity and an inviolable bond of the same. Therefore, the office of this most holy spirit, or third person in the Trinity, is concerned with

This divine spirit also operates for the distinction of the genera of terrestrial creatures, dividing them into animals, vegetables, and minerals. Finally, in the supreme heaven, it causes the genera of living beings to differ, distinguishing them into diverse natures; into gods, demons, heroes, and souls (according to *Iamblichus'* opinion), and thus in infinitely many other ways.

**C A P. IX.**
*How the tripartite division of each of the three heavens or regions of the world corresponds in its order to the three persons of the Holy Trinity.*

But so that we may prove with still more effective arguments that the entire world was made and formed according to the exemplar of the three persons in the Holy Trinity, and consequently as an image and representation of God, it will be necessary to consider that we first examine with spiritual eyes the properties and positions of the three hierarchies of the Empyrean heaven, and we shall perceive that they agree in every respect (and in a direct manner) with the three persons of the Trinity. For in the superior hierarchy, called *Epiphany*, the property of the Father is found, since this is concerned with the fervent

--- Page 39 ---
DE DIVINE NUMBERS. 37

fervent love and affection at the summit of the highest motion and in the liberation or weighing of particular judgments: Hence this hierarchy is divided into orders naturally suited to such a property. For the *Seraphim* (who constitute the superior order of this hierarchy) consist of a multitude of angels, whose role it is to understand the highest things and to be inflamed by the essential fire of God, insofar as they are closest to the formal world and nearest to the simplest dwelling of God: The *Cherubim* are filled with wisdom and knowledge. And the *Thrones* are most fully replete with divine judgment: For (as *Isidore* testifies) GOD sits upon them in His judgment, and through them disposes all things. Hence this hierarchy is rightly attributed to God the Father.

The second and middle hierarchy is called *Epiphonomia*, which signifies divine splendor and clarity with reverence, divided into *Principalities, Powers, and Dominions*: Thus the second person, who is the Word, is called the light of the world and the life of things, which we ought primarily to revere as the act of things.

The third and lowest is called *Ephionia*, as if pertaining to virtues, because the spirits of this hierarchy, whether they be *Virtues, Archangels*, or *Angels*, have the power to perform miracles, to cure illnesses of both mind and body—and this beyond the reason of nature—and to demonstrate mysteries, to which the third person is referred, since all virtues are attributed to the world by the Spirit from the mouth of the Lord.

Therefore, from the first hierarchy, as from a luminous source or center, the second proceeds as splendor and light from a fiery body, and as color arises from light, so virtues arise from the splendor of light. Therefore, the first hierarchy is like a fiery ardor, the second divine clarity, as from fiery ardor, and the third, secret virtue, as heat from both, namely fire and light. How most manifest, then, do we see here the conformity of the first heaven and its parts with the Trinity.

Now, proceeding from this heaven to the second, there too we shall find the trinity most evidently under the same relation: For in its first and supreme triplicity, embracing the *primum mobile*, the *starry heaven*, and the *sphere of Saturn*, we shall perceive the property of unity and of the Father; for just as unity is the first number from which other numbers arise, so all lower things are moved by the virtue of the *primum mobile*: Similarly, as the firmament is called the heaven composed of fixed stars, so the Father is fixed in His nature, immobile and in no way to be altered, as is observed in the nature of unity: Finally, as *Saturn* was called by the Poets the father of the other Gods, so from the unity or supersubstantial Father the two other persons of the Trinity, the Son and the Holy Spirit, are propagated.

Again, the second and middle triplicity of this heaven is compared in its disposition to the second person of the Trinity. For as *Jupiter* was the son of *Saturn*, so the second person is the Son of the first; as he is called the father of thunderbolts (carrying thunderous arrows with him), so also is this voice of the Father going forth with lightning and thunder, and accompanied by immense powers from the mouth of the Father, striking with ineffable power wherever it wills: *Jupiter* is also esteemed for justice, benevolence, religion, piety, as a preserver and friend of the human race, and as a distributor of radical moisture and innate heat, which most easily separates for the life of things. But innumerable passages of the sacred scriptures have clearly explained the incomparable power, justice, benignity, religion, piety, affability towards the human race, and operation for life and its preservation of the Son. *Mars*, also found in the same triplicity, argues for the Son's power and victory against the prince of impiety and his followers, namely the multitude of iniquity, whose role it is to overcome the beast, the false prophet, hell (Orcus), and death itself. Finally, this most holy second person is appropriated to the *Sun* in many ways: For just as mundane harmony is said to flow from *Apollo*, so in truth from the Son, or duality with His spirit, the universal symphony of matter (in the Diatessaron, Diapente, and consequently in the Diapason, which is composed of those two) is derived, as has been declared above. The *Sun* also, according to *Merc. Trismegistus*, is the *son of the material world*, and according to *Plato*, the *immortal God's*

**CHAPTER X.**
**\*On the reason, according to Mathematics, why the Godhead was first designated by number, and then afterwards by the ternary number, similarly why, according to Logicians, relation was attributed to the Godhead.\***

Now indeed we have proposed to bring forth publicly the reasons, first, why Theology dedicated GOD to number, then we will bring forth geometrical reasons, why it chose the ternary number, to express GOD, the first form of all things, the efficient cause, and dedicated the Godhead to such. First, therefore, it must be known that Theography wished to declare and explain the Godhead to us by number because of a threefold consideration, of which the first is, that it might reveal His infinity thereby, since nothing is more infinite than number, as it were, whose magnitude has no end: Second, that it might declare GOD prescient; For number was (as the wise man says) undoubtedly the principal exemplar in the mind of the creator for things to be created: Lastly, that it might indicate GOD to be immutable, for nothing is more immutable than unity, and its properties, as has been said above: For what things were, those same things are; what things are, those same things were, and always. Therefore, number insinuates God to be simple while immutable, it insinuates Him to be wise while prescient, it insinuates Him to be incomprehensible while infinite; finally, it insinuates Him to be wonderful and singular, while these three [qualities are present].

Theologians indeed chose the ternary number above others, wishing God to be the first form of all things. And that it is the principle of forms and the first and supreme root of bodies, we are taught by the most evident geometrical demonstration: For if we consider that triangular figure with diligent attention, we will indeed perceive that it is not resolved into others, nor is it subject to any principles, inasmuch as it is itself the principle of other figures for composition, but the end for resolution: For square and pentagonal figures and the rest proceed from it and return into it, inasmuch as from this surface, which is the principle of lines, it is necessary that all other surfaces, as well as bodies composed of surfaces, are derived, in whose dissolution it will again be necessary that they return to that triangular surface: Such, therefore, is God, from whom are all things, and into whom all things are complicated with a resolutory simplicity. Finally, whatever exists, receives its being, that which it is, from form, and not from matter; matter itself also receives its being from form, and form, moreover, is unsusceptible to accidents. From this, therefore, that the ternary is the principle of forms, it insinuates with wonderful and most secret truth the cause and principle of universality and of unsusceptible difference, which is alone and truly one. Again it is declared that this ternary number is most properly adapted to God alone, because it is the most perfect number, completing all things. For it is beauty, perfecting beginning, middle, and end, and having these equal and absolute, while on the contrary the binary number proceeds stripped of these three, having neither beginning nor end (because there is no middle) and consequently deprived of this sacred gift of perfection. The other numbers, however many hold beginning, middle, and end, do not have that perfection absolutely and simply, but compositely. Therefore, the ternary number reveals GOD, the principle and cause and form from the chief form, it reveals the most perfect from the beginning, from the middle, and from the end; from the beginning, as that from which all things are; from the middle, as that through whom all things are, and from the end, as that in whom all things are. Furthermore, for this reason also by number

in such a number, which is similarly like such a relation, or it is said that in the Triad the monad is found as if by itself, and the dyad as if by itself; so also in the Trinity, as if the Dyad by itself, like the Father and the Son, and again, because the monad by itself, like the Holy Spirit. Therefore the Father and the Son respond to each other by relation, and not to the Spirit. The Spirit, as if by itself, is not to be referred to the Father by name, nor to the Son. Therefore it is referred to by signification, as *the Spirit, the Spirit of the Spirator, and the Spirator of the Spirit is the Spirator: The Spirator is the Father and* *the Son, nor are there two spirators, but one, and one spirit.*

Finally, Theography uses relative predication, wishing to demonstrate God to be in agreement with Himself, indeed, truly, to indicate that He is harmony itself and a full and singular connection: *For whatever the Father does, these things the Son* *also does similarly, and the one and same Spirit works the same things, dividing to each as He wills.* An incomprehensible harmony and singular connection, so that more and of one are one, many in identity of person, indeed, more persons of the Godhead than the first of one Spirit and of the Angelic [realm]; Finally, it surpasses all understanding. Beware, I say, lest the unity of life turn its splendid face away from you, and for that reason you be again thrust down into the oblivion and deformity of darkness: Therefore, O human body, do not be so adverse to yourself, as to lightly esteem the light and spark of your clarity and life derived from formal unity, and to act so hostilely with it, but by cherishing it, render continuous thanks for it to its root and source, so that from its fount you may at last obtain full information, purification, illumination, and resurrection to angelic perfection.* But whither does the sweetest and most delightful ardor of Divinity now lead and carry away our Muse? Let us return to our matter at hand. For just as the primary order of the novenary number, formed from simple digits, revolves around the power of the sole Deity; so the second repetition of unity, proceeding with a single cipher to the composition of the second series of the novenary number, once composed, leads to the proportion of the empyrean heaven in composition; and its third repetition or addition with two ciphers contributes to the perfection of the middle heaven. Finally, the fourth with three ciphers revolves around the completion of the lowest heaven. Hence it is clear that the cube resulting and produced from the most holy ternary number expands throughout the entire capacity of the world; indeed, it even penetrates to the center of the world, and disperses itself. Hence GOD is also said to exist in darkness, and yet darkness is not darkness to Him. Psalm. Therefore, God is observed to be everywhere, nor is there anything where He is not, and outside Him there is nothing, since He Himself is the most holy Monad of monads, beyond which there is nothing. For what is prior to unity? And consequently, He comprehends all things in Himself and under Himself. From the concatenation of these numbers, therefore, it is clear what the proportion of the material pyramid is in each region of the world, namely, in the superior [region] it is simple, where a simple cipher is found, in the middle it is double, and in the lowest it is sesquialtera (one and a half times). CHAPTER XIII.
*Concerning the septenary number, and what mysteries are*
*comprehended under it.*

**T**he septenary number results from unity, the binary number, and the quaternary number, from which is born the Diapason, which is the most perfect harmony; by whose virtue and proportion God descended from His immortal and simply formal throne into the universal orb of the material world, informing and composing things. Wherefore this number was powerful and efficacious in the mystery of creation and concerning holy things.

--- Page 49 ---
teria, all things are generated, and by the same path they are also dissolved; but generation and life are a supernatural light and a harmonious force, while corruption is from the underworld and from night and rending darkness. Hence it is, that according to the doctrine of Orpheus, Hesiod, Euripides, and others, the divine Sun exists in the archetype, from which is all beauty, all adornment, all harmony, and the fount of life; in whose right hand is piety, kindness, and beneficence; in the left, severe punishment. Him they call Phoebus, Apollo, and the Sun, whom they say carries the Graces and Charities in his right hand and a bow and arrows in his left, whom by night they named Dionysus, tearing apart and rending, and breaking himself into seven parts; and in the daytime they named him Apollo, again composing those things which he had torn apart by night, and dividing them into seven parts. Therefore, by night he breaks apart and rends, and by day he unites things, as if driving away evils. For this reason, therefore, he is called Alexicacos by the Athenians, that is, the repeller of evils, and by Homer, Υ'γιων, that is, the author of health. With these also seems to agree that opinion of the Pythagoreans, who enclosed the world and the soul within seven limits. In the first place, they put unity, as if the ultimate degree of the soul and mind, through which it contains the supreme unity in the Creator, and has become one and the same with Him; for all things pre-existing in the Word were one with that Word, according to the Theologians. The second place (containing a double proportion compared to the first) denotes the progress of the soul or mind with God. The third demonstrates the entry into itself, and thus is described the emanation of the persons of the Trinity, namely, of one into another, and the return of the third again into unity. But now the emission of the Spirit of the Lord into the imperfect mass is reached, and thus the number four is proceeded to. The fourth signifies the egress which it makes from itself, so that it may be occupied with things to be created, and still formless. And thus in the fifth, sixth, and seventh (which last two limits or places consist of solid numbers) it denotes the conversion of bodies, to which the soul is joined, I say bodies: for the world consists of a twofold body, namely, of the incorruptible and celestial, and of the corruptible and elementary: So also man, in order to retain the perfect image of the world, according to the Platonists, was made of a twofold body, one elementary, the other celestial. The elementary is denoted by the cube or solid of the binary, which designates matter, and the celestial by the cube of the ternary; which cube indeed we said above to be rather a surface or a square number, for the reasons adduced by us there. For although spiritual elements are in themselves humid bodies, nevertheless if ether and air and fire are compared to solid bodies, they relate to them as a surface to a body, or as a square to a cube.

C A P. XIV.
Concerning the admirable property of the septenary number and its changes in its
square: Concerning the number filling its square: and
concerning the base derived therefrom.

Indeed, it is not to be doubted that immense secrets lie hidden in this septenary number, since it is frequently used in the sacred Scriptures, both in the performance of divine mysteries and in other matters of nature and human necessity or custom. Nor indeed should men, treading in the footsteps of fools and ignorance, say that there is no greater secret in this number than in others, and consequently, that the frequent repetition of this number in sacred writings signifies nothing more abstruse than that of any other number. For as by demonstration

Similarly, seven multiplied by itself by seven will produce 49, from the parts of which number, considered in arithmetical progression and arranged in a square manner, the base of the septenary, namely 175, emerges in a certain miraculous way (by progressing from any point of the square to its opposite). Indeed, how great the perfection is in the base of this number seven, and how much happiness the completion of this number imports to human life, seems to be clearly argued to us by that blessed age of Abraham, consisting of 175 years, about which the Holy Scripture speaks thus in Gen. 25. 7: "And the days of Abraham's life were one hundred seventy-five years, and passing away, he died in a good old age, advanced in age and full of days, etc." From which it is clear that this number of solar revolutions produces an advanced age, a happy old age, and a fullness of days; and from this it is evident that there is an infinite mystery in the consideration of this number seven. Indeed, I myself know a most learned man who, by virtue of this number seven, with the assistance of a kind of oracle, did not hesitate to resolve doubtful and uncertain questions, and even promised to divine in some way about hidden things, both present and future.

C H A P. XV.
On the Mystery of Divine Numbers in Creation.

N We have mentioned above that simple numbers or digits refer to a supernatural essence and belong to the supracelestial region, which is indeed infinite; here, however, we have proposed to treat of the divine reason of the number five, and then finally of the number ten. Indeed, just as we have demonstrated above that the monad or unity is the fount and origin of all numbers, inasmuch as from it the Dyad is derived, not as a number, but as a confusion of unities, insofar as it contains two ones within itself, which we therefore also called the principle of imperfect number, because it has a beginning and a middle, but lacks an end; no differently than we called the ternary number the beginning of perfect number, inasmuch as it has within itself a beginning, a middle, and an end, and is therefore held among the numbers of perfection: so we said that with respect to these three terms, namely 1, 2, 3, there is a relation through all other numbers, progressing to infinity. Therefore, just as unity is the root of the first perfect number, namely the ternary, which signifies the universal form. (For what difference does it make if GOD exists as unity, and the universal spirit in potential as duality, if that spirit is not informed and actualized by that GOD, so that duality may finally be perfected into Trinity?) so also duality is the root of the imperfect quaternary number, namely, and of those which arise from it. And hence it is that, as 3 relates to 1, so in the same proportion 5 relates to 3, and 7 to 5, and 9 to 7. Similarly, as one relates to 2, so 4 relates to 2, and 6 to 4, and 8 to 6, according to which simple progressions all other composite ones are deduced, but the perfection of these is unity: Wherefore, just as imperfection arises from unity in the middle movement, so by its addition at the end, the third term is brought forth, from which the first of the perfect numbers arises, namely the ternary. From which it is clear that both imperfection and perfection, that is, both evil as far as we are concerned, and good, flows from the hands of God or unity, in whose power is that which is evil, G by virtue

--- Page 52 ---
50          T R A C T. I.  S E C T. I.  L I B. I.
by the power of His spirit to render good and complete both for Himself and for humans.
Therefore, we see that the imperfection of matter produced by God, namely duality, is present,
which nevertheless becomes perfect by the presence of unity. Nor, however, should you
believe that I have said or understood the second person in the Trinity to be imperfect,
inasmuch as in the superessential world the Spirit of the Father is always present with the Son,
and consequently, trinity in unity and duality in trinity: Which indeed most excellently explains
that wondrous word Tetragrammaton, consisting of Jod, He, and Vau, He;
Where the aspiration of the letter He in both denotes the procession of the spirit, and seems to join
Vau with Jod from the right, and again Jod with Vau towards the right. Thus the Son in
the number of perfection is said to sit at the right hand of the Father: Thus also he is said to
proceed from the center of the Father, inasmuch as he is the middle of the terms of perfection.
Wherefore it must be understood that the middle of any number refers to the Son and the
center, because the middle of a number is always understood to be in odd and
perfect numbers: Thus in the number three there is duality, in five, trinity, in seven,
quaternity, in nine, quinary (five), which is also the exact middle (insofar
as the middle is considered in even numbers) of the number ten, through which God, descending
from his superformal kingdom, immerses himself into confused matter, creating that
thing from nothing, and informing the formless with his act and light.
Here, however, I want you to know that when we speak of the middle of an even number, we do not
mean its center, which is plainly empty and nothing, but its half part:
For example, the center of the Dyad (two) is nothing, because it has only two terms,
but its half part is 1. Thus the middle of the number four is two, but it lacks a center.
And so in the others, like 6, 8, 10. From which it is clear that all perfection
lies in odd numbers, where a center is found, as in 3, 1 is the center, and 1 is the
term from which, and 1 is the term to which: And in five likewise, 1 is the center,
and 2 is one half part and 2 is the other, and in 7, 1 is the center, 3 terms, etc. Therefore,
in simple perfect numbers, unity is the term from which, trinity the term to which, and duality
the middle, but in such a way that that duality is unity: Thus also trinity is the term from which,
and trinity making six, the middle, and trinity perfecting the period of nine;
but here the center is superficial; Or trinity the beginning, quinary the
middle, and septenary the end; In the same way, quinary the beginning, septenary
the middle, and novenary the outcome: In all these, the trinity of persons considered
in a supersubstantial nature is found, that is, where form is totally regarded,
and not matter. And by this harmony God acted for the ordering of his superessential
kingdom in eternity, before he had decreed anything in the sacred
council concerning the creation of matter. Here, however, it must be observed that,
as unity is, as it were, the center of all forms, so also the ternary
number is the first and nearest emanation of the divine majesty from its nature towards the
thing to be created, and the quinary number the second, the septenary the third, and the
novenary the last, so that there are five processes of the emanation of divine light,
namely, the emission of luminous form from unity towards 3, and from ternary towards 5, and from
quinary towards 7, and from septenary towards 9, and from novenary towards 1, which number by the
addition of a cipher constitutes 10. From which it is clear that if God does not enter the
abyss of matter, then he reflects his rays back into himself, or into his center and his
unity, according to that saying of Hermes Trismegistus: "The Monad generates the Monad and
reflects its ardor into itself." Nor indeed does God, considered in his superessential nature,
depart from the odd number, inasmuch as he rejoices and delights in it:
But, when he had purposed to tread the path of the formless spirit, secretly immersed in the womb
of hyle, he immersed himself through his Son, immediately proceeding from him, through the way
and number of imperfection into the abyss of imperfect matter: for he alone

He alone, who entered the field of the perfect binary number, was able to penetrate to the imperfect binary and that which exists in potential for something. Hence the super-substantial duality, by doubling itself, rendered the middle in the number seven, and in this way joined perfection with imperfection in the first degree of procession from its supercelestial nature to the mundane. For four is an even number, and consequently imperfect, but three is a perfect number, so that from the first conjunction it is probable that matter or imperfection, which is referred to by the number four, is to be joined with perfection, inasmuch as the number three, which is attributed to form, is connected with it for the complement of the number seven. Similarly, the number four is the superficial mean between two and six, denoting thereby that the Word is, as it were, the center of the operations of the six days of creation. Hence, after the heavens were established by the Word of the Lord on the fourth day, this King, informing His tabernacle, placed it in the Sun on that day. **C H A P. XVII.**
*On the reason of simple unity, which is the origin of digits, and of unity joined with a cipher, which is the principle of articles, likewise on the reason of the quinary and sixth number in supercelestial harmony.*

Since in the preceding numerations many doubts could present themselves to readers, namely, first concerning unity and then concerning the denary number, how, for instance, GOD the Father or the first property of the Trinity can be introduced at the beginning and end of digits, and then afterwards, how it repeats itself in the centennial number, and finally in the millennial; Similarly, why the second property or person, being a duality, can be found in the quinary number, when twice two produce four, and twice four eight, etc. it must first be understood that in Hebrew numbers, א (Aleph) always signifies unity, and א (Aleph) imports GOD the Father, the Monad, and the first person, just as in John in Revelation, according to the Greeks, it is called α and ω, alpha and omega. Hence the Hebrews write His wondrous names with א; such as אל, EL, אהיה Ehieh, whom Plato calls ὤν or ὄν (being or existent). Whence this word אהיה, which designates the Father, God revealed to Moses in Exodus 3, for leading the Israelites out of the servitude of the Egyptians. Furthermore, also

Finally, since the diapason draws the efficacy of its consonance from unison, therefore its harmony is connected with unity, from which it is numbered and derived. Again, if we proceed by way of proportions, we will find unity and duality to be in a double proportion (1:2), from which the diapason is formed. Still further, proceeding by a retrograde path, 3 joined with unity denotes four notes of the diatessaron consonance, and 3 with duality, five sounds of the diapente consonance; to which if the Trinity is added, eight notes of the diapason consonance will emerge. Whence it clearly appears that, however the persons of the Trinity may be taken, they are always found in concord and harmony, and are observed to be immune from all discord and contrariety. The demonstration of this Music follows here, inasmuch as it is found in the sole Trinity.

CAP. II.

*How worldly harmony relates in the same way as divine harmony, and that*
*worldly and material symphony proceeds from that divine and formal one.*

**A**S the number ten relates to unity, so also the harmony of the material world to that of the formal and supersubstantial world. And as unity was the beginning of the Music and concord of the Trinity; so also the ternary (three) multiplied by itself is the beginning of the symphony of composition, because 9 is the beginning of the denary number and the end of simple numbers. Hence, for the formation and consonance of the material world, the Spirit of the Lord (who was the third person of the Trinity), taking upon Himself the place of unity, as the Spirit of the Trinity, was carried over the waters, imparting to them fiery love and melody proceeding from the most holy harmony. Therefore, the Spirit of Jehovah (with whom is the power of the Father, and consequently, supersubstantial unity, and the wisdom of the Son, and consequently supersubstantial duality, and grace proper to Him) here, I say, found as three and one in the denary number, because it was already engaged in material composition, claimed for itself the place of unity in the universal and material essence. From whom the second person flowed forth; namely, the *Sun*, whom Plato for this reason called the *visible son of God*, nor indeed did he much err in this opinion of his, since, as the royal Prophet testifies, GOD *has placed His tabernacle in it*. The Sun is therefore, as it were, the second person in the material world, receiving its brilliant and splendid power from the first, or the fiery Spirit of GOD, which seems to illuminate the waters of the middle region of the world, as well as the lowest, in the likeness of its Father (from whom it received its power), and to infuse life into the lower parts annually. But we call the third person of the material world man, proceeding from the first and second; hence, *Mercurius Trismegistus* says, "*God is the light and life of man*", and another Philosopher teaches us, "*the sun and man generate man*. *Mercurius Trismegistus* also says in another place: *The world is the son of God, the sun of the world, and man of the sun*." But we take the world for the universal essence of matter, in such a way (if it is permissible to compare substantial things with supersubstantial ones) comprehending within itself three persons worthy of admiration, just as the divine essence comprehends its own. But God, the life of the world, and the fiery and loving Spirit, is considered the first person of the world, from whom primarily the other two, and all other things, are derived. But GOD is present to His simple and formal world in unity, but to the material world in the denary, so that He may, by the symphony of His splendid countenance, mix Himself with the formless waters, to give them form and to drive away their dissonances and strifes, and to bind the elements to each other in harmonious peace with an inviolable bond of concord.

Since, therefore, the material world is merely a type and image of the Archetype, or the supersubstantial world, we have deduced this our worldly Music and the consonances of any region or heaven thereof from the observation of that divine harmony. First, therefore, we perceive with diligent observation that the unity of the Trinity, joined with duality, produces the consonance of a diatessaron (perfect fourth) born from three intervals. Following this example, we also observe that the three hierarchies or regions of the empyrean heaven, in their disposition, produced a melodic formula not dissimilar (by the inspiration of the divine Spirit). Again we perceive that, as unity relates to duality in a double proportion, which constitutes the consonance of a diapason (octave), so also in a similar way the proportion of the upper pyramid of universal matter, or the first region, beginning from its cone or the principle of the first heaven, relates to the intersection made by two pyramids in the heart of heaven...
