of the second or ethereal heaven, since one portion of the pyramid found in the empyrean heaven is found in double proportion to that of the middle heaven, as we have more fully recounted in our mundane harmony. Then, because in the second place 2 added to 3 produce 5, which number denotes the consonance of a diapente composed of five sounds or voices; similarly, because 2 relates to 3 in a sesquialtera proportion (in which the consonance of a diapente is found), therefore this proportion is found twice between the second and third heaven; namely, once counting upwards, from the sun towards the supreme heaven, and once proceeding downwards to the elemental heaven. Finally, since in the third place, proceeding circularly, the unity of the Trinity relates to its own number in a sesquitertia proportion, therefore the consonance of a diatessaron is found in the third heaven, which is found in such a proportion, just as also between the first and last person of the Trinity. But in this place (contemplating in passing) a great mystery (as it seems to me) is to be drawn out; namely, that bodies in the ultimate and coarser proportion of the material pyramid, submerged in the most imperfect consonance and in an abyss of imperfection and as if in darkness, namely resounding in a material diatessaron, nevertheless have a relation to unity in a sesquitertia proportion, so that there is hope for the dissolution of bodies after death, through which that form and mind veiled in human bodies, which arose from unity, may return again to unity by a circular path. From these things, therefore, it appears clearer than the sun to those who diligently observe, that the consonance of the diatessaron of the empyrean heaven, joined with the superior diapente of the middle heaven, constitutes the supreme and spiritual consonance of the diapason of the greater world, beginning from God and ending in the Sun; and consequently it is indicated that the diatessaron of the first heaven and the superior diapente of the second heaven are the simplest and most spiritual consonances of the entire material mass of the world. Similarly, by joining the inferior diapente of the middle heaven with the diatessaron of the lowest heaven; these consonances joined together produce a material diapason, beginning from the Sun and ending in the earth. Whence it is clear that the inferior consonances of diapente and diatessaron tend more towards matter than towards form; hence they are called material, while conversely the superior ones are so called insofar as they regard form and fully informed spirits. We see, therefore, that there exists a threefold harmony composed of three consonances of symphony; of which the former resides in the uncreated essence, where there is no discord, in the middle world, namely the formal and the essence of the Trinity; The two latter are included in created matter, namely one in the material world, specifically in its more subtle part, the other in the denser part and subject to opacity. But indeed that uncreated symphony is united by an indissoluble bond to created harmony; namely, the supersubstantial form, to the material and substantial form in this way: namely, by adding the ternary number of the Trinity (which contains the diapason within itself) to the quaternary number of matter (for according to the Pythagoreans, two in matter is not a number, but a confusion of unities, as has been said, wherefore they hold that the quaternary number is the first even number) the septenary number is produced, which generates the consonance of all perfection, namely the diapason, which is that bond by which GOD has bound the music of life and light to His creatures and continually and liberally infuses it into the cosmos and the children of the cosmos.

C H A P. III.
Concerning the reason for mundane, elemental, and corporeal discord; and how
GOD bound the discordant daughters of chaos in concordant peace.

WE have declared above the reason why material *Dias* is considered a most imperfect number; namely, because it is destitute of the members of perfection by which it might be perfected. For although matter had already been brought into act from the deformed entrails of chaos or hyle, nevertheless it did not possess the active principle of its essence by itself;

--- Page 65 ---
ON DIVINE HARMONY. 63

...it did not possess the active principle of its essence per se; since it acquired the principle of its perfection from an absolutely formal nature, namely from the unity of divinity, which was the author of its existence. For how is it possible that perfection should be in a thing by itself (speaking in an absolute sense) for which it is not possible to exist without the help of another? Since therefore duality, multiplied in itself and divided into intervals, produces nothing but even numbers; and since all symphony is perfected by consonances, which are composed solely of odd intervals, how is it possible that from duality (producing only odd numbers by multiplication) it can in any way propagate the consonances of melody and consequently harmony? Indeed, on the contrary, it will produce discords and dissonances most opposed to harmony. From which it is clear that GOD and the most holy Trinity are the sole and unique origin of concord; but the Devil, conversely, is the parent of discord and antipathy, wherefore he has also acquired the name *Strife*. GOD therefore uses formal light for the birth of proportional and most perfect symphony; but the Devil uses matter for his dissensions and strifes.

For if we consider the ideal or invisible world, we will find a portion of each of its regions in the inner man: For that mind, a divine ray of uncreated light, is communicated to the inner man with a composite portion of created light, established in the spiritual heaven, through the will and pleasure of the Divine Maker; and similarly also, as in the visible world there are two, namely heaven and earth, of which the former rains forms onto the earth, while the latter receives and preserves them; so also in man, that celestial ray with its ethereal vehicle bestows life and form upon that muddy body, which is called man's earth. Furthermore, in both worlds there are some parts not subject to corruption, namely, supercelestial and celestial; but a certain portion of the visible world is corruptible, namely, the elemental part; therefore, in a similar way, the portions of the inner man are incorruptible, but the body and its visible parts are subject to corruption. The world is encompassed and governed by the Divine Spirit, and the human body is also moved and encompassed by this same essential virtue: He who is ultimately one, created one world in His image; and the same one also founded one animal, namely man, in His own image, in which He was greatly delighted. Not inappropriately, therefore, man has been called another world and another image of God; since he has in himself all that is contained in the entire greater world, to such an extent, indeed, that nothing whatever exists anywhere in it that is not truly and really found in man, and performs entirely the same functions in him as in the greater world: For in him is the divine mind, angelic reason, celestial spirit, elemental harmony, planetary vegetation, the senses of irrational animals: Finally, in all things he has a symbol of the world, and with all things, operation and interaction: Why then should this ultimate creature not be called by its proper name *Microcosm*, since it is in all respects most similar to the *Macrocosm*? But God the creator, since He is infinite, created the world round, and very proportional in its parts; Are not also the measurements of all human members proportional and consonant with those of the world, and agreeing with them in roundness? The center of the circular world is the earth; but the central point of human roundness is, according to some, in the navel; but we rather think that it should be placed around the genitals, since just as the seeds of things are hidden in the center of the world, so also near man's testicles lies hidden his seminal virtue. From this point, therefore, drawing a compass, we will perceive the external man to be exactly round, like the external world, as is clearly explained in the following example.

Con-

Therefore, we conclude with Trismegistus that the world is the image of God, and man indeed is the image of the world; and that consequently, because of his similarity with the world, man is not improperly to be called a lesser world or Microcosm, and in all things is to be considered in the manner of the greater world or Macrocosm.

CAP. II.
On the interior or invisible Microcosm, and that it contains within itself all the ideal parts of the world.

We call the interior Microcosm that hidden, invisible, and immortal portion of man, formed from the invisible parts of the invisible heavens of the Macrocosm, by which it not only performs its natural functions, but also is accustomed to engage in divine contemplations by virtue of its supercelestial portions. Hence it is, therefore, that both Theologians and Philosophers have called the inner man the soul, comprising living, intellectual, sensitive, and vegetative power, each of which is derived from a particular heaven of the greater world; namely, the intellect from the Empyrean heaven, the vital from the ethereal, and the operations of sense from the more formal qualities of the elements. Therefore, we say that the inner man is formed from invisible matter and a most pure and spiritual form, of which he has the material part from the substance of the ethereal heaven, no differently than the visible body has its own from the elements; but its spiritual part retains itself in its ethereal body, just as that ethereal spirit [retains itself] in the composite elemental body: For the rays of the superior region are to the inferior heaven nearest to them as life and soul. From which it is manifest that the intellectual part of man is, as it were, the soul to his ethereal spirit, which, because of its preeminence over the inferior parts of the inner man, gave man his name and being. And this is what Trismegistus meant in Pimander 1, by affirming that the inner man consists of life and light, which God himself

I 2 God

--- Page 70 ---
68	TRACT. I. SECT. I. LIB. III.

*He called God.* And in another place, *he calls the inner man immortal, but the outer mortal.* And in the resolution of Theologians it is also found, *that the outer man is corrupted, because he is dust, and returns to dust, but the inner man is renewed from day to day.* Behold the fruits of the God-like breath, by which man is exalted above all other visible creatures of the world, and is rendered similar to the Creator himself. This fiery spirit, therefore, constituting the inner man with its vehicles and appendages, we define with the Peripatetics as an incorporeal substance, *by which we live, feel, move according to place, and first understand;* Indeed, the mind itself *according to Augustine, is called, because it understands all things.* And according to *Seneca; an intellectual spirit ordered in itself towards blessedness.* Therefore, concerning each portion of the mundane heaven contributing to the constitution of the inner man, we will treat specifically and in natural order in the subsequent chapters.

C A P. III.

*Concerning the infinite and ineffable property of light, and how man*
*has a portion of every luminous species within himself.*

IN the first volume, *Treatise 1*, we proved, both by reasons and authorities, that every thing is nobler the more essential light it has within itself, and that greater or lesser imperfection arises from a greater or lesser abundance of body and matter; but greater or lesser perfection from the exuberance or diminution of luminous form. For we have said that God is pure and most pure uncreated light without any addition of matter, that is, purely formal and simply fiery: Hence he is called *the true, proper, and first light by Saint John in chapter 1.* We have also said that the substance of the empyrean heaven itself is the fiery dwelling place of the light created on the first day, which is called empyrean because fire has dominion in it: And this, neither in time (since it is created) nor in perfection (since the composition of this place is made from one quarter of spiritual matter and three quarters of most simple light), is in any way to be compared to uncreated intellectual light and splendor. Furthermore, we proved that the substance of the middle heaven derived its form from that empyrean origin; But, because it is the middle of the space between the material heaven and the formal, therefore it seems to participate equally in both extremes. Hence it is certain that the substance of this heaven is more imperfect and less formal than that supreme one; because it has more matter, but less form, than that; for it consists of two parts of grosser spirit and as many of light infused into it on the second day of creation through the diaphragm of the empyrean heaven from its source: And hence it is called *aether*, as if *aetha-er*, that is, fiery spirit, or equally composed of spirit and fire. Similarly, in the last place, we declared that light is weakest in the lowest heaven, but the substance of matter or waters is most rebellious; for it consists of three quarters of light; and thus it behaves in this extreme in quantity of matter, as in the other, namely the empyrean, in abundance of form. We have also demonstrated that light is the simplest act of all, inasmuch as it is a simple act of intelligence, and of uncreated intellect, and first diffused from the divine mind into all things, yet in a diverse manner, according to the more rebellious or more obedient nature of the body. We say therefore, that uncreated light is totally and originally in God the Father himself: *For He is the Father of lights*, indeed He is the first and true light itself, whose rays are the first acts, as *Trismegistus* testifies: Hence that: *I am the light of the world, etc.* We also affirm with Trismegistus and the sacred Scriptures, that in the *Son* there is an illuminating and exuberant splendor, *in whom is the light and life of men, as Saint John testifies*

--- Page 71 ---
ABOUT THE INNER MICROCOSM. 69

*John chapter 1.* Finally, in the Holy Spirit there is a splendor surpassing all understanding, as *Dionysius* says: But after the creation of light, its simplest portion converged with the splendor of the uncreated intellect or divine mind for the composition of Angels: whence *Dionysius* calls them *Algamata,* that is, most brilliant mirrors receiving the light of God, in which God himself is also seen. After this, a portion of this composite light descended for the formation of celestial bodies, giving them an abundance of life and effective propagation: And this light is visible splendor. Into the elements themselves, the outermost portion of light is infused, bestowing upon them fiery vigor, by which they live and constitute the lower bodies in distinct and harmonious proportions. Finally, in man there is a due portion of all these species of light, both uncreated and created. For by the breath of life is not understood the vital soul (for this is granted even to brutes and plants, by which they live) but the divine mind, and uncreated light, which is immediately infused into him by God, by which he first assumes the image of God: Then he is adorned with angelic and rational splendor, and he has this portion from the empyrean heaven, by which he is called rational; and by these two endowments he seems to excel other animals and all other creatures of the world. Afterwards, he receives vivifying, vegetative, and multiplicative light from the Sun and the splendor of ethereal creatures, by which he is corporally led hither and thither, grows, and has the increase of his species through propagation. From the light of the elements, he has the symbolization of the parts of his body and the nature and harmonious proportion of the elementary humors, according to that saying of *Trismegistus in Pimander. Woman, air and water, composed for coition, took maturity from fire, spirit from the aether, and nature cemented them together to form the species of man.* Who, finally, will doubt that all these species of light are in man, since *Saint John, chapter 1,* testifies to the origin of all these, namely the divine mind, and a portion of uncreated light in men, from whose uncreated source all other species of created light are derived. For according to that saying of the *Royal Psalmist: By the word of the Lord were the heavens established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their powers.* We conclude, therefore, that there are three species of rays, which are called acts; namely, supercelestial rays or acts of God, from which the nobler portion of the human soul is derived; Then the rays of the world or celestial rays, which are acts of nature, and the soul proceeding from it, whence man's sensitive and vegetative life is derived; And lastly, there are elementary rays, which do not prepare life, but a dwelling place for life, and are qualities properly hidden in the elements. Therefore, we will discuss these rays of the Microcosm more extensively below.

C H A P. IV.
*About the supercelestial rays, which are acts of GOD.*

**N**ow concerning supernatural rays, since we have indicated that some are in God himself, as the sacred Scriptures also testify, and others, as it were, are the substance of the empyrean heaven itself and its creatures, we say that those existing in God are uncreated, but these of the empyrean heaven are created. We call the divine ray, with *Scotus, the uncreated intellect*; but the other, that which proceeds immediately from the divine, the *created intellect.* Hence *Scotus* affirms that intelligible objects are produced into intelligible being by the act of the divine intellect, and that all truths concerning them necessarily shine forth in them; so that the created intellect, understanding such objects and, by their virtue, also the necessary truths concerning them, sees such truths in them. And then that created intellect, seeing infallible truths in such objects, is conveniently said to be...

--- Page 72 ---
**TRACT. I. SECT. I. LIB. III.**
...it can be said to see them in eternal light, or eternal rules. This also seems to be confirmed by *Theological Resolution, tract. 2, part 2, port 2, quaest. 2*, while it asserts that it can conveniently be said that the created intellect sees such infallible truths in the light of the uncreated intellect, because, namely, by the power of that uncreated intellect, objects have been produced into intelligible being, and these objects, thus produced, move the created intellect itself not by their own power but by the power of the divine intellect. From which it is clear that there is light of both the created and uncreated intellect, and that the created intellect can understand nothing whatsoever unless it, as it were, sees this in the light and splendor of the divine intellect, which they call the Mind; and consequently it is certain that for the constitution of the human soul, the divine mind concurs with the created intellect, so that through this (divine mind) that (created intellect) is accustomed to see the aforesaid infallible truths, as we shall declare below. Since, however, this divine portion could not have come to man in his creation, because of the immense unworthiness of his body, without the divine grace of the Creator, therefore God granted him the same gift on the very day of his creation, which He had previously communicated on the first day of His work to the empyrean heaven and consequently to the entire world. For just as on the first day of creation His Spirit was carried over the face of the empyrean heaven, spiritually illuminating it, so also on the last day of that creation, the Spirit of the same Archetype was carried over the face of man: For He breathed into the face of man the breath of life, which, because uncreated, was immortal life and light, as *John 1* and *Trismegistus in his Pimander 1* testify. Such, therefore, are these supercelestial rays, which are truly proper acts of God; of which the former proceeded immediately from God and are, as it were, rays emitted by God Himself, and as it were, His divine act of the Spirit and eternal splendor, nay, God Himself, present everywhere according to His divine will, so indeed that not ineptly, with the *Theological Resolution* concurring, it is said, *that in every creature there is a vestige of the Trinity*, no differently, namely, than we say the sun is in this house, or that part of the earth, when its rays strike those places. But the secondary supercelestial rays are those which were created immediately by God on the first day, to produce the matter of darkness from potentiality into actuality and to form the actual and visible world; by whose actions the darkness was driven to the center of the mundane globe, and all power was given to the heavens and all parts of the heaven and creatures: From which they can also truly be called secondary acts of God, inasmuch as they emanate immediately from the Spirit of the Lord. But these themselves are not simple, like those uncreated ones (since they are entirely formal and fiery), but they are joined, as has been said, with a small amount of the spirit of the most subtle hyle (prime matter); in which composition that passive spirit, and the active essential light and true emitted ray of God exist. But the entire substance of that heaven is called created, because from nothing, that is, with no pre-existing matter, something was produced into actuality, namely, the formless and potential spirit of darkness or most subtle water was informed by the presence of divine light. From which this heaven is also called intellectual and rational, and this simple composition is called light, and for this reason created light is understood as the mixture of divine light with the spirit which it informed, that is, for the composition of spirit with light; in which composition, because the proportion of light is triple to that of matter, therefore light gave it its name and being, and in this way light was created on the first day. Since therefore this formal light acts upon its passive (element) and the passive spirit, receiving form, is acted upon, and those actions, no differently than matter receives form, is it not therefore probable that of this substance, simply composed of two (elements), the light is that which the Philosophers called the agent intellect, which makes all potentially intelligible things actually intelligible, no differently than it reduced that matter, existing only in potentiality due to its formless disposition, into visible actuality? From which also *Francis of Mayron* called this intellect, *the light and reason of knowing*, and according to *Proclus in his treatise.*

--- Page 73 ---
DE MICROCOSMO INTERNO. 71

treatise *On the Soul*. That [intellectus agens] provides us with understanding, namely the light of intelligence; but the Spirit, which is the other part of the composition, if I am not mistaken, is that intellect which philosophers called *patient* (passive), whose role it is to receive all intellection into itself. Thus, light directs its face towards a very polished mirror, and the mirror, receiving its rays, makes the proximate subject, which was only potentially visible before the act of light, now actually appear and be seen in the mirror. And this is what Trismegistus seems to assert in *Pimander* 1, saying that the mind is in reason, understanding by "reason" the substance of the intellectual heaven, since in reason there is both action and passion. And Aristotle, *On the Soul* 3: In the intellectual soul, because of the passive intellect, an agent intellect must be posited; that is, an active form must be imposed upon its passive matter. Hence, therefore, it is that some, according to Basil in *Hexaemeron* 1.2, rightly called this heaven intellectual, and others also called it rational. And Augustine, on Genesis 1, understands angelic nature by "primary light." But angelic nature, according to Boethius, Book 3 *On the Trinity*, differs from a mere lucid form, which is uncreated; because it is subject to accidents, namely intellection and volitions, whence he says there is matter in them: But we have clearly declared this in the first treatise, volume 1, in the book: *On the Creatures of the Empyrean Heaven*. These, however, are properly called acts of God, because they proceed immediately from Him, by whose splendor man is inwardly illuminated, and is said to bear the image of God Himself, as we will explain more fully below; although we also establish that all inferior rays are derived secondarily or tertiarily from God, which Trismegistus also seems to assert in *Pimander* 3: GOD, divine nature, principle of all things, GOD, mind, nature, act, necessity, end, and renewal; and therefore consequently, he seems to affirm that all worldly rays or acts are divine and proceed from God Himself.

C H A P. V.
Whence is man called the image of God? And concerning the nobility which he receives from the supernatural rays, both uncreated and created, which are in him.

When that uncreated Creator had breathed the breath of life into the muddy body of man; that body, though dense and opaque, received the divine mind, and that mind, through its inexplicable and most lucid beauty, bestowed the most polished beauty of a most cultivated mirror upon the muddy and crude corpulence of man; so that the form and image of the Archetype was first to be spiritually beheld in it. Whence Trismegistus states that man, made in the image of God, represents the Trinity in a certain place, and likewise also the Sacred Scriptures in many places say that man was made in the likeness of God Himself: Trismegistus also in *Pimander* 1 called the mind of man the proper form of God. And elsewhere, he calls the mind of human reason God, who is intellect, life, and splendor. And according to Saint John 1: In the Word of God is the life of men, which is a light shining in the darkness, that is, in the dark human body, and this is the true light or divine form. Thus likewise Trismegistus in *Pimander* 1 says that the internal man consists of life and light; and he calls life and light God and mind, and there he speaks these words: "The Father of all, existing as intellect, life, and splendor, created man in His own likeness, and rejoiced in him as His son." In the same way, Paul, and Xystus the Pythagorean, called man and his soul the temple of God. But that polished matter, receiving these rays of uncreated light, is the spiritual and intellectual substance of the first heaven, created in the image of the Word, the first exemplar and cause of causes, which, according to the Platonists, is immediately derived from God. And this

--- Page 74 ---
72          T R A C T. I.  S E C T. I.  L I B. III.
This is the true rational substance of Proclus's soul, which he says the first Creator of the world brought forth, and consequently concludes to be the noblest of all creatures; *because, as he says, the essence of the soul's perfection comes from the superior Gods; indeed, this is that intellectual substance which Iamblichus, in 'On the Mysteries,' says is illuminated by divine benevolent will, that is, by the presence of the divine mind;* and likewise it is that which is defined by Theologians as, *'an intellectual spirit ordered in itself towards blessedness, as is found in 'Theological Resolutions':'* This substance, I say, is twofold, namely, of essential light and of the simplest spirit, like a certain keen edge and most limpid medium, implanted in the earthy body, in which a portion of that divine and uncreated idea is seen. Therefore, in such an empyrean mirror, illuminating that earthy body, GOD the Creator Himself, as *Trismegistus in 'Pimander' 1* testifies, as if looking at Himself, congratulated man, as His son, and, too much delighted by His own form, granted all His works for human use. Man, therefore, perceiving himself to have power over all things, began to observe the works of the seven governors (for according to *Trismegistus, 'Pimander,' sermon 4, man was made a contemplator of divine work*), and those governors, whom they call intelligences, rejoicing in the meditation of the human mind, each made man a participant of their own order; and after he learned their essence, becoming most skilled in Astrology, he began to ascend higher, and strove to seek out the source and origin of his own splendor and life. Whence, with the sharpness of his mind, he penetrated and cut through the circuit of the seven circles, and attempted to comprehend the power of the Governor presiding over fire: For just as the rays of fire tend upwards, towards their connatural seat; so it is the function of that divine splendor to ascend as many degrees higher than other rays, as it is known to be more subtle or nobler and more excellent than them. Hence it was, as *Trismegistus in 'Pimander' 4* relates, *'that man, by admiring and vividly scrutinizing divine works, at last found and recognized their author and his own.'* And from this also it is, that the same *Trismegistus in 'Pimander' 10* calls man *'a divine animal, to be compared not with brutes, but with the celestial Gods; indeed, he wished him to be superior to the heavenly beings, or at least perhaps to possess equal power with them.'* Finally, man alone rejoices in this honor, that in all things of this world he has a symbol and, by virtue of that divine ray, operation and interaction with all things: For he symbolizes with matter in his own body; with the elements in their fourfold composition; with plants by vegetation; with animals by sense; with heaven by the ethereal spirit in between; with Angels by intellect; and with God Himself, as he contains all things within himself. Therefore, he acts in all things and upon all things; and thus he also has power over God Himself, namely, by understanding and loving Him: and just as God knows all things, so also man can know all knowable things, for there is nothing in him in which something of divinity does not shine: And from this also *Trismegistus in the 10th sermon of 'Pimander' dared to call man a terrestrial and mortal God, and God his Creator a celestial and immortal one. And in the 3rd sermon of 'Asclepius' he says, 'it is a great miracle that man is an animal to be adored and honored: for he asserts that it passes into the nature of God, and is as it were God Himself:'* And elsewhere, *he says that man's nature is akin to the Gods, and joined to them by divinity.* And certainly this is man's greatest glory, that he possesses a true ray and act of God, by reason of which he is related by blood to God Himself, no differently than those who descend from great-grandparents and grandparents are called their blood relatives and kin. And all these perfections we have from the root of uncreated light, which we have called mind and intellect infused into us by God Himself; by which, because of that ray of divine form existing in him, we say man is an image of God, and is to be compared with Angels, inasmuch as he is intelligent and rational, and finally also has a symbol with all the heavens and the creatures of the heavens, as we declared before.

CHAP. VI.

*Concerning the mundane or celestial rays, which they call acts of nature; and why the soul of the ethereal heaven is irrational?*

Mundane or celestial rays, which elsewhere we have called secondary, we name those which are infused from the perennial luminous fount, created on the first day, that is, from the primary light, into the middle region of the world, for the purpose of bringing the spiritual substance of the ethereal heaven into activity, and for driving downwards the dark origin of privation; which, since they are, as it were, the visible soul of the world, by which the Platonists said it lives, are therefore called by some mundane rays and acts of nature, because all natural things receive from them their act, that is, life, vegetation, multiplication, and the origin of motion; Indeed, every ray or act of nature is like a living soul, if it is infused into a well-disposed body in due proportion; since by its infinite power, like things are generated from like, all things grow and are nourished, so much so that this act of nature is the bond of the elements, and the power of mixing; without which the mixtures of elements could not occur, nor could a form suitable to its species, by which that thing is distinguished and recognized from any other thing, have been impressed in any way: Furthermore, by these rays the Sun inspires life and heat into inferior things, inasmuch as the act of its rays converts all things to itself with its life-giving heat, permeates all beings and leads their qualities and virtues through all things, and disperses darkness and gloom. What else, then, is this act of nature, than *that soul of the world, which the Platonists wished to be placed especially in the Sun?* so that mundane or celestial rays are nothing other than the emission of light gathered in the solar body, and its projection to all visible parts of the world. This Iamblichus also seems to confirm, affirming that all celestial virtues are in the Sun. And according to Proclus, all the powers of all things are gathered and collected into one Sun; which he is finally believed to disseminate into this lower world through his fiery exhalations. Hence, we see the earth grow green and flourish when the Sun approaches us, but when it departs, we see it wither. It is therefore certain and manifest that this force or act of nature is the middle soul of nature, formed from the substance of primary light and ethereal spirit, which is called middle because it participates in both extremes. For it receives its nature and essence from the perennial spirit of the empyrean heaven and liberally pours its life-giving virtue upon all created things of the lower heaven: Indeed, this life-giving soul, with its spirit, penetrates even to the very center of man, carrying with it that super-celestial gift, namely the mind and intellect residing in its rational course. Hence, the Sun (that is, the life-giving soul) and man (namely, the divine breath, which is called the internal man) are said to generate man.

And hence it is that *Porphyry, in the book On Occasions, speaking of this middle soul, defines it as a certain medium between individual essence, which is intellect, and essence divisible into true bodies. For material qualities and forms are divisible according to bodies.* And in the same book he establishes a difference between *the life of this soul and that of the intellect.* And *Dionysius, in the book On Divine Names,* also seems to confirm this difference by saying; *that those things which are in the lower exist more perfectly in the higher.* And *Proclus, in the book On the Soul, asserts that more perfect souls come from the higher Gods; for those are self-moving, and less partakers of an inferior nature, while these move themselves less, and suffer more from corporeal force,* and he speaks truly: For through this soul the mind and in-
K tellect

...intellect is joined to the body. Therefore, through a more perfect soul, he understands the intellect as proceeding immediately from the supreme Creator; through another less perfect one, this worldly soul, he wanted it to come from inferior gods, namely, ethereal ones. For he asserts that some souls are derived from the Solar sphere, others from the Mercurial sphere, and some from the Lunar sphere, through which he seems to denote the diverse nature of rays following the diverse dispositions of places and spheres. Therefore, he speaks in these words: *The rational soul is nobler than the irrational soul, because the former the first Creator of the world, namely the supercelestial God, created, but the latter the junior gods produced, that is, the ethereal ones.* But this soul, vital in itself, but irrational, becomes rational through the acquisition of a supercelestial portion; And then it *

...And then they may be refreshed and rejoice in the presence of this intellectual splendor, just as plants (rejoice/are refreshed) by the Sun's approach and aspect. But so that we may prove the irrationality of the soul of this heaven by a more familiar way, we see, when the light of the intellect directs the sense of sight, that the further an object is from it, the weaker are the rays of the same kind that perceive visible forms: so much so, that sometimes even the truth does not shine upon them; for thus also the matter stands in the present case with this soul, since its medium is different from that of the intellect and it is distant from the intellectual seat through the semi-diameter of the world's medium; whence the rays of the intellectual heaven, due to the diversity of the medium, are as it were refracted in the middle heaven, and do not operate rationally. And furthermore, if this soul were rational by itself, why would it not likewise be perceived to impart reason simultaneously to all things to which it is accustomed to give life? For the substance of this heaven is in metals, as well as in plants and animals of both kinds; for the fifth essence, which is the sensible nature of all things, exists only, and not as intellectual, as Lullius testifies in his book *On the Fifth Essence*. We conclude therefore, that the empyrean heaven has its soul from the uncreated rays of God, and its substance is entirely lucid; yet not the most simple light, since that is proper only to the Trinity, as it is uncreated. Yet thus the spiritual appetite of this heaven's substance is fulfilled, so that it is entirely converted into a lucid and formal nature; whence that composition is called empyrean, that is, fiery, by whose formal substance the dark spirit of the middle region is informed; and moreover, the entire substance of the celestial region is made from a portion of this empyrean substance, which is its form, and from its own spirit, which is its matter, which composition indeed is called aether, that is, fiery air. And just as the entire substance of the empyrean heaven is the form or essential soul of the aethereal heaven; so again, the entire substance of this (aethereal heaven), which they call the fifth essence, is the soul and nature of all creatures of the lower world, except for man, who drew his greater perfection from a higher region. In this way, therefore, the aforementioned sayings of Dionysius in his book *On the Divine Names* are verified: "Those things which are in the lower regions exist more perfectly in the higher regions," that is, the higher one ascends, the greater perfection is found: For as the same author says in his book *On the Angelic Hierarchy*: "It is a common law for a superior angel to illuminate an inferior one"; so also the matter stands with the regions of the world. For the inner, or ideal, world is the exemplar of God himself, while the outer and visible world is the image of that invisible one.

C A P. VII.
On elementary rays and the sensitive soul.

Timaeus says that the essence of our soul is not constituted from the first kinds of all things, like the superior souls, but is composed of second or third kinds, where by "first kinds" he denotes the natures and substances of the empyrean heaven, by "second kinds" those of the aethereal heaven, about which we have spoken above, and by "third kinds" those of the lowest and elementary heaven, about which we will speak in this place. The Pythagoreans, as we explained above, wishing the soul to be composed of simple, double, triple, and quadruple proportions, understood by the quadruple proportion the sensitive power of the soul, which Plotinus and other Platonists called an "idol," because it is, as it were, an image and idol of that quality by which it is perceived. And Trismegistus, in Pimander 6, says: "Whatever moves the senses are idols and certain vain admirations: for it is not permitted to find good in the world, or in parts of the world: for just as the keenness of the eye does not discern God, so neither does it recognize the beautiful and the good." Saint Paul speaks of the animal man, and we call the spirit carnal; For these bodies only...

perceive, since incorporeal things are least subjected to the senses. From which it is clear that the sensitive soul participates in the body, since without its organs it can accomplish or perfect nothing; indeed, unless it is in some animated body, this function or power of the soul is nothing. Therefore, it is established that it consists rather of elements and their virtues and mixtures, than being derived from the virtues of the superior heavens. Hence Porphyry, in his book 'On Occasions,' seems to distinguish it from the superior powers of the soul in these words: *The soul is indeed a medium between the individual essence, which is intellect, and the essence divisible into true bodies; for qualities and material forms are divisible according to bodies.* Where by 'soul' he understands that vivifying soul of the aethereal heaven, by 'individual essence,' the intellectual and rational substance of the empyreal heaven, and by 'essence divisible into bodies,' the sensitive power; which he indicates to be concerned with elementary qualities and material forms, divisible according to bodies, and to arise and be derived from their actions. Hence among Philosophers it is defined that *this kind of sensitive soul is the act of a substantial, natural, organic body, by which it lives, feels, desires, breathes, and moves from place to place, whose apprehensive power apprehends and perceives species of visible things, present and absent:* for sense is as apt to receive abstract impressions of natural things as wax receives the image or character of a seal abstracted from a ring without gold or silver adhering to it. And this power is manifested both in the exterior sense, to which five species are subjected; namely *sight, hearing, touch, taste, smell or odor;* or in the interior, of which there are three differences, namely *common sense, imagination, and memory.* Moreover, by its motive power, the animated body is moved, either externally from place to place, or internally by spirit and pulse; which indeed, if it is dominant, is the *concupiscible virtue,* containing hope and joy beneath it, or the *irascible power,* under which fury, rage, insanity, fear, sadness, pain, and other such things are comprehended.

This sensitive faculty is therefore the daughter of the earth itself and of darkness, the mother of all evils, the instigator of the flesh to all evils, constantly exciting the appetite for sin in it and repeatedly presenting objects of sin to man; for by the sense of the apprehensive power, present species inciting to evil are perceived: Hence *Eve* was first enticed to sin by hearing the serpent's persuasions; then, seeing the fruit to be beautiful, and delightful to the eyes and sight, she touched that fruit, and finally tasted and ate it; so indeed, that for the completion of this sin, all those five species concurred, especially since smell is also a familiar companion to taste: But also the species of the motive power of sense concurred in this action; for she immediately coveted and desired the fruit, and to satisfy her desire, she went to the tree, and took of the fruit, afterwards, struck by fear and sadness, she fled from the face of God. From which it appears that there were three incitements for Eve to commit that sin of disobedience against her Creator; namely, the *Devil,* the *flesh,* and the *world itself.* The Devil tempted the flesh with some object. The flesh, with the apprehensive sense operating, apprehended and saw the worldly object, and overcome by diabolical persuasions, desired that sensible species, and by its motive power led her to satisfy her desire, and wonderfully delighted in that visible worldly object, which is finally subjected to her as a reward or rather a punishment for her disobedience towards her Creator. Hence, therefore, is the origin of all evils of the entire human race; which, swelling immediately from its birth, forthwith defiled the entire human condition. For the woman herself also gave of the fruit to the man, who ate, and through that sin of his, he was reduced from an immortal state to mortality with all his posterity; so that *Trismegistus* rightly described him as *an earthly, but mortal God;* for he lost his privilege of immortality through his disobedience; and forms

--- Page 79 ---
DE MICROCOSMO INTERNO. 77

...and all its forms, whose nature, according to Proclus's discourse, is from the higher regions, begin to sicken, and only this sensitive faculty begins to flourish; concerning which that first man could rightly say with the Apostle Paul: *I see another law in my members, captivating me in the law of sin:* And with Socrates in *Phaedrus*: *Our strengths are mixed with the opposite of good, and full of mutual dissension.* Hence, I say, the sentence of mortality is pronounced against Adam. For the Lord GOD says in *Gen. 2. Of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall not eat; for in whatever day you eat of it, you shall die.* Hence therefore Adam was expelled from Paradise, lest he taste of the tree of life and live forever, and thus also because of his sin all his posterity and succession are rendered mortal: for GOD says in *Gen. 6. My Spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh; for flesh has corrupted its life upon the earth, therefore I will destroy all flesh in which is the spirit of life under heaven.* This, I say, the beginning of the sensitive soul's or carnal malice, was an evident prognostication of future calamities. For it constantly drew the animal man, to use the words of St. Paul, entirely composed for the worst things, more and more; And GOD saw man's wickedness on earth so coalescing, and every thought of his heart so intent on evil at all times, that He even regretted that He had made him. *Genesis 9.* For it happened, that after Adam's fall, *the sense and thought of the human heart were prone to evil from his youth. Gen. 8.* Hence the love of bodily beauty and the luxurious gaze upon women, and the contempt for supercelestial beauty and sincere and truly fiery love. Whence *Trismegistus in Pimander 1 asserts that the love of the body is the cause of death.* And elsewhere: *He who embraces the body with the error of love, will wander in darkness, perceiving the evils of death by sense; for unless one hates his own body, he cannot love himself.*

But what finally is to be said about that abominable tribulation, which this carnal faculty introduced into the human race, by which good is distinguished from evil; which distinction man indeed ignored in his innocence, and by the benefit of that ignorance was free from troubles, was not passive, afflicted in no way by cares and anxieties, immune from soul's perturbations, of a most patient spirit and inexperienced in evil, as one who was concerned only with the goodness of the Creator, the sole good. Oh, the supreme good of man! Oh, his inexplicable happiness! But now, by his error arising from disobedience, he can distinguish good from evil, light from darkness, a tranquil soul from one tumultuous and oppressed by vexations and passions; the fire of conscience is now perceived to burn, the fury of Gehenna is feared, diabolical invasions are constantly noticed, human damnation is dreaded; besides which he is also afflicted by infinite worldly torments, even the safest of all men, and fortified with the firmest security; the mournful arrival of death, the deplorable misfortunes of friends, and our own constantly to be feared; no one in this world is secure, everyone suspicious of his neighbor, no one ever fortunate enough, or content with his state, because he is knowledgeable of good and evil. Oh, therefore, the supreme misfortune of the human race! Oh, its inexplicable unhappiness deriving its origin from the treacherous disposition of the sensitive power, and the rebellious and wanton intemperance of human flesh, the source of its miseries.

We conclude therefore that this lower portion of the soul, or its sensible function, is, as it were, a more essential elementary form or quality, wonderfully delighting in bodily changes and perturbations; concerning which *Iamblichus in De Mysteriis* seems to speak in these words: *Whatever passions are in an animal, they are not in the soul as such, but in the body, which possesses a certain quality under the soul, by which it both suffers and is disturbed.* Where he seems to understand by this quality under the soul the lower portion of the soul, which it received from the elementary form; which indeed we said in the chapter on the element of fire is the occasion of every change. For that form, although it comes from that source of vital spirit, is in K 3 first

--- Page 80 ---
78 T R A C T. I. S E C T. I. L I B. III.
derived from the first creation, yet never rests because of the inequality of the matter in which it is enclosed, never is content with its position, but always assailed by contradictions, it is engaged in a continuous war with the darkness of the body, sometimes vanquished, bringing troubles and sadness to the body, but sometimes conquering, bringing joy to it with piety, if it agrees with the mind. Sometimes also, peace having been made, there is a friendly communication between it and its dark flesh; wherefore it busies itself with vain and vicious pleasures, and with the flesh is ready to observe all the devil's commands. And then, deprived of the royal light of the mind because of the dark companionship of the flesh, it produces all the worst things. Concerning this, *Mercurius Trismegistus* also speaks, when he says, *that the plague of ignorance subverts all the earth, corrupts the soul enclosed in the bonds of the body, nor allows it to embrace the path of salvation, but causes it to be submerged in the lake of corruption and death, nor allows it to return to the fountain of life.* How its disposition, because of the malignity of the flesh and the devil, is entirely opposed to the mind, we shall declare more fully below.

C A P. VIII.
*By what vehicles or through what means the lights of any heaven, constituting the human soul, are joined to the body.*

Among philosophers, observing that divine virtues are diffused into all things, Democritus and the Pythagorean Orpheus called them Gods; by which they said all things were full. Zoroaster, however, called them *divine allurements*. Synesius, *symbolic allurements*. Trismegistus and others, *lives*; and all generally, *souls and essences*, attributing name and being to things. The Platonists, diligently inquiring into the descent of these souls into bodies and the manner of their conjunction with bodies (for they perceived that the soul is primarily and spontaneously mobile, but the body is in itself ineffective for motion, and consequently these two extremes are entirely contrary in nature, and for that reason not easily joined), observed that it occurs through some spiritual medium: so indeed, that by its intervention, those two extreme and foreign entities have some commerce with each other, and are coupled to each other by its bonds, which they further called the *aethereal vehicle of life or chariot of the soul*. And they affirmed this to be that aethereal spirit, which has familiarity with both extremes; no differently than the substance of air with fire and water, which are contrary to each other: Whence also that aethereal spirit, enveloping the soul in the middle region of the world, that is, situated between the spiritual and corporeal extremes, is defined as being neither soul nor body, but as if already soul, inasmuch as it is contiguous to the higher region, and as if not soul, but as if already body, inasmuch as it is joined to the elementary region. This spirit, I say, the Platonists observed to be that vehicle, in which and through which those wondrous gifts of forms are conferred upon lower things, and every hidden faculty in herbs, stones, minerals, and animals is propagated by the power of the sun, moon, and planets, and fixed stars. But *Trismegistus*, looking somewhat more deeply into human nature than these Platonists, discovered that *the aethereal spirit is the vehicle of the divine mind.* And although *Proclus in the book on the soul* makes mention of the garments of the human soul with these words; *The soul descending is variously clothed and at last purified,* he nevertheless speaks of them more confusedly: For in *Pimander 1* it is held, *that the garment of the mind is the soul, but the garment of the soul is the spirit itself.* Where by soul the Author understands the rational substance of the empyrean heaven, and by spirit, the informed substance of the aether. Whence in *sermon 10 of Pimander* he seems to open this same passage of the first sermon with these words, by

--- Page 81 ---
DE MICROCOSMO INTERNO. 79

through which it most effectively declares the true movement of the mind from its uncreated origin, from which, to the created limit, to which: *The soul of man is carried in this manner; Mind in reason, reason in soul, soul in spirit, spirit in body.* By which words, indeed, it not obscurely implies that the divine and uncreated mind, a ray of uncreated light, assumes the substance of the empyrean heaven, by which vehicle it descends further downwards into the formal substance of the middle heaven; for the form of the middle heaven is of the true nature of the empyrean heaven's substance, and naturally like rejoices in its like. Furthermore, that aethereal form, embracing a twofold supercelestial nature, is enveloped in the coverings of the aethereal spirit, in which, as in its own proper vehicle, it is transported into the earthy body.

Therefore, the source of the mind is that uncreated Monad, which *Trismegistus in Pimander 1 calls God's own form, similar to Himself, and Holy Scripture calls a Theiform breath:* And *Trismegistus in sermon 10 of Pimander proves that this cannot exist in an earthly mass, nor can earthly dregs receive a mind so divine, or sustain such a deity.* Hence *it is (he says) that the mind assumes the soul as a garment, because the divine soul, existing, uses the spirit as a vehicle.* Nor indeed can this divine mind be carried further into the middle region without its empyrean vehicle, than the nature of the middle soul into the lowest, except by means of the middle spirit, since the same relationship exists between the heaven of the Trinity and the empyrean, which exists between the empyrean and the middle; and the same between that middle and the lowest, which exists between the empyrean and the middle: For the soul of each higher heaven is nobler than that of its immediate lower, according to that saying of *Proclus in his book On the Soul: The rational soul is nobler than the irrational, because the first Creator of the world created the former, while the younger or aethereal Gods created the latter, that is, the fiery spirit of the intellectual heaven, which they also call rational, emanating immediately from God, the first Creator of the world, is nobler than the spirit of the aethereal heaven, inasmuch as to the latter is given only the faculty of imparting life and vegetation to lower beings, but by no means complete reason.* And hence it is that *Proclus* himself asserts in the same place, *that some souls descend from the Solar sphere, others from the Mercurial, and some from the Lunar.* From which it evidently appears that the first garment of the mind is far nobler than that aethereal one, since it is, as it were, a form for that middle spirit, by which it is received in its descent. Therefore, the mind is first enclosed in the rational spirit; but the rational spirit, with its most divine content, is received by the spirit which is vital in itself; which then, from being an irrational spirit, becomes rational and intellectual by the presence of the mind and its vehicle, according to that saying of *Iamblichus in his book On Mysteries: The soul is illuminated by beneficial divine will.* And *Aristotle* now correctly defined it *in his book On the Spirit: to be an intellectual, rational, always moving spirit:* inasmuch, namely, as those supercelestial endowments are conjoined with its nature. Finally, this aethereal spirit, exalted by both supercelestial and mundane rays, because of its constant communication and familiarity with lower beings, is infused into bodies aptly disposed and proportioned by God in creation to receive it, and running through the entire human body, it first introduces into them a sensitive power from its own proper nature, which it is accustomed to bestow equally upon other animals, namely irrational ones, as well as upon humans, and then afterwards also a rational and intellectual power, which by virtue of supercelestial lights it is accustomed to confer only upon man. And in this way is formed that inner man, comprising simultaneously the intellective, vegetative, and sensitive faculties.

C A P. IX.
*On the opinion of Theologians concerning the creation of the soul.*

IN the preceding chapter, what philosophers, even the more divine ones, establish concerning the creation of the human soul and its descent into the earthy body, we have clearly explained. Here, however, we will briefly discuss the differing opinions of the theologians themselves. The majority of theologians conclude that *the soul is infused into the body* *and created by infusion*, citing for this that passage from *Genesis 2: 'He breathed into him the breath of life,' that is, He created the soul in the body.* But Origen, along with some Greek theologians who follow the Platonic opinion in this regard, openly contradicts this assertion; all of them hold this view: *that all souls were created equally with the angels in the beginning.* This is also what certain others believe, as found in *Clangor buccinae*, where it is expressly written in these words: *Souls, which today and daily hereafter are newly infused into the mother's womb, are not created anew, but were created from fire alone in the primordial beginning of all things, and are nurtured in the mind and power of the Creator until the predetermined time when they ought to be infused into the body, and they do not depart from the body unless the spirit has first departed and vanished, and when it has departed, the soul also vanishes.* And Augustine also seems to wish to agree with these, as is found in Book 7 *on Genesis*, unless he found sacred Scriptures contradicting it; Hence, he speaks doubtfully about Adam's soul thus: *If no Scripture is found to contradict it, it seems it should be said that Adam's soul was created from the beginning with the angels, and afterwards voluntarily came to the body to administer it.* But this doubt of Augustine, in my judgment, will be most easily removed if we consider that the eternal Spirit of God, carried on fiery wings over the waters, continually infuses all virtues into the parts of every Macrocosm, according to that never-to-be-repeated enough saying of the Royal Psalmist: *By the word of the Lord were the heavens established, and by the Spirit from His mouth all their power.* For since these things are so, why would not that spirit, which the Creator once breathed into the face of the Microcosm, also suffice in the same way for all human propagation, seeing that it seems to be reserved in the mind and power of the Creator until the predetermined time when it ought to be infused into the body? Thus, indeed, so that, saving that *Genesis* passage, that intellectual soul, which, inasmuch as it is the image of God Himself, can be called infinite for the formation of humans, extends itself infinitely, no differently than that spirit which GOD gave to the Macrocosm at the beginning of creation, by whose presence the Macrocosm itself is daily adorned with infinite endowments, without a repeated creation of that spirit. Is it not also said according to Saint John 1: *that in the Word of the Lord is the life of man, and that life is the light, etc.*? And Trismegistus, *calling light and life God Himself*, says that man is created from these, by which he proves that God Himself is the life of man, through which he tastes supercelestial things, and that the mind of man, as if the divine uncreated essence of God Himself or the true image of God, is always reserved with God Himself for the creatures whom He intended to form in His image. Furthermore, that the soul is created anew, that is, from nothing, or from non-pre-existing matter, does not seem probable; since the matter of its composition is spirit, and its form is light, as the theologians themselves testify. But indeed, the sacred Scriptures testify that the general spirit and similarly that universal light, from which all form and matter of things are derived, were created only in the beginning by divine power from non-pre-existing matter. To these is added, moreover, that the Father, the Creator of all, said before the existence of the world: and immediately by His Word the heavens were established and the Spirit proceeding from His mouth [established] the virtues

And the whole in the whole and everything created are nothing but God; inasmuch as all things are said to be good, and truly nothing, besides God alone, ought to be called good, from whom alone is goodness. For by His goodness all things exist, and without it nothing could be brought into being; because God's sole goodness, light, and benevolence is the act of all things, in whom, from whom, and through whom all things that are, exist, and without whom nothing. Whatever therefore is act, is GOD, because GOD alone is act: And therefore the act and life of creatures is GOD, because in the Word was life, etc.

DE HOM. INTERN. NUM. ET HARM.     95

It also drew three properties from the starry heaven, corresponding to each of the three triplicities of the Zodiac, which properties it also joined to itself for the perfection of its office in the human body. For it drew its attractive faculty from *Aries, Leo & Sagittarius*, which form the fiery triplicity; its retentive [faculty] from *Taurus, Virgo & Capricorn*; its concoctive [faculty] from *Gemini, Libra & Aquarius*; and claimed its expulsive [faculty] from *Cancer, Scorpio & Pisces*. Then, passing through the sphere of *Saturn*, it received its receptive power from it, also gravity and constancy in its purpose, and prudence with profundity. From the orb of *Jupiter*, it seized for its portion justice, love of virtues, honesty, meekness, and the governance of the natural faculty. From the region of *Mars*, it had impulsive and irascible power, audacity, potency, and fortitude. From the *Solar* circuit, it drew its vital faculty. From the circuit of *Venus*, it took concupiscible virtue, cheerfulness, and delight in Music. From the orb of *Mercury*, it acquired its imaginative power and sharpness of intellect, love of sciences, and perfection of memory. And from the sphere of the *Moon*, it drew its power of waxing and waning. Finally, its lower portion, which we call sensitive and animal, introduces with itself, for its portion, into its dark abode, complexions, humors, and other properties suitable for the sensible organs, for the perfection and complement of elemental composition. From which it most clearly appears that the soul attracts to itself on its journey, wandering from unity to multitude, infinite properties of the macrocosm flowing from the divine harmony thereof.

And here it must be diligently observed that discords do not strike the human soul from the empyrean heaven, because that [heaven], due to its purity, divinity, and simplicity, always revolves around the good, but contentious sounds are very often perceived to come from the starry heaven, for example: *Saturn* sometimes inconveniently and discordantly infuses envious seeds into the soul; similarly hatred, baseness of life, melancholy, and other such things; *Mars* also sometimes sends wrath, sedition, strife, derision, adultery, incest, inconstancy, and other such things into the lower [parts/regions] due to its incongruous pulsations with some lower natures. Hence these are called *unfortunate Planets*; the reason for which we have reviewed in our mundane Music. Moreover, the regions of the elements, found to have an abundance of matter in them, are full of discords; because their binary number is the origin of discord and strife. And hence it happens that there are so many altercations in this region, so many corruptions of things, and their changes from one form to another. But even the elements themselves would quarrel among themselves, and wage perpetual war against each other, were it not for that honorable **medium**, by whose virtue contending things are bound and connected by the bonds of peace and concord. But indeed the mind is free from every passion and malevolent disposition of matter, and is always found constant and unmoving in its state; for it is not swayed by the influences of the stars, or the impulse of intelligences, but exists immune from every operation and action of things which are subject to its connatural seat. Hence it is manifest that the stars cannot impose necessity on bodies over which it predominates. For the wise person, sprinkled and imbued with the blessed rays of the divine mind, will dominate the stars themselves; Nor certainly do the influences of the stars and planets have that power over the intellective part of the soul, inasmuch as the rational spirit is the immediate vehicle of the mind and naturally exalted above the power of the stars: But such people who, refusing the gifts of the intellect and the benefits of the mind, are content with only the vital soul, like beasts, and preferring irrationality to rationality, and in no way contemplating divine things with spiritual eyes, look only at earthly things with a downward gaze, the animal

*Concerning the origin of the body of every creature, whether mineral, vegetable, or animal;*

That the internal man is composed of a threefold constitution of the soul, or of a primary, secondary, and tertiary act or ray, we have sufficiently clearly declared in the preceding books. In this little book, however, we have proposed to briefly and concisely explain the matter, nature, and fabric of its palace or receptacle, which is called the human body, the external man, and, according to John 4:9, the house of the internal man.

Therefore, as far as its matter is concerned, from many passages of the Holy Scriptures, we gather that it is earth and mud, Gen. 2:7, and ibid. 3:19, and ibid. 18:27, and Tob. 4:9, and ibid. 16:18. Concerning the reason for its origin, nature, quality, and opacity, we have made sufficiently clear mention in our first Treatise, on the Macrocosm; where we demonstrated that it is the dregs of universal dark spirits, driven back to the center of the macrocosmic fabric by a threefold revolution of the uncreated Spirit; yet in such a way that some dense spirits of the waters or universal spirits still lie hidden in this, as it were, dead head, with some barely perceptible sparks of threefold light, adhering from each of the three heavens or from any region of the world to the glutinous and viscous matter of the hidden spirit, and submerged in darkness. Hence the origin of minerals is perceived to come from the thickest and densest spirit of the lower or sublunar region, and from such a spark of light; whence their weight and gravity, and difficult dissolution on account of the density of the matter, which includes sparks of light. From this it also happens that metals and other minerals N more

Hence it is that this golden, vital, and incorruptible plant of the world is not hindered in its ascent by the elements: because its matter is not contiguous with them, but a substance of the middle region is interposed between fire and the empyrean, or intellectual, heaven, from which neither fire, nor air, nor water, nor earth could retain this spirit flying upwards from the earth, but only the ether, which is contiguous to it by its natural position, no differently than fire is to ether. From these things, therefore, it will be clear to those observing subtly, that the nature of the Sun, since it is of the origin of the empyrean or rational heaven, both because of the greatest vivacity of its actions, and also because of its wondrous power and virtue in the life of animal things, produced by its life-giving power those animals of every kind which were created on the fifth day and at the beginning of the sixth day. For before its appearance in the heart of heaven, no animal was created in the expanse of the lowest region or upon the earth. But indeed, after the fourth day, on which the Sun appeared in heaven, namely from the beginning of the fifth day until the end of the sixth, animated creatures were gradually produced. From which it will be reasonable to consider how an animal requires a greater quantity of heat and light for its composition and existence than a mineral or a plant, and that various kinds of animals are procreated according to a greater or lesser effect of heat and light. For at the first appearance of the Sun from heaven, the vapors of humid nature, of mists and material spirits springing forth from the rebellious mass of darkness, were still crude and less concocted, which thereafter were more and more daily subdued by the solar rays and actions, and thus having become more obedient, they subsequently brought forth more perfect and mature things. Hence, at the beginning of the fifth day, since the humors were still very crude and undigested, by the life-giving operation of the Sun, cruder animals were brought forth into light. For thus we read, that firstly, fish and aquatic animals were created immediately after the revelation of the Sun; Then, the nebulous spirit of darkness having become more obedient, more aerial and volatile animals had life and saw light in the second place; afterwards, finally, with the fifth day of creation having passed, more hot and fiery animals began to live and breathe, namely quadruped animals and reptiles. It is therefore clearly evident that the dominion of the Sun, increasingly assailing the humid nature and terrestrial mass, was the cause (with divine and immortal nature so willing) that various and diverse kinds of animals were found in the lower world; of which some were colder, others hotter, some terrestrial, others aquatic, others aerial, and others more fiery: And indeed, the bodies of all these were selected from a portion of the earth more obedient to solar and formal rays, and more corresponding to their actions; For this earth is the mother of all elements, because from it these proceed, and to it they return: Indeed, the earth is the mother and nurse of all things, which she conceived in her womb from fire, that is, from heaven, or by a celestial act: because heaven, whose emperor is the Sun, is the father of all composite things; while the earth is their mother. This (earth) carries those (things) in its depths, like a mother her fetus. For into the depths of the earth all celestial influences, and especially solar ones, flow, which, like the seeds of things, are enclosed there as in a common womb; Hence, because of the varieties of the proportions of these descending influences, diverse generations of diverse things occur in the earth, and various impressions arise, all of which happen in the muddy substance of the earth. Indeed, the earth itself is the palace of the solar rays carried in the ethereal spirit, in which they are enclosed like captives and are called vital spirits; inasmuch as by their benefit even these houses and their tabernacles live, feel, and have rea-

And, let it be said with due deference and permission of both ancient and modern philosophers (whose opinion is that all animals except man alone are irrational), other animals besides man also have certain sparks of reason; which they received from the solar nature, since its rays partake of the nature of the empyrean heaven and of its rational spirit. Whence the nature of animals is exalted in dignity above that disposition of the planets, and the flame of their heat is observed in a certain way to penetrate to the borders of the empyrean or rational heaven, on account of the solar nature, a portion of which it retains within itself. Finally, man, a wonderful animal and a quasi-divine miracle in creation, also required for his external existence an earth specially selected by the Creating Nature (Natura naturans), which it prepared with its own hands and most skillfully fashioned to the image of its own likeness.

C H A P. II.

*What is the human body? That it is pure and selected earth, precipitated downwards on the first day of creation, when the darkness of the supreme mundane region was repelled: and how it differs from the matter of other mixtures, both mineral and vegetable, as well as animal.*

Therefore, the external man was nothing else before the breath of the soul was communicated to him, than a corporeal mass formed from mud or clay of the earth, of a reddish color, as some would have it; such as philosophers imagine to be found pure and unadulterated in the center of the earth; signifying by this very thing that God chose this most perfect particle of earth of all to prepare a dwelling for His spirit of life, as being more filled with purer and more mature spirits of darkness, and thus most apt and suitable for receiving that most noble and God-like human spirit, inasmuch as *Paul*, with *Xystus the Pythagorean*, called it the temple of God. For, according to the authority of some ancients, in the foundation of the earth, completed on the third day of creation, this portion of earth was prepared and destined for this work by divine providence, and it contained and possessed the purest and most suitable potential seeds of light and ethereal spirit for receiving that God-like breath of uncreated splendor, namely, the primary acts or rays. This portion of earth, I say, the Creator formed into the likeness and essence of the external man; so that its interior might receive it as a dwelling; wherefore He breathed His divine spirit into its nostrils. And this undoubtedly differed from other kinds of earth used for the structure of more ignoble creatures, no less than the earthy composition of gold differs from that of other impure minerals, because, **as Plato testifies,** the acts of forms require impressions of matter that are suitable and worthy of their operations, that is, the soul desires such a dwelling in which it may act and dwell as it itself is. From which

--- Page 103 ---

from which it follows, that, since the mind is the most divine ray and act of the Creator, immediately emanating from His mouth, it is necessary that it also requires a most excellent dwelling, similar to itself, in which it may reign and perform its wondrous operations. Therefore, from the most excellent and polished slime and clay of the earth was that external Adam formed: From which it is clear that his earthly portion was not entirely dry, as gross earth is in its nature, but that it had in itself the substance of water, by which its dryness was reduced and tempered into a certain muddy and slimy disposition. And yet the whole denomination of the same body is taken from earth, because gross water is nothing other than subtle earth, and earth nothing other than gross water: But just as the element of fire, in its relation, is contiguous to gross earth, with respect to its dryness, and therefore also exists potentially in earth, so also in subtle earth or gross water is potentially found that subtle water or air, from which water acquired its mobility; since these two elements are continuous in the nature of humidity: And yet, because nothing in the external Adam's form, except earth alone, was seen or touched, therefore earth, clay, and dust are named in many places of the sacred Scriptures. Therefore, this mass was prepared into the softness of clay or wax, which is suitable for receiving any figure and image of any kind; and finally, God, Most Good, Most Great, with His hands, formed it into the image and likeness of the external man, according to that *Psalm 119:73: "Your hands have made me and fashioned me, etc."* And *Job 10:9: "You have made me like clay, etc."* This, therefore, is that illustrious dwelling and exalted palace, and that microcosmic body and distinguished man or external Microcosm, or that earthly basis or foundation, concerning which *Job 4:9* thus speaks: *"The body is the clay house of the inner man, who has an earthly foundation."* And elsewhere *chapter 16:18: "O earth, do not cover my blood, etc."* This is that man, whom *Genesis 2:7* *affirmed to have been made and formed from the dust of the earth; and whom elsewhere, chapter 18:27, it called "dust and ashes."* And *chapter 3:19, it said he would "return to dust."* There are also, as it seems to me, still some deeper things to be sought for the true knowledge of the external man. Hence, if, according to our intention, we diligently examine the three species of lower creatures, namely animal, vegetable, and mineral, we will clearly perceive that each order of them not only received its soul from a particular region of the world (namely, the more irrational animals from the soul of the Sun, which derived the Sun's creation from the first region; and the more rational immediately from the intellectual heaven; vegetables partly from the middle heaven and partly from the elementary form; and minerals from the light of the lowest heaven) but also that their bodies claim their origin from the darkness of each region of the world, and that indeed according to their excellence in nature. For all darkness in the beginning was called "terra inanis" (empty earth) by Moses, which earth, indeed, repelled by a threefold action of the spirit towards the center on the third day of creation, was no longer called empty earth, but was called rich and filled with species of minerals and vegetables. Therefore, from the upper portion of the empty earth, or palpable darkness, were formed the bodies of the Sun and of man himself; but the bodies of other animals were composed partly from the same darkness, and partly from the shadowy spirit of the middle region; Similarly, the bodies of vegetables partake of the darkness of both lower regions, and the remaining bodies of minerals came forth from the portion of the darkness of the lowest region alone. Hence it is, therefore, that mineral bodies differ from vegetable bodies in density and solidity, and likewise vegetables from animals; For the bodies of minerals are harder and more compact, those of vegetables less so, and those of animals least of all. Is this not also most clearly argued from the diversity, nobility, and ignobility of the natures compared to each other in these bodies? Has not nature operated and been engaged N 3 of the Sun
