...of the Sun in the animation of these animal bodies, which were made immediately after its exaltation and placement in the heavens, as in a subject more natural and convenient to itself? Have not these composite species also received their sites and stations according to the position of the heavens themselves, namely minerals towards the center of the earth, but vegetables in its upper region, and animals upon its surface? What is more evident than this very thing among the wise? But what is more absurd than it among fools? Are not the bodies of minerals, vegetables, and animals opaque? But if therefore all are opaque and dark, whence this disposition of theirs except from darkness? But perhaps you will assert that this discrepancy of theirs arises from their form; to which reply of yours, if we give place, what then follows? Does not form usually require a subject suitable for its actions? Hence, the nobler the form will be, the nobler a body or passive subject it requires for itself, upon which to act. And therefore superior lights descending into the darkness of the lower world, require darknesses more suitable for their bodies, in which they may dwell. What passive subject therefore, or what darknesses are more suitable for the actions of the mind and intellect than the human body? Certainly none; because experience teaches us that the intellect with the mind chooses only the human body as its dwelling place and no other. Hence it is clear that the human body, among all species of darkness, is most known and familiar to that divine intellectual spirit, precisely as if already then, once even before the creation of the world, the darknesses of this body had been the misshapen matrix of that spirit. Thus also we see that the celestial spirit with its soul is more suited to vegetables than to minerals, because it is found more abundantly in the former than in the latter; and so in other things. From which indeed we can clearly see what kind of earth, or dust or clay and that corporeal mass, from which GOD formed man, and how it differs from the external matter of other mixed species.

**CAP. III.**
*Concerning the Geometric proportions of external man, and how through them we can most aptly delineate the world.*

**W**ill not this seem wonderful and miraculous to men stained with the blemish of ignorance, that in the nature, position, and Geometric proportions even of external man, the idea, image, and proportion of the material world is found most exactly? Hence man is not unsuitably called by Hermes Trismegistus, the image of the world and Microcosm; because in him, as in a mirror, the parts of the world, both ideal and material or visible, are seen. For we find that, just as the earth is the center of the greater world, from which lines or diameters are drawn to the circumference and as it were the matrix of all elements, from which all generations, growths, and multitudes proceed; so also the center of the lesser world is the point of the genitals or pudenda, and the root of the penis: from which if we shall have measured to the xiphoid process (bone of the pointed cartilage), and then from that to the base of the throat, situated near the clavicles, and further from it to the crown of the head, we shall find the Geometric proportions of the Microcosm corresponding with equal distance to those three regions or heavens of the Macrocosm. For by proceeding and ascending from the pubic bone or from the center or point of generation to the xiphoid process, we shall find that the lower heaven of the Macrocosm, or the elementary region, corresponds in all respects with the lowest portion of the Microcosm, since in its re-

Thence from the diaphragm to the throat, observing the same measure of height as was previously found in the dimension of the elementary region, one ascends. This region is therefore called the thorax, which relates to the Microcosm as the middle or ethereal heaven relates to the Macrocosm. For through the middle of this region passes the orb of equality, in which the vital soul of this lesser world is situated: For, just as in the middle region of the Macrocosm the Sun occupies the sphere of equality; so in this lesser world the heart is observed to possess the sphere of equality, inasmuch as in it the celestial heat and ethereal moisture are joined in equal balance, and to which also, as to the Sun, the other planets offer obedience in this region: For according to the opinions of learned Physicians and Astrologers, *Saturn found in Aries presides over the chest, and in Taurus regards the heart; similarly Jupiter passing through Aries is referred to the heart, in Pisces to the chest; Mars also entering Cancer presides over the chest, but entering Leo looks to the heart; The Sun in Scorpio is beneficial to the chest and passing through Sagittarius is most friendly to the heart, indeed however the Sun may be, it presides over the heart of animals, and its sign Leo holds firm possession for it; Venus visiting Leo is referred to and predominates over the chest, but in Virgo over the heart; Mercury contributes to the heart if found in Libra, but in Virgo, which is its own house, it is conducive to the chest; Finally, the Moon passing through Libra has dominion over the chest, passing through Scorpio over the heart,* and thus in this region of the Microcosm all the effects of the Planets, as well as the signs of the Zodiac, are investigated subordinately. But nevertheless the Sun itself, the emperor of life and native heat, always holds the first place in this region, both in this machine of the Microcosm and in that of the Macrocosm.

Furthermore, this region is distinguished into three cells related to the three hierarchies of the empyrean heaven; namely, into the ventricle of the common sense, and into the ventricle of fantasy or imagination, and the memorial (ventricle): And what is no small miracle, by virtue of this heaven of divinity, the Microcosm has familiarity with the holy Angels and contemplates God Himself through contemplation, addresses Him, and is united with Him, through the mediation of the divine Spirit. And just as it is found in the Macrocosm that the rage of demons inhabiting the lower region is suppressed, and they are rendered so obedient, and are restrained and governed by an inviolable bridle through the virtue and power of God and the good Angels inhabiting the third and supreme heaven; so also by the virtue of the mind and the directions of intellect and reason, anger arising from bile and impatience, envy proceeding from the spleen, concupiscence born from the liver, and fear and despair and sadness and other such things are corrected, made mild, and from rebellious become subject. C H A P. IV.
*Concerning the correct position of the Microcosmic body according to the four*
*regions of the Macrocosm.*

[Ornamental Q]UITE arduous and difficult though it be to find a suitable position of the Microcosm, corresponding to the four regions of the Macrocosm, nevertheless, we deduce from the source of the sacred scriptures that there is a certain suitable relationship between these two worlds. For in many places in them we read that in prayers and in the manner of praying, the face of the supplicant should be turned towards the East. Similarly, in Matthew 24:27, we find that lightning will come from the East and extend to the West. And in Numbers 35:5, it is read: "Measure also to the East side, etc., and to the South side, and to the West side, and to the North side, etc." Furthermore, it is also written in Job 23:8-9, according to Pagnini's translation, where the inquiry of the place and seat of Jehovah is discussed: "Behold, I go to the East, and He is not there; and to the West, I do not understand Him; or to the North, while He works, I do not see Him; He hides Himself in the South, and I do not see Him, etc." Indeed, Jerome interprets this passage of Job thus: "If I go to the East, He does not appear; if to the West, I do not understand; if to the left, what shall I do? I will not apprehend Him; if I turn to the right, I will not see Him." Tremellius also translates that passage of Job into these words: "If I go forward, He is not there; but if backward, I will not perceive Him; when He acts to the left, I still will not see Him; He will cover the right side, and I will not look upon Him." Most clearly, therefore, from these things we can perceive the proper position of man in the world according to his nature. For from that passage in Numbers we gather that man, in every operation, should primarily look to the East, then in a circular respect to the South, West, and North.

From the words of Job, however, we discover that the Eastern region, both according to Jerome's and Pagnini's translation, should be referred to the face of man, that is, as Tremellius interprets, to the front or his anterior part, and the Western part to his posterior parts; from which it necessarily follows that his left part turns towards the North, just as its opposite part, namely the right, looks towards the South. Therefore, the sacred Bibles teach us that this disposition of the Microcosm to the regions of the Macrocosm is more congruent with it according to the laws of nature. Now, diligently examining the nature of the matter, let us inquire whether this position of the Microcosm to the site of the Macrocosm, according to its physical constitution, agrees with the nature of the world or Macrocosm, or not.

Therefore, with accurate observation, we find that every region of the lesser world corresponds to every quadrant of the greater world in nature, temperament, and disposition. For we attribute the light of the eyes to the solar splendor, and intellect and reason to the prime mover, which rotates its spheres from East to West; and we rightly compare the human heart to the Sun, as its principle; inasmuch as it is written that Jehovah placed His tabernacle in it; and thus all things of man, both internal and external, rejoice to salute the Sun, as the luminous tabernacle of the Creator, with devout prayers and thanksgivings preceding to their Creator and Lord; since it is the repeller of sadness and darkness, the author of joy, gladness, and light. Conversely, the posterior parts of man are not undeservedly referred to the West. For just as the East usually brings day, light, and joy; so, on the contrary, the West imports night, darkness, and sadness. Thus, also through the posterior parts of man, only a single way and a sole passage is found, through which foul and useless substance is compared to the empty earth, inasmuch as the nutritive faculty and power

--- Page 109 ---
DE MICROCOSMO EXTERNO. 107

...lost almost all ethereal spirit (extracted from it for the sustenance of the heart) and likewise elementary virtue (exhausted from it for the nutrition of the liver and blood); whence it can be called a quasi-dead head, useless dregs, and as it were a messenger of night and darkness; and therefore that part is not unsuitably compared to the West and the darkness of night. The left part of man also seems necessarily to be referred to the North. For just as Boreas from the North sends forth towards the South its cold and dry blasts, inducing snows, hailstones, frost, ice, and melancholic dispositions. So the human spleen, the source of melancholy, situated in the left part, sends forth and disperses its melancholic, cold, and dry blasts throughout the entire Microcosm, and especially towards its right side or south, through the so-called colon intestine, by which its hypochondria are disturbed as if by a whirlwind. Indeed, just as that Macrocosmic wind tends upwards towards the ethereal region, but is finally repelled downwards, that is, its violence is reverberated by the power of the aerial diaphragm. So also the blast emitted from the spleen strives with utmost effort to ascend upwards to the region of the thorax, where the heart dwells; but it is impeded by the diaphragm and finally repelled downwards. Therefore, the left arm of the Microcosm is, as it were, the arctic pole, just as its right is the antarctic, upon which the Microcosm seems to be carried in the image of the greater world. For human shins are as columns by which the Microcosm is sustained; but arms are as wings by which it is governed, inasmuch as they contribute both to its sustenance and to its protection and defense. Thus a bird has shins and feet by which it is sustained; but it is directed by wings in its affairs. Finally, there is a great relation between the right part of man and the nature of the Southern region. For the liver of the Microcosm is hot and humid in its nature, generating blood and dispensing it through the rivulets of the body to irrigate the entire human garden, no differently than the Southern region of the world is observed to bring forth clouds and rains for the fertility and growth of the entire earth. Behold, O men imbued with true Philosophy, how notable is the relation, and how admirable the affinity between these regions of the greater world and those of the lesser, by which they are perceived to correspond most exactly to each other in the same nature, condition, and situation.

C A P. V.
A brief anatomy of each Microcosmic region.

The head of the human body, which we compared above to the empyrean heaven, some have called the supreme belly, which terminates at the neck, and contains the spark of the mind in its rational vehicle. Of this head, physicians distinguish its external part into the forehead, sinciput, occiput, vertex, temples, and face, and again observe its hairs, their manifold use, and the dense, hard, dry, and thick skin to which the roots of the hairs adhere; But its internal part they distinguish into the cranium and its adhering parts, and into the brain with its parts. They divide the cranium into five sutures, one of which is posterior, called Lambdoid; another anterior, coronal; the third is called straight and sagittal; the two remaining ones are called mendose (false), squamous, and temporal. A certain membrane surrounds the convex surface of the skull, arising from the thick meninges through the sutures, which is therefore called the pericranium and periosteum. Beneath this skull also two other membranes meet, covering the brain in a circle, of which the one that is thicker and harder, and adhering to the concave surface of the cranium, is called the dura mater; while the other, intimately joined to the brain, is thin and soft,

--- Page 110 ---
108 TRACT. I. SECT. I. LIB. V.
and is called the pia mater. Finally, the second part of the head, namely the brain, is divided into three ventricles: And from the cerebellum nerves arise, which are the instruments of sensation and motion. Furthermore, in this region the eyes are also included, for the structure of each of which five tunics come together; namely the white (sclera), cornea, uvea (in which are the pupil and iris), sagena (retina) and aranea (hyaloid membrane); and three humors, namely the aqueous, vitreous, and crystalline. In this region also the ears and nostrils are found, and similarly the tongue, consisting of the bifurcated bone called hyoid, and of nerves, arteries, veins, and muscles. Furthermore, also the trachea extends up to the clavicles. Physicians call the second region of the body the middle belly and the Thorax; because it is circumscribed on both sides by the clavicles down to the diaphragm and by the ribs, containing the vital parts. In this region the heart has its principal station; its structure is its capsule. Furthermore, the major parts of the heart are its two chambers; namely the right, to which are attached two veins, namely the vena cava and the pulmonary artery, and the left, to which are connected the arteries, the Aorta and the pulmonary vein. But the minor parts are the two auricles, namely the right and left, and the orifices (valves). Similarly, this region contains the substance of the lungs, and three membranes by which it is enveloped, namely the Diaphragm, the Mediastinum, and the membrane surrounding the ribs, called the Pleura. The third and lowest region of the human body, extending downwards from the Diaphragm to the pubic bone, comprehends the liver, spleen, gallbladder, kidneys, bladder, seminal vessels, and other such things. The substance of the Liver consists of flesh and nerves, from which arise veins—the portal or ramified, and the vena cava—and arteries. But the Spleen, gallbladder, kidneys, and bladder are members prepared for the use of the liver, namely, for carrying away superfluities from the liver. Similarly, this region contains the stomach, mesentery, and the upper and thinner intestines—namely the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum—and the lower and thicker ones—namely the cecum, colon, and rectum. Finally, we could fill entire volumes with observations of this anatomy, and thus afflict the eyes of readers with more weariness regarding things common to the world, than soothe them with delight or the pleasant murmur of novelty; therefore it pleased us to pass lightly over the anatomy of the human body in this place at least, so that we may gird our mind for things more new, and not so commonly known, and yet true and demonstrable.

CHAP. I.
On the comparison of the harmonic constitution of the regions of the Microcosm
with those of the heavens of the Macrocosm.

[Large decorative initial C] The human body, which we called the external man above, is formed from the same matter as the world. And although the spirit of the world, on account of that subtlety which it received from the property and presence of light, is known to be diaphanous, clear, perspicuous, and transparent: nevertheless, that clarity and diaphaneity of its spirit often becomes black, shadowy, and obscure through thickening and condensation (which usually happens more or less according to the greater or lesser absence of light, or the dominance of thickening cold), just as is seen in the transformation of air into a dense cloud; and again, by the congelation of cold, that cloud or condensed aerial spirit is changed into a kind of white earth, as in hail, ice, snow, indeed even into the densest earth itself, as is demonstrated by considering the matter of a thunderbolt. For it is certain that the species of earth are of diverse natures, that is, participating more either in the purity of fire, or the disposition of air, or the quality of water. And yet all these species of earth are for the most part opaque and by no means transparent.

Thus, the brain is observed to participate in the fiery element, the heart and lungs in the aerial, the stomach, liver, and humors in the aqueous, and finally the spleen and intestines in the gross earthy element, because these parts of the body became receptacles of those elementary natures after the soul was placed into them, as we will teach below. But indeed, all these portions of earth, differing in disposition, are observed to have, as it were, the same dimension of length in the geometrical symmetry of the body, nor is one part more opaque than another: which indeed happens because GOD fashioned this external dwelling place of the soul or breath of life before He breathed the soul into it. For from this it follows that although the element of water is greater in dimension than earth, and air than water, and so in the others (which happens because the same thing, when dilated, requires more space for its existence; similarly

And so He formed man from soul and body, that is, from eternal and mortal nature, so that an animal thus formed could satisfy both its origins, and marvel at and pray to heavenly and eternal things, and inhabit and govern.* Nor indeed shall we find Mercury's words to be vain, if we consider the matter rightly. For since it is the nature of the free mind and also the disposition of the intermediate soul, indeed even the property of the denser fire itself, to neglect lower things and to regard higher things by instinct of nature, when they are free and loosed from dense bonds, it is necessary that they be enclosed in an opaque body, and possess material organs, by whose direction they may be occupied with corporeal, dense, and lower things. For the nature of the soul, and much more of the mind, is so much conversant with spiritual and invisible things, that it could not perceive visible and corporeal things, unless it were enclosed in an opaque body, so that through material, terrestrial, and lower organs it might observe them. This therefore is the reason why the rays of both mind and nature operate around opaque things. For if they were freed from the bodily prison, leaving the earth empty and void, they would leap with a light bound into the heavens. The mind therefore is given only to man, so that it may distinguish his vital soul from the souls of other living beings, and exalt it above others in dignity. And although the vital soul itself was granted in creation to plants as well as to other animals, yet the bestial soul in animals, immediately strengthened and augmented by the virtue of the Sun, is superior to the soul of vegetables both in reason and in motion, inasmuch as the latter was infused into them before the Sun's position in the sky. From the foregoing, therefore, we see that the regions of the Microcosmic body do not differ in thinness and thickness, following the example of the regions existing in the Macrocosmic body, because the former was prepared before the inspiration of the soul, and consequently remains such after the infusion of the soul as it was before; but the latter, having been sent into it by that divine soul which was carried upon the waters, immediately received preparation and disposition in thickness, thinness, place, dilation and constriction, transparency and opacity. But the nature of the mind is of the purest disposition and lucid form, and therefore it follows that the brain is also most inclined to a lucid and humid nature, and supremely accommodated to it. The reason, however, why the brain is neither more subtle nor more transparent than other members is drawn from the creation of man, inasmuch as it is clear that the human body was created and prepared by the Creator before its soul was infused into it; The reason for this was that the soul, obscured by darkness, might perceive, distinguish, and observe bodies through material organs; which indeed it could not have accomplished unless veiled by dark flesh, since by itself it understands nothing but invisibles, that is, things like itself, while nevertheless, with the aid of the body, it sees visibles and gazes upon them with bodily eyes.

By this way, therefore, God rendered the dark mass subject to Himself and subjected both earth and heaven to His will, and stirred up dark bodies with respect to their condition. The middle region of the body, however, insofar as it relates to humidity and heat, can be compared to air, since it relates to the brain as air to fire; therefore, we deem the entire thorax of the Microcosm to be referred to the element of air. As for the opacity and density of the heart and lungs, the reason for it is the same as that alleged above.

The watery region in the Microcosm is also the origin of multiple humidities found in its lowest distinction. For the chyle of the stomach, the thick blood of the liver, and urine or blood serum constitute the watery sphere. Therefore, the stomach, liver, kidneys, and other parts of this region are much grosser in their hidden nature than the upper members: which is indeed proven by their effect; inasmuch as these very parts produce purer and more invisible spirits. For example; the brain contains animal spirits, which are invisible, and the heart contains vital or arterial spirits, which are almost invisible; but the earthy dregs are terminated and preserved in the intestines and spleen, which are found near the center of the Microcosm, just as the element of earth is found near the center of the Macrocosm.

From these things, therefore, we see that the regions of the external Microcosm are distinguished by symphonic differences no differently than the entire disposition of the elements of the Macrocosm is known to differ in quality and situation; the harmony of which, indeed, we have depicted quite evidently in our treatise on the Macrocosm. And indeed, that composition of this harmony in the elementary region was nothing other than a similitude of the universal mundane harmony, derived from the mutual action and resistance between the source of all light and the abyss of darkness. For the element of fire relates to the element of earth as light to darkness; similarly, the region of humidity between fire and earth relates as the universal intermediate spirit to the two extremes, namely light and darkness.

From these things, we can diligently consider how great is the similitude between the proportions of the human body and the mundane elements, and by what metrical dimensions these two can be reduced to music, so that they may agree with each other in harmony.

Moreover, that human harmony agrees with the sympathy of all things is demonstrated in this way: God is light; light is concord, and concord is the origin of creation and existence, and the consonant word, and that which effects the beauty of things and moves spheres from their starting point to their destination, and again to their principle, as to a unison, from which all concords have flowed.

And just as these two pyramids differ in position, so also the natures emanating from their bases are perceived to be opposite in disposition. For we see that the soul, emanating from the center of the formal pyramid, the longer it is in the body, the more perfect and vital it becomes, and is observed to grow younger in its faculty and wisdom or prudence; whereas, conversely, the body, the more advanced in age it becomes, the more it is known to diminish and weaken, as if by a certain old age. Furthermore, the stronger the soul, the weaker the body, and vice versa. We conclude therefore that the human body consists of four elements: but in flesh and bones, because of their fixed and solid earthy substance, earth is most apparent. Similarly, the element of water has its force and existence in the humors; but air, besides being found abundantly in the blood of the lowest region, is also perceived to dwell in the lung, as in a place more proper to it. Hence it happened from the beginning that that member of the body is always in motion, and serves as a fan for the cooling of the heart, lest it, inasmuch as it is the principal seat of igneous virtue, be consumed and dissolved by excessive heat. Therefore, the shape of the heart is pyramidal, and in this shape it is adapted to the flame of fire; because in an upward-ascending flame of fire we see its base similar to the base of a pyramid, and its summit sharp like the cone of a pyramid. But in the body, the matter stands with the heart as in the world with the Sun. For the base of the solar pyramid is in the body of the sun, but its cone tends downwards, contrary to the nature of common fire, and this by singular divine will. For a similar reason, the cone of the human heart, by which both the lower and upper parts of the body are refreshed by its benevolence, is observed to tend downwards. But since this fiery power was not present in the body before the breath of the divine spirit; and indeed our intention in this little book is to discourse concerning the body alone in its simple nature, without any consideration of the internal man, we will not say more about this subject, but we will proceed with a swift foot to its manifold dispositions, mixed with its internal aspects, and their explanation, so that, by finally departing from this, as it were, nothing—from this, I say, vile mud, and from these ashes and dead earth, still devoid of all divine grace—we may hasten with more intense joy and gladness, and with a cheerful mind and hastening foot, to the admirable operations of divine light (which, a little later, inhabiting it [the dead earth/vile mud] and breathed into it by a Deiform breath), and its hidden sympathy with the body, by which that [light/spirit] moves, this [body] is moved; that acts, this suffers; that vivifies, this lives; that through this [body] feels, sees, hears, tastes, smells, and touches; and by still more admirable virtues, by the astounding power of its rational and intellectual spirit within it [the body], ineffably leads to a happy culmination and outcome.

### CHAP. I.
#### *On the creation of man.*

[A large historiated initial 'A' depicting figures, possibly related to creation or anatomy, within a landscape.] The human soul, according to the manner and reason alleged in the first book of this work, gliding down by musical proportion and spiritual vehicles from the higher heavens to the lowest, and prepared for entry into its dwelling, is finally infused and inspired by the breath of the Maker into that [dwelling] made from earth, dust, and clay, adapted by the hands of the Creator Himself to receive such a Deiform breath, as has been said above, and moves, vivifies, and animates the external man by the life-giving power of its presence. And in this way, man was created twofold in a single individual, and became a living creature, endowed with reason and intellect; a wonderful (I say) animal, an earthly God, created immortal in himself, but made mortal because of sin, finally, the ineffable image of his Maker. But since we have treated copiously elsewhere in *Our Theologico-Philosophical Treatise, on life, death, and resurrection* concerning the breath of his life and concerning his body, in the state of innocence, its purity, cleanliness, transparency, clarity, and perfection, and likewise concerning his placement in Paradise, together with a description and explanation of the pleasure of Paradise itself, we will pass over these lightly in this place, so that we may occupy ourselves solely with the opinions of the ancient Philosophers, discussing the actions of the internal man in his external [body]. Therefore, in the former part of this book, we will treat concerning the operation, dominion, and power of the human soul, both from the supernatural part, and from the celestial and elementary part, inasmuch as the soul is considered with the body in creation alone or generation. We therefore perceive creation to differ from generation in many respects; Nor do we wish, however, this term 'creation' to be considered so strictly,

--- Page 125 ---
DE MICROC. INTERN. IN EXTERN. 123

we wish, as do those who define it as the production and origin of a thing from non-pre-existing matter, that is, from nothing: for in this way we do not correctly say that man was created; inasmuch as in his beginning his external part was made from pre-existing matter, and prepared for the work: namely from mud and earth, which was suitable for the composition of his matter; but we rather and more correctly define creation as that by which species of things, not existing before, now begin to be. Thus the first species of man received its beginning in the creation of Adam, that of the Lion in the first production of terrestrial animals, etc. In this, therefore, creation and generation differ: that the former is concerned with the origin and production of non-pre-existing species, while the latter is concerned with the propagation, multiplication, and conservation of pre-existing things or creatures, and of the species already created by the first FIAT, and until the ultimate PERISH. In the former, therefore, GOD the Creator operates immediately, but in the latter, the second image of the first mind, which is created nature itself, or the daughter of God, having proceeded and been derived from Him before all creation.

CAP. II.
*On the free disposition of the middle spirit, by which it is accustomed to partake*
*of one or the other extreme, and on the cause of the inner man's blessedness,*
*and the reason for his dejection and misfortune.*

[Large initial D] IVINE Paul, agreeing with Xistus the Philosopher, constantly asserted that the human soul is the temple of God, the reason for which is also demonstrated by *Merc. Trismegistus, Pim. 12.* in these words: *The Good Daemon, he says, declared the soul to be in the body, the mind in the soul, the Word in the mind, and God to be their Father. The Word, therefore, is the image and mind of God; the purest portion of matter is air; the soul is of the air, the mind of the soul, and finally* GOD *of the mind. God, indeed, is concerned with all things, the mind with the soul, the soul with the air, and the air with matter.* Hence it is that others, more strictly defining human nature, have composed it of three parts, namely, soul, intermediate spirit, and body; meaning by 'soul' both mind and soul. But these, as it seems to me, did not so exactly distinguish the inner man, that is, they did not distinctly describe the portions of the inner man which he acquired from each of the three heavens, and consequently, they left it imperfect, since all perfection consists of a beginning, a middle, and an end. Therefore, in this place, we will rather listen to the opinion of the Platonists, which does not differ from that of Hermes Trismegistus, who ascribed three parts to the inner man; namely, *the supreme, the lowest, and the middle.* By the supreme, they understood that divine part, which they call mind, illuminated intellect, a portion of uncreated light, and an act or ray of God, which is the superior portion of man, in which portion of the soul *Merc. Trismegistus*, ascending higher, by the counsel of the good and never-lying Daemon, assertively declared the Word to be present, to which *Saint John* also seems to assent, *calling the Word the life of men and the light of darkness,* and likewise *Merc. Trismegistus* calls it *the life and light of which man consists.* And elsewhere he says: *The Word in you sees and hears, Pimander 1.* Thus Moses calls it the *breath of life,* immediately inspired by God himself into the external man. And this superior portion of man, embracing the illuminated intellect, is that by which man, excelling other animals, approaches the nature of the Godhead itself; Hence it is called *the image of God and the son of God* not only by philosophers, but also by the scriptures themselves. Therefore, by mind, the Platonists understand intellect and reason

Q 2 volue-

--- Page 126 ---
124 T R A C T. I. S E C T. I. L I B. VII.

wished. By the lowest part, however, they seemed to signify the airy and lowest portion of the internal man, or the action of the elements, which is, as *Mercurius Trismegistus* testifies in the place cited above, of the entire elemental region, which, gathering to itself, in proportion as matter exists more subtle and tenuous, the formal dispensations of the elements, and with the superior guides or portions of the soul simultaneously assisting and preceding into the body, acts according to the corrupt disposition of flesh and darkness, inasmuch as it is more familiar to these by its nature and position. Hence this portion of the soul is more prone to the affections of the body and lower things, than it is by its nature suited to the mind and divine matters. And this lowest portion of the soul is called the sensitive soul, which *Paul the Apostle* called the animal man, and an idol drawn from the bosom of corporeal matter, which, when the body is dissolved, perishes along with it, or whose shadow does not long survive in the vapors of its dissolved body, participating in nothing of immortality, but returning to the deformity of hyle, unless it too is united to a higher power, by whose virtue alone it can acquire immortality. This portion of the soul is the moving power, vivifying, governing the body, and the material origin of the senses, through which the soul itself unfolds its powers of sensing in the body. For it senses corporeal things through the body, moves the body through space, governs it in space, and nourishes the body with the body. In this portion of the soul, therefore, there are two most powerful virtues, one of which is *Phantasia*, or imagination or cogitation, and the other the nature of sense. Finally, by the middle Spirit they understood the middle or ethereal and vital act and ray of nature, connecting both extremes, namely the mind with the animal soul. Hence it happens that this middle nature participates in both extremes, and thus has both from the virtue of the Sun, on account of its light's relation to the empyrean heaven, a spark of reason, which is subsequently augmented by the presence of the mind and intellectual spirit, and also from the lowest extreme and the subtle elements a sensitive faculty. Hence it happens that this middle nature, as if equally uniting the extremes and joining the intellectual portion with the animal or sensitive soul, that is, carrying the mind with its rational spirit and vehicle to lower things, is in its nature as it were free, so that it is permitted to adhere more to one or the other: namely, either to be more occupied with lower and sensible things, than with supercelestial and divine things, or also vice versa; just as if GOD were to say to this intermediate spirit dwelling in free will: *Which of these you prefer, take, or according to the words of the Priest Moses: You have before your eyes life and death, choose which you wish, or according to the Apostle's choice: either be children of the world, or of the heavenly kingdom.* And similarly it is also said in this way: Adam tasted of the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, who in the beginning contemplated nothing but the secrets of the mind, and consequently was a partaker of goodness alone. But how the matter stands, listen, I pray. This intermediate spirit, full of vital spirit and moreover imbued with reason, both solar and especially of the mind and empyrean, from these gives the body the power of living in general, that is, it bestows upon the body all the functions of life, through sensitive organs adapted to the faculties of life. But truly, since every action of life revolves either around good or around evil (since nothing happens in this world except these two extremes), the former of which is a gift of light, the latter of darkness, it is necessary that this movement of the spirit in life tends either towards goodness, that is, towards the nature of God and the father of light, or towards the malice of the Devil, the prince of darkness. For it is impossible for it to incline with an equal balance to both extremes simultaneously: For hence *Christ* says: *You cannot serve God and man at the same time.* *And Saint John 1st epistle: The children of God cannot be children of the world, nor vice versa.* From these, therefore, it is clear that this spirit, as if an Elector prince, tends either more towards higher things, or also towards the nature of lower things or the animal soul, that is, that it tends either towards the world, depravity, darkness—

--- Page 127 ---
DE MICROC. INTERN. IN EXTERN. 123

the nature of darkness and vices, or may regard the disposition of supracelestial goodness and virtue of heaven. If, therefore, this intermediate spirit, with its light, constantly adheres to the mind, it is beatified; because this supreme portion never sins, nor consents to evil, and always resists errors and exhorts to the best things, as *Mercurius Trismegistus* describes more fully in 1. Pimander. And therefore, finally, by the virtue of the mind, such a Spirit, because of its obedience, is transferred to God, according to that saying of *Proclus*: *The soul, through acquired knowledge, becomes similar to the mind or intellect itself.* But conversely, if that spirit approaches the animal soul, or adheres to the lower part, it is depraved, defiled, and is submerged and detained in darkness, until from a good Daemon it becomes evil; because that lower portion, namely the animal soul, is always submerged in evil, sin, and concupiscence, and, as *Saint Paul* testifies, draws to the worst things. His words are these: *I see another law in my members, captivating me in the law of sin.* Hence also arose this divine saying of *Bernhard*: *O soul, adorned and made beautiful by the image and likeness of God, espoused to the spirit by faith, aided by angels, companion of blessedness, heir of salvation, partaker of reason, what have you to do with the flesh?* Indeed, *Bernhard* did not see everything: For the spirit very often, in a treacherous manner, by flattering, draws the middle soul to lower things, and encloses it in the opaque body, where it very often leaves it alone and idle, and it accomplishes this by the blandishments of the sensitive soul, to which it is more inclined to adhere than to the mind, because of its moist and material disposition, which rejoices more in its like. But nevertheless, where the proportion of the middle soul's nature is ample (which is always found in the spirit), there it makes its spirit more obedient to the mind; because the middle soul, or the act of the world, and the ray of nature, is of the remote nature of the mind itself, or the act of God; whence it partakes of its property. Therefore, matter naturally tends towards the works of darkness, but form towards the disposition of light, as we see in the flame of burning fire. Is this, O readers, a new and unheard-of doctrine? Is this, I ask, the opinion of the Platonists in any way dissenting from the truth? Examine yourselves, I beg you, and you will finally discover that this matter cannot be otherwise. For example. To someone among you, perhaps, some crime to be committed will be proposed, that is, he will decide with himself either to commit rape, or adultery, or theft, or murder, or treason against the Prince, or some similar crime. But nevertheless reason, which is always the companion of the mind, will resist this intention of his to the best of its ability, nevertheless it very often happens that at the end of this struggle, the spiritual sense and the appetite of the flesh are fulfilled, and the admonitions of the mind and reason are rejected, and thus that destined crime is accomplished. Here therefore we see that this intermediate spirit has neglected the counsel of the mind, and by adhering to the sensitive soul, has immersed itself in darkness; But conversely, if the spirit, struck by the fear of the Creator, and following the footsteps of reason, strongly adheres to the mind, and leaves the conceived crime uncommitted, and, inflamed by repentance and a kind of hatred for its evil counsel and intention, converts itself to a better life, there is an evident sign that this intermediate spirit has constantly embraced the mind, and that it has held the animal soul or idol in contempt. But what need is there for more extensive discourse? Is it not clear to us that there are two extremes in the world, namely light and darkness, virtue and vice, good and evil? It follows therefore, as if from granted premises, that likewise there is also a certain and determined medium between them, which is apt to partake of this or that extreme, according as the object of one or the other seems more pleasant and delightful to it. And without doubt the human soul, or the internal man, is composed of these parts, inasmuch as he is perfect and complete, and consequently is judged to consist of a perfect number, namely, from a beginning, a middle, and an end, that is, from mind, spirit, and idol, or the animal soul, or which is the same thing,
                                                                                                      Q 3              is,

C A P.  I I I.
*On Reason; and why the mind is enclosed in an opaque body, and concerning its*
*dominion in the human body.*

**I**t is admirable to consider by what harmony those two things, contrary both in the nature of their essence and in their spatial position, namely Mind and body, can be joined together into one: And yet we perceive this to happen, by means of an interposed spirit, with our intellectual eyes. Similarly it will seem wonderful that this most excellent image of God, nay, indeed, the very ray of God himself, is removed so far from its connatural seat, and so debased in its condition, that although it is a most splendid, most efficacious, most divine, immortal, and purest light, it is nevertheless cast and enclosed in a prison so dark and gloomy, and earthly, and subject to corruption, and moreover, unclean and foul. But we acknowledge that this was done by the divine providence of the Creator, so that it might both cherish the nature of particulars, and yet be concerned with the multitude, and also regard the

--- Page 129 ---
CONCERNING THE INTERNAL MICROCOSM IN THE EXTERNAL. 127

a certain trace, following the exact determination of the first mind:
which secondary mind is nature itself or the mundane act. Therefore, the first mind or ray of God, immediately emanating from the supersubstantial nature, enters into the empyrean or rational spirit; where it formed divine creatures, produced on the first day of creation, and endowed with divine keenness. The image of this first mind also shone forth on the second day of creation in the midst of the abyss, and produced the ethereal heaven and the life-giving soul of the material or visible world: Which image of the prior mind and second mind is not undeservedly called Nature itself or the mundane ray. And this is granted to individual animals and the other visible creatures of the world. Wherefore *Mercurius Trismegistus, Pimander 12,* called this secondary mind the nature of brutes and vegetables. To this opinion *Synesius* assents with these words in *Hymn 3: The mind fallen into matter, the immortal mind, offspring of divine parents, small indeed but wholly theirs, that one and everywhere, wholly infused into the whole, turns the vast cavity of the heavens, preserving this universe, distributed into diverse forms it is present; A part of it is the course of the stars, a part the assembly of angels, a part also by a heavy bond, has obtained an earthly form, and separated from its parents, has drunk dark oblivion, etc.* Similarly elsewhere the same *Mercurius Trismegistus* seems to confirm that with these words: *The Mind, he says, IS GOD in men, and therefore some from among men are Gods, and their humanity is as close as possible to divinity: For the good Daemon indeed proclaims immortal Gods, but mortal men as Gods. In irrational animals, however, that mind is of nature. For wherever there is soul, there is mind; just as wherever there is life, there also is soul in living beings without the discourse of reason.* But indeed the middle soul in its nature is empty of the first mind, although it itself is as it were a second mind, which suffices for the life of any creature. Hence, says *Mercurius Trismegistus, Pimander 10: The soul, destitute of the mind's presence, can neither do nor say anything: But often the mind goes out of the soul, at which time the soul neither hears nor sees, but is like an animal lacking reason:* So great, I say, is the power of the supreme mind, which abandons a soul of this kind entangled in the body, and drawn by the same as if to the underworld. For this eternal essence, to speak with Mercurius Trismegistus, is very far from the ignorant, the wicked, the lazy, the envious, the unjust, murderers, and such, or at least it is absent in its dwelling, leaving them to the will of the avenging Daemon, who, striking with the sharpness of fire, afflicts the senses, and more and more arms man to commit crimes, so that, guilty of a fouler fault, he may be subject to a harsher punishment, and without any intermission inflames him to insatiable desires, fights with him in the darkness, examines sin, and in a wondrous way excites and agitates the impulse of fire for his torment. But indeed to souls whose spirit adheres to it, the mind will be present most benignly and most auspiciously; inasmuch as it is accustomed to flow into the holy soul and to raise it to the light of wisdom; for it will be benevolent to good, pious, pure, religious, and holy people, its presence brings them aid, and thus inclines them to give thanks and to bless piously, so that they may immediately know all things; it makes them indeed surrender their body to its death, and disdain the allurements of the senses, inasmuch as they clearly discern how deadly are the enticements of the senses; moreover, the mind itself, acting as a doorkeeper, by no means permits those falling into the body's snares to achieve their purpose; for it constantly blocks the entrances through which base flatteries are accustomed to flow, and extinguishes all fuels of lusts. Hence *Mercurius Trismegistus, Pimander 12: To whatever souls the mind presides, it illuminates them with its splendor, resisting their evil habits, just as a skilled Physician afflicts the body of a sick person with pains, burning and cutting it for the sake of recovering health: in the same way the mind afflicts the pleasure-seeking soul, so that it may uproot the roots of pleasure, and purifying the body from evil, it procures the good of the soul no differently than a Physician procures the health of the body.* Indeed, even more wondrous is this divine mind's

...whose efficacy in bodies he declared in his fourth discourse of Pimander, where he speaks in these words: *Whoever are supported by this creature of God, according to the comparison of their works, are held immortal instead of mortal; by their understanding they embrace all things that are on earth, and that are in the sea, and if there is anything beyond them above heaven: and they demand themselves from God, that they may also behold the good itself: which indeed when they perceive, they consider the life by which we live here, a kind of misery.* Conversely (as is clearly evident from the foregoing), as many human souls as are by no means strongly governed by the mind, suffer the same things as the souls of brutes. ...[the soul, when it] uses the mental rewards granted by God for what is fitting, differs in nothing from immortals; moreover, freed from the chains of the body, it is led by both [God and His creation] to the chorus of the blessed, and simultaneously to God. The Platonists also put forth such a saying: "The mind is above fate in providence"; therefore, it is affected neither by the influences of celestial bodies nor by the qualities of natural things; therefore, only religion governs it. But why shall we recite or adduce more authorities of others in this place, when the most evident reasons, drawn from the sincere depths of philosophy, are at hand, which clearly demonstrate that the mind and reason of man dominate the stars and their influences, and that it is not subject to the actions of the visible heavens. Will it seem just that a most eminent king be governed by his subjects, or be subjected to their punishments and passions? Indeed, it would be unjust to be led by such an imagination, that the Creator should be compelled by his creatures to anything contrary to his will, or that an act and ray immediately emanating from Him, and yet in no way separated from His divine essence, but perpetually connected to Him, should be subjected to creatures established and strengthened by that very mind and word. What then do the stars or creatures of the intermediate heaven have to do with the creatures of the superior heaven, and especially with their author and creator? Therefore, without a doubt, gifts are poured forth downwards from the empyrean heaven through the divine benevolence of the Creator, and are received in the desired manner; but they are not again cast back upwards by the creatures receiving them. For this would be to ungratefully return that which is freely received for oneself and for inferiors, and, in the manner of the prince of darkness, to forget the Creator's beneficence, and to be carried aloft on the wings of pride, and foolishly seek higher kingdoms.

Therefore, elsewhere, we have explained sufficiently and copiously that this matter is otherwise; where in our Mundane Music we declared that the Sun, emperor of the middle heaven, had received its gifts from the sublimity of the empyrean heaven, God the Creator so willing, through the power of the consonance of the Diapason, so that from its abundance it might pour a portion of life, every day, hour, and minute, into the lower regions, likewise by the power of the material consonance of the Diapason, into the earth. From which it is clear that the lower region of the world receives its measure of life from the middle, in the same way that the middle receives it from the superior. Now indeed it would be held as absurd if anyone were to say that the Sun and the middle heaven receive their life and formal nourishment from the lower region, or the supreme from the middle, just as if one were to infer that the cause proceeds from its effect, or the principle from its derivative. For the Sacred Scriptures acknowledge the distinction of the works of the first three days of creation. The matter, therefore, briefly speaking, is thus: The human soul, which we have declared above to be the internal man, is composed, as we have said, of three portions derived from a threefold heaven. It acquired the nobler portion of its composition from the empyrean heaven, indeed, immediately from God Himself, carried in the empyrean spirit; namely, the ray of the mind seated in a rational chariot. Its middle portion, which gives life to the body, acquired its power...

--- Page 132 ---
130 TRACT. I. SECT. I. BOOK VII.
namely, and consisting of light, it will not be surprising if the stars and Planets make an easy impression on it, and govern it according to their will, and thus bend it towards all worldly concupiscence. Similarly, the lower portion of the soul most eagerly embraces their influences, and esteems and acknowledges them as gods alone. And hence it is that, of the constellations of the Zodiac, some produce bilious and choleric, others melancholic, others phlegmatic and sluggish, and others lascivious and sanguine effects. Whence *Mercurius Trismegistus in Pimander 13. says the Zodiac consists of a tabernacle of twelve Avengers of darkness, which elsewhere he calls horrible; and he makes one Avenger Ignorance, the second Sadness, the third Inconstancy, the fourth Cupidity, the fifth Injustice, the sixth Luxury, the seventh Deception, the eighth Envy, the ninth Fraud, the tenth Wrath, the eleventh Rashness, and the twelfth Malice:* And under these, as a subordinate genus, many more are contained, which, through the body's enclosed prison, compel the sorrowful man to suffer through his senses. Afterwards, descending into the realms of the Planets, *Saturn* renders a man abandoned by the mind envious, vile, poor, sad, avaricious, etc., and especially indeed, when he himself was stronger at that man's nativity. Thus *Jupiter*, found to be the lord of the horoscope, makes him ambitious. *Mars* makes him devoted to quarrels and disputes, a drunkard and unchaste, and an adulterer. *Sol* (the Sun) makes him bilious and proud. *Venus* makes him luxurious and submerged in concupiscence and worldly desires. *Mercurius* (Mercury) makes him inconstant and of light or easy credulity. *Luna* (the Moon) makes him drunken, sluggish, and negligent. From these things, therefore, we see how much power the visible heaven and its creatures have over the lower portions of the soul, devoid of mind and reason; for like rejoices in like; and the middle spirit, with its light looking only downwards, is delighted by material and worldly pleasure; and this all the more, because it is instigated to it by the blandishments of the sensitive or elementary soul. Whence it happens that it forgets its Lord, and thus, perceives neither worldly vexations nor the torments of the Demon, until, totally abandoned by the mind, it pays the penalties, and in desperation, or too late repentance, cries out: *I have sinned;* and thus adheres eternally to its mud, nor is able to ascend higher, because, abandoned by its divine Lord, through whom it ought to have risen, it lies prostrate in darkness and is submerged. Therefore, let the scrupulous no longer say that the stars act with no necessity upon men devoid of mind, since we have most clearly proven, by the reasons already alleged, that they are in every way subject to the stars and the visible heaven. And in this way we see that it is not outside the nature of things to judge, by astrological virtue, concerning theft, murder, rape, or other such human vices. But indeed, that axiom of the Bishop is also preserved; *namely, that the wise man will rule the stars.* For, as was said before, when the mind flows into the holy soul, it elevates it to the light of wisdom, which has a dwelling higher and more powerful in virtue than that of the stars. For, according to *Mercurius Trismegistus, those twelve Avengers mentioned before are repelled by the presence of divine splendor through ten powers: For from its assistance there descends to us first the knowledge of God, by whose presence ignorance is driven away; Then there descends to us the knowledge of joy, by whose presence sadness utterly flees; By the act of this power, constancy is also produced, by whose aid inconstancy is abolished; and constancy is a most sweet force. Continence is also produced, which is the victorious force over all desires. And this degree exists as the foundation of justice, inasmuch as by its rise and approach injustice is expelled from all works, and we, with injustice absent, are made just. But the sixth power also descends into us by the presence of the mind, namely, a fortification against excess and luxury, which being expelled, truth will also appear, and deception will soon be driven away: Whence, with truth present, absolute good will be with us: envy will also depart; for good is innate to truth, along with life and light, nor will avenging wrath approach further. Indeed, by its presence all the Avengers with a sudden impetus*

Being carried to the middle, it becomes more prone to the delights of the flesh and immerses itself in the allurements and blandishments of darkness; forgetful of the mind and divine light, neglecting higher and spiritual things, it regards lower and corporeal things. Certainly, it will be subject to corporeal passions, struck no less by the fear and disturbances of diseases and death than the sensitive soul itself. And then its lucid soul, or ray of nature, in its ethereal course, that is, by adhering to the disobedient intermediate spirit and looking as if into a mirror, will perceive many deceptions and illusions of darkness, by the sight of which it will be disturbed; because the divine mind, image of truth, has abandoned its society on account of the disobedience of that spirit, and permits it to be disturbed by the deceptions of darkness and the Devil. Therefore, in this mirror of its own, it will behold these monsters or fantastic passions, and as it were, chimeras of falsehood: namely, foolish love, detestable hatred, immense desire and concupiscence, tremendous horror, feigned, spurious, and non-durable joy, intolerable sorrow, vain hope, fatal despair, impudent audacity, ineffable fear, irrational or bestial and tremendous wrath; and these indeed are enumerated as the eleven passions by which the soul, abandoned by the mind, is afflicted. Nevertheless, there is a certain power in the lucid soul of recalling its spirit, thus fallen and immersed in darkness, to heaven. For since it is of the same lineage as the mind, it very easily draws the mind to its aid by prayers and the cry of penitence, so that by its protection and direction it may again be led to the holy kingdom and the palace of its parent. Hence, quite divinely, *Porphyry in the book On Abstinence* says: *When we strive with all our might to return to our pristine state, it is necessary to completely separate the soul from sense and imagination, and from every irrational condition that follows therefrom, and from such passions, as far as the necessity of nature permits.* But truly, if the soul consents with its spirit, and having already fallen with it into the love of the body and the world (if indeed it has persevered in evil to the end), it will taste nothing of immortality, nor will it enjoy good; that is, it will not return to that perfection of form and light from which it was derived, but will always remain captive in chains, and submerged in the abyss of matter. For it is impossible for the soul to be freed from the captivity of matter, unless it happens through the mediation of the mind and the life-giving Spirit of the divine Word, by whose wings alone, and not by those of others, it can be elevated and sublimated from earth to the peaks of heaven; for it is very easy for matter to descend, but very difficult for it to ascend and return without fiery wings, by whose aid the ponderous Spirit is carried and lifted to heaven much more swiftly than molten metal by the power of fire, or a cannonball shot into the air. Finally, we say that the ray of the mind in the first creation, the more it descended from the fount of unity, the more deeply it immersed itself in the multitude of matter, as was said in the harmony of the soul. Hence it happens that although the ray or act immediately proceeding from God is simple and most pure, yet the ray produced from it (which is called the second mind and nature itself) becomes more entangled in the chains and coverings of matter (which we called spirit above), as was said in our Macrocosm. And therefore it requires the aid of the first mind for its redemption. Therefore, by this way the world will be renewed and exalted in virtue, as testified by the Prophet Isaiah in these words: *The sun will be ten times purer and more excellent in its beauty*, since all these things will be perfected by the presence of the Word residing in the mind, which therefore most rightly claimed for itself the name Alpha and Omega.

CHAP. VI.

Why the human mind and reason inhabit the superior region of the Microcosm,
the Empyrean heaven?

IN our little book concerning the external man, it has been shown that he is divided into three regions, according to the disposition of the macrocosm, the superior of which we have not ineptly or without most evident reason compared to the Empyrean heaven. For just as in the Empyrean heaven of the macrocosm, the place and connatural seat of the divine mind and rational spirit exists, according to the opinions of the most learned philosophers and theologians alike, so also by philosophers and medical doctors, the place and dwelling of reason and intellect is observed to be located in the head or the superior microcosmic region. And indeed, even if we consider common experiments, a sphere made of hollow glass, however much someone may have tried to submerge it by force in water, will always be found to rise to its natural place, since the nature of its content (namely, air) is to float on water. We perceive this same thing also in wood, because of its airy and fiery disposition. Such therefore is also the reason why the mind, since it is supreme among all things, should possess the superior part of the place in which it is. For although the rational or Empyrean spirit is its vehicle, and the mundane soul with its ethereal spirit is again the chariot of the intellectual spirit, and for all these, air is like a wagon in which the mind with the others is introduced into the body; the human mind nevertheless possesses the summit of the entire animal being, and like a most divine king or emperor, it always occupies the superior seat, both in the internal and external part of man, and seems to claim for itself the office, as it were, of a sailor, cutting the corporeal ship through the fluctuating perturbations of the world and the tempestuous and stormy waves of this life, and directing it safely to the land and port of happiness, if its other ministers, namely, reason, life, natural spirit, and the senses, are rendered obedient to it. But if they are rebellious and do not listen to the governor's precepts, they will undoubtedly produce an inevitable and fatal shipwreck for themselves, in which they themselves will be absorbed into the abyss of the world's sea with the corporeal ship or boat, and swallowed alive by the chasm of darkness, while meanwhile the sailor or governor, seeking the heights with immortal wings, will return to his blessed homeland with his rational spirit; since he (the rational spirit) is always accustomed to being obedient to it (the mind), inasmuch as it is not subject to fate. Hence it is, therefore, that just as the ship's governor sits in the superior part of the stern, and directs the lower sailors in their duties, so that they may make their journey prosperously and favorably; and the sailors themselves are partly in the inferior part of the stern, and partly in the superior, as occasion moves them; so also the mind inhabits the superior region of the human body, to which the other ministers, namely the vital soul and the natural and sensitive soul, are present at its beck and call, and are ready to diligently perform and expedite all its commands. But, I ask, what more evident argument can be sought for the mind inhabiting this superior region of man, than that we see him standing more erect and upright among all other animals, from which it is most manifest that at his apex and summit there exists a most eminent power and act, raising and lifting the senses themselves towards heaven, no differently than how the heaviest bodies are perceived to be lifted high by the power of artificial fire: Indeed, so efficacious is this divine fire (which Hermes Trismegistus asserts is accustomed to putting on a fiery garment as soon as it has been separated from the body) that not only human bodies

--- Page 137 ---
DE MICROC. INTERN. IN EXTERN. 135

...bodies to be erected at right angles, but also to be snatched upwards and elevated,
as we shall declare more clearly below. From these things, therefore, more clearly than
light, is apprehended the true seat, location, and position of the mind in the human
body, and that it alone is the divine empress and God-like governor of the microcosm,
both internal and external.

C A P. VII.

*That light throughout the entire mundane orb is the same, and similarly the Spi-*
*rit is the same; and how light tends towards the purifica-*
*tion and elevation of Spirits on high.*

In very many places, cited previously in our macrocosmic book, we have abundantly and lucidly revealed the concise and very close relation of the light of each heaven. For we have explained that the light of the supreme region of the world, created on the first day, is the icon or image of the divine mind, and that the secondary light, which informed the middle heaven on the second day, is, as it were, a ray or likeness of the former and superior light, and finally the third is an idol and effigy of the second; similarly, that by the power of the superior light, the rational or empyreal Spirit was created and called the ray of the mind, which is the ray of God; and that likewise also the middle spirit, by the power of the middle light, was made vital or ethereal, or the fifth essence, and is called the ray of the world, the soul of the world, and active nature itself; and furthermore, that by the action of the lowest light in the lowest spirit, the four elements were produced and distinguished on the third day, and it is called the ray of the elements, and as it were, the element of fire, or a thin portion of light leaping downwards into those parts. Therefore, all these alterations arise from the actions of divine light, whose entire endeavor is to purify the impure and to subtilize the coarse. And by this action of its universal Spirit of the world, which, according to Saint Peter, is nothing other than Water, it is distinguished into regions differing in purity and impurity, tenuity and density, and into the disposition of the four elements. From which it is clear that the universal light of the world is unique, and of the same action and nature, derived from the eternal source, and that the differences in its operations exist not in itself, but in the diversity of the resisting matter. For that which resists more strongly requires a stronger action, and that which is weaker in its resistance needs less impression; and yet the principle of action is always the same. Similarly, the principle of passion proceeds from the diversity of matter, differing in density and tenuity. For that which is dense and compact more difficultly yields to the impressions of the agent; whence it happens that celestial light, due to the minimal resistance of its spirit, seems to warm us imperceptibly, although it nevertheless excels in its luminous function. Thus also we see the same light, due to the constriction of its rays in dense spirit, becoming and turning into destructive fire and intolerable to the sense of touch; indeed, we are taught that the more it penetrates towards the center of the earth, the more vehement is its burning and destructive faculty; since its rays, tending more downwards, continually find coarser matter, and thus are finally compressed in an ineffable manner. Whence it happens that it burns not without the greatest torment, and produces common fire. Thus also, nothing else makes the flame of fire visible than the contraction of inflamed rarer parts of the air, or the gathering into one of the hidden and diffused rays of light in the air. In which very way we also see humid air, invisible in its subtle nature, condensed by contraction into a visible and palpable cloud, which

--- Page 138 ---
136 TRACT. I. SECT. I. LIB. VII.
which, thus contracted, is observed to moisten things. From these things, therefore, it is clear that the parts of universal light do not differ from each other, but are of the same nature, and so the cause of its difference as far as we are concerned is the diversity of operation. Likewise, the entire matter of the world is the same, namely water; which nevertheless is known to differ according to the greater or lesser proportion of light found with it and in it. Hence, therefore, we teach that inferior light acts in its aerial spirit in such a way according to its proportion, as middle light acts in its own; and again, that middle light acts in its ethereal Spirit no differently than the light of the superior heaven in its own; and consequently, that the whole difference consists in this: that inferior light is resisted more because of the smallness of its proportion and the multitude of matter; but middle light, because of its equality with the ethereal spirit (which, what kind it is, we have shown above from the harmonious adaptation of the formal and material pyramid), is resisted less, inasmuch as it finds the Spirit obedient to it in the same proportion; and thus also furthermore, superior light, as if excellently abundant, acts with even less or minimal struggle in the empyrean spirit, inasmuch as it is very scarce and therefore incorporeal, and is plainly called metaphysical, that is, placed beyond the bounds of nature. And this is that most evident reason by which men, illuminated by divine mystery, and to whom consequently God is not demonstrated a priori, ascend as if by a ladder from posterior (experience) so that they may arrive at the knowledge of God: for through the hidden operations of water with fire, which we observe here on earth, we can infer concerning the effects of middle light in its spirit; and thus also from the manifest actions of the Sun in the air, it will not be impossible to judge concerning the power of primary light in the secondary spirit; and finally, the reason for the action of middle light with its spirit having been found, it will not be entirely denied to a diligent inquirer to effectively contemplate, to some extent, the actions of the superior heaven and their effects; and thus finally it will be perceived that light, which has emerged from the divine source, tends towards the purification, cleansing, and attenuation of matter, and consequently to its elevation and exaltation from the gross to the subtle, and from a place subject to corruption to a seat most full of formal light, which may satisfy all its desire. For the disposition of the divine essence is benevolent and inclined to always work towards the preservation, salvation, redemption of things, and their promotion from darkness into regions of light; and so it is always engaged in the reformation of deformed things, and desires to reduce ugly dispositions to beauty, to reveal the deceptions of darkness and strife to the world, and to bestow and distribute the gifts of its benevolence to everyone, and finally to seal all things with the characters of its divine love. Do we not therefore observe in this elementary region that the flame of fire, by natural instinct, neglecting superior and sublime things, seeks inferior things with all its might? Nor indeed can we turn it away from this inclination of its own without its sensible extinction. Thus in the nature of artificial molten (substance) we observe that, as soon as its fiery disposition is brought into action, its heavy body is raised upwards against its own disposition. From which we can see how eagerly luminous nature seeks its connatural seat, and strives to leave its corporeal mass and extricate itself from its bonds.

CAP. VIII.
On the unequal proportion of the body and the luminous soul, and that light alone
works here on earth for the body's elevation towards heaven
and the purification of its impurity.

The matter of the body stands in proportion to its luminous soul, as the spirit of the lowest region of the world to the light of the same; which we said above is found in a sesquialteral proportion; inasmuch as there, namely, one part of light and three parts of material Spirit are found. Hence it comes about that the body is said to weigh down the soul and impede it in its actions; so much so, indeed, that what the soul wills, the body does not permit to be accomplished, and it strives with all its might against the soul's actions, which tend to elevate the body upwards. That the soul, however, is many degrees weaker in the body than matter, is shown by experiment. For if someone descends from a mountain, this movement will be very suitable for the body; since everything heavy, by a certain natural instinct, tends downwards; indeed, the external man rejoices, because the descent seems easy to him; which movement, however, is contrary to the nature and disposition of the soul, as has been declared in the case of fire and the fuse: But in ascending a mountain, the external man is fatigued, and the life-giving soul (which, however, is merely like a spark) acts vehemently and with all its strength for the elevation of that heavy weight, and makes its dwelling labor for this purpose: Whence it is manifest that the mass of the body exceeds the measure of its luminous soul by many proportions: since the whole man seems to delight in descent, which occurs according to the appetite of matter, but is burdened by ascent, which is according to the desire of light. But indeed, if the faculty of the luminous soul were more abundant than the mass of the body, conversely, man would be burdened by descent and would rejoice in his ascent; since the luminous soul strives upwards with every natural effort, indeed, even the Spirit itself vehemently desires to ascend upwards with its spark of light, which is always ready for such a task, as was said in the elevation of the ignited fuse. And indeed, the same thing is also demonstrated by the following experiment.

Let there be

For if you expose a fictitious kite made of paper, to which a sufficiently long thread or string is tied, to the wind, we will see that the wind very easily lifts that sufficiently heavy machine upwards.

From these things it is clear that not only light, but also its vehicle, tends towards the raising of bodies; indeed, to such an extent that even when, due to its smallness, it cannot accomplish that work, it is then accustomed to move bodies and animals standing on columns or feet, here and there from the side, namely rightwards and leftwards, or forwards and backwards, and upwards and downwards, in the manner that has been stated. But, to omit these artificial things, we also see the same disposition in plants; for in them, portions of light rising from the earth, with the sun's rays leading the way as an aid, lift themselves upwards towards their connatural place with their entire bodily mass. *And now, so that we may dwell on the investigation of animals, I heard from a certain maidservant that she once, having caught a certain older and larger cat unawares in the very act of gluttony and devouring, because of its remarkable rapacity, and lacking another weapon, yet unwilling to let slip the opportunity of the present occasion from her hands, harshly tried to crush it with her feet, and thus by trampling, to suffocate it. But when, having placed one of her feet on the cat's throat, and the other pressed and fixed on its heart, she stood upright, tormenting and afflicting that miserable little animal without any pity in a deadly struggle because of its greedy gullet, she perceived such great strength in its body, and such vigor and efficacy in that small part, and as it were, a spark of light or act enclosed within it, that, struck by a certain admiration, she constantly feared lest at any time, even despite such a great burden, she might be lifted high and thrown down, while she perceived, namely, the immense vigor of the enclosed Spirit to carry upwards and to lift high the mass of its body.* From these things, therefore, it is most evident that the vital Spirit with its active light has the greatest power, not only in things made by art, in which, namely, saltpeter obtains the place of the aerial spirit, inasmuch as it is nothing other than congealed air, and that sulphurous nature supplies the place of light, whose luminous nature, brought into action, is moved by the virtue of that Spirit, but also in vegetable
