bus; since in these the ethereal Spirit leads the solar ray, enclosed within them, upwards to its homeland (whither it would also most easily ascend, were it not impeded by heavy air along with the still heavier elements of earth and water); and likewise also in the lower animals, in which, as we said above, some rational power of heaven resides: Hence it happens that their light is more efficacious and stronger for lifting heavy bodies than that light of vegetables, derived from the solar orb alone. For it must be diligently considered that just as the light of the empyrean heaven is stronger than the light of the middle heaven, and this again is stronger than the light of the lowest heaven, so too, where a portion of these lights predominates, there a stronger or weaker movement and effect towards higher things is found. Hence, as was said before, the fixity and immobility of minerals; whose soul is produced from the light of the lowest or third heaven; whence, due to the weakness of the light and the strength of the matter compacted by nature, they rest around the center. So also a plant, although more vital than a mineral, so that it rises above the earth, yet it is affixed to the earth by its foot, nor can it move by itself.

But indeed, an animal is free, and is seen to move its body locally here and there, and sometimes to lift the burden of its body from the earth by a leap: Hence the most evident difference of creatures in the disposition of light and its corresponding spirit. Nevertheless, before we proceed to describe the excellence of human light, which surpasses all other species of light in other creatures, we will here, only briefly and lightly touching upon it in passing, mention a certain experiment devised by us, from which we indeed learned two notable things; namely, first, that human light is far more worthy, excellent, and powerful for lifting the body upwards than the light of other animals. For if the weight of some living animal is explored, and then again that same animal, strangled without any loss of blood or excrement, is weighed on a scale, you will perceive that this dead body is far heavier than it was alive. And indeed, all notice this difference between living beings and their corpses. Hence it is manifest that that animal had its lightness from vital light and such a spirit, inasmuch as they acted constantly with an upward-tending action; but because the heavy body was an impediment to them, they moved only sideways and forwards and backwards; and this is the reason why a living animal is lighter than after death.

So also we see that a man, having drawn in aerial spirit into his lungs by inspiration, is not easily submerged in water, but is held above the water by the lightness of the drawn-in air. So also a flask filled with water and placed in water will suddenly submerge: similarly, if a flask, melted by the violence of fire, is coagulated into a mass, and thrown into some pond, we will see it suddenly seek the bottom no differently than some heavy stone: but if the same flask is filled with air, its weight will be lifted by the power of the air, it will be sustained on the surface of the pond or water, nor will it move to the bottom.

Similarly, if you consider the weight of a living human body, and compare it with the corpse of a dead one, and diligently examine the difference, you will perceive that its corpse surpasses the living body in weight by its gravity; indeed, you will observe that the proportion of weight and gravity in the human body and corpse far exceeds in measure and number that of the bodies and corpses of other animals, if indeed trustworthy people are to be believed. Wherefore it is evident that the vital light in man (which is not only solar and mundane, as in other animals, but also divine and supreme, insofar as it is instilled into man by a God-like breath) has greater efficacy for the elevation of the human body upwards than the light of other living beings has.

Moreover, we can also investigate by a certain experiment how much essential light was lacking in the living human body, so that it could have been lifted upwards. For if the living body of a man weighs 200 pounds...

--- Page 143 ---
DE MICROC. INTERN. IN EXTERN. 141

pounds, and its cadaver weighs 240 pounds, it is certain that the vigor of light with the vital spirit in the living body would still have required 60 actual proportions by which that body would be elevated into the sphere of the Sun. For the solar body is suspended in the middle place precisely because it is composed of an equal proportion of light and matter; so that it is placed in the middle, where the pyramids intersect, and thus is always suspended forever by the power of incorruptible light, until the bonds are dissolved by the Creator, in whose sole power it is, as the Apostle testifies, to divide the soul from the Spirit. Nor is it to be believed that this body of ours, polluted by filth and stained by darkness, can be elevated in such a form. For it will be transfigured by the power of abundant light, just as we are taught by the doctrine of the sacred Scriptures as well as by the histories of the Philosophers. For first we read in the scriptures that Moses' face shone so brightly that the Israelites could not gaze upon him. So also we read that Christ was glorified and transfigured on Mount Tabor by the light of the Holy Spirit. Thus Paul confesses that he was caught up to the third heaven: But these, returning to themselves, died on earth. It is also reported in the historical records of the ancient pagans: that Socrates was so transfigured that he surpassed the light-bearing wheels of the Sun with his radiance, and that Alexander the Great, surrounded by great danger in India, his soul so blazed forth that, as the barbarians themselves watched, he seemed to emit light. The father of Theodoric is also said to have emitted sparks from his whole body; And it is written of a certain wise man that sparkling flames shot forth from him here and there, even with a sound; Similarly, in the book of prodigies, a story is found about a certain man from whose head a rather large flame of fire was seen to leap forth: In the sacred Bible we also have it written that, by virtue of this light and the divine Spirit, Philip the Apostle, after baptizing the Eunuch in India, was immediately found in Azotus; And concerning Habakkuk, a similar account is found in Daniel; So also in 1 Kings 18:12, "The Spirit of Jehovah will carry you, I know not where, etc." And in 2 Kings 2:17, "Lest perhaps the Spirit of Jehovah has taken him up and cast him upon some mountain or into some valley." Philostratus also relates that by the same power Apollonius of Tyana, passing invisibly, suddenly appeared to the eyes of those standing in the tribunal, and a little later spoke to one of his disciples near the city of Cumae. So also Enoch and Elijah, surrounded by a fiery chariot and immense light, were taken alive into heaven; but on the way they were transfigured and purified from all mortal impurity by the power of light that purges and burns away filth; for no one with a corruptible face can behold God. The pagans attributed a not dissimilar power to Zoroaster and Romulus; for they wrote that the former was transfigured and taken up bodily; the latter, the Romans recorded in their monuments, was snatched up to heaven in a wondrous thunder by his father Mars. Avicebron the Moor, Avicenna the Arab, and Hippocrates of Cos recognized the power of this divine light with the Spirit, and furthermore, the entire Chaldean school confesses and teaches it: for the unanimous opinion of all those who observed the progress of this light was that there is a certain wondrous power in our mind, by which they say it is possible for the mind, fixed with its whole focus on God, to be filled with divine power, and thus filled with divine power, by pouring forth rays through every medium even to this thick, dark, heavy, and mortal body, surrounding and enclosing it with its copious and efficacious light, renders it like a star, and equally sparkling, and moreover, by the fullness of its rays, lifts it on high with a certain remarkable lightness, like tow set on fire, or animated by gunpowder, and by that means also sometimes transfers the body, as if it were a spirit, instantly to remote places. But I, persuaded by these opinions, as well as by the preceding examples and by reasons drawn from the treasury or sanctuary of philosophy, am compelled to agree; inasmuch as I see most clearly by them that without the presence of the divine mind, transfiguration, regeneration, and resurrection cannot occur, and consequently, from all other creatures

...has been denied, except to man alone; because in him alone, and not likewise in others,
resides the breath of life and the sacred gift of mind and intellect. Therefore, that
light possesses, according to its greater or lesser proportion, the faculty of elevating
the bodies in which it is contained, we have demonstrated above: But since, as usually
happens, elemental bodies in the lowest region of the world prevail over souls and
portions of light, therefore creatures do not have a sufficient quantity of this light
from their creation to fully perform its office. Nor did God give to any creature
more light than is sufficient for its adequate perfection; so that it cannot impart
of its light to others, while remaining whole itself. Thus, therefore, appears the
foolishness of those who try to prepare an infinite tincture from a portion of common
gold. For thus the Sun itself, the noblest creature of the visible world, by its virtue
would constantly grow richer in light and tincture, would then seek a higher place,
and would gradually ascend towards the apex of the intellectual world, until it reached
the point of unity, leaving multitude behind. Wherefore we are mistaken concerning
all such immense power which, remaining in itself in its state and incorrupt, could
provide so much form to a corrupt body that it might be elevated to higher things.
Whence therefore shall we obtain this gift, since it can nowhere be drawn from a
created thing? From the mind alone, namely the divine ray of God; whose it is to
bestow more-than-perfection upon all, since in God alone and in the rays not divided
from Him, the highest and only gift of more-than-perfection is found. For how is it
possible that that which has attained only the perfection of its own species can give
and confer more-than-perfection to another? From God therefore, and His Word and
Spirit, to whom the rays of the mind are continuous, that gift is drawn and infused
into holy men; and by a certain magnetic force and admirable harmony it is attracted
from the essence of unity into these lower things, in the manner and by the reason
which follows. Since in every man there is this virtue from the root of his creation
(which nevertheless varies in strength and weakness of operation in different men),
a way is revealed by some saints, Prophets, and Sages, by which, from the luminous
fount through a continuous ray of this divine virtue, it may be attracted to lower
things and consequently into man himself. For a pious soul adhering to the mind
will most easily be filled with pious gifts. Hence in his *Hymn 1* Synesius thus sang:
"The Mind now cares only for the intellectual worlds; for thence the good origin
of the human Spirit is indivisibly shared: And the mind fallen into hyle (matter),
the immortal mind, offspring of divine parents, indeed small, but wholly theirs,
this and one everywhere, wholly infused into the whole, turns the vast cavity of
the heavens, and preserving this universe, is present distributed into diverse forms;
Part of it is the course of the stars, part the assembly of angels, part also by a heavy
bond has obtained an earthly form, and separated from its parents, has drunk dark
oblivion, admiring the earth with blind anxieties. Yet there is, there is some light
for open eyes; there is also in those who have fallen hither, a certain power recalling
them to heaven, when, emerged from the waves of life, they joyfully enter the holy
path to the royal court of the parent: Blessed is he who, avoiding the voracious
barking of hyle, and emerging from the earth, directs his steps to God with a light
leap: Blessed is he who, after fates, after labors, after bitter earthly cares, having
entered the paths of the mind, sees the height refulgent with divine light, etc."
We conclude therefore, that just as God gave perfection to all creatures in creation
and in His sacred tabernacle, so also it is in His power alone to impart more-than-
perfection to them. For if it were in the power of a creature to give more-than-
perfection, it would be necessary for it to do this either by a new creation, or to
receive such a gift from elsewhere. But if it were in its power to create new things,
it would have to be equated with God Himself, whose alone it is to create; but if it
were to receive such a gift from elsewhere, it would follow that it had obtained it
from God alone, the Maker of all things. Therefore, just as no creature is infinite
in itself, so also more-than-perfection cannot be given to infinity by a creature.
But truly, if anyone (and indeed not so

--- Page 145 ---
DE MICROC. INTERN. IN EXTERN. 143

...so absurdly) were to object, that, by virtue of a single spark of fire, infinite [sparks] can be multiplied, and by the presence of one candle innumerable others can be lit, and that therefore, since fire and light are creatures, it follows that creatures can bestow infinite light and tincture upon similar things. **We respond** that light is the true image of God, and, as it were, the very presence of God. Hence *Augustine* says, *that, as much light as something has in itself, so much of God it seems to claim for itself.* How, however, that divine light dispersed itself into hyle at the creation of the world, the divine *Synesius* has taught us quite clearly in the immediately preceding cited passage. Nor indeed is there any multiplication of light or fire in the multitude of candles illuminated by one spark, but it is a manifestation of light dispersed and attenuated in the air, and invisible due to its rarity; so indeed, that fire is everywhere and always permanent, but invisible to us and to be perceived only by the intellect and by variation of the air; but that [fire], when thickened and compressed, renders the object or matter and Spirit, to which it adheres, colored, bright, and luminous. Thus also we see invisible air converted into a visible cloud, that is, thin and invisible air becoming dense and visible by coagulation and compression. Therefore, common fire is nothing other than the accumulation and gathering of dispersed fire, not any multiplication; for there is not, nor ever will be, more or less fire in the world than there was at creation. Therefore, the property of light is magnetic and wonderful, since its single spark attracts infinite [things] to itself. And this is the reason why fire, when contracted into a denser subject, burns and destroys, because it acts vehemently towards dissolution, in proportion to the manner in which the density of the subject is prepared for strong resistance. But on the contrary, the same fire, expanded throughout the entire air, is observed to warm and refresh bodies. This, therefore, is an argument that fire emanates from the throne of the Father of lights, because, namely, as far as we are concerned, it seems to be multiplied infinitely; but indeed, in itself it is, as it were, a formal unity, from which all things, as from a form, inasmuch as it is also the sole mundane act, are procreated. Hence it is evident that light is derived immediately in creation from God alone, as the sole source of forms in created things. Therefore, having rightly considered these things, we will perceive that the mundane act is nothing other than the progression and diffusion of God's rays in creation, and that, conversely, the universal Spirit is, as it were, the medium receiving those rays, and that likewise matter, formed from the cubic spirit, is, as it were, the subject receiving their impressions in itself, and that finally, the whole in this world is nothing other than the implication of fire into spirit; from these two, fire by itself and in its nature tends upwards, but Spirit, without the aid of fire, tends downwards. Thus the world was made, and from the world or the elements of the world, creatures [were made]. It is not surprising, therefore, if the nature of fire is to attenuate the dense, and to make beautiful from the foul, to drive away darkness, to vivify dead things, and to lead from potentiality into actuality, etc. Since all this is the intention of the Creator, namely, to create things that are uncreated, to give form to the formless, to animate the inanimate, to save the condemned, to purify the foul, to raise the fallen, to free and illuminate things overwhelmed by darkness. From which it is manifest that light is the image of the divine essence, dispensed everywhere throughout the universe, and mingled with the mundane waters like a saffron dye joined with a liquid.

CHAP. IX.
*On the communication of human souls.*

FROM the premises, it will seem difficult to some, who view these things only with bodily eyes, that the soul of one human being, by virtue of its spiritual splendor, can communicate and have familiarity with the soul of another, even one far distant, no differently than one person is accustomed to converse with another, inasmuch as it is covered and obscured by the veil of the flesh. Indeed, even the solar light itself, from which the middle soul of creation is derived, can be hidden and obscured by a thinner impediment of opaque substance than the impenetrable human body, as appears in rainy weather; wherefore much more so the soul of man fallen from heaven. Similarly, following these sayings of Hermes Trismegistus: *The soul, deprived of the nature of things, and conscious of good, deprived of eyes, entangles itself in bodily passions, etc.* it is clear that the soul, covered by a corporeal mass, is as if destitute of eyes, so that it cannot perceive what is outside and in darkness.

To these doubts, however, we respond that the matter indeed stands thus when considering the soul inasmuch as it regards life alone, which is merely the middle portion in the composition of the human soul. But inasmuch as it is united with its mistress, the mind, without which the human soul cannot exist, to that extent the walls of the body can no more compress and retain its rays than the water of a crystal-clear torrent can impede the solar rays from penetrating all the way to the bottom.

For Hermes Trismegistus says that the mind can be drawn by its keenness to higher things. And elsewhere he assigns the reason, namely in Pimander 12: *Because the mind is by no means divided from the essence of God, but rather connected to it in the same way that light is connected to the body of the sun.* Wherefore he called the mind God in men, and says that the humanity of men is most proximate to divinity; whence his good Daemon called men mortal Gods. From which it is manifest that the keenness of the human mind and the rays of its light are so subtle and penetrable that the pores of the body, or its dark mass, can in no way impede them from penetrating the very throne of the Creator and circulating everywhere through the world.

Hence it happens, as that aforementioned Philosopher testifies, that by the presence of the mind, which he calls the nature of God, man embraces by his intelligence all things that are on earth, and in the sea, and whatever else there is beyond those things that are above heaven, and moreover raises himself up to behold even the Good itself.

The middle soul, therefore, is raised by a supreme and God-like gift, and with it providing a way and opening opaque pores, it invisibly pours forth its rays hither and thither to external things. Nor indeed is this surprising, since that mind is an act immediately emanating from God, to whom, to speak with the Royal Psalmist, darkness is not darkness, but night is as clear to Him as day itself.

And this ray of God is as it were a spark of His divine wisdom, without which it is not possible for the human soul to judge concerning manifest things that are before its eyes, much less concerning those that are in heaven. But the truth of this matter can be clearly seen from the following discourse of the Wise Man (Wisdom 9:15): *For the corruptible body burdens the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things, and we estimate with difficulty what is on earth, and what is in sight we find with labor: but who will investigate what is in the heavens? And who will know your mind, unless you give wisdom and send your holy Spirit from on high, etc.*

It is necessary, therefore, that the spark of the divine ray, enclosed in man, be refreshed from on high, by the abundance of which regeneration may occur and a perfect union between the augmented mind and the intermediate Spirit. Hence prophecy, and the foreknowledge of things done in remote parts; whence Prophets were accustomed to be called as it were 'seers'. Hence also the truth of dreams, and the correct explanation of things through visions; because by virtue of that spiritual and invisible splendor, united with the rays of the two lower portions, the whole soul

--- Page 147 ---
DE MICROC. INTERN. IN EXTERN.      145

Just as I myself, once living in Oxford, was asked by a certain friend of mine, Master Cox, about the health of his brother, who was following the war or fighting in Ireland, by the power of my soul, calm and undisturbed, but entirely intent on this business, I saw my hand guided in such a way that, having made a projection of points and constructed a Geomantic figure, I indicated through the information of my soul that his brother had been killed in battle, and stabbed with a wound from behind; which indeed, as I predicted, the event taught. We also find in the Gallic Chronicles that a certain King, named Gontranus, having by chance strayed from the company of hunters during a hunt, and accompanied by only one friend, lay down exhausted under a certain large tree, and finally, with his head reclined on the lap of that companion of his, peacefully fell asleep: Meanwhile, while the king slept, this companion of his perceived a certain very thin animalcule emerging from the king's mouth, and formed from air, scarcely visible; He, diligently observing its movement and path, discovered that it was hurrying towards a certain small stream, and anxiously seeking passage there through some safe ford. Therefore, he, rising and unsheathing his sword, placed it on both banks, and thus laid down as it were a bridge; by which this animal immediately hurried to the further part of the water, and entering a hole at the foot of the mountain, not staying there long, returned by the same way, and re-entered the King's body. It happened, however, that Gontranus, spontaneously awakened, narrated to this companion of his all those things that had occurred to him in a dream, which that royal companion had seen in the animalcule or as it were the idea of an animal; namely, he indicated that he had been greatly troubled in his dream while crossing the river, and finally, having found an iron bridge, had safely crossed the ford, and then, having entered a certain cave under an immense mountain, had found an incomparable treasure there: Whence, having heard his companion's account of the animalcule, he entered the mountain through the cave, and found an immense treasure there. But truly, when the Supreme Spirit powerfully infuses its divine impressions into the human soul, greater things are accomplished there than these; and indeed, even with the powers of the soul not leaving the body, but remaining entirely within it. Thus Saint Paul confesses that he was raptured to the third heaven: thus holy Prophets were accustomed to perceiving the secrets of others even in very distant places, and to see with eyes as it were of the mind, or with rays of the divine soul, as if with a certain holy splendor and charity, as is most abundantly demonstrated in many places of the Sacred Scriptures.

CAP. X.

That the illumination of the mind, from the influx and inspiration of the divine Spirit, becomes the cause of prophecy.

Divination or Prophecy, according to the opinions of ancient Philosophers, is that by which men, inspired by a holier order and life, both deduce the causes of present things and foresee the events of future things. And the Wise men believed this virtue of oracle descended into men either from Gods or from Demons, since they taught that this divine spirit was inspired and infused by them. Whose opinion indeed does not seem to differ much from the words of the sacred Scriptures. For in Deuteronomy 13:1 these things are written: "If a prophet or one who claims to have seen a dream arises among you, and predicts a sign or a wonder, etc., you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer, for the Lord your God is testing you." Likewise: "Whoever, corrupted by arrogance, wishes to speak in my name what I have not commanded him to say, or in the name of other Gods, shall be put to death." Deuteronomy 18:22. From which it is clear that by "Gods" the Ethnic Philosophers understood the same as the sacred Bible by "Jehovah," or persons in the Trinity, or the one, sole, and true God; and by "Demons" the same as the sacred Scriptures by "foreign Gods." And yet we also see that those intelligences cannot produce such wonders except by divine permission, since all divine spirit flows from God, as from the supreme source, and not from elsewhere. Hence Jehovah said: "You shall not listen to the words of the dreamer or prophet, for your God is testing you," as if He had said; "He has stirred up His ministers to test you." For Satan himself can do nothing against God's permission, as is declared in the history of Job, and by these words of the Prophet Micah, 3 Kings 22: "I saw the Lord sitting on His throne, and all the host of heaven standing by Him on His right hand and on His left; and Jehovah said: 'Who will entice Ahab King of Israel, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth Gilead?' And one said such words, and another otherwise. Then a spirit came forward and stood before the Lord, and said: 'I will entice him,' etc. 'I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.' And Jehovah said: 'Go out and entice him, and you shall succeed,' etc." From which it is made manifest that no prophecies can occur without God's permission, and that the spirit of Prophecy proceeds either immediately from God Himself, or mediately from some of His intelligences or spirits; who likewise act either with a lying spirit for the punishment of sins, or with a spirit sometimes producing true wonders and signs for temptation. But all prophecies proceeding immediately from God are always true and infallible, because none of God's words can fall to the ground in vain. Hence 1 Samuel 10:5: "A faithful prophet is a sign, when none of his words falls to the ground." And Deuteronomy 18:22: "If a prophet speaks in the name of Jehovah, and the thing does not happen, this is what the Lord has not spoken." But leaving these things aside, let us return to our purpose. This divination occurs according to the Platonists because of the descent or influence of superior souls into ours, which they call "illapses." And Hermes Trismegistus calls it the senses of Demons and the souls of Demons, whom the ancients called Eurideans and Pythons, accustomed to entering the bodies of men and using their voices and tongues for predictions of future things: Of this kind were those Pythoness women, who, moved by a divine Spirit and as if rapt out of themselves, and standing upon the tripod of the oracle, situated near the cave, uttered the oracles of Apollo, in a prophetic manner, with a bold voice, as is read in Diodorus Siculus and others. Authors testify that those ten Sibyls were possessed by such a spirit, who are said to have left behind many things written in verses about God Christ. And that Merlin, the eternal glory of England, whose simi-

divine inspiration, so that, as if snatched from himself, it renders a man different from what he was before, according to those words of Samuel cited above: "And you shall be changed into another man." Indeed, we see by common experience that the sun's power can lift upwards an eggshell filled with spirit or May dew: How much more, therefore, will this splendor, illuminating the human spirit enclosed in the shell of the skull, be able to lift it upwards with its spiritual rays? since such is the efficacy of this divine power, that it renders man's eyes, closed by Adam's fall, open and capable and fit to see the vision of the Almighty, and thus, by expanding his spiritual ears, makes him capable of the word, so that he can hear and understand the words of the mighty God and know the understanding of the Most High, as in Numbers 24:15-16. And elsewhere he says: "Whoever are supported by this divine nature are considered immortal among mortals, by comparison of their works; they embrace all things with their understanding, what is on earth, and what is in the sea, and if there is anything beyond these above heaven; and indeed they raise themselves up so much that they also behold the Good itself," Pimander 4. And he asserts this to be the reason that many of the Prophets, when fire is applied, are not burned, namely, God repelling the fire by breathing within: Whose words indeed are also confirmed by the sacred Scriptures in the story of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, Daniel 3. Some also, although they are burned, nevertheless feel nothing, nor perceive stinging, nor gnawing, nor any torments. Christ walked upon the waves of the sea. Moses was carried through fire into the presence of God: And Elijah was lifted into heaven in a fiery chariot: Moses through the Red Sea, Joshua and Elijah passed miraculously through the Jordan River. All these things Iamblichus also relates that a priest performed in the Cataballa. By these things he seems to argue that the Prophets, at the time they are inspired, live neither a human life, nor an animal life using senses and impulse, but a divine one, and that their soul is at rest, because he says God is there instead of the soul and moves it, as a more excellent soul. But we cannot entirely assent to or adhere to these reasons of Iamblichus: but rather we think that the human soul in an inspired person behaves in such a way, and moves with almost such a motion, as the Planets are said to move by natural motion from east to west. For just as the primum mobile, according to Hermes Trismegistus, is swiftly carried by the breath of the divine Spirit from east to west, and yet the natural motion of the stars from west to east is not removed or extinguished; so also is the case in the Microcosm, when excited by the inspiration of the divine power. For the divine Spirit, beyond doubt, joined to the mind as if to the primum mobile, rotates the human mass with a certain swift motion; so indeed that the entire Microcosm seems to be moved in such a way, and to be carried around and agitated by this swift motion, just as the entire Macrocosm is rotated around by the motion of the primum mobile; while nevertheless, in the Macrocosm, the planetary spheres, and in the Microcosm, the middle soul, which is of the nature of the stars, are recognized to move by their own proper motion, although on account of the violence

Therefore the **Mind** or internal divine Spirit, joined with the external and divinely infused divine spirit, moves man's intellectual sphere against the motion of the animal sphere, which is led by the middle soul; and thus, although the soul seems to rest, it is nevertheless moved by its own proper motion; but the Spirit, having dominion with the mind, both over the soul and over the body, snatches the whole living man to the contemplation of divine vision, and unites the soul itself with itself, and makes it temporarily abandon the human state, and connects it to divinity, according to that saying of Samuel cited above: *And you shall be changed into another man than you were before, etc.* We also see that a lit candle, exposed to solar rays, seems to completely lose its power because of the glorious splendor of the Sun, so much so that its light, as if submerged by the Sun's glory and brightness, does not appear to human eyes, while nevertheless in reality it is such a light as it was before, and in its action and power it is not diminished, but rather its heat and activity are exalted by the power of the Sun. So it is also with the inspired soul. For if, according to Jamblichus's opinion, the human soul with the mind were entirely devoid of action, or even completely at rest in the body, then necessarily as a consequence that body, with that divinely infused spirit again departing, would remain inanimate, or totally deprived of the power of action, because it is the property of light and primary action that it either always acts, or also, when it does not act, it ceases to exist. Indeed, rather it follows that it acts by the presence and illumination of greater activity and splendor, and thus even more readily, because united force is usually stronger. Therefore, against these arguments of Jamblichus, it is necessary that the action of the inspired Prophet not only proceeds from God or the divine Spirit, extraordinarily infused into him, but also that the soul itself with the mind, as if snatched away by the presence of the divine Spirit, is stirred by an unknown motion of nature, and in a way foreign and unaccustomed to the body. Hence no reason for this motion is perceived by the soul and sense, and the powers of the soul, lifted upwards, forget the lower things, and, snatched by intellectual sense, contemplate the higher mysteries of God. Therefore the pious soul attracts the mind to itself, and the mind, embracing its pious vehicle and cherishing it with divine splendor, by the magnetic power of its divinity, attracts divine rays, most full of the divine Spirit, to itself, so that by their beauty and gifts it may reward that soul according to its merit, and lead it from the earthly to the heavenly way, according to that saying of Hermes Trismegistus in Pimander 10: *A good soul, when it has all the commands of virtue and piety, certainly becomes either God or mind.* Here therefore we must diligently observe that the miraculous works of the Prophets are not done by any power either of the stars or of that portion of the human soul which is derived from them, nor by the body itself, but by the pure and free power of God. But, if anyone perchance should say that the middle soul can be the immediate cause of this divine power or gift, we will demonstrate by an inviolable argument that the matter stands otherwise. For, since this portion of the middle soul is contained in a single man, and overshadowed by a perishable body, it is impossible that it should have power or virtue sufficiently efficacious for a divine work. Hence it is clear that, if anyone is divinely inspired, it follows therefrom that he has a divine benefit, with holy illumination flowing from above, through which he also seems to be a partaker of God's action. For if divine works were from the soul, it would follow that the soul is by its own nature and power possessed of wisdom and divinity; and consequently, that every other soul also has the same property of divinity. But every soul is known to be far removed from such power. For, that soul which seems to be perfect is still imperfect with respect to divine things. *Wherefore not the soul (may I now use the mouth of Jamblichus) as the prime mover, but divinity is the promoting cause for divine works.* Which indeed, if it were not so, religion would be in vain, since without the worship of God we would be masters of divine

From these things, therefore, it is clear according to our intention, that the middle portion of the human soul has received all its power and essence from intellectual light; just as the light of the middle heaven received its splendor from the external light of the empyrean heaven; which itself borrowed its glory from the most splendid fount of unity. And consequently, it is certain that it received its good from the mind and the spiritual heaven. CAP. XI.

How men, by virtue of an illuminated mind, or divine inspiration, can not only perceive things done in distant and remote places, but also understand the secret whispers of people far absent, and perform wonderful and ineffable things?

By virtue of a divinely inspired mind, or of the divine spirit sent from on high and united to the human mind, it is possible to accomplish and expedite absolutely all miracles that the human heart can conceive or imagine in any way, because all virtues or powers that are found in the world and its creatures are comprehended in the Holy Spirit, and remain in Him. Hence, therefore, those miraculous operations of Seers or Prophets, with respect to which they are called in the Holy Scriptures "men with open and uncovered eyes." Num. 24. And commonly they are called Seers, thus 1 Samuel 9:9: "Let us go to the Seer." And in the same place: "Is there a Seer there?" Likewise, that men of this kind, inspired by God or the divine Spirit, are called Seers 1 Chron. 19:29 & 2 Chron. 12:15, etc. Nor is it surprising, since they not only foresee future things (whence Balaam says in Num. 24: "I see it, but not now; I behold it, but not near") but also present things, which are done in the most remote and distant places, thus Jahaziel openly saw from afar the Ammonites and Moabites having pitched their camps on the summit of the torrent, which is opposite the wilderness of Jeruel, and warned King Jehoshaphat and all Judah to go up against them and fight. 2 Chron. 20. Similarly, Elisha revealed the secrets of the king of Syria, who was fighting against Israel; indeed, he saw their actions and knew their counsels, as is read in 4 Kings 6. And all these and infinite other miracles they performed by the virtue and assistance of the divine Spirit, in whose splendor, guiding their eyes, they perceived things done in distant places, and through the purest and most refined Spirit, they also heard and understood the voices and speeches and counsels of men living in places remote from them, no differently than if they were nearby. These things, indeed, cannot seem impossible to those who rightly know themselves. For whoever rightly considers the virtue of the internal man, constituted as it is from the middle soul as its subject, and from the mind as its divine form, will perceive that by the virtue of the mind, even more arduous things can be brought to the desired end, since its power is so widely expanded that even the spirit cannot comprehend it, but it is present everywhere and in every place, and yet is incomprehensible, inasmuch as it is of the essence of God. Hence, therefore, Hermes Trismegistus says, that man, supported by this divine nature, embraces all things with his intelligence, both those on earth and those in the sea, and whatever else is above heaven, and moreover raises himself up so that he may also behold the Good itself.

--- Page 154 ---
152 TRACT. I. SECT. I. LIB. VII.

For we see in common experience that if we turn the gaze of our mind to Rome, immediately to us, even if we remain in England as far as the external man is concerned, a person, and a place or thing previously done there before us, presents itself, so that suddenly, and as if in the blink of an eye, we behold it, etc. And so also in any most remote places, namely in Judea, etc. Indeed, we even raise the simple ray of the human mind in earnest contemplation to God Himself. What then will this admirable essence accomplish if it is illuminated by the Divine Spirit, from whom, as a ray of God, it first emanated? But indeed the human body is so deadly and deceptive to the soul without the influx of this divine grace, that what seems to the soul, is not, and what truly is, does not appear to it. Hence it happens that the whole man not illuminated by such a Spirit is carried away by deceptions. Indeed, every external sense is deceived concerning its proper objects; much more therefore the interior sense, which is covered on all sides by the veil of the flesh. And Proclus seems to confirm this with these words: *Matter,* he says, *seems to possess all things, when in truth it possesses nothing.* Hence it happens that carnal men are so distrustful and incredulous, and utterly deny those things which are not subject to the senses, deriding the truth of philosophy describing the inner nature of man, and the very investigators of mystical and spiritual nature. For they are unwilling to admit by any reason those things which they have not seen, or touched with St. Thomas. For just as men illuminated by the presence of the Divine Spirit regard only spiritual things, and despise all corporeal things, holding them to be false and trifling, so also conversely, worldly men and those occupied solely with the senses are accustomed to regard spiritual things as chimeras and deceptions, but corporeal and sensible things as infallible, and thus they are deceived. The reason for which thing Solomon certainly declares clearly to us in Wisdom 9 with these words: *For the thoughts of mortals are timid, and our plans are uncertain. For the corruptible body burdens the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that muses upon many things, and we estimate with difficulty the things that are on earth, and what is at hand we find with labor. But who will investigate the things that are in heaven? And who will know your mind, unless you give wisdom and send your Holy Spirit from on high, etc.* From which it is clear that the external man cannot become internal unless he is illuminated by divine illumination. Hence from what is said in 1 John, we perceive that there is one son of the world, and another son of God, and that the son of God ought not to perceive the world or its dark deeds, because the world does not know the sons of God or their deeds. But now we will adduce the reason why those inspired by the power and presence of the Divine Spirit, and by its conjunction and union with the mind of the inner man, can elicit and perceive the voices and secret whisperings of absent men. The Holy Spirit of discipline, although it expands itself everywhere throughout the whole world, and imparts power, motion, action, sound, and voice itself to all things; yet it is not powerfully present with its aid to all, but only to those to whom God abundantly grants it out of His clemency. For in some it is simply present for the function of life, in others in a double proportion, and in some in a triple, etc. Hence arise the various gifts of that Spirit recounted by Saint Paul. This, I say, the most holy Spirit, abundantly inspired by God into some, makes the man, into whom it is poured, hear and understand at will any voices of animals, because it itself is the cause of the production of vocal sounds: Hence, when it fell upon the Apostles in the form of fire, it rendered them skilled in every language. And Philostratus narrates that Apollonius of Tyana, by a certain divine power, understood the chirping and speech of birds, or the meaning of those voices. Indeed, this divine Spirit, governing the universal spirit, and expanded through all its members, narrates to the man in whom it dwells, and as it were, echoes to him the same voices and tones that are heard in more remote places: Nor indeed will this seem impossible to the wise, since the Apostle Paul himself...

--- Page 155 ---
DE MICROC. INTERN. IN EXTERN. 153

Paul relates that he was snatched by the power of that Spirit into the third heaven; where he confesses to have seen wonderful things and to have heard ineffable words. We also see by a familiar example that the flame of a lit fire at night is seen far and wide; and we know that this happens constantly and immediately without any resistance from the medium. We are also taught by experience with a thread stretched out over a long distance, that if one end of it is struck, the other, opposite end also vibrates at that blow. So also, if the upper part of a strongly stretched musical string is struck alone, it will make the whole string resonate and produce sounds. What then will the light of lights and the spirit of spirits not be able to achieve by its divine vivacity, both in the multiplication of a single voice through infinite air space from one to another, and in the vision of a thing through the remote distance of scattered places? The Wise Man seems to hint at all these things in very few words, in Wisdom 1, with this kind of discourse: *“For the Spirit of wisdom is benevolent, and will not absolve evil speech from his lips, because God is witness of his deeds, and a true searcher of his heart and a hearer of his tongue; because the Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of the voice; therefore, he who speaks unrighteous things cannot be hidden, etc.”* Therefore, these things having been considered, it is evident that to whom the presence of the divine Spirit is abundantly granted, to him is given the knowledge both of voice and of vision, according to that [passage] *Numbers 24:15 Balaam, a strong hearer of the word of God, and knowing the knowledge of the Most High, sees the vision of the Almighty, falling, but with his eyes uncovered, etc.* Concerning other miracles also flowing from the illumination of this Spirit, many things may be read and perceived everywhere in the sacred Scripture; to recite all of which in this place to the reader would perhaps be tedious and seem superfluous.

OF THE FIRST TREATISE,
OF SECTION I.
BOOK VIII.

Concerning the action of the middle Microcosmic soul in the body.

CHAP. I.
Concerning the properties of the vital soul with its ethereal spirit in the human body.

What this mundane portion is, constituting the medium of the human soul, we have openly and clearly explained in the first book of this work; namely, that considered in itself, it is, as it were, a spark of light of the soul of the world descending from the sphere of equality; which soul of the world we have called the mundane ray, the nature of things, the second act, the fifth essence, and the origin of the life of animated beings; and this indeed, insofar as it is considered in itself in its nature, and without the admixture of mind or sensitive soul. But indeed, insofar as it is a middle portion in itself, both in the composition of the universal world and of the human soul, to that extent it is rightly defined by Hermes Trismegistus, Pimander 12, as being life devoid of mind, and according to its being, it is divided into matter, which is pure spirit, and form, which is light carried in that Spirit as a vehicle, and acting indefinitely upon it as its proper passive element. Hence, that form or light is properly called by Philosophers the innate heat of the animated being, and this ethereal Spirit is called the radical moisture. These two, essentially conjoined, constitute life, and therefore, according to Porphyry, they do not die; and by their sole virtue and presence, the four elements in composition are balanced with such justice, and by the bonds of this fiery Spirit they are so connected to one another in harmonious peace, and ordered to vital and symphonic motions, that the life of animals and plants, indeed, even of the most compact mineral itself, is thereby created. Therefore, a total violation of the bonds of this soul induces death and dissolution; while a partial violation induces disease and sickness; inasmuch as it is nothing other than a relaxation of the bonds of celestial harmony, and a disagreement of one unbridled and rebellious element against its companions, which are naturally unsuitable for it; concerning which later

--- Page 157 ---
DE MICR. ANIM. MED. ACT. IN CORP. 155

This. But the Sages have shown that there is a twofold reason why this soul is infused into the human body by divine will. The first, namely, is with respect to the mind, which is the superior portion of the soul. Hence, Mercurius Trismegistus, Pimander 10, says: "Since earthly dregs cannot receive a mind so divine, nor sustain such a divine power confirmed in a divisible body, the mind assumed the soul, as a garment; moreover, the soul, being divine, uses the vehicle of the spirit, and the Spirit pervades the whole animal, etc." And for this reason, this soul is not ineptly called "the temple of God" by Paul and Xistus the Philosopher, as was said before. Conversely, the mind rewards the soul itself in infinite ways for its blessed labor and office, inasmuch as the soul finds its highest good in the mind. For this soul was full of mind and God in man from the beginning, as Mercurius Trismegistus testifies, agreeing with the sacred Scriptures in this. Hence it happens that, just as the soul by itself is the cause of life, so also the mind joined with it, and the soul firmly adhering to it, is the cause of a pious, holy, honest, and blessed life, which is the beginning of eternal life. And hence Mercurius Trismegistus, Pimander 10, uses these words: "The human soul, not all, but

--- Page 158 ---
156          T R A C T. I.   S E C T. I.   L I B. VIII.
carried and introduced with itself into it. This [lower soul], therefore, although by disposition it is most suitable to it [the divine light], nevertheless its presence is so much more exalted, the more it is able to attract the middle portion of the soul to itself; and consequently, it is inflated with so much greater pride, the more eminent a victory its prince (namely, of darkness) obtains against the portion of divine light, present there and bearing the image of the prince of light before itself. Hence it happens that that lowest portion of the human soul first tempts the intermediate spirit with worldly delights and pleasures, so that afterwards it may so much better and more easily deceive its soul, with this Spirit tempting it. Did not the serpent tempt Eve, the woman or the patient one, in this way, so that afterwards it might circumvent Adam, the man or the agent, indeed, to such an extent that both of them were thereby deprived and bereft of God's presence? Indeed, for this reason, the moist nature of the Spirit or Eve, and the active light of heaven or Adam, by consenting to the counsel of the animal or sensitive soul and adhering to it, lost the presence of the divine mind. Hence their misfortune and loss, which could never have been repaired or mended, except by that abundant presence of the fleeing mind, which we received from the Savior of the world and the infusion of the second mind, in which is the Word of God. Hence our enigmatic explanation of the described pleasure of Paradise is revealed, which we expounded in our Theologico-philosophical Treatise on Life, Death, and Resurrection. For Adam's soul, through the abundant presence of the mind, was inclined to contemplate only the higher things; but when it preferred to adhere to the blandishments of the sensitive soul, and the false and malicious instigations of the Devil, there the portion of the mind flew away, and, as it were, in its place, death succeeded; and thus likewise again, by the repeated abundant infusion of the mind into these lower things, in which is the Word, the regeneration of the inner man, and the resurrection of both the inner and the outer, follows. But now we will bring forth the authority of the Philosophers, speaking of the blandishments and allurements of the sensitive soul or idol, and also speaking of its lethal disadvantage and ineffable unhappiness. *Merc. Trismeg. says that the soul, conscious of the nature of things and of good, deprived of eyes, entangles itself in bodily passions, and that it is necessary for it to look around with the eyes of the mind, lest it utterly perish.* And elsewhere he says, *that the impious soul and one loving the body, remains in its own nature, and torments itself too much.* And elsewhere: *he calls the soul, because of its disjunction from the mind, not standing but falling;* Thus also in his *Pimander 10* he asserts, *that the soul destitute of the mind's presence, is able neither to do anything nor to say anything, and he says that this soul differs in no way from the soul of brutes.*
Such, therefore, is the hope of the carnal and worldly soul; such is the reward of the animal soul, which it renders to the vital or middle soul for its descent from the heavens; such is its reception; this is the end of carnal hospitality; these are its riches, the effects of which are nothing other than frauds, lies, deceptions, illusions, and nothing of certainty, since all truth emanates solely from the rays and virtue of the mind, and in no way comes from elsewhere. And certainly, this was the most unhappy fate of the soul, by which, descending into such a dark abyss of matter, as into a dark inn and prison, and utterly alien from its dignity, and indeed against its will, it migrated. This is also confessed by *Iamblichus* in these words:
*The soul, which slides downwards, meets [it], dragging with itself signs of chains and punishments, and shows itself burdened by the composition of material spirits, and occupied by disturbances unlike matter.* Which opinion of *Iamblichus* the wise man seems to confirm. *Wisdom 9* in the place cited above: *'The body,' he says, 'which is corrupted, weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the sense or the mind thinking many things, and we can scarcely discern the things that are before us.'* To this also, in my judgment, is consonant the opinion of Plato and Proclus, which holds that it is not natural for souls to live with bodies and to be involved in generation, but on the contrary to be separated, and that an immaterial and incorporeal life is rather agreeable to souls; and they say that
                                                                                                                  when

--- Page 159 ---
DE MICR. ANIM. MED. ACT. IN CORP. 157

...and they say that *when they are involved in generation, they are like men inhabiting a plague-ridden region, and that, when they live outside of generation, they are like those cultivating meadows.* This therefore is the reason why *Proclus in his book on the soul affirmed that all forms sicken in the body.* And for the same reason also *Porphyry* said, *that the soul, which is always most vigilant in itself, sleeps in the body.* Hence also *Synesius* said, *that a part of the mundane soul, having obtained a form by a heavy bond, and separated from its parents, has drunk dark oblivion, admiring the unpleasant earth with blind anxieties.* Since the soul, enclosed, is afflicted by all these perturbations of the body, there is no doubt that its descent into the bodily tabernacle of man is against its nature; no differently than the disposition of fire, which always seeks higher things by its nature, is sometimes forced by violence to tend downwards. Whence then is this unnatural conjunction between these two extremes? Certainly from the divine will, that it might enrich both lower and higher things with its living blessings; and especially, *that man, made in the image of God, might contemplate both lower and higher things.* For the *Universal Creator* sent the mediating soul into man for a twofold reason: Firstly, namely, because, to use the words of *Hermes Trismegistus*, *neither could earthly dregs receive a mind so divine, nor could such a divine power, confirmed by a divisible body, sustain it. Therefore the mind assumed the soul as a garment; because even the soul, being divine, uses the vehicle of the spirit; but the spirit pervades the whole living being.* Furthermore, *Hermes Trismegistus* brings forward a second reason in *Pimander 3.* *The human soul, he says, is veiled by the shadow of the flesh, to receive the discourse of the celestial Gods, for the works of God and the progress of nature, for signs of good things, for the knowledge of divine power: a certain portion is allotted for the judgment of good and evil, and for finding various good arts, etc.* From which it is manifest that the soul in its nature is good and most useful for the constitution of man. Indeed, it is that mediating nature in the composition of the human soul, without which its two extremes cannot be joined to each other. But it is deceived by the flesh's inclination to worldly pleasures and the deceptive allurements of the sensitive part; and thus through the excessive dark overshadowing of the opaque body, separated from its parents, it drinks the oblivion of truth, and deprived of its eyes, it entangles itself in bodily cares and passions. Hence *Hermes Trismegistus, Pimander 10.*: *When the compact body disperses and distracts the soul into its mass, then it is subjected to oblivion, and deprived of the vision of the beautiful and the good. But oblivion itself is wickedness, etc.* Whence the assistance of divine illumination is necessarily required for its salvation, since without it it can produce nothing good or holy in this life. Blessed therefore is he whose soul firmly adheres to the divine mind. Blessed is the soul that, avoiding the ravenous barking of matter, and emerging from the earth, with a light leap, carried by the wings of the mind, directs its steps towards God. Blessed is the Spirit, who after the fate and dissolution of the body, after hard labors and bitter earthly cares, having entered the paths of the mind, sees the summit and height of happiness shining with divine light. Blessed therefore is the Spirit with the soul, and thrice blessed is he who, most faithful and constant to the mind, endures to the end, for such a one will taste the cup of happiness, and will taste of the eternal fruit of immortality. Therefore, do not look back, O my soul, at the deceptive allurements of the flesh and the world; joyfully raise yourself, according to your own disposition, to higher things; be nobler than common fire, whose nature it is always to tend towards higher things, and to despise and by natural instinct shun lower things. For since you are adorned and made beautiful in the image and likeness of God, betrothed to the Spirit through faith, bought and redeemed by the blood of Christ, helped by Angels, companion of blessedness, heir of salvation, and partaker of reason, what do you have to do with the flesh, with sense, and with the world? But now we will speak briefly about the manner in which this soul, with the mind and Spirit, enters the body formed from clay.

Mercurius Trismegistus asserted that the Word passes into the mind, the mind into reason, reason
into the soul, and the soul into the spirit, and this [spirit] into the air; and then all these [elements], slipping downwards through the aerial sea, are transferred into the body with and in that [air], as the ultimate vehicle. We would also in a certain way prove this same thing, were it not that we consider the mind itself
to be a ray of the Word of God. For, as testified by Saint John, chapter 1, in the Word itself was life,
and that life was the light of men, etc. Whence, when Jehovah had uttered that word:
"Let man be made," etc., the clay, prepared by the hands of God, passed into a living animal, and by the power
of the breath, with the Word having proceeded from His mouth, all virtues were produced.

actual expansion, having carried along a portion of itself as a vehicle, and that thereafter,

and thus penetrating even to the center, introduced a portion of any mundane region,
according to its lightness or gravity, into the regions of the human body,

just as the elements possess the lower place of the world. Now that experiment
is as follows. Let a fourth part of a glass be filled with water, upon which artificially pour
red wine, so that it floats on the water, as can be done by means of a crust of bread,
and so let this wine occupy the second fourth of the glass; then gently and skillfully pour upon it
the best Spirit of wine, so that it likewise floats on the previous wine, and in that way fills
the third fourth of the glass; which being done, let that Spirit be ignited, so that it burns:
Thus by this experiment it will be demonstrated how ethereal nature floats above air
or elementary nature, just as wine floats on water, and then afterwards, in what manner empyrean
nature floats above ethereal nature, and finally fiery Spirit above empyrean nature, as in the
following demonstration.

From these things, therefore, it is to be gathered how these natures behave

thinner part is the Spirit of wine, constituting the empyrean region, but the thicker part

lowest heaven. From which it most evidently appears that the Spirit of the aethereal
heaven participates in the nature of both the lower and the upper heaven, both in the world
and in man. And this is that infallible reason by which we are exactly taught that the nature

to the rays of the mind as air to fire, and the mind to the Spirit as fire to air, or aether to fire.
Hence therefore it is clearly established what the position of the parts constituting the inner
man is in his external [body]: namely, that the mind with reason dwells in the head, as if
in the empyrean heaven or its natural seat, and indeed with the rays of the mind also
claiming a superior place for themselves there. Then, that the soul with the aethereal Spirit
inhabits the heart in the middle of the trunk as a solar orb; And finally, that the aerial Spirit
with the animal soul chooses the lowest part of the trunk for its natural station, where it uses
the liver as its inn or laboratory. The rational Spirit gives action to the senses, diffusing its
invisible powers through the organs of the nerves into the entire body; so that with reason
and judgment we can see, hear, touch, taste, and smell things. The soul of virtue with its
Spirit, possessing the middle of the Microcosm, no differently than the Sun possessing the
center of the visible heaven, transmits rays of life universally through the external man,
upwards and downwards through the arteries, so that by their power he can live and move.
The animal soul or idol, or aerial virtue, formed from the shapes of the elements, and
receiving its virtue partly from the elements, partly usurping the offices of the superiors,
acts and operates in the liver, so that it may transmute the nourishment of chyle into blood
for its own use, which it also pours and disperses upwards and downwards through the veins
into its entire bodily machine to preserve the parts of elementary composition in their integral
state. Therefore, the mind is contiguous to reason; wherefore it governs all operations. The
rational Spirit is contiguous to the aethereal Spirit: and therefore they act through the rays
of both natures: for arteries communicate with nerves and nerves with arteries: and moreover,
a small branch of the arteries covering the brain constitutes an admirable network there: but
the branches of the nerves are admirable, and argue for the true seat of the mind. For as God,
sitting in the height of heaven, is the root and unity of all things, pouring down only into the
world the rays of His action, and bestowing reason and life and sense upon creatures; So also
the mind itself, placed at the summit of the Microcosm, is the root of all nerves, whose branches
run downwards only, so that they may refresh the lower parts with the moderation of reason
and sense. For God in the Macrocosm and the ray of His essence in the Microcosm, not
emitting rays upwards from His essence, as if from their root, argues that there is nothing
among the things which the Creator created above His own existence, no more than a number
can go backward beyond unity. Therefore, the lower Spirits are as it were subjects of the
superiors, of all of whom the Mind is King and Emperor; To whom if the soul reigning in the
middle is obedient and faithful, this Commonwealth will be most happy; but if rebellious, most
unhappy, and that soul will pay the penalties for its disobedience. Hence it happens that the
rays of the mind through the intellectual Spirit are terrible to the rebellious soul; but gracious
and amiable to the obedient. For to the rebellious soul they are accustomed to bring cares,
sadness, fear, distrust, despair, anger, rage, hatred, gluttony, drunkenness, and other such
things; while conversely, to the obedient [soul] they are observed to induce joy, gladness,
boldness in truth, faith, hope, patience, meekness, spiritual love, temperance, and other things
of that kind. But how this is, briefly understand it thus: Galen on loc.

Here it must be observed incidentally that the superior region, because of the presence of mind and reason, commands, and acts at will, like God, that is, voluntarily. But indeed, we perceive the action of the vital and natural region, which we called animal and idol above, to be involuntary, and as if governed by a superior power or a higher divine will. From the aforesaid authors, therefore, we gather that involuntary vital action consists either only in the dilation of the heart, whence joy, hope, confidence, love, mercy, humanity; or in the dilation and contraction of the heart simultaneously; whence the motion of the pulse, consisting in systole and diastole; or only in the contraction of the heart; whence sadness, despair, fear, hatred, envy, anger, fury, shame, and other such things proceed. O Christian men, observe, I beg you, how closely these Physicians, Heathens, and Philosophers have approached the shadow of truth! For what better and more correctly could they have depicted by these things than that opinion and intention of ours concerning creation?

For in the first place, we perceive that vital action, situated and rooted in the middle region of man, and likewise natural action, located in the lowest belly, are involuntary, that is, they depend on the ordination and disposition of a superior power: Then, in the middle region, as it were, in whose heart or midpoint life consists, we clearly see the actions of the three regions of the world; inasmuch as in the dilation of the heart are born joy, hope, love, confidence, mercy, humanity, and similar actions of the holy soul, which are recognized as infallible gifts of the mind and of God, and therefore denote the obedience of the soul, and its society, communication, friendship, and fidelity with the mind. For how much joy and gladness, what faith and confidence, and what ineffable love, mercy, and humanity God pours into holy and good souls, the Sacred Scriptures copiously declare, manifoldly confirming the assertion of Hermes Trismegistus. Hence that willing, ready, and prompt dilation of the bulwark of life, so that it may receive with joy the blessings sent by God and His mind: For it does not fear the actions of God, which it always finds salutary for itself, but eagerly desires them as its highest goods, and receives them by desiring. For we are taught by experience that no disturbance or evil can befall the soul where the aforesaid gifts of God and the mind are found. Such, therefore, was the action of Adam, still living in Paradise; for his heart was filled with the gifts and benefits of the mind, and always open and dilated to receive divine and superior actions: Whence also doors or gates are found in the uppermost part of the heart, signifying that the heart expects the benefit and joy of life from above: But Adam, after his disobedience, was excluded from this exquisite pleasure; indeed, he was deprived of the joys of the highest heaven, inasmuch as he partook in the knowledge of evil; Whence now he has his highest pleasure from the middle heaven, as it were, whose nature it is to partake of both extremes, namely, of the goodness of the highest region and of the wickedness of the lowest region. For inasmuch as his nature is composed of the disposition and property of both extremes; namely, from formal light and material spirit, it thus happens that the heart
                                                                                                X          of this

--- Page 164 ---
162 T R A C T. I. S E C T. I. L I B. VIII.

of this region acts partly by dilation and partly by contraction: Whence the pulse arises, in whose motion matter contracts, but form dilates, hence systole and diastole. And through this involuntary action the soul with its Spirit, partly by gifts infused from the empyrean Spirit and mind from above, but partly by malignant vapors of darkness, is affected, borne aloft on the wings of perturbations and strife. Hence the inequality of human life, now joyful, now sad, now affected by hope, now afflicted by despair, now seized by love, now infected by envy, now merciful, now plunged into cruelty and rage, now gentle and suddenly, as if in an instant, disturbed. Do we not also perceive that the same properties of the middle heaven, and the same effects, are infused into us from above in a certain fatal way? Indeed, that Jovian and Venereal and Solar influences are for the most part good, but Saturnine and Martial influences are generally sad, fierce, and inauspicious for us, we are most often taught by Astrological experience. Finally, that involuntary vital action, which consists in the contraction of the heart, is miserable and unhappy for the soul inhabiting the middle region of the Microcosm. For through this very action that soul, already having fallen from the happiness of the supreme region to a mediocre state, is further cast down to the lowest abyss of misfortune, since, receiving all hope and solace from the supreme region, it is submerged in the whirlpool of darkness. For since it regards the sensitive soul more than the rational soul and the mind, therefore it is abandoned by the perfect mind and reason: whence it is oppressed by cares, doubts, sadness, despair, fear, hatred, anger, shame, and sorrow, and finds nothing but the horrible barking of dark matter, and all things seem dreadful to it, because it is deprived of the eyes of true reason, and is destitute of the illuminating light of the mind. However, it does not perceive these horrible things until finally, when, having fallen into the sensitive pleasure of the lower belly, it has long lingered there, neglecting the mind and supercelestial things, and at last returns to the memory of its place, birth, and origin, seeing that it has been caught as if by material snares, so that it cannot extricate itself from them without the wings and aid of the divine mind. Thus it finally realizes that through its disobedience it has neglected the mind. Hence sorrow, hence tears; hence in it constant suspicion and fear, lest its stronghold be soon invaded and destroyed; hence its frequent contractions, and constant passions and perturbations lacking all reason. But some, devoid of reason, will exclaim how it is possible for this to happen; And since all these things are in nature, they will say; show us the natural reason for this thing, so that we may better understand that these things are so, and not entirely reject these reasons of yours. To these unbelievers we also reply, that just as the Sun of the world, placed in the center of the heavens, shoots forth its rays through the Spirit both upwards and downwards, and therefore its rays springing forth from above are most full of divine grace, by which it infuses life into lower things, and indeed this would not happen unless there were a certain magnetic force in the sun, implanted in it from creation, to perform such things, so also the matter stands in that middle portion of the world-soul (which is from the sun) situated in man's chest or middle belly: For if it eagerly expects benefits from the superior mind, and attracts good to itself from it by the magnet of piety, most easily and without difficulty, its gifts will flow down to the lower parts of the lowest belly; and while its arterial branches tending upwards will abound with the Spirit of light, since the nature of the soul looks upwards towards the supreme region with the nature of fire, and by its motion captures higher things through a certain divine appetite; And then its lower branches will either be filled with a foul or thicker liquor of the vital Spirit, or will remain more empty, since their more excellent part, rejoicing in the vision of the mind, now aspires upwards.

--- Page 165 ---
aspire. And then the soul, if it has been constant in this action of its own, will acquire blessedness, according to this saying of Mercury Trismegistus in Pimander 10: "A good soul, when it has submitted to all the commands of virtue and piety, becomes either God or mind." Whence he also elsewhere called such a soul a "standing soul, and not a falling one." This, therefore, is that soul which we said rejoices in the aforementioned gifts, by which its bulwark or heart is dilated. But truly, conversely, if, contrary to the constitution of divine nature, the vital rays of this soul and the purer fluid of that Spirit, by descending through the lower branch of the arteries, have listened to the blandishments of the Spirit or soul of the lower belly, then they will be retained there, and infected by the poisonous allurements of the flesh; and thus the more impure Spirits in the arterial branch, conspiring with evil and the lower region by reason of their gravity and position, will be elevated upwards instead of the true fifth essence; whom the rays of the mind flee because of their impurity: And in this way, the darker rays of the soul, which otherwise naturally tend downwards, now being elevated upwards, produce an eclipse between the sun of the mind and the moon of the soul fallen into the lower belly. This, therefore, is the inner chaos of the Microcosm, whose confusion of elements we can discern here with true eyes, and whose irregular disposition is reduced to harmony only by divine illumination (whose acts even Demons are compelled to obey). Hence those infirmities and passions of the soul which we mentioned above, namely sadness, despair, fear, etc. Concerning which Mercury Trismegistus speaks in Pimander 10, when he says that "the impious soul remains in its own nature, and torments itself too much": And elsewhere: "The soul fallen into the human body, if indeed it has persevered in evil, will taste nothing of immortality, nor will it enjoy any good." Hence, therefore, arise all the terrible effects of melancholy, from which reason is estranged; hence madness, lycanthropy, insanity, incubus, fear-inducing dreams, vain apparitions, and infinite things of that kind; all of which are driven into darkness by the union of the mind with the soul, and completely vanish, and are found to be nothing other than the deceptions and illusions of the Devil hidden under the veil of darkness, by which the most wretched soul, submerged in the mists of sadness, is tormented, so that it despairs of the benevolence of God and the mind. We have, therefore, here in the Microcosm all the regions or "bellies" of the Macrocosm. And just as in the lowest region air is almost everywhere expanded, and water is refined by the operation of heat and turned into air, and fire is drawn out from subtle air, so also we see that in the lowest belly of man, the chyle of the stomach, which we compared to the sea of the Macrocosm, by the virtue of the operating liver, becomes blood, and is converted into air, namely into a sanguineous mass, having within itself the hidden nature of the other elements; whose subtle or fiery nature is pushed into the gallbladder; while the more crude part is poured downwards, as into the lowest place of springs, or the abyss of the earth, and likewise also the coarser portion is committed to that part which is compared to earth, namely the spleen. Similarly, we see that the vital Spirits in the heart, as in their home and root, where they are prepared, draw forth food similar to their own nature from the external air, namely an ethereal nature, invisibly inherent in the air, by which silent inspiration the vital Spirits are nourished and refreshed daily and every minute, as with the sustenance of life, and they nourish those bonds of the body's members, by which the elements are connected in harmonious peace, lest due to their defect the elements, having gained freedom, should discord among themselves, and thus the harmony of life be interrupted by discords; whence either dangerous diseases, or death and the complete dissolution of the whole would follow. The rational Spirit also receives the most subtle nourishment and a kind of similar sustenance for itself from the air drawn in both through the mouth and nostrils,
X 2 then
