164 TRACT. I. SECT. I. BOOK VIII.

then also by subtle bodily inspiration through the thin passages of the head. But the Mind remains perpetually immobile and constant in its nature, like that supersubstantial essence from which it is derived. Hence, therefore, it is clear that the natural faculty of the lower heaven acts for the nourishment of those parts of man similar to itself, namely, the elementary and corporeal: Whence it is established that solid parts are nourished by it, and in the same state, by the apposition, union, and assimilation of blood, they are nourished and preserved. From the waves of this red fluid, the heart also draws to its chamber, through diapedesis, that ethereal substance which is due to it. Similarly, the vital faculty, governing the middle region, is known to nourish the innate heat with the radical moisture; by the increase of which the vital Spirits are more abundantly dispensed throughout the entire body, and the bonds of the elements are preserved inviolate. Finally, the animal faculties, strengthened by a certain proper nourishment, render the sense whole, the imagination prompt, the memory effective, and the motion and action of the muscles more efficacious through the organs of the nerves. But the Mind in the higher region always directs its gaze to its homeland, and perpetually engages in meditations on supercelestial things, and entices man to contemplate sublime things, and wholly carries him away to the knowledge, worship, reverence, and love of God; if the soul offers itself obedient to it. Whence Proclus says *On the Soul* that the soul, through acquired knowledge, may become similar to the mind itself or the intellect. etc. The Rational Spirit, with a certain remarkable harmony, infuses these ideas of the mind into the well-disposed soul through the sieve or diaphragm of the first region to the second; and the soul, inspired by these influences of reason, rejoices vehemently, and as if carried away by the contemplation of higher things, does not regard lower things, unless its duty demands that it infuse the actions of life into it.

The natural soul, or the lowest part of the inner man, full of the world's desires, first tempts the appetite of the ethereal Spirit with carnal blandishments, because it itself is of the nature of elementary matter; and it (the ethereal Spirit) thereafter, deceived by the allurements of the idol, further deceives the soul itself, and draws it with itself to lower things, and thus both are most miserably deceived. For did not this same thing happen to Eve and Adam? But the allurements of this sensitive soul are the love of the body and the desires and pleasures of worldly things, which arise from the liver; the gallbladder extols the praises of vengeance, wrath, ambition, contention, and arrogance; the stomach is irritated by the stimuli of gluttony and drunkenness; the spleen brings forth a disposition to envy and a life full of cares and anxiety, and invites the soul to its melancholic dwelling; the male members draw the soul by the pleasure of flesh and coitus, etc. Therefore, if the middle soul consents to these, and slides into the theater of these iniquities, the reason of the Spirit also, being coerced and made false, and straying from the truth of the mind, uses false reasons for things instead of true ones, and feigns illusory and fallacious things to be true, and thus the soul is miserably deceived because of its rebellion.

CAP. III.

*How the middle soul is sometimes called immortal, and sometimes*
*mortal, and for what reason it is said to be in a place.*

We have spoken of the immortality of the soul in *our Treatise on the Microcosm, book 4, last chapter*. Here, however, we have proposed to treat of its mortality, along with the reason for its immortality. The soul is indeed truly said never to die, inasmuch as it is the image and likeness of the Creator; nay, it is indeed the very spark of the Creator's ray; whence it is impossible that it should be enclosed by the boundary of death; since, inasmuch as it is an act of God, it can never lose its life and being. However, according to a certain mobility of its own, by which it can become either better or worse, it must be considered mortal; for it is then thought to be subject to death, when it loses living well; although even then it is called immortal, inasmuch as it cannot lose living miserably.

Hence, if it adheres to the animal soul and to the flesh, and is subjected to the world, it is said to die, that is, to be thrust down from happiness into misery. But indeed, if it is fixed by constant contemplation on Him, it is thought to live and acquire the name of immortality, and to obtain it happily. In a similar manner, also, with respect to the incorporeal God, it is corporeal, since nothing invisible and incorporeal by nature is to be believed except God alone, that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who is called incorporeal and invisible because He is infinite and minimally circumscribed, simple, self-sufficient in all ways, and, since He is everywhere, is known to be invisible and incorporeal in Himself: But every rational creature is corporeal, that is, compounded from Spirit as matter and light as form. Thus we say that angels and all virtues are corporeal, although they do not subsist in flesh: From this we affirm that intellectual natures are corporeal, because they are circumscribed by place; just as the human soul, which is enclosed in flesh, and therefore can also be said to be in a place and local: In a place, namely, because it is present here and elsewhere; but local, because what is present to something is not wholly elsewhere. Yet the soul does not have corporeal dimension, nor corporeal circumscription, because it is devoid of corporeal quantity; But because it is enclosed by its presence and operation, it is itself called local; Yet not like a body, to which, according to place, a beginning, middle, and end are assigned.

With respect to incorporeal nature, which is immutable everywhere, the soul is called corporeal, because it is not such a thing itself, nor is it stopped or moved through space, so that with a larger part of itself it occupies a larger place, and with a shorter part a shorter, and is less in a part than in the whole. Indeed, it is wholly present simultaneously through all particles of the body, neither less in smaller parts, nor greater in larger parts, but somewhere more intensely, somewhere more remissly, and it is whole in all, and whole in each. For just as God is everywhere in the whole world, and in every one of His creatures, so the soul is everywhere in its whole body, as in a certain world of its own, namely, the Microcosm; Yet it is more intensely in the brain, just as God is said to be more abundantly in the empyrean heaven, and acts rationally there; Similarly in the heart, as in the Sun of the ethereal world; where it operates effectively and vivaciously; just as God is said to be in heaven. But in the other members of the whole body, according as they are more or less worthy, it is perceived to be more or less remiss and effective. From these things, therefore, we see that, as long as the soul contains itself in heaven
X 3

--- Page 168 ---
166 TRACT. I. SECT. I. BOOK. VIII.
contains itself, it seems to taste of heavenly happiness, and to be wonderfully equated with God himself, from whom it is, and as it were to drink in the Spirit with immortal blessedness. But indeed, if with Lucifer it plunges itself downwards into the multitude of matter, and abandoning heaven, into the lower abyss, obeying the higher things not at all, and casting itself down by despising their rites, it will seem to be covered and overwhelmed by death, that is, by darkness and the tomb as if of oblivion, and thus, having fallen away from the happiness of immortal life, by looking back at mortal things, it is not foolishly said by metaphorical expression that the happiness of heavenly life dies and becomes mortal.

CHAP. IV.

*That the breath of life was given not only to humans, but also to beasts,
and concerning the difference of each breath, likewise concerning
the creation of souls.*

Since we gather from the sacred Scriptures that that breath of life was given not only to humans, but also to other animals (for in *Genesis 7* it is thus read: *All humans and everything in which the breath of life is on earth, are dead.* And in the same place *chapter 6: I will destroy all flesh in which is the spirit of life*), therefore no small doubt can arise as to what the difference is between the breath of life of humans and of beasts. For the solution of which doubt it must be understood that the breath of life in creation is

--- Page 169 ---
DE MICR. ANIM. MED. ACT. IN CORP. 167

the dark mass of external man; and this not immediately, namely as the other creatures of the world received it from the world, but it was done immediately by the Creator Himself. Whence man is as complete in his essence as the world itself: indeed, there is no nature in the world that is not likewise found in this most noble creature, man, as we have clearly explained above. Hence, therefore, as it seems to me, no doubt or scruple can remain regarding that opinion which asserts that the soul originates by propagation. For if the first breath of life suffices for the perpetuity of the world and the continuation of its creatures, since, as the Psalmist says, "from the Spirit of His mouth proceed all the virtues of the world and its creatures"; why should not His second breath likewise suffice to accomplish the same without repetition and renewal in the succession of men, as the first did in the continuation and preservation of species in other creatures? Wherefore the contrary opinion seems rather to detract from the power of God than to add any honor to Him; inasmuch as it seems to argue that God was not as strong and powerful at the end of His creation as He was in the beginning: for otherwise His Spirit would be believed to be as strong at the end as in the beginning, and consequently to accomplish the same in the conservation of the Microcosmic species as it accomplishes in the Macrocosm and its creatures. But indeed, if a single breath of God can continue and preserve the succession of mortal men until the very end, what need will there be for more, since, as the *Philosopher* testifies, it is done in vain by many means what can be done by fewer. Therefore, having considered these things, we see, first, how great is the difference between the breath of life in brutes and that which is in man, namely, that the former is immediately from the world, and therefore is devoid of manifest reason; but the latter is immediately from God, whence it adorns the inner man with clear intellect and reason, uniting him in his nobility with his Creator: Then we see that the divine breath in man in no way differs from that which was communicated to the world. Yet the one and same breath of the world suffices to perpetually maintain the species and virtue of the world and its creatures. Wherefore the breath of man will likewise be sufficient to continue the human species, and consequently there will be no need for the constant creation of souls. However, we will say no more about this argument, since we have discussed the reason for this doubt quite openly above.

**C A P. V.**
**On the nature and diverse grades of the soul in the body, and on the reason for the vigor and**
**strength of the body, and on the reason for the differences in created species,**
**and how the middle spirit of man differs from the middle spirit**
**of other animals?**

IT follows from what has preceded that there are many grades of inferior souls, and that the dignity of the human soul is to be preferred above all others. But since we perceive one man to surpass another in excellence of intellect, and in the abundance and readiness of soul and reason, while in another we find more excellent effects of the middle soul, inasmuch as he is more lively and agile than others; and again we observe another to be more robust in bodily vigor, and more powerful and stronger in strength, we deem it necessary to diligently inquire into the reason for this matter. It must therefore be known first of all that the effects of reason and intellect emanate from the act of the mind and the rational spirit. Whence it happens that a strengthened spark of the mind and a ray of reason multiplied within itself produces stronger effects,

--- Page 170 ---
168     TRACT. I. SECT. I. LIB. VIII.
effects, rendering man sharper in intellect, graver in reason, and in divine contem-
plation far deeper than others, because it emits its invisible and spiritual rays
further and more strongly. Whence it happens that it raises and exalts the soul's meditations
higher towards God's throne. Hence Proclus says concerning the soul: *More perfect souls are*
*more prompt for invention: but the more imperfect ones need more external*
*aids: for the former are more mobile from themselves, and less partakers of a worse nature;*
*but the latter move less themselves, suffering more their bodily lot. These also, when they are perfected,*
*namely, rising from the body, and gathering themselves from matter, they become more fertile and inventive,*
*immediately concerning those things in which they were previously sterile and ambiguous, because of*
*the inept sluggishness of life contingent on matter, and the sordid torpor contracted from generation.*
Through which Proclus seems to ascribe greater or lesser effects of the rational soul,
not to its strength or weakness in its essence, but rather to the good
or bad disposition of the body or its opaque veil: which, although it contributes something
to aid or hinder, yet so great is the power of the mind, presiding over the rational spirit in man,

resist its influences, because the divine splendor illuminates the darkness itself; indeed, darkness is not
darkness to it, but night
*is as clear to it as day.* Moreover, *the word, which, according to Mercury, is in the mind, exists for life,*

the body is not an impediment to the actions of the mind, but rather, either the mind itself, unwilling to act
in a malignant body, is said to be idle, or its Spirit is not augmented and multiplied by the Supreme Being.
Hence Mercury says: *the mind is not given to all;* And elsewhere he says,
*that it is given to all, but in some, namely in the malignant and impious, it does not act at all,*

and is multiplied by influxes into another. Hence
therefore we see the reason for the variety in the actions of the mind, and that the diversity of its operations
is the cause of exaltation and dejection in man, since a more intense
benevolence or full presence of it makes one wise, but its neglect
and absence makes one ignorant and not much different from a beast. The reason, however, why one
man is more agile and lively than another, consists in the good disposition of the middle soul,
which, since it is present in irrational as well as rational animals, produces the same
effects in any animal. Hence the animal's lightness in jumping, swiftness
in running, ease in movement and life. And this disposition usually occurs
even in those animals whose bodily members are not strong, but weak:
Whence it is clear that this animal faculty arises from the source of the middle region, namely,
from the heart, in which the middle or vital and ethereal soul is nourished. The cause, therefore,
for greater or lesser action of the middle soul is provided by the multitude or scarcity
of the mundane ray or secondary light, or of the soul of the middle heaven, which is also called the soul
of the world. And here we acknowledge with Proclus that the body can do much
to impede the operations of this soul: because this is that portion of the human soul
which is said to be burdened by earthly dregs and weighed down by the shadow of the flesh.
But indeed, an abundant proportion of this soul produces its effects even against the body's will,
as we will clearly demonstrate with experiments described below.
Also, one animal of the same species differs from another in the strength of its body and limbs.
For this man, or that horse, is stronger and more robust than this or that one in constitution.
This habitus of man or animal does not proceed from the middle soul, but from
the natural or lowest faculty, or the nature of the animal soul or idol, whose

whose function it is to preserve the body's members in their strength and vigor, and to render solid parts, consumed by weakness and leanness, strong and robust. Therefore, a stronger or weaker disposition of this lowest portion of the human soul consists in the good or bad habit of this faculty. For a good constitution of the liver produces good and copious blood; and consequently supplies the members with the best nourishment, by which they become more solid and robust. But a bad (constitution) generates bad, scanty, and poorly nourishing blood; and for this reason, it poorly nourishes the members and leaves them weak. The strength of the members and of the entire body is either joined to an agile and lively soul, or governed by a sluggish and slow (soul). Such was the difference in the strength of Hercules, Cacus, and Antaeus. Such was the discrepancy among the sons of Jupiter and the Titans. A difference of this kind is found in brutes: a mouse differs from a toad, a horse and a stag from an ox, a pig from a dog, a tortoise from a cat, etc. All these differences of the soul's portions proceed from a greater or lesser proportion of luminous activity. For a greater quantity of substantial light produces a more vivid effect; a lesser (quantity) a lesser (effect); and this is observed in different individuals of the same species. For example, we see that a doubled portion of gunpowder multiplies the expulsive force of a war engine; and consequently, it is known to carry the burden of an iron or lead ball higher or farther.

[Two illustrations of early modern artillery pieces, specifically mortars or cannons, on wheeled wooden carriages.]

Hence also arises the difference of all species in every genus of animals and plants. For just as infinite points, as it were, are counted between the starting point and the end point, so also there are infinite proportions and degrees of the vital and natural soul, by which one species is observed to differ from another, and one individual of the same species to vary from another. In this, however, the disposition of degrees in different individuals of the same species differs from that of different species: because the sparks of the soul in individuals of the same species are found indeed in a greater quantity, but in the same spirit; but indeed in different species, the difference is such that, just as they differ in the nature and proportion of light, so also they seem to differ in the disposition of the spirit in which that soul swims and is carried. Thus the spirit of minerals, which is from the darkness of the lowest heaven, differs from the spirit of vegetables, which is partly from the middle spirit, and partly from the lowest: Hence vegetables are related to minerals in origin and nature, but their spirits are diverse. So also the spirit of animal life is simply from the middle heaven, and its vital light is also of the same condition. Just as, furthermore, the human spirit is partly from the empyrean heaven, inasmuch as its rational spirit is derived from it, and partly from the ethereal heaven, from which it received its spirit of life; as also its light is mixed with diverse spirits, as was said before. And this is the cause of variety in created things. Therefore, the spirit Y and

and light in man differs from the spirit and light of other animals no less than

For, just as fire from the spirit of wine is composed of a spirit partly aerial and partly ethereal (whence its thinner part, when ignited, does not burn), but the fire of a lamp retains only an aerial and thicker nature, so that it burns an inflammable thing, so also the matter stands in the difference between those two souls; namely, of man and of brutes. For just as the spirit of wine is far more subtle than oil, and yet both are spirits; so also the spirits of both species are both indeed of a spiritual disposition, but they differ in rarity and purity like the spirit of wine from oil, or air from ether, or ether from intellectual spirit.

C A P. IV.
That the human soul by itself embraces unity, but with respect to
matter inclines to multitude.

The human soul by itself in its nature and origin embraces unity; for its chief and summit is the mind itself, or a ray of unity itself, so connected and continuous with supernatural unity or essence, as a ray of the Sun to its body. Therefore, through the mind, the middle portion of the soul is raised to unity; as we see in the nature of fire, which, ascending upwards, forms an acute angle, visible to bodily eyes, signifying by this very fact that with spiritual wings it vehemently attempts and desires to ascend to the cone of the material pyramid; for at the extreme of the cone or angle, uniformity and unity alone are found. Moreover, the middle soul, since it is a ray of the world, or secondary light, is also called, as Merc. Tris

--- Page 173 ---
DE MICR. ANIM. MED. ACT. IN CORP. 171

But the multitude of matter, desiring to be informed, divides that universal soul, which revolves around unity, into infinite parts, and gives these to each member of the multitude: Hence the multitude of species and individuals; hence the ignorance, self-forgetfulness, and errors of the uniform soul, divided into parts; hence its sadness from this kind of captivity. For according to Proclus, *souls sicken and rave as if in a human body; or, as Porphyry would have it, they perpetually sleep as if in the body.* For this reason, Iamblichus says, *that the property of souls is a declination towards multiplicity and the motion of generation, although by themselves, and in their nature, they look towards the unity of the Deity, which is permanent in itself, and yet the unmoving cause of motions.* For since the nature of the soul is always to move, inasmuch as it is a simple act, to that extent, by its accidental motion, through generation, it produces multiplicity. For bodies enclosing souls, and blinding them, are accustomed to turn the motions of souls towards their own appetites, which revolve around multiplicity. And hence it happens that the soul's motion in bodies produces generations and the increase of individuals of every species. This same thing also happens in human bodies, which enclose the most noble form, and whose unique privilege it is, by virtue of divine splendor, to possess a soul more exalted than other creatures; Hence it happens that the soul itself, although bound in its prison by spiritual chains, nevertheless sometimes remembers its homeland, and its gaze is sometimes lifted high on the wings of divine rays, according to that saying of Iamblichus: *The soul in the intelligible world heard divine harmony, of which it here remembers, when it hears melodies bearing a trace of the divine; and remembering, it is vehemently affected by it. Similarly, according to Synesius; there is also in those who have fallen down here, a certain power recalling them to heaven, etc.* Indeed, to holy people, and even in this life, a way is revealed, by which the human soul, leaving multiplicity, can return to unity, which Mercury calls *the way of regeneration*; namely, the inspiration and influx of the divine spirit. And Proclus also seems to describe a certain way for us, by which we can return from multiplicity to unity; namely, the acquisition of knowledge: Hence he says, *that the soul through acquired knowledge becomes like the mind, that is, the soul, leaving multiplicity through the virtue and illumination of knowledge, approaches unity.* For all multiplicity is so diverse in itself, that some things seem contrary to others in every respect. Hence it will be necessary, if we wish to ascend to unity, where there is no contrariety, that we apply ourselves to true knowledge, in which multiplicity has no contrariety: For although affections are contrary to affections, similarly senses to senses, thought to thoughts, and opinion to opinions, nevertheless no knowledge is found contrary to knowledge. For in knowledge, we gather a multitude of propositions and notions into one, and we connect the number of sciences by a certain single bond; and so far are they from being contrary to each other, that even notion serves notion, and lower sciences minister to higher ones, and thus these have their beginnings from those. Thus we see very many notions of Geometry contribute to a single Theorem and its demonstration: thus we observe points, lines, angles, and surfaces with their notions, are referred to the body or three dimensions: Thus we see numeration, addition, subtraction, and multiplication depend on each other, and are necessary for division and root extraction: thus also rules or propositions about sounds, tones, semitones, Diatessaron, Diapente, Diapason and notions designating the proportions of temporal signs lead to the truth of a single symphony; And although such notions are in multiplicity, they nevertheless denote a single thing, namely melody; Thus we perceive Arithmetic, Music, Geometry, and Optics lead to the knowledge of astrological truth. Therefore, there is no contrariety in the multitude of sciences, since they lead to unity, but in the multitude of matter, which always distracts and wanders.

--- Page 174 ---
172 TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK VIII.

and departs from unity. Therefore, having understood the multitude of sciences, it is necessary to hasten from those which merely propose some one thing, to that very one. Therefore, let compositions, divisions, and multiple discourses be laid aside, and let a transition be made to intellectual life and simple contemplations. For, *to use the words of Proclus, science is not the highest peak of cognitions, but intellect is more eminent than it, and an illumination of the soul: for it is through intellect alone that we come to know the terms, namely, the one of unity, and the other of multitude.* Therefore, the multitude preceding through the degrees of cognitions in their order must be avoided: but we shall also proceed similarly hereafter through the degrees of knowable things to prove this very point. All sensible things are to be avoided; because they are aggregated and divisible and utterly mutable. From these, therefore, let us transfer ourselves to the incorporeal essence. For every sensible thing has an adventitious unity, and is by itself dispersed and full of infirmity. Therefore, its good is also partible and adventitious and distant from itself and distrustful, and residing in an alien seat. But when we have ascended thither, and have been placed in the body, we shall behold that animal order moving above bodies from itself, acting through itself, possessing its substance in itself and from itself. Therefore, let us abandon the multitude alien to souls, and by cutting through the ether, and ascending still further upwards, let us betake ourselves to the intellect and intellectual realms, so that we may possess the unity of things, and there become contemplators of that nature. We shall behold that nature [marginal mark] remaining in eternity, a vigorous life, a vigilant intelligence, to which nothing of life is lacking. Therefore, when we have found this, we shall most easily observe how much more suitable and better it is for souls, and we shall see whether any multitude is found in it, and whether it is uniform or multiform. Here, therefore, you will perceive that highest good, to which the human soul always desires to attain. Here is the source and origin of all created things. Here is the summit and pinnacle of joy and gladness. Here is the true and sole simplicity and that truth of which Plato and Pythagoras speak, when they *so earnestly admonish us to flee the multitude, so that we may attain the most simple truth.* And indeed, to do this, they prescribe a method and a way for us, not disagreeing from the way of Proclus; namely, that we ought to avoid the varied multitude, *first indeed of affections, then of senses, thirdly of imaginations, and fourthly of opinions dependent thereon.* And indeed, the judgments of these do not seem to differ in any way from our intention. For, since the soul is enclosed in darkness, it uses sense as if it were some guide. Whence its keenness then, in the third place, is turned about so many subjects, so that they produce uncertainty and inconstancy in the soul; and thus the soul's rays, distracted by so many and great objects of the senses and their contemplation, allow their keenness to be blunted, so that they cannot penetrate to the throne and seat of unity; and in that way the soul is doubtful and uncertain as to where it should turn to find truth, inasmuch as it is deceived no less in matter than by the illusions of matter itself revolving around it. Wherefore Proclus not inaptly says: *just as matter seems to have all things, when in reality it possesses nothing, so also the soul, laboring under a twofold ignorance, seems to itself to possess what it does not have.* And this happens because of the manifold effect of sense. For this reason, the multitude of external senses must first be cast aside. Finally, we also ought not to conceive in our imagination things that are fictitious, vain, and false, which are like phantasms conceived in the air; because these likewise distract from that unity which is the sole truth. And moreover, we do not at all believe that credence should be given to the opinions of men which contradict themselves and the truth. Thus, finally, afterwards, by ascending through the degrees of a thousand-rung ladder, returning towards unity, we shall ascend to the middle heaven, where we shall find greater certainty and perfection. Thenceforth, from that, by elevating ourselves higher through the degrees of a hundred-rung ladder, we shall arrive at the intellectual world, through whose

--- Page 175 ---
DE MICR. ANIM. MED. ACT. IN CORP. 173
by ascending whose steps of ten we shall at last reach the royal palace of formal unity; and thus by this path the soul will be freed from multiplicity, and will return to its pristine simplicity.

CHAPTER VII.

Why this middle soul granted only vegetative life to vegetables and plants, while bestowing sense along with vegetation upon all animals?

Indeed, we have already spoken somewhat in previous sections concerning the variety and difference between the soul of vegetables and that of animals. However, in this place, we shall discuss more extensively the difference and distinction of that soul in these kinds of creatures. We have declared elsewhere in the premises that the souls of vegetables are from the more limpid spirit of the middle darknesses, reverberated downwards from the middle heaven of the world on the second day of creation, with potions or sparks of the second light enclosed within it. And we likewise demonstrated there that this same soul is also the soul of all animals. But to some, perhaps, this will seem absurd, or scarcely probable, that the same light with such a spirit (since these differ so greatly among themselves) should be the origin of both kinds of living things; for they will argue that the same things cannot differ so much from themselves. To these, we respond that the soul of a plant does not differ from the soul of an animal, except according to more and less. We shall briefly declare here the reason why a plant has less of the middle nature, while an animal has a more abundant portion of it. That plants and vegetables, emerging from the pores of the earth, were created with the earth itself on the third day of creation, the sacred Scriptures teach us; at which time, indeed, the celestial rays were not contracted into the Sun, but diffused throughout the universal mundane spirit, and especially dilated and dispersed around the celestial spirit. But just as, according to that ancient axiom of the Philosophers, *united force is stronger; thus, that which is dissipated is weaker*. Hence, therefore, it came about that the soul of a plant was not so strong, luminous, clear, and thus efficacious in performing its functions, as is the soul of animals, inasmuch as the latter originated from celestial rays constricted and simultaneously collected and united into the solar body: For on the third day of creation, before the creation of the Sun, light was equally dispersed around the earth and mixed and enveloped with dense and thick hylean vapors: whence it happened that it was obscure, and no more to be compared to the beauty of the Sun than the splendor of a shining cloud can be compared to the Sun, or air illuminated by fire. But after all the rays of heaven were gathered to the solar spirit, which was rising upwards from the earth with its sparks of light, suddenly the marvelous effects of the rays thus contracted together revealed themselves to the world, and first fish, then birds, and finally animals were procreated, and thus, according to the increase of solar dominion or its predominance over the rebellious vapors of matter, which were raising and exhaling themselves upwards from the earth into the elemental region, the soul was gradually produced stronger and more powerful day by day through creation and brought forth into light. Hence, therefore, the admirable operation of the Sun in the production of more perfect creatures is clearly demonstrated, and consequently the defect of vegetables is explained, inasmuch as only dilated rays of light and grosser spirits concurred in their creation; so much so, indeed, that no aid from the Sun, that most noble and vivacious creature, which was produced from rays contracted together with spirit, was involved in the vegetable work. Therefore, having considered these things again and again, we shall perceive,
Y 3

--- Page 176 ---
174 T R A C T. I. S E C T. I. L I B. VIII.

we perceive that the spirit of vegetables is coarser and denser than the spirit of animals, since its rays were weaker; because the rarefaction and purification of spirits consists in the multitude and vigor of the rays of light; so that, just as the power of light is, namely greater or lesser, such also is the rarity and purity of the spirit, greater or lesser. But light before the creation of the Sun was more diffused: Therefore less powerful, and consequently it follows that in plants the portion of the soul is coarser in spirit, and less and thinner in light, than in animals. Therefore, for this reason it happens that the souls of both these kinds of animated beings differ from each other. Indeed, we even find another difference between the nature and essence of those said souls, since the soul of animals, flowing from the Sun, claims for itself the property of solar nature, which we said above is formed from light and Spirit emerging from the darkness of the empyrean heaven; and consequently we have demonstrated above that it is a participant in reason. But the soul of vegetables, drawing its origin from the spirit and light of the darkness of the ethereal or middle heaven, neither has spirit and light capable of reason, nor can it be compared in simplicity and purity of form with the soul of animals. Hence it happens that, while plants are slow in their movement and are fixed to the earth, and remain immobile, we see that animals are light, subtle, agile, swift, and move hither and thither with a certain will. This, therefore, is the difference in lives in both those kinds of animated beings, this is the reason for dignity in one, and for depression and abjection in the other, since one is richer in fire and celestial Spirit; while the other is more cast down by poverty and humidity.

C A P. VIII.

That the vital soul is composed of innate heat and radical humidity, and
that it partakes of the nature of the Sun; Likewise concerning the pyramidal shape of the heart, and that
it is the palace of the vital soul; and how this soul,
by means of the Spirit, is distributed
throughout the entire body.

Since both ancient Philosophers and the chief of Physicians are accustomed to make not infrequent mention of innate heat and radical humidity, from the mixture of which they say life arises, it seems worthwhile that we briefly explain this very heat and likewise also this humidity. Those more skilled in the secrets of nature are accustomed to say that heat is derived from motion, and motion from action or the moving principle. Nor indeed is heat anything other than the effect of motion, just as motion is nothing other than the action or act of visible or invisible light. Hence it is manifest that where there is heat, there also is motion, and consequently with motion, essential light, as the mover. Hence it happens that by some, heat is taken for the effect of motion, or for a mere quality, or sometimes for the mover itself: For in Hippocrates we find it thus written: That mortal thing which we call heat, when all things were disturbed, flew up into the highest region, which the ancients called aether. Here therefore Hippocrates did not take heat for a mere quality, or an accident, but for an essential thing endowed with immortality; namely, for the universal substantial light, from whose nature that portion of animated beings is derived, which is called innate heat, without whose motion and heating effect the lives of creatures could in no way have been induced, because its presence [overcomes] the rebellious dispositions of the composite elements.

--- Page 177 ---
DE MICR. ANIM. MED. ACT. IN CORP. 175

...become obedient, and are quietly retained: indeed, the greater the proportion of this heat, the more efficacious and excellent is the act of life, and the healthier the composition of the whole composite body. From which it is clear that this nature is nothing other than a ray or spark of secondary or ethereal light, immediately infused into creatures with the ethereal Spirit; which Spirit is, as it were, the vehicle, nourishment, that passive and moist element, by whose presence and intervention heat and light (by metonymy, taking the effect for the cause) are carried downwards (because Spirit has a relation to Spirit) and acts upon a well-disposed subject. And this spirit is therefore called radical, because it is conjoined with heat in the first creation: Or it is, as it were, the root and tree of solar fruits; or it is the root and origin of the material creature, through whose joints or members it flows. Thus also that light or heat can be called innate, inasmuch as it is the first limit and point from which it moves towards generation; Or it is called innate, as if connatural with that natural moisture, which is the ethereal Spirit, in which it lives, and gives life to the creature in which it resides. Having considered these things well, we will perceive that this innate heat in its radical moisture is nothing other than that fifth essence, by whose consonance in a Diapente (a perfect fifth), the dissonance of the quaternary, which is an even and imperfect number, is reduced to harmonious peace. Therefore, philosophers, both theoretical and those engaged in the practice of alchemy, have handed down wonderful things concerning the virtue and power of this fifth essence. For they seem to acknowledge that it is nothing other than the union of the ethereal Spirit with its luminous soul: wherefore they assertively said that the fifth essence of a thing is the same as that vital soul, which they affirmed emanates from the middle sphere of the aether (which sphere they called the sphere of equality, and in which they placed the soul of the world). For even rustics, entirely ignorant of literature, know and have discovered by experience that plants and trees revive annually, and as it were, rejuvenate anew, and by its abundance, as from a glorious fount, have a multiplication of visible light. Furthermore, it is also the opinion of the more sagacious philosophers that the Sun and man procreate man. From these things, therefore, it is evident that the lives of creatures are of the essence of the Sun and are, as it were, seeds emitted downwards from its perennial fount. Hence some have said that the heaven is, as it were, the masculine part of the universal world; while the earth and its elements are the feminine part; indeed, that the earth is the universal matrix, receiving within itself the golden seeds of heaven and the Sun, which, in the womb of matter, pass through digestion into innumerable creatures of every species. But now, I will say what I have discovered by experience concerning these things in the anatomy of a vegetable creature. Indeed, I found its vital soul by the most subtle inquiry, in which I discovered the truest icon and image of the soul swimming in its Spirit; by the sight of which, I certainly perceived the composition of the celestial Sun in matter and form: For I found an immobile crystalline figure, most full of rays of light; which rays indeed seemed to extend hither and thither through that medium. This mobile matter indeed suddenly liquefied upon the application of fire, and became like blood; but then it was suddenly reduced to its pristine immobile form, like a crystal adorned everywhere with golden rays. Hence I evidently observed what that vegetable Spirit was, what light, what innate heat, what radical moisture, what the agent and what the patient, and finally what its vital soul was, what the fifth essence, and what the bond of the elements, connecting them to each other in harmonious peace; I also saw clearly enough that the Spirit there was the garment and vehicle: Whence I perceived with intellectual eyes that, by the same reasoning, the soul is the garment of the divine mind, just as the Spirit is the garment of the soul. Therefore, having now understood what the soul is, what the Spirit, what innate heat, and what radical moisture, and what the bond of the elements in the body, let us finally inquire how the soul-

how this whole soul may be infused into the whole and into any part of the body, and what may be the principal seat of this soul in the human body: For thus it is said that God's throne is in heaven, although His presence is everywhere present; or rather (lest indeed we compare divine things to earthly ones) we see that the solar body is in the heart of heaven, and yet its rays and presence are found everywhere through action. Therefore, we recognize through diligent inquiry that the principal seat of the vital soul is no less in the heart, which is situated in the middle of the middle region of the Microcosm, than the seat of the Sun is in the middle of heaven. If we have rightly considered the figure and position of this palace of life, we will perceive that it was ordered and disposed from creation according to the image, likeness, and position of the pyramid of the formal world; since its base tends upwards, but its cone downwards. By which it seems to become known that this corporeal organ is an instrument most occupied with the vital form: indeed, whose pyramidal figure the vital rays have undoubtedly delineated for us, whose nature it is to cast forth their rays downwards towards the earth. Therefore, this life-giving Spirit is present here with its royal light in the heart, as if in its own sphere. From which it disperses its rays, which are connected to its essence, throughout the entire body in no other way than the Sun from its middle sphere in heaven is accustomed to emit and cast forth its rays to the lowest and most remotely distant parts of the world. Therefore, it runs through the veins into the sanguineous mass or sea, and the aerial waves of the body, and finally through the limbs and more solid parts, in no other way than the Sun's rays through the elements into the aerial and watery sea, so that they may finally refresh the earth and its dense members. And hence it is that we are taught in the Sacred Scriptures that blood is, as it were, the garment and receptacle of souls. How this happens, however, is succinctly demonstrated by divine Philosophers. The soul, carried downwards through its medium, is first infused into the middle point of the heart, which is the center of the human body, and from there is diffused through all parts and members of the body, when it joins its chariot to natural heat, through heat to the Spirit arising from the heart; through this it immerses itself in the humors, through those it adheres to the members; and it is equally close to all these, although it is transfused through one into another; just as the heat of fire adheres most closely to air and water, although it is carried to water through the air. Thus it is clear that the ethereal vehicle of the immortal soul is enclosed by a coarser and mortal body. Similarly, Hermes *Trismegistus* says: *The Spirit diffused into the veins, arteries, and blood everywhere moves the animal, and holds the mass of the body suspended and carries it around, the soul in the spirit, reason in the soul, and mind in reason.* By these words indeed he teaches us most excellently how all the internal particles of man, by means of the Spirit, are dispensed throughout the entire human body. However, in this we cannot in any way agree with him, that the mind, or reason, or vital soul are transferred into all members of the body through the Spirit, and are present everywhere in equal portions in their essences. But we say that the mind inhabits the upper region of the Microcosm in the rational Spirit, as a more dignified place; and that the soul possesses its middle region, as its connatural seat. But nevertheless we say that these things are so in their regions, as God in the highest heaven and the Sun in the middle. For God, sitting in heaven, sends the rays of His presence into all parts of the world, according to that of the Wise Man (*Wisdom 1*): *The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world.* And (*Jeremiah*): *He made heaven His throne and the earth His footstool.* Thus also the human mind, derived from a divine stock, disperses the rays of its presence everywhere through the nerves, as through media, into the lower parts of the body, yet it itself constantly sits at the summit of the Microcosm, above the intellectual Spirit, as if carried by the wings of the winds. Similarly, as the Sun, possessing a position in the heart of heaven, communicates form to the lower things by its rays, and is said to be diffused everywhere through the elements by its power, essential light, and influx; so also the essence of the soul, constantly sitting in the human heart, sends its rays of life into all parts of man

--- Page 179 ---
...parts of man, both solid and fluid, is known to disperse, yet remaining in the heart, no less than the essence of the Sun in the middle of the sky or the solar body; which is not ineptly referred to the heart. Therefore, the aerial spirit, most familiar to the body, flows into and permeates all its members in the form of blood and humor, carrying with it traces of the ethereal Spirit, in whose streams the rays of ethereal light or rays of nature are carried; in which intellect and the rational Spirit, like certain atoms, or rather insensible habits, are emitted from on high, above and in which the Spirit of the Lord and the very subtle rays of the mind itself are perceived to swim immediately. Thus, from a certain source, in which there is either a mass of saffron, or a collection of blood, or even a cloth recently dipped in ink, we see the entire stream flowing from it being dyed, although the dyeing principle always remains in the source itself. Hence, therefore, every member of the body, with reason showing the way, is moved according to the mind's pre-established purpose towards good or utility. Hence it also happens that every member, by virtue of the rays of the vital soul, is moved both according to the direction of the rational Spirit, that is, by voluntary motion, and according to the faculties of life, by involuntary motion. For the middle soul moves the limbs and members of man to life, and reason governs that motion, so that it occurs according to the mind's institutions, unless that soul, subject to the natural soul, moves with irrational course like brutes. Therefore, the middle light becomes the primary motor in the animated being, and its Spirit or vehicle is that which is moved first: by whose motion, finally, the body is agitated and impelled to perform its functions. For it will not be impossible to derive a most evident demonstration of this from contracted inferior light or common fire with air; since we see that in the presence of fire, external air is moved, and led here and there according to the motion of that fire or life. Hence we also perceive images depicted on paper, along with the paper itself, to be moved around by the power of an illuminated candle, as we shall say below, where the light of the candle excites motion, and motion in turn stirs the air, and the air by its motion and agitation moves around the corporeal dimension of the paper and images.

C A P. IX.

*That the soul is like a spark of celestial light; that it is nourished by its own proper food; And concerning the reason why the luminous soul is suffocated when deprived of fresh air.*

We are taught by many observations, and with respect to a most worthy consideration, that the soul of any creature is, as it were, a spark of infinite light diffused through the universal spirit. For if you have diligently perused the treatise of this first volume, you will find by trustworthy demonstrations that the Empyrean heaven relates to the ethereal as the ethereal relates to the lowest and elemental heaven. By which we have proven that this elemental fire, which they call artificial, moves in its aerial medium in a similar manner and almost the same proportion, and performs its actions, as that celestial and solar fire moves in its ethereal vehicle; and likewise, the ethereal also produces operations in its spirit very similar to the operations of the supercelestial fire or light created on the first day in its spirit. This indeed happens because our common fire is immediately derived from the ethereal, and the ethereal from the Empyrean. However, we find this difference between the actions of one and the other, that the Empyrean fire commands much more than the ethereal fire, because its spirit is in a certain way pa-Z tiens

tient, entirely almost fiery, and on account of the smallness of its proportion and the tenuity of its substance, it is rendered formal. Whence it happens that, beyond human imagination, it is made obedient to the reason of its form. But indeed, ethereal fire, because it is joined with an equal portion of spirit, is more hindered in its operations or action by the resistance of that spirit: and hence it happens that this light does not govern its spirit with as much command as that light of the supreme heaven: Finally, the lowest portion of light is most strongly hindered on account of the multitude of matter residing there, and is constrained by the density and resistance of the matter; as you will find clearly expressed in *Tract. 1, vol. 1, chap. On artificial fire*. Hence therefore it is manifest that the reason of motion is the same in the lowest fire as it is in the middle, and the same in the middle as it is in the supreme. But the action of the lower is more blunted on account of the abundance and copiousness of resisting matter than the action of the celestial, and again, that celestial action is also more repressed for the same reason than the supercelestial. We conclude therefore that it is permissible for us, through experiments taken in this lowest region from the mutual actions of fire and air, to investigate higher mysteries and in some way to perceive the mutual operations of the heavens. Hence therefore we deduce that since common fire, like a spark or the flame of a lit candle, has the power to agitate the surrounding air in such a way that it rotates and moves a machine made of paper, such as is seen in almost every barber's shop at night, there is no doubt that by such a spark of celestial light or innate heat moving its ethereal spirit or radical moisture, the particular microcosmic machine is led hither and thither; and that by the virtue of the moved spirit, provoking the internal air by its motion. It is also proven that this inferior fire is very close in affinity to celestial fire, and even by this alone, that by its virtue, in due proportion, it is accustomed to hatch eggs and produce chicks, just as successfully as the natural heat of a hen derived from superior sources. For this experiment has been discovered and demonstrated not only in parts of Africa, but also in Europe itself, and proven in these our days; namely, that chicks, by the benefit of a moderately warm furnace, have been brought forth from their own shells or coverings, and brought into the light, who nevertheless lived according to the custom of nature. Similarly, in a heated hypocaust, we perceive flowers and shoots not yet budding suddenly to blossom by the power of igneous heat, and to push forth their inner parts.

But, to ascend now to celestial fire, do we not say that the Sun and man procreate man? Where by "Sun" the entire igneous substance of the heavens is understood, from whose spark, with the specification of man, man is generated: Do we not also see that worms of the earth receive their bodies from the earth, and their form or soul, by which they live, from the ethereal region? Whence philosophers wish them to be generated through putrefaction. This was also the poet's opinion regarding the generation of the serpent Python from the rays of the Sun and the mud of the earth, mixed with a little watery humidity after the deluge. By similar experience, we ourselves have also been taught that the entire substance of a dead crow, suspended in a sunny or exposed place, was converted by the life-giving power of the Sun into innumerable worms, and indeed within the space of a few days. We also read in some authors that bees emerged in great abundance from an ox's head, with celestial heat operating; which certainly had their souls not from a dead thing, but from celestial rays. Is that heat of horse dung, by whose virtue hairs are very often converted into worms and snakes, also much inferior to this fire? Animals of this kind I have seen with these my own eyes. What also shall we think about that monster, which, bearing the form of a Dragon, was found in a certain cave receiving putrid and foul waters, with the blood of animals flowing there through a channel from the kitchen of a certain English nobleman. That indeed, without doubt, received its soul from the light of putrefaction full of heat, but the substance of its body from putrid and quasi-menstrual matter, following the example of that Python. Diodorus Siculus also narrates that after the inundation of the Nile, when the water had almost dried up, and the earth, having become drier, had acquired the form of mud from the Sun, many beasts were, as it were, newly created, among which he reports some were created only in half, while others were found in complete form. From all these examples it is manifest that vital souls, suitable for living bodies, are nothing other than, as it were, rays and celestial sparks derived from the luminous fount of the universe, which we have named above as acts of nature.

Since therefore the matter stands thus in these two inferior heavens, why should not reason and intellect also proceed from that universal fount of supercelestial light, whose rays they are, since they are acts of that Creator; which supercelestial and divine rays not only philosophers but also those more skilled in theology have spoken of? Here, however, a doubt not unworthy of resolution comes to our mind, namely: Is the soul nourished by some food or not? It is certain that the soul no less requires its own proper nourishment for its presence than other things in nature need their food: this indeed can be demonstrated by many arguments. For we see that every action of the body proceeds from the soul: But indeed its entire operation revolves around nourishment, namely in the appetite for food, its preparation, attraction to the stomach, retention, sanguification, and other similar things. Wherefore the vital soul seems to require nourishment both for itself and for the sustenance of its machine (body). Furthermore, experience teaches us that if the nourishment of air is diverted from the heart due to a lack of inspiration for a single quarter of an hour, immediately the soul itself, as it were...

--- Page 183 ---
DE MICR. ANIM. MED. ACT. IN CORP. 181

the light of the soul is extinguished and dies. We also observe that fire requires the presence of air, as if it were the nourishment of its life. For if a burning fire is enclosed in a place surrounded by walls, so that air cannot enter there, it will suddenly be extinguished, and as it were, killed: Whence it is certain that the nourishment of inferior fire is air, and that the nourishment of ethereal fire is the ethereal Spirit. But what of this? Will the vital soul therefore die? Certainly, as far as we are concerned, it dies, and, as far as we are concerned, it requires nourishment, although, if we consider the nature of light with intellectual eyes, it is clear that it neither requires nourishment nor dies. For, although the soul and light and fire seem to seek aerial fuel for themselves, they do not do this out of a necessity for food, as if they could not live without it; but rather so that they may obtain a passive [element] in that way, upon which they may act, as upon a well-disposed subject. For it is impossible for light, which is pure act, to subsist unless it acts upon some subject: for it always acts, nor does it cease to act upon some subject to a greater or lesser extent. However, the effects of its action do not aim at nourishing itself, but at first warming the passive subject, and through its heat attenuating and refining it, and finally exalting that refined [subject] and making it spiritual from a corporeal thing. Hence, therefore, we see that when it cannot find other sufficient nourishment upon which to act, it consumes its own dwelling; as we see in the consumptive: Whence it is certain that it does not operate for its own sake, but for the sake of the matter, both spiritual and material, with which it dwells. But that innate and connate moisture is suitable for it, and durable with it forever; and it is as if Psyche joined with Cupid in complete love. And although fire, when wood is burned up or air is excluded, suddenly seems to be suffocated, it does not die, but due to the deficient succession of denser air, it is dissipated through the air, either enclosed or open, and thus becomes invisible again, as it was before. For all air is filled with invisible fire; which indeed is invisible because it is dispersed and rarefied throughout the medium. Therefore, fire seems to be extinguished and to lose its life when it returns to its invisible nature: since those things which we see in the body and matter behave differently and in a contrary manner in the soul. For the body, the more it ages, the more it is weakened, while conversely the soul, the longer it lives in the body, the more it rejuvenates, and is enriched with knowledge, counsel, and prudence: so also the weight of the body is in gravity, but that of the soul is in lightness and subtlety; inasmuch as its perfection consists in these degrees. And so in other things. It is therefore clear how the soul requires its nourishment, and how it is then thought to die and be extinguished, when in reality it is regenerated and freed from the constraints of the body.

### CHAP. I.
*Concerning the properties of the sensitive or animal soul, or the inferior portion*
*of the inner man in the human body.*

[Large decorative initial 'Q' containing a floral design.]
Although the middle soul by its nature is of the freest condition,
and of infinite dignity, knowledge, beauty, and perfection;
nevertheless, inasmuch as it is comprehended with the mind, which it carries with itself under one
species, and is too much overshadowed by the perishable body, to that extent it is depressed, and contrary to its nature, to contemplate inferior things,
as if destitute of spiritual eyes, it is rendered prone. And hence it is that it is led by sense contrary to its nature, and,
looking downwards against that nature of its own to contemplate and admire
vile and abject things, it is rendered prone; because its natural disposition,

C A P. III.

*How the soul is obscured by carnal sense and forgets itself: And by what
reason, it (the soul) itself passes through vices or sensual things into the nature
of the body; then also conversely the flesh is accustomed to migrate through
virtue into the nature of the spirit. Similarly concerning the virtues of the soul
in general and concerning the senses.*

Just as this mediating soul, adhering to the mind, or illuminated by the rays of wisdom, looks back to its principle, and contemplates the highest good, and knows itself; so also, deprived of the mind's rays and divine illumination, it is lulled to sleep by bodily passions and drawn outside itself through sensible forms, and seeks outside itself those things which it can find within itself, indeed, it completely forgets what it is, or what it has been, and, remembering nothing else that it has been, it believes nothing exists except what is seen: it is occupied solely with sense concerning bodies and imagination concerning the likenesses of bodies and places, and in these it is exercised whether waking or sleeping.

The absence of the mind's rays, therefore, is the cause of such great friendship between body and soul; according to which friendship *no one hates his own flesh*. For although it is weighed down by the companionship of the flesh or body, according to that saying of the Wise Man: *The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that muses upon many things*, etc. nevertheless, it loves it in an ineffable way, and loves its prison; and therefore it cannot be free, but is vehemently afflicted by those pains; it fears destruction, though it cannot die; it fears decay, though by nature it cannot decay, it feeds on the sight of eyes, is delighted by sonorous voices, rejoices in the sweetest odors, and is refreshed by lavish feasting. And, although it (the soul) in no way uses these things itself; yet it is afflicted with grave sorrow if they are withdrawn.

Hence also, vices contrary to reason sometimes creep in, while the soul, by indulging too freely in the body's delights, is known to give place to sin. The manner, however, in which this happens, is as follows: through the senses the soul proceeds to move and vivify the body: there are also nine openings in the human body through which, according to natural temperament, everything flows in and out, by which the same body is nourished and governed: There are also certain similarities of both; namely, the highest part of the body, and the lowest part of the spirit, in which, although without a personal confusion of natures, they can nevertheless be easily joined in union: For like rejoices in like, and so the soul, which is spirit, and the flesh, which is truly body, are easily and conveniently united at their extremities. In the imaginative faculty of the soul, there is indeed not a body, but something similar to a body, as will be said in the following harmony, nor in the sensuality of the flesh, which is almost spirit and cannot exist without the soul. But just as the highest part of the soul, namely intelligence or mind, bears the image of its superior, that is, of God; whence it could receive Him, and received Him for personal union, when it willed, without any diminution of its nature; so in a similar way the highest part of the flesh, that is, the sensuality of the soul, bears a likeness, and is able to receive its essence for personal union. Nor is that wonderful, since even in the sense and memory of a beast there is a certain modification of rationality, and in its appetite a modification of will, and in those things which it shuns a modification of reprobation: for the corporeal spirit, which is truly body, discerns among many things by natural sense, and chooses by the power of concupiscibility, and rejects by the power of irascibility. It is therefore clear from these things that these are the most suitable intermediaries between flesh and soul; namely, the sensuality of the flesh, which is fire, and the imaginative faculty of the spirit, which is fiery vigor

--- Page 188 ---
186 TRACT. I. SECT. I. LIB. IX.
is called vigor. Hence, I say, arises that wonderful society which exists between flesh and soul, between the spirit of life and the light of the earth. But since the soul, possessing its rational faculty, and without flesh, is rational, concupiscible, and irascible, it follows that through its rationality it is capable and fit to be enlightened to know the truth within itself, and above itself, and in itself, and beside itself. For thus it knows God above itself, itself in itself, the Angel beside itself, and whatever is contained within the ambit of heaven below itself. Similarly, through concupiscibility and irascibility it is capable of affections for desiring or fleeing something, for loving or hating. And therefore from rationality every sense of the soul arises; just as from the other two all affections [arise]; namely, from concupiscibility joy and hope, and from irascibility sorrow and fear arise: which four affections of the soul are, as it were, certain principles and common material of all vices as well as virtues. And it seems no small wonder that the same affections of the soul can produce offspring and children so contrary in nature, such as vices and virtues, since virtue is defined as _a habit of a well-composed mind; vice, on the other hand, a habit of a badly disposed soul, and overwhelmed by darkness._ But, unless I am mistaken, there is the same difference between enlightened and obscure or dark reason as there is between virtue and vice. For reason lacking illumination is prone to dwell in darkness and error, and to produce vices of every kind; while however the same reason, when enlightened, is governed by intelligence and directed in the way of truth. And this is what we said above, namely, that the Spirit adhering to the mind produces virtues, but when deprived of the mind's rays, it generates vices and errors, or contracts them for itself. Hence, I say, it is that of the rational soul lacking illumination, the concupiscible power gives birth to carnal joy and worldly pleasures; inasmuch as it is accustomed to generate impudence, gluttony, the allurements of the belly, sloth, ambition, avarice, vain glory, and countless other vices of this kind, and to produce them as effects. So also its irascible power is observed to generate and bring forth rage, fury, bestial anger, quarrels, war, unjust hatred, injury, fear, shame, audacity and pusillanimity, betrayal, dissimulation, falsehood or lying, and innumerable other things of that nature. When however, conversely, if the rational soul is enlightened by the mind, its powers (namely, concupiscible and irascible) produce fruits of a contrary nature; namely virtues, which are habits of a well-composed mind: for in the light of the mind we compose, institute, and order the affections of the soul to that which they ought to regard, and how they ought, so that they can perfect virtues: Hence it happens that without such light the aforesaid affections of the soul very easily slide into vices. When therefore a holy splendor is present to our souls, then prudently, modestly, bravely, and justly our loves and hates will be instituted, and will rise into those four original or cardinal virtues; namely, into prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance. Similarly, through hatred of the world and of ourselves we progress in the love of God and neighbor; through contempt of temporal and inferior things we grow in the desire for eternal and superior things. From these things therefore we see that, just as the soul by its presence vivifies the body or flesh, so also it itself through such a vivifying power is so bound to this body that it cannot, when it wishes, separate itself from it, nor even, when it hears the voice of the Creator, be retained therein. Indeed, the life of the body consists in the life of the soul, and from the death of the body descends the death of the soul. For just as the soul makes the flesh living by its life, and irrigates it from the fount of its nature by animating it, so the flesh, through the corruption of its matter, kills the soul if it binds it with illicit desires. And, since one leans upon the nature of the other, each passes into the nature of the victor; so that either the soul renders the flesh spiritual by its virtues, or the victorious flesh makes the soul carnal. C H A P. IV.

*On the origin of the external senses; Why they are expressed in the face; that*
*they are causes of errors in man; similarly, on the*
*origin of imagination.*

IN the anterior part of the brain or face, the senses are thus formed. There is something in the body most subtle and most active, and from this most similar and close to the soul, indeed almost an external effect of the operative faculty in the soul itself, which Philosophers have called light. This central light is first diffused through the eyes, and shines forth in the rays of the eyes for beholding visible things; then it constitutes hearing, smell, taste, and touch through a certain mixture, first indeed with pure air, then with dark and cloudy air, thirdly with a more corpulent humor, and fourthly with earthy grossness, and thus it perfects the five senses with sight itself or the sense of the eyes. Where, however, sight alone excels because of the purity of its act. These senses are expressed in the face alone, as I believe, because the Lord God breathed into the face of man the breath of life, when he was made into a living soul. For the anterior part is deservedly preferred to the posterior; because the former leads, the latter follows; from the former, senses; from the latter, movements, just as counsel precedes action. These faculties can be called faculties of both the soul and the body, because they are made by the soul in the body, nor can they be produced without both. But so that we may declare this matter still more clearly, it must be understood that the human body is composed of four elements; and that in flesh and bones, earth is especially discerned, water, however, in the humors, air, furthermore, is contained in the blood and lung; which indeed, always existing in motion, is like the fan of the heart, lest it be consumed and dissolved by excessive heat, since the seat of ethereal fire is in the heart. Hence one part of it is sharp, like the tip of a fiery flame, the other part, however, is broad, like the base of a flame. There is, moreover, a certain fiery part tempered by air or ether; which ascends from the heart to the brain, as if from the ethereal heaven of the body into its empyrean heaven. This, however, purified and filtered through the eyes, ears, nostrils, and other instruments of the senses, proceeds outwards, and, formed by contact with external things, constitutes the five bodily senses, namely sight and hearing and smell, and taste and touch; which sense of touching, passing from the anterior part of the brain to the posterior parts, thence through the neck and spinal marrow, is diffused throughout the whole body by the power of the nerves originating therefrom. Furthermore, this fiery power itself, which is formed externally, is called sense; and the same form, through those very instruments of the senses, through which it emerges, and in which it is formed, by nature operating, is drawn inwards to the phantastic cell, all the way back, and imagination is produced. Afterwards, the same imagination, passing from the anterior part of the head to the middle, touches the very substance of the rational soul and excites discernment, to such an extent now purifi-

--- Page 191 ---
DE ANIMÆ SENSIT. ACTU IN CORP. 189

...purified and made subtle, so that it may be immediately joined to the spirit itself; yet truly retaining the nature of the body, and its property or rather its likeness. This imagination, in brutes, does not transcend the phantastic cell. In rational beings, however, it becomes purer, and advances and is carried up to touch the rational and incorporeal substance of the soul. Imagination is therefore a likeness of the body, conceived externally through the bodily senses from the contact of bodies, and reduced inwards through the same senses to the purer part of the corporeal spirit, and impressed upon it; namely, at the summit of the corporeal spirit, and at the base of the rational spirit, informing the corporeal and touching the rational spirit; which I call air or rather fire, which, due to its subtlety, cannot be seen, and inwardly vivifies bodies by vegetating them. This force, moreover, vegetates certain things and does not sensify them, such as trees, herbs, and all things germinating in the earth; certain things it vegetates and sensifies simultaneously, such as brute animals, in which some have sense but do not have imagination; while others have both sense and imagination. Since, therefore, to be sensified is more than simply to be merely vegetated; it is certainly evident that this force is more subtle; And where it is more subtle, there is more spirit. And consequently, it indeed approaches incorporeal nature more when it forms imagination than when it provides sense. For nothing in the body can be higher, or nearer to spiritual nature, than that wherein, after sense, the power of imagining is conceived. And this is so sublime that whatever is above it is nothing other than reason. Hence, therefore, it is manifest that sense and imagination consist of corporeal spirit; but the former from a denser and more perceptible spirit; the latter, however, from a more subtle spirit, and one closest to the rational spirit in its tenuity; so that the spirit of sense can be likened to air, and that of imagination to ether; from which the visible world consists. But truly, if we wish to reach the ultimate limits, it will be necessary to purify our spirits yet higher by one degree. If this is not done, it will be impossible to pass from corporeal and sensible things to spiritual and intellectual ones, from the visible world to the invisible, from darkness to light, from the deceptive power of the devil to the vision of God and the investigation of truth. From the sensible and intellectual spirit, therefore, is forged the existence and power of the animal or sensual and sensitive soul, or idol, whose violence makes the soul more prone to flesh and worldly pleasures, as we declared above. Hence the struggle of the animal soul with the mind, because just as it rarely receives the mind's rays, so the rays of the flesh arise from animal sense and motion. The animal force, therefore, was produced from the mind no differently than Lucifer from God: Lucifer, partaking of matter and darkness, became rebellious against his Creator; The animal or sensitive soul, brought forth from nothing into noble action by the operation of the mind, has become rebellious against the author of its existence, joins itself with flesh and body, and moves it against the laws of illuminated reason, unless it is hindered by divine rays and governed by the bridle of most holy justice, according to that of the Wise Man, Wisdom 9.
*We estimate with difficulty what is on earth, and what is before our eyes we find with labor;*
*But who will investigate what is in the heavens? And who will know your mind, unless you give wisdom and send your spirit from the highest heavens? And thus the paths of those who are on earth were corrected, and men learned what pleases you. For by wisdom were healed all those, O Lord, who pleased you from the beginning.*
Whence it is manifest that the disobedience of the senses and the flesh is removed by the splendor and power of the spirit descending from on high, and that their malice is converted into goodness, and thus the never-satisfied appetite of the body now rests in the presence of divine wisdom, is lulled to sleep, and rendered obedient to illuminated reason.
