*CHAPTER V.*

*Concerning the exterior senses; and first concerning sight and hearing, and why the senses*
*are deceived concerning their proper objects.*


Therefore, the exterior senses, which we declared above to be five in number, receive their power and effect from igneous virtue, through nerves and other organs, as if through dispersed instruments, by which, also through the vital color of the muscles, sensible spirits are moved downwards from the animal faculty, and are observed to move the muscles and other parts by involuntary motion, according to the instinct of reason. Of these senses, however, two are principal *and simple*, namely *Sight and Hearing*, as is demonstrated in the preceding chapter. The others, however, are *less principal*, namely *Touch, Smell, and Taste*. We call those principal, therefore, because they regard the simple parts of the world's constitution; these, however, *less principal*, inasmuch as they embrace the entire substance of the world, consisting of matter and form, and affect it by their movement. By simple parts of the world's composition, we mean that simple spiritual matter, which we recalled above is called and named "waters" by the scriptures by a universal name, and light, which is the more formal part of the world, as it is by whose presence the universal waters or spirits, still potential and formless, were made actual and formal out of nothing. Therefore, universal spirit or air is the medium around which Hearing is concerned; and light is the unique object that is seen, and through which bodies are said to be colored, and in which all things are perceived. For nothing is seen except luminous things; because whatever is discerned, we behold it in the splendor of light. Sight, therefore, is concerned with the divine image, by whose virtue the Israelites, led by Moses, beheld the glory of God immediately emanating from His face with remarkable splendor, and even now every creature of the animal world endowed with eyes joyfully contemplates the same glory, proceeding mediately from Him through infinite reflections. This is indeed most strongly confirmed by the fact that the property and nature of light are so strong and effective over all things that exist in the world, and especially over spirit, which claims the second place in the world, so that no thing, and indeed not even the density of transparent spirit itself, can impede its penetrative faculty. We perceive its excellence over aerial spirit from this, that in the crash of thunder, the light of the flash is discerned sooner than the sound or crackle reaches the ears. From which it is evident is the efficacy of light over that of matter, and consequently, that it is the effigy or image of the Creator Himself, whose movement and influence nothing can resist: For just as the will of God is immediately accomplished without any obstacle; so too the effect of light is discerned and seen from afar, and as it were in the blink of an eye, without any impediment from the medium, since, just as God is a unity which, multiplied in itself, always results in itself, to such an extent indeed that He Himself will always be the same as He was from the beginning, so also light seen from afar, though it is only one, reaches the acuity of the eye in the same way it emanates from a cloud or other subject, without any division of its essence. But indeed, sound or voice or crash is divided, and multiplied many times in the air, and in its multiplication, it is partly continued, partly divided. Hence it happens that the crackle of a cannon seems smaller from a distance than it truly is. From these things, therefore, it is evident that the sense of sight is to be preferred to hearing by as many degrees as light is preferred to Spirit;

--- Page 193 ---
DE ANIMÆ SENSIT. ACTU IN CORP. 191

to Spirit. Similarly, that sight is a simple sense, and more active, and inherently so, inasmuch as it is completed by the power of a luminous act, but hearing is indeed likewise a simple sense, but more passive and incidentally so, inasmuch as that medium, through which hearing occurs, is subjected to the actions of light, and conveys sounds to the ears by various reverberations and multiplications. Therefore, the effect of sight is admirable, since by its power a true artist, following the discipline of mirror optics, can behold the icon and likeness of God, in the multiform color of the rainbow, and also in a thousand other ways, not without stupendous admiration, indeed, so that by such an artist's gaze, those divine colors of the Deity and His glory, which it once beheld with spiritual eyes in its supracelestial homeland, while it was still free, seem to be recalled to memory. How ineffable, therefore, is the power of this sense due to the nobility of its object, and how admirable, how abstruse and hidden things it is able to reveal to us, human ingenuity has scarcely ever been able to explain to the world, if indeed it was permitted. Similarly, the Spirit itself, which is the medium without which hearing cannot occur, comprehends miraculous and arcane things within itself through the presence of divine light; which indeed the wise have not wished to reveal, or to publish and promulgate; nay, they have not dared; lest they incur the Lord's curse. In these two, therefore, consists all operation of magic, both natural and supernatural, all governance of animal life and the universal act of the world, and the effects of the heavens and the stirring of the stars. By these, the eye of the world sees all things that occur in the cavity of the world; by these, angels behold these lower things, and look up to the throne of God; by these, animals are accustomed to distinguish good from evil; by these, the intention of one person is understood by another; by these, one thing is perceived to differ from another; and by these, the harmony of one soul, enclosed in a body, is perceived to accord or disagree with the harmony of another. Indeed, we could fill an entire volume with the praises and virtues of these two senses, were not the necessity of this subject to call us to other matters. But here I wish the Reader to understand in a single word, that the corporeal eye beholds very few true and certain things, but infinite falsehoods and deceptions; the reason for which is the dominion of darkness within us, which deceives us with fallacies, and makes those things appear to us which are not such as they seem. For whatever is perceived, is seen in the body, which indeed is nothing in itself, since whatever it has, it receives from the luminous form. Therefore, we follow matter; but we neglect form, and thus we are deceived, because matter is from darkness, and darkness is from nothing, and therefore also, that which is corporeal, is nothing per se and in itself: But if anything exists, it receives all its being from form, which is from light, from whose source is the life of things; for the Word, in whom and from whom is life, is the sole truth, and whatever exists outside this truth is deceptive, and from the prince of lies. But now let us hear the Ethnic Philosophers. _Proclus, as it were, concludes all this in one word: "Matter," he says, "seems to be all things, though in reality it possesses nothing."_ We also see in the variety of mirrors a varied figure of the same thing and a differing dimension of that body appear, although the truth of the thing is unique. Thus we observe the same face in a convex mirror contracted in length, but excessively widened and extended in breadth, while in a concave mirror we see it horribly drawn out and extended in length, but wonderfully contracted in breadth. But in a flat and polished mirror, we again behold this same image arranged in a just manner, and according to the indication of the natural eye. Therefore, we are all deceived; and it is impossible to discern what is true, unless it is done in holy splendor and truth; in which we behold all things as they truly are: For how many deceptions, illusions, and fascinations an impious magician is accustomed to induce with the help of the devil, both historical accounts and innumerable oral narrations have indicated to us; yet the effect of which is nothing

are nothing else than visual deceptions, and vain things, which are not truly such as they seem to be, no more than a painting of a man is truly the man himself, to whom it is assimilated. Hence says the Wise Man, Wisdom 9: *For the corruptible body is a load upon the soul, and the earthly habitation presseth down the mind that museth upon many things. Therefore, by these things we are taught how fallacious, uncertain, and miserable human life is without the true knowledge of Christ, who is the sole truth, life, and light of things, since without it all things are vain, deceptive, and fallacious. I would also like you to observe this unique experiment concerning the sense of hearing: that its medium is both water and thick air, nor is air anything other than thin water. For *when I was living in Nîmes in Languedoc in France, in its famous bottomless spring (as they say, because its depth is not known), sometimes in the evening hours, around sunset, I swam for recreation and refreshment, and having taken two stones separately in each hand, I immersed myself quite deeply, for the sake of making an experiment, into the water among the bare rocks protruding everywhere, and thus remaining underwater, I struck these stones against each other. From which it happened that a horrible and scarcely credible sound was heard.* By which I was assured that hearing, because of the density of the medium, becomes many degrees more distinct and powerful in water than in the air itself, inasmuch as in the latter all things are more kindly, mild, and more suitable to human nature.

                                   CHAPTER VI.
                          *On Touch, Smell & Taste.*

JUST as God in the creation of man placed and situated the mind and reason in its highest and noblest region, namely in the head; so also he joined to it five bearers or ministers, by whose use and movement, or rather through whom, as bodily and sensible organs, it might exercise its powers concerning things to be perceived. For it is the nature of the human mind to behold and contemplate spiritual and insensible things by itself, without body or sense. But truly, inasmuch as it regards sensible things, it is necessary that it acts through the body and its external senses, inasmuch as without these it cannot judge concerning gross, visible, tangible, and similar other things. Therefore, the five senses offer to the sight of reason whatever things are necessary to it for the knowledge of bodies; and they show to it those things by which it is aided in the knowledge of things pertaining to visible, audible, tangible bodies, etc. These, moreover, serve the human body no differently than sailors serve for the direction of a ship, whose captain and principal leader, or governor and guide, is the mind in its reasoning capacity, directing the course by a certain magnetic power, and observing the ship's course at its summit by the property and direction of the marine needle, which points to the Arctic pole. But through these its ministers, reason is warned concerning external occurrences happening to the ship, and concerning its prosperous journey, or concerning a rock threatening danger to the ship, so that, what evil to it

--- Page 195 ---
DE ANIMÆ SENSIT. ACTU IN CORP. 193
ON THE SOUL'S SENSATION AND ACTION IN THE BODY. 193

that threatens it on its path, it may avoid, and what is good and salutary for it, it may wisely choose. Moreover, to each of these bearers, its own distinct property is separately assigned. For sight, by its own property, is concerned with ten things; namely, concerning light and darkness, color and body, figure and actions, remoteness and proximity, motion and rest; all of which, however, as has been said above, are reduced to the sole property of light. For darkness is known through the opposition of light, color is discerned through the operation of light on the surface of a body, and so in the others.

The property of hearing is to be concerned with two kinds of sounds; namely, concerning animal and non-animal voices; of which the former are either rational, pertaining to human speech, or irrational, such as the roaring of lions, the neighing of horses, the chirping of birds, etc. but the latter are devoid of animal life, such as the sound of a drum, a pipe, the rustling of winds, thunder, etc. Concerning these two, moreover, as the principal bearers of reason, we shall not write much here, since we have spoken above about their internal dispositions. For I myself have been taught by experience that all foulness comes from the element of fire, mixed with impure spirit or air: Then also air produces some foulness, but less than fire, because of its impurity and uncleanness, which it has from the other elements. But all sweetness, by which the soul is delighted, flows from heaven, where ether with light obtains equal weights and proportions in harmonious peace and in Astræa's scales and balances; just as I myself have often experienced with admiration in the chemical anatomy of bodies. Indeed, coldness is contrary to the faculty of any sense, affecting the organs rather with numbness than offering them any help. For it is in every way contrary to the faculty of the senses; since their perfection requires the presence of tempered heat, by which they may operate. But coldness is accustomed to remove this by its predominance. Similarly, the dilation of pores and organs is required for the complete function of the senses. But it is characteristic of coldness to obstruct and close passages. The senses also desire subtle spirits, by which they can swiftly and effectively perform their functions. But it is characteristic of coldness to condense and thicken what was subtle, and consequently, it is most opposed to the senses in its nature. Hence it is, therefore, that coldness is accustomed to induce the obstruction of pores and the thickening of membranes, blindness of the eyes, and also the thickening and condensation of humors in the optic nerve. Likewise, it harms hearing by obstructing the organs and by thickening and drying the viscous matter and by affecting the limbs with torpor and numbness; whence coldness is also adverse to Touch. It also obstructs the nostrils and extinguishes the natural heat of the organs, by virtue of which the sense ought to distinguish odors correctly. It harms Taste by numbing the parts of the tongue, by whose benefit this sense is accustomed to operate; and sometimes it is observed to induce mortification and gangrene in the throat and gums. All these things being rightly understood, it is certain that earthly coldness is not the cause of odor, whether foul or sweet; but rather, the sense of smell and olfaction always occur because of the presence of heat. And although some perhaps will object that *opium itself, being cold, emits a very foul odor*, nevertheless that does not happen because of the coldness of the medicine; but rather it is recognized to emanate from a hidden hot disposition. For in the same simple substance, contrary qualities and natures are often observed to exist. For example: *Fumitory or earth-smoke*, although it is cold and dry in operation, yet no one of sound mind will doubt that it has drawn its bitterness from fire. And so, the dispositions and natures of the external senses having been explained quite clearly, as it seems to us, we will briefly bring this part to an end.

C A P.  VII.

**On the natural faculty that all vegetation occurs from the liver**
**or the aerial mass of the Microcosm.**


REGARDING the natural faculty in the generation of blood, and in the composition, preservation, nutrition, and maintenance in the same state of the body's parts and elements, we have spoken somewhat in the preceding [sections]. Here, however, we will show that the principal reason for the body's vegetation depends on this internal faculty of man. It must therefore be known first of all that all vegetation and multiplication of the body, both in animals and in plants, proceeds from an aerial disposition. Yet, aerial nature cannot accomplish this by itself, unless it is aided by superior [influences], both Macrocosmic and Microcosmic. For the natural faculty, according to the opinion of Astrologers, is principally governed by the Moon and Venus, which increase and foster the natural, vegetative, and generative power and spirit; to which Jupiter also wonderfully joins itself in such work by its disposition, inasmuch as it is humid and hot in the most temperate degree.

CH A P. IX.

On our principles of the Microcosm, and how they agree as much with the principles of divine letters as with the intentions of all Philosophers and Chemists?

Now furthermore we will demonstrate how this our doctrine or Philosophy is consonant and in agreement with all the opinions of both Theologians and also ancient Philosophers and Physicians in the description of human physiology; and first indeed, proceeding methodically, we will begin from the primary principles of all things. Therefore, in the first book of our first Tractate, where we treated of principles, we clearly declared that the principles of all things are Darkness, Waters or the intermediate Spirit, and Light; and we said that darkness is the origin of deformity and the immediate cause of formal privation, declaring that it is not a mere accident, but is to be understood as a certain unimaginable thing overwhelmed by darkness; which indeed seemed to be between something and nothing. Moses spoke of such Egyptian darkness in Exodus, which he called palpable. Therefore, this darkness was

--- Page 203 ---

darkness, as it were, a veil of a thing scarcely imaginable and utterly formless. This *Moses* acknowledged in *Genesis 1*, when he says that darkness was upon the face of the deep. By the empty earth, he also understood darkness devoid of all informing light; from which, by means of light, the earth, germinating, green, and fertile, was created on the third day and produced in the center of the cosmos by the light-reflecting power. Hence, therefore, the health and infirmity, life and death of the body proceed from the humors, and by their succession the members of the body arise and are nourished. CHAP. I.
*On the first kind of vision, by which, namely, the soul perceives corporeal things*
*through sense; and how it is sometimes deceived*
*in this vision of its own?*

[Large decorative initial 'T' set within a square frame, depicting figures in a landscape with trees and a building]
We have observed three kinds of visions in the soul from their infallible effect; the first of which is corporeal, by which, through the senses of the body, colored bodies of things and their dimensions and other things obvious to the senses are perceived. For although the substance and condition of the soul is invisible, and consequently remains invisibly in the body; nevertheless, looking out from the body and, as it were, invisibly going forth, it sees bodies through the body, namely, heaven and earth and the creatures in them, visible to our eyes. And this vision of the soul is accomplished through the external senses of the body. The second kind of vision in the soul is spiritual, by which the likenesses of bodies are perceived by the spirit alone, and not by reason or mind. For whatever is material, and yet is not a body, that is rightly and deservedly called spirit. Therefore, by a certain hidden and spiritual force, the soul is so rapt that it sees their expressed likenesses in place of bodies, as if in a mirror. The third kind of vision is intellectual, by which those things are perceived which have neither bodies nor forms of bodies; such as, the mind itself, God, justice, wisdom, and every good affection of the soul. For by intellectual vision the soul is never deceived. For either the soul understands, and what it understands is true; or if it is not true, it does not understand. But in corporeal vision the soul very often errs and is deceived, according to that old and true axiom of the Philosophers; the sense is deceived concerning its proper and true object, when it thinks that what appears in the imagination happens in the bodies themselves. For example. To those sailing, the land, cities, trees, and similar things seem to move; similarly, to those standing firmly on the earth and looking up at the sky

--- Page 207 ---
ON THE TRIPLE VISION OF THE SOUL IN THE BODY. 205
the stars seem to stand still; yet diligent observation has taught men that all these move from east to west, and vice versa. Furthermore, when the rays of the eyes are divergent, a single object will appear to have a double form, and a broken stick will appear in water, and many other things of that kind. Indeed, among all other senses, *sight* especially, though the most excellent, is deceived. For in a mirror we sometimes see a larger image, sometimes a smaller, and sometimes an equal one; similarly, in another [mirror], the right will appear to be the left, and vice versa; so also what is up will appear to be down, and vice versa. Sometimes the image will appear outside the mirror, as is proven in concave ones; sometimes indeed inside the mirror; And likewise in one mirror, namely in an oblong concave one, an object will appear longer than it is, while in a convex one shorter than it is, and in a plane one it will appear as it exists in its natural form: However, in plane mirrors the right will appear

Thus the Ram of the sky seems to have the likeness of an earthly ram. And the Milky Way appears to be such as it is not, but rather it is a likeness of what it appears to be. We also attribute intellect and the soul's vision through it to supracelestial things, in which neither body nor the image of any corporeal or sensible thing is found, such as God, the rational and intellectual mind, reason, the cardinal virtues, chastity, piety, and whatever else is of that kind, which we enumerate, discern, and define by understanding or thinking, as has been said above. even between the vision of the sleeping and the true cognition of the waking, no distinction is made, but continuously their flesh is moved, and against their own purpose, or against lawful customs, they seem to lie together, and what is naturally collected, they emit through the genital passages; which action indeed physicians have called *nocturnal pollution*. This movement chaste waking people restrain and curb, which the sleeping therefore cannot suppress, because they do not have in their power the expression of the bodily image, by which the flesh is naturally moved, whence follows that which, when restrained, was wont to follow, and, what cannot be done without sin by the waking, happens in the spirit, and many things are imagined at will, or are shown beyond will, while images of bodily things appear. For the soul itself, which by its own motion is always in motion, because it is not limited by the body, or indeed is plainly not allowed to feel bodily things, or to direct the force of its intention towards bodily things, therefore, with the body asleep, it acts by itself in spirit, just as it is accustomed to turn over images of bodies by thinking from itself, or it beholds subjects, when it is taken up by some spirit to see them.

But I would like you to note, O Readers, reading these our works with an open mind, that we are not now speaking of the mind; which we have proven above to be subject to no passion or changeability, but of the middle soul in the body, mixed with senses and the corporal spirit attributed to imagination, which if it is joined to the body through sense, that is, if it beholds corporeal visibles by corporal vision, it can be called corporeal by its effect, but if it is engaged through phantasy concerning the vision of spiritual things and similarities of bodies, it is called spiritual, and so also, if it is occupied through intellect concerning vision, in which neither bodies nor similarities of bodies are seen, it is called rational and intellectual. For if this soul adheres to the mind, then its vision is more engaged with the mind and intellect. But if it is more subjected to the sensitive soul, then it uses its lower visions.

This soul is therefore a spiritual substance, formed from light and a middle spirit, and consequently simple and indissoluble, incorporeal, passible and mutable with respect to the abundance of its spirit, which is passible; but indeed, as to its lucid form, permanent, fixed, and immutable. Therefore, the more it inclines downwards, the more it is submerged by spirit, and consequently subjected to passion. But the more it is elevated upwards towards the mind, the less it is burdened by the perturbations of matter. Hence, in the region of the mind, where it produces intellectual visions, it always beholds true things, because of its freedom from passions and the excellent operation of the most powerful light. But indeed, in its lower visions, it very often contemplates false things for true, because of the coarseness of the medium in which it swims. Thus an oar or straight stick, plunged into water, will appear to be broken and bent because of the density of the medium; whence such things will appear to be what they truly are not, and thus the soul will be deceived.

The soul also lacks weight, shape, and color, inasmuch as it is invisible and not to be grasped by sense. Nor indeed is it to be taken as a part, but as a creature of God, nor even of the substance of God, except insofar as it participates in His lucid good: nor is it made of the matter of the four elements, but created from nothing with a fifth essential spirit, for if God had made it from Himself, it would by no means be subject to vice, passion, changeability, or misery. Furthermore, if it were made from elements, it would be corporeal. Therefore it has a beginning, but it is certain that it lacks an end. And since it is spiritual and ethereal, it has nothing earthly mixed or concreted with it; nothing of airy or watery humidity, and nothing of the heat and dryness of the fiery element. As therefore its nature is invisible, so also it remains invisibly in the body, and invisibly departs from the body, through the body it sees bodies, such as heaven and earth, and what in them are visible to our eyes. But through spirit it beholds the similarities of bodies. For whatever is not body, and yet is something else, is not foolishly called Spirit. Through intellect it sees those things which are not corpo-

are bodies, nor do they have the forms of bodies, as has been deduced above.


                              C A P. III.

  *On the soul's visions, likewise on dreams & their five kinds:*
               *On Phantasm, Ephialtes, & finally*
                             *on Ecstasy.*

Of those things which are not bodies, but spiritual likenesses of bodies, such as we perceive through imagination, some are ordinary visions, others appear to those sleeping, and some are perceived in ecstasy. Those visions which are ordinary and human, either arise from our spirit, or are in some way suggested to the spirit by the body; just as, when people have been affected either in body or mind, not only do they, while awake, turn over their concerns in their mind by thinking in the likeness of bodies, but also, while sleeping, they deal with that which they need by dreaming. For they both conduct their affairs out of mental desire, and long for feasts and drinks, if perchance they have fallen asleep thirsty or hungry. We also know that thoughts have been instilled in the waking by some hidden instinct, by which they might divine; just as Caiaphas the High Priest prophesied, though his intention did not have the will to prophesy. Therefore, from what has been said above, we see that the soul sees many things, and that the nature of all visions is the same, whether in the waking, or the sleeping, or the sick; because things of this kind, which are seen, are not of a different kind than the nature of the spirit, from which or in which are the likenesses of bodies: For it has obscured ways of sensing, so that it sees what dreamers see. Indeed, the visions of the frenzied are similar to the visions of dreamers, and similar to the thoughts of the waking. Indeed, for those sleeping, the path of sensing which leads intention to the eyes is lulled to sleep in the brain, and therefore the intention itself, turned elsewhere, perceives the visions of dreams, as if bodily forms were present; so that the sleeper seems to himself to be awake, and to behold not images of bodies, but the bodies themselves. Nor certainly without remarkable admiration do I contemplate, and in contemplating am affected by no small astonishment, with what speed and ease the soul fabricates images of those bodies which it sees through the eyes of the body. Whatever the nature of those visions may be, it is beyond doubt not a body. For visible bodies do not create those images in the spirit, nor do they have the power to form anything spiritual; but the spirit itself accomplishes this in itself with wonderful speed, inasmuch as it is spiritual, intellectual, and rational.

Those things which seem to appear to sleepers, according to Macrobius's opinion, are distributed into five kinds, namely into *oraculum, visio, somnium, insomnium & phantasia*. *Oraculum* he defines as being when in dreams a parent, or some serious and holy person, or a priest, or God himself, openly announces something that will happen or will not happen, or something to be done or avoided. Concerning which the sacred Scriptures have explicitly treated many things in many places, and Iamblichus recited very many things in his mysteries. *Visio* is when one sees that which happens in the same way as it appeared. *Somnium* is covered with figures, and cannot be understood without interpretation, that is, veiled in enigmas. Whence *Numbers 12. Jehovah speaks to Moses face to face, and shows himself not through dreams and enigmas and figures, as he was accustomed to reveal himself to other Prophets; but he openly beheld God, and gazed upon the likeness of Jehovah*. *Insomnium* is when that which fatigued the waking person intrudes upon the sleeper: of which kind are the concern for food, or drink, or certain studies, or arts, or infirmities; for according to the studies which each person has pursued, he is accustomed to dream; Likewise, images of familiar arts, presently impressed upon the mind, will appear

--- Page 211 ---
DE TRIPL. ANIM. IN CORP. VISION. 209

...appear in dreams. Furthermore, also, according to the diversity of infirmity, different *insomnia* occur, and likewise they vary according to the variety of manners and humors; since the sanguine see some things, the choleric others, the phlegmatic others, and the melancholic others; these see red and fiery things; those white and black. A *phantasma* is, when someone has barely begun to sleep, and still thinks they are awake, and seems to themselves to see others as if rushing upon them, or forms wandering everywhere, differing and various, and these either joyful or turbulent: under which genus indeed *Ephialtes* or incubus and succubus are numbered; which rumor has it, suddenly and unexpectedly invades those resting, and burdens them with its weight. Which indeed, according to the opinion of physicians, is nothing other than a certain vapor ascending from the stomach or heart to the brain, and there compressing the natural faculty. In ecstasy, the soul is alienated and turned away from all bodily senses, more than in sleep, but less than in death. The soul in this is not deceived, but is divinely aided by the mind itself, as is explained in the Apocalypse of John. Great indeed is this revelation, since, when it is assumed with a good spirit, the soul cannot be deceived; because holy Angels in wonderful ways make their visions true through a certain easy and very powerful union or mixture, and reform their vision in an ineffable way in our spirit. For they themselves indeed preside over indicating and ministering to these bodies, and so dispose their significant likenesses in the spirit, and treat them with such power to some extent, that they can mix them by revealing them to the spirits of men. Hence it is, that the Angel of Jehovah appeared in dreams to Joseph, saying: Do not fear, take Mary your wife. And again. Take the child and flee. But God through the Prophet Joel says: And I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams, etc.


C A P. IV.

*On the transformation of men into the forms of beasts through the deceptive operation of witches. How good or evil Demons assume the spirit of man; And by what way evil Demons foretell future events, and deceive with false apparitions?*


It happens sometimes, according to the opinions of some trustworthy persons, that, by a certain magical art of women and the power of Demons, men, transformed into wolves and beasts of burden, like brutes, carry whatever is necessary, and this work completed, they return again to themselves and their original form, yet in such a way that the mind in them does not become bestial in the meantime, but is preserved as rational and human. This, which also Saint Augustine faithfully recorded for us in his writings as having happened in Italy in his time. But this, if I am not mistaken, is to be understood thus: that Demons indeed do not know how to create natures, but they can nevertheless do something such that it appears to be that which it truly is not. For neither by any magical or diabolical art or power can the soul, nor even the body, truly be converted in any way into bestial limbs and features; but it can indeed be converted into a fantastic man; since he is also varied by thinking or dreaming through innumerable kinds of things, and although he is not a body, he takes on the forms of bodies with wonderful speed. Therefore, with the senses of the human body lulled and oppressed, a truly corporeal figure can be produced for the senses of others, but only in such a way that the very Dd true

--- Page 212 ---
210 TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK X.
true bodies of men lie somewhere, indeed alive, but much more pleasantly and deeply than in sleep, with their senses locked away; but that illusory form, as if shaped into the image of some animal, may appear and present itself to the senses of others: In which case, that man will indeed seem to himself such as he sometimes appears to himself in dreams, as if he were carrying burdens.

Which burdens, of course, if they are true in body, are carried by Demons, so that these men, given over to illusions, may be deluded by their actions, while they see partly true bodies of men, partly false bodies of beasts of burden. Also, a good spirit sometimes, and an evil spirit sometimes, assumes the human spirit: nor can it be easily discerned by which spirit it is assumed, except in this, that the good one instructs towards good things, and leads into the way of truth, but the evil one deceives, and with its deceitful machinations deludes the soul, even in manifest good things, so that when it has been believed in such things, it may draw and seduce it to follow its own will.

Thus it often seizes the human spirit, so that by a hidden mixture of both, the spirit of the vexed and the spirit of the vexer may seem to be one and the same spirit: just as we once observed in demoniacs and those afflicted with a certain bad kind of Epilepsy.

*For while I was living in Marseille, Gaul, I noticed a certain demoniac girl agitated among the priests by the sign of the cross; who, though she was entirely ignorant of sciences, uttered some Greek words as if by her own inspiration, and revealed many things to the multitude, both about the past and the present, not without great admiration from those standing by.*

Which truly could not have come from her own Spirit; but because of the mixture made with the malignant Spirit, she uttered such things as if with a single breath. And here we think it worthy of note, how the malignant spirit is accustomed to join itself with the spirit of the slanderer, for the execution of the impious purpose in the slanderer.

For the mother of this girl, weak and consumed by illness, because of the neglect of her daughter—whether because she, as it was indeed reported, had lost some money, or because she had wasted it on trifles—infecting her with dire imprecations, finally burst into these words: *'I wish (she said) that the devil with his legions would suddenly enter your body.'* And this having been maliciously uttered, the effect immediately followed the will. For the girl was suddenly possessed by evil Demons, and indeed, as the Devil himself confessed through the girl's mouth, by six Legions, and miserably tormented by them.

Therefore, the Demons immediately entered the spirit breathed out by the mother in a malevolent and wicked manner, and thus Satan, because of the proximity of nature between the spirit of the mother and the daughter, most easily penetrated into the spirit of the daughter, carrying with him a crowd of Demons. But it must be noted that while Demons are permitted to possess the spirit of men, it is nevertheless impossible for them to penetrate into the lucid region of the mind and reason; because that is only the seat and tabernacle of the Trinity, no differently than the heavenly sun, as the *Royal Psalmist* testifies.

And yet Satan is said to fill someone's mind and the principal part of the heart. But this is understood to happen, not indeed by entering into it, and into its sense, but by fraud, iniquity, and all malice, by which he entices and seduces that rational soul to himself, deceiving it and making it believe through thought that those things are good and virtues which are truly full of falsehood, vices, and illusions. For the Devil is a deceitful, wicked, and fraudulent deceiver of souls.

Therefore, not by participation in the nature or substance of the rational soul, as some think, does the Devil occupy the lucid soul of man, or become its inhabitant; but joined from part of his composition with the aerial spirit of man, through fraud, deception, and malice, he is said to possess the mind and soul, that is, by obscuring the splendor of reason through fantastic imaginations in the sensual spirit of the possessed man, which he is accustomed to excite by his artifices, so that those things appear to be which are not. Nevertheless, the sense is rendered subject to the Devil. Hence the tongue of the possessed speaks, and those apparitions of fantasy, as he indeed supposes, he sees as certain and infallible,

For that good which God has bestowed upon His creatures, only the Trinity is accustomed to enter; but to the Devil it is given to possess a denser spirit, that is, an airy one, in which he deceives the senses and imagination. And yet through his cunning, the mind, that is, the true and immediate ray of God, suffers the Devil's mischief no less than the Sun of heaven endures the obscurities of an airy cloud, or the crashes and noises of thunder. Which things, although to the earth and earthly beings they may appear to be dark and dense clouds, or horrendous thunders, or dreadful flying Dragons, or prodigious Comets, etc., nevertheless the Sun of heaven is in no way disturbed by them, but is always constant in its motion, always the same in its beauty and splendor; because God is always present to it, since it is His tabernacle. In a similar way, I say, the matter also stands between the Devil's deceptive obfuscations and the mind or rays of light in man. For althou

For although he seduced the soul of some unbelieving woman, and subjugated her to himself through her infidelity, he immediately transforms himself into various kinds and images of persons, and to that soul, which he holds captive in darkness and deludes as if in dreams, he shows now sad, now joyful, and now unknown, now known persons, and thus leads her astray through all sorts of remote paths. But since we will speak and discuss these matters more extensively in our Treatise on death, or the dissolution of the soul from the body, we will omit them in this place.

C A P. V.
Of the third kind of vision of the soul, namely the intellectual,
which never deceives.

The third kind of vision of the soul is intellectual, as stated above, by which those things which have neither bodies nor forms of bodies are perceived. And indeed, by this kind of vision, the soul is never deceived. But in sensible and fantastic visions, it is often deluded and led astray, for the reasons alleged by us above. Therefore, through intellectual vision alone can the mind arrive at true self-knowledge, and in no way through those former visions of sense and imagination, since these rather deceive the soul and make it seem to itself that which truly is not. Therefore, by withdrawing from the senses and the images of bodies, the inner man usually attains knowledge of himself and of God; since this is the only way by which he, unknown to himself, learns to know himself. But this labor, this work, requires constant practice and great constancy in withdrawing from the senses, so that man may abstract his mind from multiplicity towards unity, that is, that he may recall it to himself and retain it within himself. Indeed, by these senses the soul is hindered from being able to perceive itself and its creator, which it alone and simply ought to behold without eyes. Wherefore it is necessary that, leaving behind the sensible steps, it should transcend to the goal of reason, treading the path of justice. For the rational soul surpasses all those things which were made by God, and therefore, when it is pure and closest to God, and indeed, in so far as it adheres to the charity of the mind, suffused and illuminated by that intellectual light, it certainly perceives God not through bodily eyes, but through its own principal part, that is, through intelligence, in whom is the most perfect beauty and the most blessed vision, by which vision it itself becomes blessed. Therefore, it ought to remove from its consideration all notions which are received externally through the senses of the body: since corporeal things, and their likenesses, and even the

--- Page 215 ---
DE TRIPL. ANIM. IN CORP. VISION. 213

the senses themselves also and imaginations revolving around them, and clinging in memory when it remembers them by recalling, pertain to the outer man, although the soul perceives external things by these as if by certain messengers. The soul also is simple and free, to which nothing is more present than itself, by a certain internal and not simulated, but true presence. It sees itself in itself; for it knows nothing so much as that which is present to it, nor is anything more present to it than itself to itself. For it knows itself to live, it remembers itself to be, to will, to think, to know, to judge; these, I say, the soul knows all in itself, nor does it imagine them outside itself, as if some sense of the body might touch them, just as any corporeal things are touched; from the thoughts of which nothing accrues to it, so that it might think itself to be something of that kind; whatever remains to it of itself, that alone it is. For nothing is so illuminated in the soul as the soul itself, nor does anything know the soul as the soul itself does; for when the soul asks what the soul is, it certainly knows that it seeks itself and knows that it is the soul which seeks itself; for it seeks nothing else concerning itself than itself. While therefore it knows itself seeking, it certainly knows itself entirely. But if it knows, certainly everything that it knows, it knows entirely. Even if, a part having been found, it does not seek itself entirely; nevertheless, because it seeks itself entirely, it is entirely present to itself, and nothing can be more present to it than itself to itself. But what it seeks concerning itself, what it was before, or what it will be, or what it is now, it seeks, that is, how similar or dissimilar to God, how humble and devout, how beautiful and how holy. But because it is in these bodies, which it thinks about with love, and with which it has grown accustomed to mix love, it cannot see itself without their images. For these external living things cling to it with such glue, that even when these are absent, their images are present to the one thinking. Therefore it cannot separate them from itself, so that it may inspect and see itself alone. Let the soul therefore return to itself, and stand in itself, nor let it seek itself as if absent, but let it take care to discern and perceive itself as if present; and let it fix the intention of the will, which wanders through other things, in itself, and let it think of itself, so that it may know and love itself. Thus it will see that it has never not loved itself, never not known itself, but that, by loving other things with itself, it has confused itself with these; so that it cannot be separated from them without great labor, to which it clung with great love. Therefore it is deformed by the phantasms of corporeal imaginations, these being deeply impressed, and even when freed from the body, it is not divested of them. For if it is not cleansed here from the corruption of corporeal affections, having been stripped of the body, it is held by corporeal passions. For there is a very great coherence, as has been said, between the spirit of the soul and the body; so that if the spirit of the soul clings to the corporeal spirit, the beauty and blessing of the mind being neglected, then that elemental and sensitive spirit, after the soul's departure from the body, clings and connects itself to its airy spirit; and thus the soul, stripped of the body, will be held by such passions as it was subject to while existing in the body. For as we see in the growth of a plant, that the ethereal spirit with its soul or spark of light, flying and tending towards its homeland, raises itself upwards above the earth, to which another portion of the element of fire is connected, inasmuch as it is contiguous to the ethereal heaven; but to fire again air is glued on account of the dignity of its place, and water to air, and finally water to earth; and thus the active will of light and the ethereal spirit is depressed by that gross and heavy dreggy spirit, so that against its will it is detained in the air, and cannot be carried or lifted further upwards. So also, if the ethereal soul of man does not cling to the portion of the mind, but is neglected by the divine ray, which is from the empyrean heaven and has no connection or familiarity with the elements, it behaves in almost the same way as the soul of a plant or a beast. For by the fiery force of the elements it is bound with the body and with the airy spirit of the sensitive [soul], and sometimes it is also chained with a more subtle portion, so that it is depressed from the place of joy and gladness, and is detained in a place subject to those passions by which it was disturbed in the human body; because all

Here are demonstrated three visions of the soul, namely insofar as it is *sense*,
insofar as *imagination*, & insofar as *reason, intellect & mind*. When it is *sense*,
it sees, hears, smells, tastes & touches bodies & visible things as they are, that is,
it perceives all those things immediately in their composition through the exterior senses.
Therefore, the soul is more deeply engaged in the multitude of things, while it claims the appellation of sense,
& consequently, it is more remote from the contemplation of divine & spiritual things.
Hence it happens that sense perceives only the mere chest or rind of things, or
the covering & veil of truth; and it cannot discern truth itself hidden in the center,
nor perceive it with the organs of the exterior senses. Therefore, the corporeal & visible
world is presented to the sensitive soul, to whose earthy portion Touch corresponds,
to the watery Taste, to the gross & mixed airy Smell, to the simple & subtle airy Hearing,
& to fire with aether Sight. Furthermore, the soul residing in the anterior part of the inner
mountain or Microcosmic head is called *imaginative*,
or phantasy itself & imagination; because it perceives not indeed true images,
but similitudes & as it were shadows of corporeal & sensible things. Hence it
speculates on the ideas & icons of the world & worldly things, insofar as it is imagination &
things in the abstract, but it does not apprehend real things, or things in the concrete,
& as they are. In the center of the brain, however, the soul neither sees in a fantastic manner,
nor considers bodies with sensible regard, but contemplates intellectual things with the spirit
of reason & the light of the mind, which were neither in sense, nor are comprehended by
phantasy alone, but are held & esteemed as true things by reason itself. For never
did the secrets of intelligences fall under sense, nor the ineffable mystery of the triune Essence.
Moreover, imagination cannot even comprehend their ideas;
since reason itself & the acuteness of human intellect can scarcely ever attain such grace,
& only by immense illumination of the mind. Hence it happens that reason itself,
through divine speculation, first rises to the intellect, & then from the intellect raises itself
with a light leap into the sphere of the mind, so that in its light it may behold spiritual things
from afar, & through this kind of vision be, as it were, raptured with immense joy,
& behold Jehovah, according to the Prophet *Isaiah*, sitting in heaven, & elevated on the highest
throne, & placed above the mundane palace, where His throne is heaven, & His palace
most full of glory, light itself, so that it always, as if in ecstasy, beholds supercelestial things,
neglecting inferior ones; let it cling, I say, to the contemplation of things so noble,
abstracted from vile sense. Finally, in the last part of the brain, the soul is called
*memorative & motive*: for in that part it stores, guards, & recalls the objects of visions,
both of the sensible, as well as the imaginary & intellectual world. Similarly, it is called *motive*,
inasmuch as through the spinal cord it gives & sends down motion to every member of the lesser world.

#### CHAP. I.
#### *Concerning the Principle of Generation and Multiplication.*

[Decorative woodcut initial I]N the secret of generation, many mysteries, both of supercelestial as well as celestial and sublunar things, commonly still unknown and not yet revealed, need to be elucidated and diligently observed. Therefore, as far as it primarily concerns supercelestial things, it must be noted, according to the doctrine of Iamblichus, *that living beings are divided into 4 orders, namely, into Gods, Demons, Heroes, and Souls, that is, into God, Angels ministering to God like architects in the worldly work, Olympic spirits or governors of the Planets and celestial bodies, and Souls.* Hence, according to his opinion, there seem to be two semidiameters, drawn from the center or earth to its extreme circumference, that is, the upper capacity of the empyrean heaven and the elemental heaven; of which the former is considered the dwelling place of God, and the latter of souls; Demons and heroes, however, are said to claim intermediate places for themselves: Hence it happens that Demons, because of their proximity to the fiery tabernacle of God, are said to participate in His property, which is unity. For *their properties are, according to Iamblichus, to contain within themselves the gifts of the Gods, in an inferior manner indeed than the Gods, but under the idea and principle of them, to obtain a worse condition.* Hence they participate in unity and stability. But the property of the soul inhabiting and operating at the other extremity, tending more downwards (since it is a declination towards multitude, motion, and natural things to be filled with vital motion, and towards perfecting generation), is observed to be most distant from the nature of unity or the property of God; inasmuch as it tends towards number and plurality. Heroes finally

--- Page 225 ---
**ON SEED AND GENERATION. 223.**

Finally, since they incline more towards the state of souls, they agree with their natures in almost everything. For their characteristic is understood under the condition of multitude and motion, and the disposition of mixture, state, and excellence; just as it has been more broadly declared by us above, in the division of the mundane pyramid into square and cube roots. Therefore, Daemons differ from Heroes in this, that Heroes incline somewhat more towards *particular and mobile things, to use Iamblichus's words, than Daemons*. For those two intermediate kinds, namely Daemons and Heroes, are composed from the properties of the extremes, namely God and souls; which indeed are denoted by simple digits and the joints of the first composition or roots, in the material pyramid mentioned above; but in Daemons there is more of the divine, in Heroes more of the human. From these things, therefore, it is clear that the governors of the Planets with their legions dwelling in the elementary region, whom they call Heroes, infusing life into lower things from their orbits, and consequently agreeing with souls, promote multiplications in vegetables and generations in animals. And the place of these Heroes is described in the order of the squares of the material pyramid, just as souls are known to be submerged in the depth of its cubes. God indeed, since He is the purest and simplest form, and the most exact and primary light, made the purest and simplest generation of the monad, reflecting it into Himself: so that unity might remain in its nature whole and untouched, without any pollution of matter. For matter itself was the cause of multitude and the increase of number, just as will be declared from this enigmatic history or fable that follows.
*Demogorgon, who is the highest and first God, surrounded, accompanied, and adorned by eternity before the origin of the world, and reposing in it, beheld formless Chaos with the ineffable splendor of his eyes, and perceiving its belly to be wonderfully agitated and disturbed by contention, struggle, and tumult, stretched out his hand to aid the birth of that pregnant Chaos. From this, Strife immediately and at first sight took its origin, which, produced into the circuit of the world by the benevolent favor of Demogorgon, indeed with a dishonest and immodest face, and accompanied by an unheard-of clamor, sought to be carried on ambitious wings high and upwards to the peak and summit of the sky. From this it happened that it was deservedly cast down and ruined by Demogorgon into the deepest abyss. Chaos, truly the mother of all things, remaining purer now after the birth of this rebellious firstborn of hers, burned with sweat and fiery sighs, and again began to labor, pregnant, for another birth, and again, with the assistance of Demogorgon's hand, she brought forth a second male offspring, whose name was Pan, signifying nature, matter, or the universal spirit; whose starry head signified the heaven of the stars, his two ears both poles of the world, his long beard the solar rays tending downwards, his pipe made of seven reeds the seven Planets with their harmony, and his goat-like feet the nature of time. Again, after the birth of Pan, his three sisters, namely the Fates, were brought forth and born from the womb of Chaos, indicating the vicissitude of things. Finally, Polus, Titan, Earth, and Erebus followed in linear succession.* From this account, therefore, it is demonstrated that matter or Chaos, constituted from a collection of formless spirits or waters, was, before creation, the origin and matrix of generation; which nevertheless could have begotten or produced nothing, had not the act of Demogorgon been present, inasmuch as without his assistance the powers of Chaos could by no means have been brought into act. From this it is manifest that God, by His unique essence and formal property, which is unity, brought into act a fertile nature, which the Pythagoreans placed in the number of imperfect things, namely in duality. From this, thereafter, unity informing the formless spirit, the disposition of the ternary and the Trinity was produced; so that by the virtue of unity an imperfect duality was brought forth; which, by the addition of enlightened unity, was reduced from an imperfect number into the most perfect number and nature, namely into the Trinity. Thus God in the Word, the Word in the Spirit flowing from both

--- Page 226 ---
224 T R A C T. I. S E C T. I. L I B. XI.

itself,¹ and God in all things. Thus the Word of God filling the entire world in every nature or spirit. Thus God with the Word and the Spirit everywhere. And thus through the symphony of this divine harmony, peace, with strife already then cast down from heaven to earth and driven into its center, will be continued among the elements until the very end. MAY IT PERISH!² Thus perpetual happiness will always be present for the first region of the world, lasting friendship for the middle, and rest with little disturbance for the lowest. But indeed in this lowest region, sometimes the tumult of opposing winds, the conflict of waves and waters, the generation of meteors formed from contrary qualities, and countless other accidents, contingent upon this lower world because of its proximity to strife, are very often found. Therefore, these things understood, the reason is at hand why lower things are more apt for generation than higher ones; since a denser and more efficacious part of the matrix of chaos is found in this region. Whence the earth is called the mother of all things, which fire has sent into its matrix. Nor indeed is there further doubt about this, since we observe that neither air, nor fire, nor aether is suitable for the generation of animals, vegetables, or minerals in its own region. Therefore, from Chaos was the matter and substance of generation, which received its form, soul, and act from God for its essence and existence. For generation cannot occur without action upon a well-disposed passive [element], and consequently, God, who is unity and a monad, does not by Himself generate multitude, but through the abundance of the matter of Chaos, or the fertile spirit, or the humid nature, which, as Mercury Trismegistus testifies, the Word and pure light and fire cherished, or the Spirit of the Lord, who moved upon the waters, souls prone to the multitude of particulars arise; and by the Heroes or Lords of the Planets, pouring forth prolific and vital matter downwards, these souls are solicited, attracted, and strengthened for continuous generation and procreation. Therefore, the dominion of Heroes and souls extends from the solar sphere down to the center or earth; because from that point, progressing downwards, the cone of the formal pyramid tends from formal universality to its particularity, namely ending at the point of the cone in the earth; while conversely, the base of the material pyramid, resting on the earth, supplies a multitude of matter to the paucity of form found there in the cone of the formal pyramid. Hence arise so many generations on earth, and so many corruptions and mutations or alterations. For abundant matter, never content with the paucity of form, desires to change its state daily, so that it may acquire a nobler form, by whose presence and act it may fully satisfy its appetite. But indeed, ascending upwards from the sphere of the Sun, nothing of generation can be found, because the part of the material pyramid tending upwards is progressively more and more subtilized, while it gradually approaches the base of the formal pyramid. Whence such matter, because of its subtilization from form and light, is altogether inept and infertile for generation, since its matrix becomes too tender and subtle, so that it cannot retain the seeds of light due to their intense strength. Hence, therefore, souls are said by Philosophers to possess the lowest part of the world and the last order of intelligences, and to claim for themselves a place near the earth, or in the lowest region; because there their appetite, occupied with particulars and the multitude of generation, according to Iamblichus' opinion cited above, is sufficiently fulfilled.

**C A P. II.**

**On generation, and what is the difference between it and creation?**
**That the heavens are the origin of the generation of things.**

Philosophers of the Peripatetic school, faithfully treating the natural generation of things, and diligently inquiring into the reason and disposition of generation, finally perceived that Genesis itself, or generation, is nothing other than a change from a single, original, substantial form into another; that is, the progress of matter towards a substantial form which is not yet inherent in it, but will soon be. *For example:* They hold the generation of an apple to be the progress of the germ, as matter, towards the apple, as a substantial form; because an apple is a substance; but the form of the apple is not inherent in the germ, but will soon be, once generation is complete. But truly, as it seems to us, and with due respect to the Peripatetics, the form of the thing to be generated is actually inherent in the sperm or germ itself from the very beginning, although it may not immediately become manifest to our senses, but rather operates more and more secretly day by day within the mass of the seed from the moment it is cast into a matrix suitable for generation, towards the perfection of the thing to be begotten, as we shall declare below. Now, what the difference is between generation and creation has been stated above, where we lucidly explained that *creation is the origin of a non-pre-existing species, and consequently of any individual of the same species immediately and primarily emanating from it; whereas we say generation is the method of preserving and continuing a pre-existing species produced in the world by creation.* From which it is clear that creation is concerned with a non-pre-existing thing, while generation is necessarily concerned with a pre-existing thing, existing in the nature of things by the benefit of creation. Furthermore, from this we deduce that, just as God is the author of creation, or the father of created species, so also the creature itself is recognized as the father of the generated thing; since without the creature's sperm, it is impossible for any generation to occur, inasmuch as without the hidden seminal virtue, matter cannot assume the form and species of animated bodies. Hence, therefore, it is established that nothing generated is good, inasmuch as it is a passion produced by a passible and imperfect father, according to that saying of *Hermes Trismegistus, Pimander 6: "Generated things are not good; for generation is a passion; but where there is passion, there is in no way good; where there is good, no passion is posited; just as where there is day, there is no night, and where there is night, there is no day."* Furthermore, what is generated is not good, inasmuch as it is imperfect. This is also confirmed by the words of the same *Hermes Trismegistus, Pimander 4,* which are as follows: *"Whatever is generated is certainly imperfect, divisible, growing and diminishing; but to that which is perfect, none of these things happen."* Therefore, the Father of the creature was the sole good and the highest perfection, namely the Monad, the principle, root, and origin of all things, truly without beginning; which contains every number, contained by none, generates every number, generated by none; which communicated of its goodness and perfection to the first creature. Whence all created things are called good: Which perfection and goodness, however, was disturbed by the sin of Adam. For he who had obtained only a portion of form for his own composition and perfection, by wishing to contribute that portion to the generation of others, and thus prodigally imparting it to others, became, from a perfect creature, an imperfect creature, stained by the pollution and defilements of darkness. And just as the Creator Himself
Ff was

--- Page 228 ---
226	T R A C T. I. S E C T. I. L I B. XI.
was the Father of Adam, so he himself, further foolishly desiring to ambitiously create others in a divine manner, thence plunged himself into the sphere of generation, and from the perfection and pinnacle of contemplation of his Creator, he was cast down and ruined into the abyss of misery and imperfection; and consequently, all other creatures after and because of him, indeed even the earth itself, received a curse from it. From the foregoing, therefore, it appears that, just as God himself, through His most holy Word, was the immediate author of creation, so also heaven or nature is the origin of generation, *according to that [passage] of Hermes Trismegistus, Pimander 1: 'The circuit of the celestial spheres, just as the mind itself willed, fashioned animals from the lower elements.' And elsewhere, Pimander 9: 'The revolution of the world, stirring up generations, produces qualities, infecting some, defending against evil, and purifying with good.'* Astrologers are taught by experience that the matter stands thus. For evil Planets, otherwise called Misfortunes, are accustomed to deprave the dispositions of men; while fortunes convert them into better ones. We have nevertheless declared above that the Mind is free from all fate and celestial influence, although meanwhile it is beyond doubt certain that good influences of the holy heaven render the soul more obedient to the mind; just as, conversely, evil influences make it (the soul) more subject to that portion of the inner man which is opposed to the nature of the mind. From these things, therefore, it is evident that the power and property of generation are derived from heaven. Indeed, the wise have acknowledged that man himself cannot be generated without the Sun and man. But as for those ignorant and foolish ones who foolishly and imprudently assert that heaven does not act upon these lower things, let their intentions vanish into smoke, and let them be perpetually considered ungrateful; inasmuch as they impudently strive to deny their first and principal parents, while they deny that they are begotten by heaven and celestial beings, as ministers of the Creator through divine will, and thus try to abjure the power and virtue of heaven that produces them, with harsh mouth and deceptive sense, and consequently are not ashamed to falsely infer that that glorious ornament of the world serves no purpose. Do you, O fools, wish to be partakers of the celestial kingdom, and yet presume to penetrate to it without a medium? Could *Saint Paul have been caught up to the third heaven, unless he had passed through a medium?* As if someone were to say that motion occurs from a starting point to an end point, or from a beginning to an end, without a medium. You deny the operation of heaven in generation, and yet you daily draw your life from its heart. O foolish nature of men, while it does not believe that those things which it does not see or touch exist in the nature of things, and thus, neglecting the truth, it grasps at vain, false, and deceptive things, and intoxicated by vanities, it also conceives a vain faith, and for that reason, infected by darkness and rejecting light, it holds true things for false, and vainly embraces false things for true. But may God, the Best and Greatest, reform all these things for the better according to His good will.

C A P. IV.

*On the operation of human sperm after its insertion into the female womb.*
*And how the Planets act for the completion of the fetus;*
*And on the true twofold time of female birth,*
*and on the reason for the same.*

The visible sperm having been received into the female womb with its invisible seed, the womb is suddenly closed, nor is it opened afterwards until the perfection and completion of the fetus; unless this happens due to a reason compelling beyond nature, which also usually brings dangerous effects with it, such as abortion, etc. Therefore, the sperm having been established in the womb, those three ampullae designated above, separately or divided from each other, are produced within a space of seven days, and become manifest to sight, which indeed on the fifteenth day are transformed into those three principal members, which are called the brain, heart, and liver, of which the first is the seat of the mind, reason, and animal spirits, the second of life and the vital soul, and the lowest of natural faculty; so that we can perceive veins protruding from the liver, and arteries emerging from the heart, and nerves gushing forth from the brain; by the power of these afterwards, with the cooperation of heat, the other parts are also gradually produced, namely the lungs and other parts of the thorax, the stomach, intestines, and those which cover them; similarly the bladder, kidneys, and lastly the other parts of the entire body. Then on the thirtieth day, males usually appear, and on the thirty-seventh, females. Therefore, the members and organs of the body having been completed, the fetus still remains in the uterus for its complete maturity and ripening, until the completion of nine months. And sometimes it also emerges alive in the seventh month; but if it exceeds the seventh month (i.e., is born in the eighth), it does not live; but in the seventh it lives, as both experience and Philosophy itself testify. But those born in the eighth month die, but in the ninth they live;

Therefore, if the infant is born then, it can live; but if it is not born, it will be weakened. **But in the eighth month, Saturn**, by constricting the womb and the fetus, will predominate. CH. V.

Why the animal soul does not act as quickly in the fetus as life and motion?

In previous (sections), according to the opinion of Hermes Trismegistus, it has been said that the garment of mind and reason is the soul, and that the vehicle of the soul is the spirit. The receptacle of all these, however, is sperm, which is a subtle extract of all the elements concurring in the composition of the progenitor, from which, as from a shoot, a new tree or a new body arises, not dissimilar to the body of the progenitor in species, limbs, figure, and organs. But since, as that Hermes Trismegistus testifies, the mind cannot exist by itself in this earthly mass, and cannot sustain such a divine power confirmed by a divisible body, the mind assumed the soul, as a garment; similarly the soul, also being divine, uses the spirit: For the mind in its nature, and the luminous soul itself derived from the mind, and as it were the image of the mind or a secondary mind, are so contrary to the nature of the opaque body that they require spiritual, or rather, very subtle and very soft material vehicles, without which they cannot be joined with the body. Therefore, with the spirit enclosed, the motion itself, from the soul contained in the sperm in a hidden way, gradually and successively inflates the spermatic substance, which invisibly contains within itself the likeness of the body to be generated, and causes it to gradually extend itself and rise in the form of a vesicle; and the mind, which is a ray of God, stirs the soul to construct such an edifice. And in the mind, says Hermes, is the Word of God, which orders and institutes all these things. And certainly, since man was made by the Word, his succession is also continued by the Word through generation, and consequently, the character and seal of the Word is not only in the complete man, but also in him who is not yet formed; since the Word of God is said to remain forever; indeed, Saint John testifies that all things were made through the Word, and without Him nothing was made that was made. For in Him is life, and that life was the light of men, and that light shines in darkness. Does not Hermes Trismegistus also say, agreeing with the Evangelist, speaking as if with the mouth of God and Mind? Consider that in you the Word of the Lord sees, but the mind is God the Father, for they are not distant from each other; the union of these is life: And the Royal Psalmist, Psalm 139:15. My substance was not hidden from You, when I was made in secret, skillfully wrought, as in the lowest parts of the earth. Your eyes saw my unformed substance, and in Your book all these things were written, the days when they were formed, when as yet there was none of them, etc. Similarly, Psalm 119. Your hands
