*Your hands made me and fashioned me.* Thus also in *Job. 10. 9.* we find:
*You made me like clay: did you not pour me out like milk? And curdle me like cheese?*
*You clothed me with skin and flesh? And wove me with bones and nerves? With life you exer-*
*cised kindness towards me? And your visitation preserved my spirit?* And finally, according to *Psal. 22.*
*11. Since you are the one who brought me out of the womb, making me trust at my mother's breasts. Upon you*
*I was cast from the womb, from my mother's womb, be my strong God.* From these things, therefore, it is evidently clear, unless I am mistaken, that God is in the womb itself, and there acts for the production of the human structure, and consequently; that the Word of God is in the mind, and with the mind, and for this reason in man himself, and in the sperm remaining in the womb, so that it may conform to the existence of the human species, and to that divine exemplar. But just as the Word is said by *Mercury* to be in the mind, the mind in reason, reason with the Word and Mind in the soul, and the luminous soul with all these in the body, and thus a progression occurs from unity to multitude; so it will be necessary that the Mind, as a duality, be moved by the Word, and the rational Spirit by the mind, and the soul by the rational spirit, and that thus finally the spirit may immediately operate through the soul itself to perform its office in the spermatic body. Therefore, the airy or ethereal spirit acts in the body, as if in its likeness, to build a palace for its heavenly king, and adorns it with organs and members, and storerooms and workshops, suitable for every ray and internal spirit, and for that which has descended from above. The soul therefore vivifies the spirit for such a work, so that the spirit is the instrument and vehicle of the soul; Reason vivifies the soul, and the soul with reason constructs that admirable divine work, or the divine tabernacle of the divine ray. The mind also imbues the rational spirit with ineffable sharpness and dignity. And the Word in the mind carries with it a supersubstantial splendor; by whose presence the eternity and perpetuity of the species are preserved, as we described in the aforementioned. Hence, therefore, it is that Mind and Reason appear last of all. For the spirit, by virtue of the soul's hidden action, causes the mass and embryo to be augmented and grow day by day from the beginning by its breath. And yet life or the living soul does not yet appear then; although it is manifest that it operates hiddenly through the production, or rather the manifestation, of arterial, venous, and nervous ampullae. Therefore, with the bodily organs augmented and made sensible, the movement of the soul and its effect also become more sensible. Hence it happens that life usually appears in the middle of augmentation, and thus the fetus is then also perceived to move by the sense of touch itself, nor does the mind with reason seem to act, except by a certain mystical movement in the soul, which human sense is in no way able to perceive. For just as the spirit acts in the body, so the soul acts in the spirit: but just as the actions of the soul cannot be perceived by bodily sense without the spirit, so neither can those of the mind and reason without the vivifying effect of the soul. Hence it is clear that the acts of the spirit are familiar to the bodily senses, because they are closer to them, and as it were, contiguous. But the acts of the soul are not so familiar to them, because the spirit is interposed between the body and the soul. Similarly, the acts of reason are still more difficult for the bodily senses to know than the acts of the soul, because the spirit and the mediating soul are interposed between the body and reason. But most difficult of all for the bodily senses to perceive are the acts of the mind and the operations of God, because they are further distant, and are, as it were, in the center of spiritual mysteries. But the operations of sense are placed on the outermost surface. Indeed, it will be extremely arduous for a sense dwelling and acting on the surface of the earth to perceive the secret operations that are performed in the center of the earth, and the mysteries of nature that lie hidden there; much harder and more difficult still will it be for gross and earthly matter to understand those mystical operations and intentions that are produced in the supercelestial heaven. Hence, therefore, it is that mind and reason, as far as human sense is concerned, seem to rest in the spermatic mass, though nevertheless by a hidden and mystical

--- Page 235 ---
DE SPERMATE ET GENERATIONE. 233

mystical way in the soul, so that it also, finally moving in the lowest spirit of the sperm, is accustomed to build the human structure and dwelling. And
just as we see in the first creation of the world, that the impressions of the supernal light upon the elemental sphere were weak, and as it were imperceptible before the appearance of the Sun (whence no animal, but only vegetables and minerals were produced, since it did not act for animal life, but only for vegetable life.) Similarly, as we observe, that after the increase of the vegetable mass, by the power of increased vivifying heat, animal and vital bodies, but devoid of evident reason, were produced; namely aquatic, flying, and terrestrial [animals], and that at the end of creation, reason with mind was inspired into man, the noblest animal; so please observe how the matter stands in the fetus during its stay in the womb.
The world with its creatures was created in the space of seven days from water and light. Water, by condensation or rarefaction, is distinguished into elements diverse in nature and position. And such a mixture was made on the first three days of creation. Thus, the origin of sperm is water and light, through whose diverse mixtures the four elements are produced, and from the subtlety of these, semen or thick water. This sperm, for three months, solidifies into three bodily regions, formed from three ampullae representing the three regions of the world: Thus, we declared above that the world is divided into three regions corresponding to the first three days of creation; and the completed vegetable mass began to grow and increase. But in the remaining and final days of creation, animal life was produced, and the power of the Sun operated: And so also, through the other three months of the fetus dwelling in the womb, animal life appears in the vegetable mass. Finally, on the sixth day of creation, the elemental region having been purged of its misty clouds and rebellious vapors, reason with mind was inspired into man, by means of the word. So therefore, also around the sixth month, sparks of reason from the human species are seen to leap forth in a certain way, though very slowly. And just as on the seventh day the fabric of the world and its creatures was completed, so also the infant, now perfected in the image of the world, is accustomed to be brought forth into the light, or due to maternal defect, in the ninth month.

C H A P. VI.

Concerning the ages of man, and why they are subsequently shorter; and the reason for purifying corrupted elements on the last day.

Indeed, the number seven is of marvelous power, since in it the animals of the world were preserved in Noah's ark from the flood, and likewise also through its institution the entire course of human life is governed. For just as it is granted to the fetus to continue in the mother's womb for seven months before its complete perfection; so also after its exit from the womb, the course of its life is measured by seven other intervals of time, which are called ages, and each of them is again circumscribed by seven years. For from the connection of seven-year periods comes that dimension which the wise called the climacteric year. But as we declared before, that a certain Planet separately governs each month of the fetus in the womb according to order; so also it is always observed that one of these Planets presides over each age; of which, therefore, the first [is governed by] Gg Luna-

--- Page 236 ---
234 TREATISE I. SECTION I. BOOK XI.

The Moon claims for itself that it completed and perfected the infant in the womb and worked for its emergence into the light; and therefore also from then on has power over its disposition during the space of the first age. Thus, *infancy* is deservedly attributed to the *Moon*, because the lunar power is observed to follow its entire disposition, since in it we live according to nutritive and vegetative power. Hence it is that this age is fluid, tender, watery, and more cold and humid than the subsequent ones. The *second age*, namely *childhood*, is given to *Mercury*, since in it Mercurial dispositions are most found; for in it, according to *Proclus'* opinion, we exercise the study of letters, the lyre, wrestling, and similar games, and man's imagination is varied and light, and prone to many things. The *third*, which we call *adolescence*, is subject to *Venus*; hence it is that in it the limbs swell in females and we are immediately aroused to procreation. The *fourth*, namely *youth*, is called *Solar*, in which the vigor and perfection of age are conspicuous. For this part of human life, being in the middle, behaves as the Sun does in its disposition in the middle of the sky. The *fifth* age is between youth and evident old age, which by some is called the *bilious and irascible* age, inasmuch as the *Martial* planet predominates in it: In this, therefore, we seek powers and victories, and are easily provoked to anger. The *sixth* age, which is called *green old age*, is assigned to *Jupiter*, since in it we desire prudence, an active and civil life with a certain natural inclination. The *curved and decrepit seventh* age, however, is that which *Saturn* governs; since in it it is natural to cease from generation, to separate oneself from bodily appetites, and to compose and transfer oneself to another and incorporeal life; hence this age is called *contemplative*. From these things, therefore, it is clear that, contrary to the blind opinions of fools, the stars wonderfully operate in humans and govern almost the entire human life very effectively. And certainly, if we consider the matter correctly, we will discover that human life is nothing other than a certain passage or journey from a point or terminus of imperfection and crudity to a terminus of perfection and maturity. Indeed, it can be very well compared to the solar course, which constitutes the year and moves from the winter solstice towards the summer solstice. For as the sun hastens towards the northern parts, the perfection of plants and the maturity of fruits are increasingly induced, as can be seen in cherries, apples, and similar fruits, which, by heat, maturity, and color, are perceived as if ascending to the peak of youth, and then afterwards again, as if descending to the goal of old age through the path of corruption, with the Sun and Cancer retreating towards the south, to such an extent that even the very leaves of trees are observed by common experience to fall when the *Sun* passes through *Libra*. But also in the nature of a growing apple, we can exquisitely perceive the reason for human life and its movement: For in the beginning of its movement, it is crude and undigested, like the *Moon*; then it proceeds in a linear path through all the dispositions of the Planets to complete maturity, which we compare to youth. Then afterwards, gradually decreasing, it again tends towards corruption. Here, therefore, we must observe that the corruption of the body is nothing other than the multitude of the vivifying soul. For as the body matures, the vital soul becomes stronger; which, now hastening towards its liberation from the bodily prison, first attempts to corrupt the body; this, indeed, is perceived to gradually and progressively endeavor, both in fruit and in animals, beginning its movement towards corruption, both from complete maturity in fruit and from intense youth in man. We also see that this human life can be compared to the path or journey of man, progressing from the seventh northern climate towards the first climate near the equator. For the *climate passing through Flanders and England is attributed to the Moon*; hence the people of that climate are found to be more humid and colder than others. The *sixth* is assigned to *Mercury*, cutting through *Gaul*; whose inhabitants are to the English

DE SPERMATE ET GENERATIONE. 235
warmer than the English, and not so humid; whence also in their dispositions they are more tender and light, as if living in a childish life. The fifth divides Italy, which is governed by Venus: Whence this nation is affected by delights, songs, and other such Venereal pleasures; And in this region of the world the sphere of adolescence seems to move. The fourth climate, dedicated to the Sun, passes through the Mediterranean Sea, and cutting through Greece, renders men learned and represents the state of youth. The third, subjecting the holy land to itself, is attributed to Mars; in which victory, war, and anger have exercised their effects from the beginning: here the traveler finds heat in its full vigor: then man, in the course of his life, passing through Egypt, finds there the nature of Jupiter ruling the second climate: Whence he becomes more civilized and prudent, and more inclined to the true worship of the Gods and religion. And finally arriving at the last climate, which divides Ethiopia, he finds Saturn ruling there, decrepit, and contemplating divine things, neglecting earthly ones, considering heavenly things. In this climate the body is found to be weakest, but the soul strongest: Whence the soul, now earthly, and indeed also neglecting its own body, raises its gaze to heaven, and with the bonds of the animal and sensitive soul broken, it desires to tend towards its supercelestial homeland, and to fly away with spiritual wings, and therefore diligently prepares itself for this journey: Therefore the body grieves, the soul rejoices. And so the pilgrim man arrives at the end of his worldly and mortal journey, so that by a more joyful and pleasant pilgrimage he may seek the kingdom of celestial and immortal life.

But now I will turn to that hidden reason, by which it is demonstrated, Why human age according to the age of the world is successively shorter and more curtailed. It must therefore be understood that in the beginning God created all elements most pure, inasmuch as He, as it were, intoxicated them with that primordial fifth essence, by the bonds of which they, departing from confusion, were reduced to order and harmonious concatenation. Nor yet were they equal in purity in all respects in the first creation, but one existed purer and cleaner than another according to the greater or lesser quantity of the fifth essence which it possessed. Since therefore man especially, and moreover also other creatures likewise, were made from such pure elements in their creation, therefore it was necessary that in these newly created creatures there should be a most exact and purest composition of bodies, and that consequently they could not die or be corrupted or dissolved; inasmuch as they were immediately created by the immortal God, according to that of the Wise Man, Wisdom 1:13. God did not make death, nor does He delight in the destruction of the living; For He created all things that they might exist, and the generations of this world are salutary, in which there is no deadly poison nor the kingdom of the underworld upon the earth. But justice is immortal. If therefore this was not the will of the Creator, that any thing He made should perish, or that the earth itself, now corrupted, should be subject to the traces of death or the underworld, whence arose this depravation of creatures and so great a defilement of the elements? Whence did it happen, I ask, that these four elements so created, namely pure and clear, by reason of that perfection in which they were established, have now at last fallen away from that perfection of nature, so that creatures made from them are now compelled to die? We respond, that this happens because of the impurity of the elements, and especially of the earth itself, which is therefore more prone to corruption, because in its creation it had a smaller portion of the fifth essence; and therefore this corruption undoubtedly proceeds from the first generation; because, as creation was most pure, inasmuch as it was made immediately by the Creator, in whom and from whom nothing but purity can proceed; so also generation is not from the Creator, but from the Creature, namely from Nature; whence it brings imperfection with it; because the Creature does not have more perfection than suffices for its own perfection; and consequently cannot give complete perfection to others; since this is the office of the Creator alone, who alone is more than

Therefore, what is evil and impure, submerged in the dark abyss, will fall upon evil and damned Demons; but what is pure, upon the blessed. It is clear, therefore, that through the presence of more than perfection, all things will return to their destined place, which was assigned to them in the beginning, the impure being separated from the pure, the dark from the light, the good from the evil, etc. Nor indeed is it to be believed that this earth, which we tread here, is a pure element, but rather that it is elemented from its fifth element: For by the reasons alleged above, a major portion of the fifth essence has departed from the earth, and its major portion is impurity, dregs, and as it were a caput mortuum, that is, a body, without a soul, on account of the infection designated above. Therefore, in the center is the true virgin earth and the true element, which fire will not be able to consume on that tremendous day, and whatever besides this is not of the pure truth of the elements, will burn, and be reduced to ashes and as it were nothing on the day of judgment. CHAP. I.
That human Music is fittingly referred to the cosmic: And concerning the

[An ornate woodcut initial 'P' depicting a figure in a landscape.]
The Pythagoreans taught in their writings that in the fabric of the world the Monad or unity refers to the craftsman or creator; but the Dyad or duality to spiritual matter with its dreggy base, and the Triad or Trinity to form or light, by which all things are informed: and thus they assertively said that the whole world was constituted from the ternary number. Similarly, from the composition of the aforementioned, they affirmed that man, the most worthy creature of the earth, was born, namely from the Hexad. For 1, 2, 3, added together constitute 6. For from the more worthy, more composite, a more worthy, less composite thing was made, namely man. For God first fabricated the world from the ternary number in the first composition, whence the world was called the son of God by the Philosophers; and from the composite parts of the world, as if from its ternary number, man was born, whom for this reason the ancients called the son of the world. The same Pythagoreans also say, not disagreeing with the Platonists in this, that the human number is septenary; nor indeed without reason; since the septenary is made up of the formal number, which is ternary, joined with the material number, namely the quaternary. They said, however, that the being and life and existence of other creatures were made from the denary number or ennead. From which it is clear that the human number approaches the nature of unity more than the number of other creatures, and that it corresponds to the unity of the world, namely the seat of the mind, in the consonance of the Diapason; which consonance consists of the Diatessaron and Diapente, which consist of seven intervals, inasmuch as the Diatessaron is constituted from two tones with a minor semitone, and the Diapente from three tones with a minor semitone, which intervals connected together make seven. And yet if both semitones are joined together,

--- Page 242 ---
240	T R A C T. I.  S E C T. I.  L I B. XII.

...so that they constitute a single tone, it can also constitute a hexad. And for this reason, both these numbers are found in man in one way, according to the opinion of the Pythagoreans. We also, from a diligent inspection of the formal and material pyramids found in man, have discovered such music. For first, descending from the spiritual pyramid of matter, we find the Diapason between the apex of the mind and the sphere of the heart, because the proportion of the vital spirit in the heart to the spirit contiguous to the mind is as 2 to 1, namely it is double, from which the Diapason is constituted, comprising the consonances Diatessaron and Diapente. Similarly, the disposition of the spirit of the heart is referred to the disposition of the lower region, where the natural faculty originally acts, as 2 to 3. For three portions of spirit seem to reign there, inasmuch as the base of the material pyramid is found there. Therefore, in this proportion, the consonance Diapente is found, and at the very point of the pyramid's base, almost no light, but only mere dregs (namely, in the intestines) is found, and, as it were, a dead head, deprived of all light and, as it were, vital grace. Hence, there are 4 parts of matter there, inasmuch as almost no light is present, and so this portion relates to the portion of the higher elements as 4 to 1, which is in the sesquitertian proportion, in which also the consonance Diatessaron is found.

C A P. II.

*On the symphonic melody between the soul, spirit, and body.*

IN common observation of Music, we see that its system or scale consists of a triple series of letters or notes, which the Artists have called keys. And all of these, except three, are called hidden. But those three are clearly expressed to distinguish the difference of the aforementioned invisible keys. Therefore, the first series of keys is $\Gamma$. A. B. C. D. E. F., expressed by simple letters of the major order, as you see; which are called *grave keys* (low keys), as if bases and foundations of the remaining higher ones. And the manifest key of these is F, which is expressed thus $\daleth$: the second order of letters is such: g. a. b. c. d. e. f. And this series is called *Middle*, and its letters are called excellent and acute (high-pitched); from which the parts of the middle melody arise, and properly the *middle song* (tenor/alto range), just as the *Bass* is drawn from the lowest. There is also yet another series, more eminent, more excellent, and more acute (higher) than these themselves in vocal elevation, from which the *Alto* song is formed; and this is of this kind: gg. aa. bb. cc. dd. ee. ff. Which letters indeed are superexcellent and very acute (very high) and supreme in all human power. From this kind of harmonic proportion, in a triple septenary number, the machine of the world is constructed; whose elementary portion, consisting of a graver (lower) symphony, seems to support the other parts of the mundane harmony. For the elements are heavier than the other regions of the sky, and are as it were bases and foundations; Similarly, the middle heaven is assimilated to the series of acute and excellent letters, inasmuch as it makes the first melody with the elements or Bass; whose seven Planets are the seven keys; And just as ascending from g. a. b. c. we find that c. is the principal key, by the manifestation of which the others not expressed are understood; so also ascending from the Moon ($\leftmoon$), Mercury ($\text{\mercury}$), Venus ($\text{\female}$), Sun ($\odot$), we find that the Sun ($\odot$) becomes as it were that open or manifest key of the heavens, by whose visible presence the other planets, hidden in themselves, are manifested, sound harmoniously to the lower grave (heavy) things, are illuminated, and vigorously operate in the elements and things composed of elements. Finally, the superacute and superexcellent letters are referred to the supreme region; where the cone of the material pyramid defines itself in a superacute manner, beyond which there is no passage for a created spirit. But as we have demonstrated in the preceding (pages), that man is called by the wise a son of the world, because from the simpler parts of the world, his subtle, invisible, and internal (being) was made, just as

just as likewise from the denser parts of the world, or its elements, the gross,

By these means, three species of melody, indeed most distinctly differing in sound and
variety, but most excellently linked together by harmony or consonance in the Microcosmic

soul is formed from superexcellent voices, constituting a spiritual and lucid, or formal,
Diatessaron, Diapente, and Diapason. Also, the harmony of the spirit is made from
middle voices or excellent degrees; which in its symphony agrees both with the
superexcellent or supercelestial, and with the grave or elementary harmonies. Finally,
the human body is, as it were, the organ or instrument of the entire human harmony;
whose lowest degree of melody or grave accent occurs in that subtle part of the
elements from which the sensitive soul and natural faculty arise. Of this chord is the
elementary spirit, or grosser or subtler air, which the fiery or more formal force of the
elements is observed to strike, and the pulse of the spirit makes some harmony of the
elements sound to the ears of reason. And the principal origin of this Music is in the
lowest region of the Microcosm; but nevertheless, the effect of its harmony is dispersed
and disseminated throughout the entire human fabric, and is observed to move the
natural harmony with the higher parts no differently than in common Music the sound
of the Bass part is heard to resonate indifferently with the sounds of the Middle and
High parts, or the melody of one part is accustomed to be mixed with the essential and
natural part of another by a certain mixture of life. Hence, veins with arteries, and both
with nerves, are perceived to be distributed simultaneously everywhere throughout the body.
So also the middle spirit or aether is struck by the middle soul, by whose vibration an
excellent melody is made in the middle of the instrument, attributing tones of life or
vivifying sounds to the entire body no less than when a struck lyre string makes the
entire lyre resonate. Furthermore, this chord, by its pulsation, creates the melody of the
rational heaven by its high reason with ineffable magic, and joins it with grave music.
And thus complete music, constituted from three diverse melodies, is observed to sound
in the human body; namely, *sensitive*, *vital*, and *rational*. *Sensitive* acts in the
preservation of the flesh and vegetative parts; *Vital* in the vivification and agitation of
the mass, or machine; and *Rational* in the governance and direction of the entire fabric.
Therefore, the *Bass* of the Microcosmic song is cubic, because it is elemental or corporeal.
The *Middle*, however, is superficial or quadratic, because it is spiritual. Finally, the *High*
is radical or linear, because it is formal. And although in this our harmony we have named
three spirits, or three lucid forms, striking those three spiritual chords, and three distinct
regions: nevertheless, generally considering the Microcosmic machine, it stands in the same
respect with the universal Macrocosm, in which there is nothing but a single resonating
spirit, a single organ receiving sounds into its cavity, and a single striking light; but because
of the grosser or subtler disposition in substance of the same spirit, that which is one and

the same light, on account of the various degrees of density or subtlety in the spiritual matter in which it resides, is said to be varied, when in reality it is nothing but a single light derived from the uncreated light, which is the father of light, and created on the first day, but unequally dispersed in the world. In a similar way, there is also a single musical organ of man, a single spirit or monochord, a single player or light; but if there is any difference, this whole thing occurs on account of the multitude or paucity of spirit and light in this or that degree of worldly dimension. We see therefore from these things that there is a single music in the lowest region of the world and man, where the cone of the formal pyramid is found, and the base of the material pyramid. And this music is more bass and slow and grave, because there three parts of matter reign and only one part of luminous form. Wherefore, that paucity of light acts slowly and sluggishly in such a mass or multitude of matter: Hence the gravity and ponderousness of matter renders voices slow, base, and low. But in the middle region, where the two halves of the pyramids meet, voices are rendered, both from the part of the spirit and from the part of the light, medium and equally sounding: which are therefore called excellent, because in purity and clarity they excel those which are called grave, since here there is more form and less matter. Hence here the actions of form are freer and more external than in the lowest region, but in the higher region light is still freer from the bonds of matter, inasmuch as in it there is only one part of spirit, namely the cone of the material pyramid, and three parts of luminous form. Hence here the sharpest and superexcellent voices are produced, because in this place light exceeds the quantity of matter by two degrees. Here, however, I would have you observe that from this kind of musical observation it clearly appears how opposite the disposition of matter is to the disposition of form. For the higher one ascends from the cone of the formal pyramid towards its base, the sharper or more slender the accents, and the more subtle the works performed: But in the material pyramid, the more one progresses from the cone towards its base, the graver and denser the sounds become, and the coarser, more opaque, and visible the works become. And the reason for this is certainly at hand; namely, because the formal utterance of light more strongly disperses the spirit, and consequently, through their subtlety, renders voices clearer and more effective. Oh, how distinct, clear, and sonorous was that admirable and ineffable voice, that incomprehensible uncreated Word, by which the luminous Creator wondrously fashioned the world and man, inasmuch as by its power or accent the horrible and terrible shadows themselves were agitated and reverberated downwards, and the waters or humid nature were purified from their deformity, and all things were made from nothing, the elements bound in harmonious peace, and the heavens themselves wonderfully established, the earth balanced with equal scales, propped up by firm columns, and suspended in the middle. Indeed, this ineffable Word of the Creator also performed wonders in the very fabric of man; for He made his soul a palace and tabernacle for Himself, or rather a temple, to speak with *Saint Paul and Xistus the Pythagorean. Hence Mercurius Trismegistus, speaking with the mouth of the divine mind, says: I believe that in you the Word of God sees and hears, etc. Many passages of the sacred Scriptures, which are to be believed above all, also seem to confirm the admirable power and harmony of this holy Word, both in the creation of the world and the making of man; and also by the divine Philosophers, the power of the divine voice in creation is commended in their eternal monuments. ON THE HARMONY OF THE INTERNAL AND EXTERNAL MAN. 247
where both beginning and end are lacking (because duality has no middle), all discords, daughters of darkness, are produced; but truly, harmonies, the offspring of light and truth, arise from a perfect and odd number. Hence it happens that, if the unity of light, which is the soul, is joined with the duality of matter, it produces an odd number, which is full of harmony; and likewise also, if the trinity of the soul, which is the same in essence with unity, is added to the quaternity of matter, then it produces the number seven, in which the most perfect consonance is perceived to sound, which contains Diapente (a fifth) and Diatessaron (a fourth) within itself; and consequently this union of the soul with the body now renders that wonderfully consonant, which before was dissonant; that, I say, it now makes regular, which before and by itself was rebellious and irregular, and altogether adverse to motion or action. Whence we find that man is nothing else than a unity and a multitude collected together in admirable harmony.

Thus we see that the Sun of the world is unique, the soul is unique, but its rays are diverse, indeed infinite, which are common to the soul. Thus also we observe all rays of light to be derived from the one Jehovah, as the Father of lights, that is, from a unique source, or supersubstantial essence; whose rays, flowing from Him both mediately and immediately, are in no way divided, but rather connected in the same way as light to the body of the Sun; which nevertheless is known to be present in earth, waters, air, and composite things. Hence the soul is called one, because of its indivisibility from its primary form; just as matter is called a multitude because of duality or quaternity, which consists of a multitude or number of units; to which, however, an imperfect number is the principle, and not unity. And this is the reason why Democritus, Orpheus, and many of the Pythagoreans believed all things to be full of Gods; all of whom they referred to the one Jupiter, as a multitude to a unity.

But to return to this human Music of ours, we have composed it from three strings and three organs joined together, and introducing three parts of melody, of which each string and each organ corresponds to each region of the world. But since the two upper strings, namely the spiritual and the formal, coincide equally with the harmony of the string in the lowest instrument, no differently than we see in the music of diverse melodies the Bass part mixed with the Middle and the Middle with the Alto, and the Alto with the lowest parts, with an equal disposition of melodies, so indeed, that the multiform harmony is found there in the same consensus; therefore to each triangle or pyramid we attribute seven keys, differing from each other in double or quadruple proportion, from whose consonance and mutual relation to each other we can most easily conceive and behold the symphonic composition of the internal with the external man.

Therefore, intellectual light sounds the accent of reason into the spirit, as a medium, rendering it rational; and the spirit, moved by the action of light, as a medium, expands itself through the ventricles or organs of the brain as a receptacle, and thus the rays of reason flow downwards to produce other consonances with the vital and natural faculty. Then, through the Diapason consonance, rational harmony is joined with imagination and the spirit of life. Therefore, the voice of reason vibrates the chord of life and the imaginative spirit, whose vivifying harmony, mixed with reason, afterwards pours itself out and disperses through the entire natural spirit or elemental chord, resonating in the subtle grave sounds of the elements and mixing the corporeal or material Diapason with acute and very acute tones: Of these modulations, the human body is the receptacle, a general organ and as it were an instrument of human music, in which the mundane harmony is comprehended, and from whose organic parts proportional effects of the same are elicited.

In the figure delineating the spiritual cube, we have described the principle of the proportion of matter, both mundane and Microcosmic. The material cube, in the description of the world, is referred to the elements, for it tends downwards due to its gravity and density. But since the formal cube behaves in the opposite way, inasmuch as it tends upwards due to its lightness and is elevated to the peaks of the heavens, therefore the middle part of both the formal and material descriptions is recognized as having almost the same principle of form, since the square surface of one corresponds to the square of the other figure. But we see that the summit or line of the material demonstration is entirely contrary in position and situation to the line of the formal description, inasmuch as that formal one tends downwards; By which it is clearly declared that the greatest force of matter dominates downwards in the world and in man; but the greatest virtue of form is found upwards and is contiguous to the lucid fount. Therefore, if these two figures, as they are described here, are joined to each other, they will demonstrate the exact composition of the world and man from matter and form. Moreover, it must be considered here incidentally that the world in its composition is simpler than man. For the world was made from a simple composition: but man is compounded from the composite, that is, he is said to be made from the mundane composition. Hence, in his composition, he is more overshadowed by diverse mixtures than the world. And hence it is that, just as the Philosophers called the world the visible son of God, so they handed down that man is the son of the world, made immediately from the world no differently than the world from God. The world from the beginning was divided into elements wonderfully distinct and balanced, from the mixture of which, confused with each other and bound by a natural bond in harmonious peace, man was made. We see therefore that in the conjunction of the formal cube with the material line, the square of one is also united with the square of the other, and consequently the formal line tending downwards is joined with the material cube. By which it is clearly declared that the smallest part of form, namely its line, is joined with the greater dimension of matter; just as conversely the smallest portion of the spiritual figure is united with the greater dimension of light. But the two middle parts, since they have the same form, easily agree and produce life. And in this way we have also explained the principle of the pyramids of mundane composition, which we have often cited.

For just as this region is hot and humid, so the salty nature of the sea adds heat to the marine water, and itself inherently possesses humidity. With similar respect, through Diatessaron, the lowest region of the air is related to the highest; whence both these spheres of air are hot and humid; but in a different way, inasmuch as one is colder due to its proximity to water, and the other hotter due to the vicinity of the element of fire, to which, however, the middle region of the air seems to be dissonant, inasmuch as it is intensely cold; a quality it acquired through antiperistasis. The lower part of the element of fire, mixed with vital air, is related to the Sun, its summit to Jupiter, the upper region of the air to Venus, the Moon to Jupiter in humidity and in hidden heat. Similarly we see that, just as earth is, as it were, the dregs of the elementary region, so also the Moon is the coarser and denser part of the ethereal region. The middle region of the air sounds a Diapason with Mars, and that unhappily and with a contrary quality. Whence it happens that, although this Planet in heaven and in its nature is as good as the others, yet in respect to lower things it is called an inauspicious Planet, and a misfortune for the human race. And hence it happens that great disturbances, namely thunder, lightning, flashes, and other such things dreadful to humans, are said by Astrologers to be stirred up in this region. To this Planet, however, the element of water corresponds in double proportion, simply dividing the lowest region of the world into four elements, just as Jupiter to air, as has been said in our Macrocosmic harmony. But these two explanations tend to the same thing. For Jupiter, to which *e.* is attributed, corresponds to the upper portion of the air, which is warm and humid, and favorable to life. Astrologers also confirm that such is the nature of Jupiter; wherefore it is called a fortunate star and most friendly to human nature, and for this reason it is called the Greater Fortune, just as Venus is called the Lesser Fortune. Finally, Saturn, to which *f.* is attributed, insofar as its Diapason ends in fire, is considered an inauspicious star by those inhabiting the lowest spaces of the world, although in itself it is as good as the others. For although its dryness agrees with earth, whose $\Gamma$. is related to *f.*, to which *g.* is contiguous, it does not, however, agree with the dryness of fire, insofar as it is joined with lethal cold, which is entirely contrary to igneous heat. But now at last we have arrived at the supreme series of keys, commensurate with the supreme region of the world; where the sphere of will *gg.*, marked to the nature of the supersubstantial essence *ggg.*, is found in Diapason, because God does all things according to His will in the heavens and on earth. Whatever, moreover, lies beneath this sphere, is moved by this sphere, as by the prime mover. For lower bodies are said to be moved involuntarily by this sphere in no other way than the world is carried around by its power with a rapt motion. For bodies naturally desire to rest, wherefore the Sun and the other Planets are said to move according to the motion of the prime mover. We see therefore how miraculously the spheres of both worlds, namely the lesser as well as the greater, harmonize with each other; so that the keys of the upper heaven with the keys of the middle, and the keys of the middle with the keys of the lowest, together constitute symphonic melodies. Thus water with earth, for the constitution of the Moon, denotes the act of will and the subject agitated by involuntary motion: The Moon and water denote the mutability of will in humans: Earth, which is the basis and foundation of the whole, denotes the stability of God's will: Water also, fluid by its nature, denotes the mutable nature of Mercury, and joins these together in their relation to the sphere of reason in Diapason. Hence the variety of human reason, the multitude of opinions and sects; and hence Mercury is said to preside over intellect, science, arts, and Music, and so it also follows from this that, just as sense is referred to the element of fire, so imagination, the companion of reason, is referred to water; Sweet water also and the lowest part of the air are referred to Venus, and Venus to the intellect, which is fiery love. These three therefore agree in the act and passion of love: Air also, the Sun, and Mind denote mind, soul, and spirit, which are joined together in optimal harmony. We could bring forth countless other reasons for this harmony in this place, but since the secret of Music is not open to everyone, and it would perhaps be more tedious than pleasant for the reader to unravel or explain them in this place, therefore I shall now pass over them in silence.

In the preceding demonstration, we have explained the numerical system of the entire mundane fabric, which we declared above to be derived from the harmony of the divine essence. For from simple unity, or the supersubstantial property of the first essence, duality flowed forth, which is nothing other than unity repeated twice, or a monad from a monad or with a monad, that is, the most fitting connection of two unities of the same essence, producing the number Dyad; by the movement of which again towards unity, three unities of the same supersubstantial and uncreated nature are added simultaneously, which produce the first number, adorned with the complement of perfection; in which unity is the beginning, unity the middle, and unity the end; and therefore the whole is nothing else than sole unity in trinity, and trinity in unity: which quantity of the most complete number, multiplied by itself, will produce the last odd number from the simple and uncompounded numbers or digits, namely 9. By the multiplication of which (9) in its root (3), those composite numbers are produced, according to whose order compositions of a threefold kind are made in the three regions of the world: For the number 27 is the most complete number of mundane compositions, whose first novenary number denotes the nine first articles of numbers, namely 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70,

Moreover, we see that sea water has its saltiness from the Sun; The concupiscible power is proper to the first Venus, in the region or sphere of the earth; where plants and animals have their germination, and with concupiscible appetite constantly await a celestial form from on high; The Mercurial power is in metals and their sphere; and finally, the vegetative power given to the Moon by the central Sun; from whose rays growth and germination proceed on the surface of the earth. But indeed, the more light something has in itself, the more of God it can claim for itself, as *Saint Augustine* testifies, because God is the Father of lights, from whom is all Light, which is the origin and foundation of truth. Having diligently considered these things, we will perceive all harmony of things to be derived from the soul itself, which was propagated from God, and is as if God Himself, or a ray immediately emanating from God Himself. Therefore, in the foregoing demonstration, we have nine accents or voices constituting the Diapason of the soul's operations, namely four from the Diatessaron and five from the Diapente; and in this way, we have human Music produced in the nonary number. # OF THE FIRST TREATISE,
# OF SECTION I.
### BOOK XIII.
## On the Practice of the Music of the Composite Soul.

### CHAP. I.
#### *What is the Soul? & concerning its infinite power, and how it differs from the spirit?*

[A large decorative drop cap 'I' featuring a sun-like face and foliage.] Now at last, before we arrive at the use or practice of the simple soul's harmony by itself, and then its harmony with the spirit, and finally the symphonic melody of all three among themselves, it is necessary that we recognize their differences, by which they are distinguished from one another. We will here repeat many definitions of the soul, almost all agreeing, approved by the school of ancient Philosophers, both Pagan and Christian. For some define it thus: *The soul, insofar as it is adorned with mind, is a certain substance of reason adapted to the governance of the body, convertible to good and evil.* And therefore, it is said to be mortal in some respect, namely insofar as it can be alienated for the worse and from the will of God, by participation in whom it is good; and immortal in some respect, because it cannot lose the sense by which it may fare well or ill after this life. But in this description, the soul seems to be understood together with the spirit. We, however, taking the soul simply by itself, without any mixture of it with the created spirit, understand it as a mere formal light immediately emanating from the Creator himself. Wherefore, as it seems to us, accepted in this way, it is not badly defined by some as *being an incorporeal thing adorned with every beauty of light, assimilated to the Holy Trinity, and made equal to eternal glory.* Or: *The soul is an incorporeal thing circumscribed by all members, colored by no color, assimilated to the Most High God, and the most beautiful of all things.* Now indeed it must be known what the spirit itself is, which is joined with the soul, the tincture of life, the form and the purest and simplest essence of light. Hence, first of all, we must consider in how many ways "spirit" is understood, since "spirit" is referred to in multiple respects. For God himself is called Spirit, and thus also this air and wind, and breath to the heart's

--- Page 267 ---
ON MUSIC. THE COMPOSITION OF THE SOUL. PRACTICE. 265

we call the spirit drawn to these chambers. But this spirit cannot be called soul, because it is dissolved by the variation of air; but by that spirit, which is joined to the soul or light, we understand that vehicle of the soul, by which it is carried as something placed in a place, or a flame in the oil of a lamp, or the splendor or ray of the Sun in the air. And hence it came to pass that the Platonists divided man into a lucid soul, *an intermediate or ethereal spirit, and an opaque body.* The soul, therefore, is called that spark of light which moves the spirit, in which, as in a ship, it seems to navigate first in the sea of the world, and then in the bodily fluid, and animates the body, that is, vivifies it. The spirit, however, is taken for a spiritual nature, namely, that which breathes in the body, is called spirit. Furthermore, soul and spirit seem to be the same in the body, although the soul denotes something different from the spirit, because simple light cannot exist in the body without spirit; nor can the spirit act by itself without a spark of light: the spirit, therefore, refers to substance, while the soul refers to form and vivification. The soul therefore acts and the spirit suffers, and both are so essentially and according to the laws of nature joined to each other, that no one except God alone can divide these two from each other. This also the Apostle seems to hint at with these words: *For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing even to the division of soul and spirit.* By which he seems to argue that it is impossible for any division to occur between soul and spirit, except by the word of God alone. Which indeed I myself can testify, having learned by experience in the anatomy of a certain creature; where I saw a virginal and clear spirit, adorned on all sides by the rays of the soul; which human ingenuity was ignorant of how to divide from each other. Therefore, although they differ from each other, as matter and form, or agent and patient, or air and fire, yet since they are so ordered by nature or created by the Creator, they cannot exist otherwise, until those indissoluble bonds are dissolved by Him alone who tied the knot. Hence the spirit is said to be of the same essence as the soul, and light and spirit seem to fuse into that same thing which we call soul; they are, I say, the same in essence, but differ in property no less than the Father in the Trinity from the Holy Spirit; who nevertheless are both the same in supersubstantial essence. For one and the same spirit is spoken of in relation to itself, and in relation to the body of the soul. Furthermore, Spirit is also called, insofar as it is a rational substance endowed with reason, while soul, insofar as it contributes to the life of the body. Hence in the Scriptures that is found: *Whoever loses his soul will save it,* that is, whoever for the sake of God willingly despises this life, which now consists temporarily of mortal bodily vivification, will in the future receive the same eternal and immortal life of the mortal body and soul. From which it is clear that the soul, in its proper appellation, is sometimes taken for life or vital faculty. And yet sometimes the meaning of soul extends more broadly, and is taken for the union of mind, rational spirit, and a spark of life with the intermediate spirit, its vehicle, and then we call it by a more fitting term, *animus*, which we take for the entire inner man. Hence *animus* is used for heart in the sacred Scriptures. For just as the heart is the center, and the inner part of the body, so also the soul, or rather the *animus*, is the nucleus of the invisible and inner man. For the *animus*, enlightened by divine wisdom, looks to its origin and knows itself. But we read almost everywhere in the sacred writings that the soul, taken as the life of a creature, is attributed not only to humans but also to animals. But indeed, sometimes the word 'soul,' and indeed most often by Philosophers and Theologians themselves, is used for the inner man or *animus*, and we ourselves have also sometimes used this word for the inner man. But, to return to our subject, the human soul, which has being in the body and outside the body, can equally be called soul and spirit. Not, however, two souls, namely the sensual and the rational, the other

--- Page 268 ---
266 T R A C T. I. S E C T. I. L I B. XIII.
namely, the one by which man lives, and the other by which, as some think, he perceives, but one and the same soul lives in itself through mind and intellect and provides life to the body through human sensation: For the body can neither live nor be born without a rational soul: But it is nourished, moved, grows, and receives human form in the womb, just as we see shoots and herbs (without a rational soul, of course) move and have growth. But nevertheless, in the sperm of man lies hidden a seed, in which mind and reason, as far as we are concerned, seem to be absent, though in truth they operate secretly and in an imperceptible manner, and gradually and by degrees excite the vivifying soul, which also operates in a hidden manner at the beginning, to prepare its palace; which by its hidden action inflates the vegetative spirit, and causes it to swell in the elementary composition; which act we indeed call the vegetative soul, so that beyond doubt vegetation is nothing other than the first effect of the vital soul operating secretly; which soul is indeed moved by the mind and rational spirit hidden in the center, and most secretly exciting the soul to motion.

C A P. II.
*On Mind & Reason, and again somewhat on*
*Soul & Spirit.*

Mind, according to some, is said to derive from *Mene*. *Mene* in Greek is called *Luna* or *Laune*. And indeed, just as the Moon waxes and wanes, and changes with various vicissitudes, and yet restores itself to what it was with a certain perfect newness; so the mind now raises its head to the highest things, now descends to the lowest, now referring itself to itself, refutes falsehoods with truths, sometimes is turned to governing corporeal things, sometimes adheres to eternal reasons or consultations, according to that saying of *Mercurius Trismegistus: "Whoever are supported by this nature of God, according to the comparison of their works, are held to be immortal instead of mortal; they comprehend all things by their intelligence, which are on earth, and which are in the sea, and if there is anything beyond these above heaven, and moreover they raise themselves up so that they may also behold the good itself."* The aspect of this divine essence is reason itself, by which it discerns good and evil, chooses virtues, and loves truth. For by its direction, the mind is capable of all things, and marked by the likeness of all things; indeed, it is even said to be all things by a certain nature, power, and natural dignity. Therefore, it comprehends the invisible causes of things through intelligence, and gathers the visible forms of actual things through the affections of the senses, and either through the senses it is inclined towards sensible things, or through intelligence it ascends to visible things, draws the likenesses of things to itself, knows present things, understands absent things, inquires into the unknown, and occupies itself with what has been found. O marvelous operation of divine nature! O ineffable disposition of the divine ray! Since it is said to be all things, all things are subjected to it, and offer a certain obedience. What then is this most powerful essence? Is it indeed nature, or truly God himself? It is indeed nature itself, producing all things in the world by the power of the Word inherent in it, and providing life to them. It is likewise God himself, since it is an uncreated spirit and a ray of uncreated essence, no less indivisible from the Creator than light or a sunbeam from the Sun. It is therefore all in all, by which all things were made, and into which all things, as from multitude to unity, must return. This divine mind is that rational and intellectual light by which we reason, in-

--- Page 269 ---
ON THE PRACTICE OF THE MUSIC OF THE SOUL'S COMPOSITION. 267

understand and are wise; which is so made in the image of God, that no intervening nature is formed by truth itself. Hence it happens that, according to some, it is called Mind, because it stands out in the soul, more eminent and excellent, since it is a power of the soul, from which intelligence proceeds, through which the soul understands truth itself, and through wisdom loves it. For wisdom is the love of good, which is also indeed called the savor of good: Therefore, the vision of the Mind is called intelligence, its taste wisdom; the former contemplates, the latter delights. From these things, therefore, we can clearly perceive that the eye of the soul is the mind itself, pure and immune from all bodily stain, whose gaze is reason, to which intellect and vision are joined; for these three are necessary for the soul, that it may have healthy eyes, with which it may gaze when it has been purged and removed from mortal desires. The soul gazes when it fixes its eyes in the light of God's contemplation; it sees when in that contemplation it perceives how great are the joys, how great is the gladness, how great is the seriousness, and how great is the pleasantness. Health makes it secure, gaze makes it upright, vision makes it blessed: For when it is free from all dregs and washed clean of stains, then at last it most gladly holds itself within itself, and fears nothing for itself, nor is anything done by any fault of its own. And then with a certain immense and incredible joy it proceeds into God, that is, by the contemplation of truth; for indeed, the vision of God itself follows a right gaze, which is the end of gazing.
Similarly, the spirit itself (which we declared above to be a certain power of the soul inferior to the mind, where similarities of corporeal things are expressed) has its own proper vision: This spirit is not a body, but similar to a body. Therefore also, those things which are seen by the spirit are not corporeal, but similar to a body. For the spirit is something intermediate between non-body or light; and a body composed of elements. Therefore it cannot be seen as a body, but as almost a body, or an image or likeness of a body. Indeed, the face of man is known to us externally, and in memory it has its image, incorporeal indeed, but similar to a body. The wonderful beauty of this world is also present to us externally, and in our memory it has its image, likewise incorporeal, but similar to a body, to which we return when we think of it with closed eyes. From these things it is gathered that just as for the bodily sense a body is perceived in a place, visible to bodily eyes, so also for the keenness of the soul, the likeness of a body is discerned by the eyes of the spirit in memory. For there is a certain intensity of pleasure in joining the seen body and the vision: and this same intensity of pleasure is in joining the image of the body, which is in memory and the vision of thought. I would reveal many hidden things in this place concerning this subject, were not necessity calling me away to other more common matters. For as it seems to me, we have deviated too far from the scope of the soul's harmony. Therefore, I will now in turn turn the thread of my discourse to that.

C H A P. III.

*How through the five interior powers of the soul we ought to ascend to higher things, to the ineffable harmony of the soul and to the throne of the Creator. And concerning the property of each degree of the system or ladder.*

When we wish to raise ourselves from lower to higher things by the harmonious consent of the spirit, and by the ladder or system of the soul, we need the first step of the ladder or system, namely sense, to offer itself to us, then imagination,

with carnal eyes, and also conceives many things with fantastic imagination, and
everywhere it is stretched, moved, raised, and seems to fluctuate, not going out from itself,
but wandering within itself as if traversing a great space, nor does it go out to those things,
but represents them to itself by its own considerations. For imagination indeed has in itself a certain
breadth and depth. For through charity it embraces God and all faithful to Him;
through meditation it meditates on all things which God has wrought from the beginning of the world
to the end for salvation; through contemplation it contemplates heavenly things, which are above.
Reason, however, which is the third degree of the musical system in the soul, is that power of the soul
which perceives the natures, forms, differences, properties, and accidents of corporeal things,
all indeed incorporeal, but not existing outside bodies, except by reason of their subsistence;
for it abstracts from bodies, which are founded in bodies, not by action, but by consideration,
namely the nature of the body itself, according to which every body is a body. Furthermore,
intellect also, which is the fourth degree of the spiritual system, is that virtue of the soul
which apprehends invisible things, such as Angels, Demons, souls, and every
created spirit; finally, intelligence, which constitutes the last and highest degree
of the aforesaid system, is that power of the soul which is immediately
placed under God, for it discerns the supreme good itself and the unique true,
and truly immutable. We have said, therefore, that the human soul perceives
corporeal things by sense, similarities of bodies by imagination, natures of
bodies by reason, created spirit by intellect, and finally, uncreated spirit by
intelligence and mind. Whatever, therefore, sense perceives, imagination represents,
thought forms, ingenuity investigates, reason judges, memory preserves, intelligence
comprehends, and leads to meditation or contemplation. Ingenuity,
therefore, is that power or intensity of the soul by which the soul extends and exerts itself
towards the knowledge of unknown things. Ingenuity therefore inquires into unknown things, reason discerns
what has been found, memory stores what has been judged, and still offers things to be judged.
And in this way, ascent is made from lower to higher things through an admirable harmony,
and for that reason, the lowest depend on the highest. For intellect is the image and likeness of intelligence or
mind, reason is the image and likeness of intellect, the phantasm or imagination is the image and likeness of reason,
the spirit is the image and likeness of the phantasm, to which also the supreme body of the body, fire, is joined by a certain
similarity, and air to fire, but water to air, and earth to water. Sense
informs imagination, imagination informs reason, and makes science or
prudence; again, the divine presence encountering reason informs it, and makes
intelligence or wisdom. There are therefore, as it were, two members in reason, since there is in
it something tending towards higher and heavenly things, which is called wisdom; and something
looking towards transitory and perishable things, and that is called prudence. For these two are from
reason, and consist in reason. With respect to these, reason divides itself into two;
upwards, namely, into wisdom, and downwards into prudence, as if into a man and a woman,
so that the man is superior and rules, but the woman is inferior and is ruled. Whence it is said:
"Better is the iniquity of a man than a woman doing good." For better is he who,
inflamed by heavenly desire, afflicts the flesh by withholding necessities from it, than
                                                                                                                             he who

--- Page 271 ---
DE MUSIC. ANIM. COMPOS. PRAX. 269

who, dissolved by carnal affection, strives to satisfy it in all things that are agreeable. But returning to our scale or system, we see that sense is aided externally; because the eye of the flesh, although by nature it has the faculty of seeing, nevertheless never by itself attains vision, nor the ear hearing, except by the benefit of external light and sound, and so in other things. Similarly, imagination is aided externally, because it is conceived from the senses. Reason is aided internally, because the rational spirit, by the gift of creation, is capable of knowing the true and loving the good; which, unless it has been suffused by a ray of inner light and inflamed by heat, will never attain the affection of wisdom or charity. Intellect and intelligence are aided from above; because God is both fire and light. Light therefore emits from itself that splendor which it contains within itself, and by it illuminates the mind and intelligence to the knowledge of truth. Fire, however, emitting heat from itself, but not losing it, inflames the affection for the love of virtue. And just as the eye does not see the Sun, except in the light of the Sun, so intelligence cannot see the true and divine light, except in its own light. Whence the Prophet says: *In your light they shall see light*. Therefore, when the mortal shall have put on immortality and this corruptible incorruptibility, then according to our measure, through the illumination of the mind, we shall know all things, and through the lightness of the incorruptible body, we shall be able to be everywhere, we shall fly with the mind through contemplation, we shall fly with the body through incorruption, we shall discern with the mind, and we shall discern with the body; since our bodily senses will be turned into reason, reason into intellect and intelligence, and intelligence will be changed and will migrate into God. Thus, as Isaiah the Prophet testifies; *The moon will be like the sun, and the dignity of the sun will be multiplied sevenfold, and exalted, etc.* We conclude, however, from what has preceded, that visible things are perceived by sense, and that in imagination are contained the images and likenesses of visible things; similarly, that to reason belong the reasons and definitions of visible things and the investigations of invisible things, and finally, that to intellect and intelligence pertain the comprehensions and contemplations of spiritual and divine things. Sense and imagination, however, do not ascend to reason, but remaining below, they can to some extent lead it, and as it were from afar show certain things, to which they are not able to arrive. In a similar proportion, reason can aid intellect and intelligence, but it cannot ascend to their state, because it has its own boundaries and proper limits, which it cannot exceed: We have sense and imagination in common with other animals, since they see visible things, and remember things seen. Indeed, in some things, beasts surpass us, because it was just that to brute animals, to whom nothing was granted of intellect, something peculiar in sense should be given, according to those verses:
	*The boar surpasses us in hearing, but the spider in touch,*
	*The vulture in smell, the lynx in sight, the ape in taste.*
And thus, conversely, a greater necessity is imposed on man for exercising reason, by how much greater a defect he suffers in sensuality. Reason, however, begins there, where something occurs that we do not have in common with animals. Therefore, it must be diligently considered that there are three things in the inner man, namely, some things are placed below reason, some next to it, and some above it. Below reason are those things which we perceive by sense, such as hard, soft, hot, cold, white, and black, etc. Next to reason are those things accessible to reason, which we perceive by reason, such as convenient, inconvenient, true, false, just, and unjust; for reason is a certain movement of the mind, sharpening the sight of the mind, and distinguishing true things from false. Finally, above reason are those things which neither sense teaches, nor reason persuades, but are either comprehended by divine revelation, or believed by the authority of the sacred Scriptures, such as, that God is three in one substance, and in three supersubstantial
								Ll 3		persons

persons, one, and that God is the universe of things, yet in such a way that meanwhile there is nothing of individual things; and thus it is not subject to the movements of reason, because reason is only about something specific. These, therefore, are the degrees of the soul's system, which are all properties of the soul, and are no less called the soul itself, than the liver, heart, brain, muscle are called one flesh, while nevertheless they differ in property. Thus the consonance of a Diatessaron is called harmony, and likewise a Diapente and a Diapason, and a Diapason with a Diatessaron, and a Diapason with a Diapente and a Disdiapason: namely, all these are harmonies, and yet they differ in the diversity of their sounds. Therefore, the soul has many names according to the function of its operation: For it is called *life*, while it vegetates. *spirit*, while it contemplates, *sense*, while it senses, *mind*, while it is wise, *intellect*, while it understands, *reason*, while it discerns, *memory*, while it remembers, *will*, while it wills. And yet all these do not differ in substance, as they do in names, because all are one soul, just as the aforementioned members of the body are the flesh of one body; for indeed the properties are diverse, but the essence is one. Nevertheless, there can be a difference between spirit and soul, because every soul is spirit, but not every spirit is soul. For, as was said in the preceding [text], spirit is not soul, unless it is prepared for this office by a due portion of light. Furthermore, regarding the difference between soul and spirit, we see that one is the property of an inferior spirit, another me-

ON THE MUSICAL COMPOSITION OF THE SOUL. PRACTICE. 271

substance consists, full and perfect, in these three, namely, in rationality, concupiscibility, and irascibility, as if in a certain trinity of its own: And this whole trinity is a certain unity of the soul, and the soul itself; yet it differs from God in this, that God is all His own, while the soul is only certain things of its own; these indeed being natural and all of them. Therefore, the whole essence of the soul is contained in these powers, yet it is not divided into parts, since it is simple and indivisible; but if it is sometimes said to have parts, this must be understood by way of similitude rather than concerning the truth of composition. For the soul is a simple substance; nor is reason anything other or less in substance than the soul; but one and the same substance acquires different names according to its diverse powers. Therefore, through the first power, namely, rationality, the soul is capable of being illuminated to know something, namely, below itself, and above itself, and beside itself, as was said before. Indeed, it knows God above itself, and the Angel beside itself, and whatever is contained within the circuit of heaven, below itself: Through concupiscibility, it is capable of desiring and loving something; and through irascibility, of fleeing something and pursuing it with hatred. Whence it is gathered that all sensation arises from rationality, and all affection from the other two: We call reason the soul's gaze, by which it beholds truth through itself; but ratiocination the inquiry of reason. Therefore, the former, namely reason, is necessary for seeing, the latter, namely ratiocination, for inquiring. Moreover, affection, which arises from the other two powers of the soul, is recognized as fourfold, namely from concupiscibility, joy and hope, while we now rejoice in what we love or hope to rejoice; and from irascibility, sorrow and fear arise; for we now grieve over what we hate, or fear that we will grieve. These four affections of the soul, therefore, are as it were certain principles and the common matter of all vices and virtues. And, since virtue is a habit of a well-composed mind, therefore the affections of the soul must be composed, instituted, and ordered to that to which they ought, and as they ought, so that they can produce virtues, otherwise they will easily slide into vices. When, therefore, love and hate are instituted prudently, modestly, bravely, and justly, they rise into virtues; namely, into prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice, which are as it were the origin and hinges of all virtues, and all these are effectively and virtuously instituted in the soul. Also, through hatred of the world and of oneself, the soul progresses in the love of God and neighbor; through contempt of temporal and inferior things, it grows in the desire for eternal and superior things. Hence, therefore, it is clearly evident that reason is not immune from error, unless it is illuminated by the mind. Whence it happens that its good affections, produced by the illumination of the mind, are called virtues, while bad ones, proceeding from a defect of illumination, are called vices. For the mind is always illuminated by God, but it does not always illuminate. For the first light in God is supereminent above all intellect: Wherefore it cannot be called intelligible light, but that light, when it is infused by God with immediate radiation, is called intelligible, because it can be understood. Then, when, distilling through the mind, it is joined to reason, it becomes rational, and can not only be understood, but also thought. Afterwards, when through reason it is infused into the idol of the soul, where fantasy or imagination operates, it becomes not only thinkable and rational, but also imaginable, yet not yet corporeal; but when it thence migrates into the ethereal vehicle of the soul, then for the first time it becomes corporeal, yet not manifestly sensible, until it has passed into the elemental body, whether simple airy or composite, in which it becomes light manifestly visible to the eye. Finally, as regards harmony and the consonances by which these powers or virtues of the soul consonant with each other, it must be understood that they are proportioned to one another in this way. The proportion of the consonance Diapason (octave) is found between rationality and concupiscence; but between reason

Furthermore, it must be known that, if reason is illuminated by the mind, an admirable harmony and consonance is found in man; by whose symphony virtues, daughters of God, are produced; indeed, even anger itself and hatred are converted into good. But on the contrary, where the illumination of reason is lacking, there virtues are deformed into malignant vices of the Devil, and all things are submerged into evil and errors.
