As for the *disposition of the dreamer's body*, it must be known that *there are four ways of sleeping*: some lie supine or on their backs, so that, with eyes and hearts intent, they may await the gift of prophecy from the Creator: *Others*, while sleeping, lean on their right side or right flank to praise their creator and the creator of all animals, and to see the truth proceeding from God; In this manner, Prophets and righteous people were accustomed to lie down when they wished to dream: *Others* lie on their left side when they sleep, so that food may be digested and the soul may be filled with joy, as we read in the *Treatise attributed to Solomon*: although we, agreeing with physicians on this point, establish that better digestion and greater comfort for the soul are conferred if one inclines to the right side rather than the left while sleeping; nevertheless, in this case, sometimes empty dreams occur, arising from drinks and foods, which are fallacious, ineffective, and vain: *Finally, others* usually sleep prone, or with face and belly downwards: And such *dreamers are called diabolical*, because by looking downwards towards the region of darkness, they cannot rightly contemplate God. Furthermore, those most skilled in magic also command that *the dreamer's room and external conditions also be adapted*, so that for the effect of divine vision, not only their internal but also their external self may be accommodated; Therefore, whoever wishes to receive divine dreams should be well-disposed in body, with the brain free from vapors, and the soul immune from disturbances and cares, and on that day should abstain from supper, lest they become intoxicated: The room in which one intends to dream should also be clean, neat, and sacred, in which, after an incense offering, and with temples anointed and bound, according to the instruction of the Magi, with dream rings on the fingers, and a celestial image and sacred paper placed under the head, the dreamer, having invoked the divine power with sacred prayers, should go to bed, with focused thought and regard for the matter they wish to know, for thus they will see the truest and most certain dreams, preceded by the illumination of the mind and intellectual spirit. This is the opinion of the ancient Magi, although we, adhering to the Sacred Scriptures, believe that without these ceremonies of the Magi, we can attain the mysteries of true dreams in the manner of the Patriarchs and Prophets of God. Finally, the time more suitable for this work is *night*, when the senses are freed from wandering objects and daily errors and vain affections, and no fear troubles the mind: This is also confirmed in many places of the sacred Bible; Thus it is said, *Gen. 15. 12. Now when the Sun was already set, when it was blind night, behold, a smoking furnace appeared, etc.* Thus *Gen. 40. 5. They both saw a dream in one night, etc.* Thus *Judges 7. 9. The same night the Lord said to him: rise and go down to the camp, etc.* And so in many others. From this it is perceived that night is the best and most convenient time for dreams; inasmuch as the prophetic Spirit acts more aptly and properly in humans during this time, due to the reason and disposition of the things previously mentioned.

Thus also from common histories we learn that an Angel appearing to Hannibal the Carthaginian in the form of an infant predicted the future ruin of Italy, and that Alexander, King of Macedonia, saw in a dream that Cassander's hands were poisonous and deadly to him, just as he was eventually killed by a poisoned cup. The poet Simonides, when he had humanely and religiously buried a certain dead man cast out without burial in the port of the sea, saw the spirit of that buried man in a dream the following night, warning him not to board the ship the next day with others who were going to travel, for that day's journey would be dangerous and deadly. Terrified by this prediction of the spirit, the poet rested that day and did not wish to entrust himself to the sea. It happened therefore, that subsequently on that very day, that ship, on which the poet had decided to travel by sea the preceding day, was submerged and utterly lost with all who had boarded it, due to the harshness of the storm and the violence of the waves. Croesus also foresaw in a dream the destruction and death of his son Atys, nor could any cunning or skill sufficiently resist it. Thus Astyages' dream warned him about his grandson by his daughter, who would be the future cause of his deposition from the Kingdom. Alcibiades dreamed that he was covered with the rags and cloak or small mantle of his mistress or female friend, which indeed happened, but far differently than he had hoped: For, having been killed by the soldiers of Pharnabazus, he is said to have been finally covered by his dear female friend with her cloak. Attila confessed that he had seen two men, holding drawn swords in their hands, and hovering over his head, threatening death unless he spared Pope Leo. To Darius, King of the Persians, the divination of impending evils was presented in a double dream; For the Macedonian phalanx seemed to him to be consumed by its own fire, and then in his sleep he saw Alexander being brought to him in the attire in which he himself had been hailed as king, and riding a horse through Babylon, and suddenly, with the horse itself, removed from his sight. This indeed was a divination of a foreboding mind, from which afterwards the Persians were also conquered by land and sea. Finally, innumerable examples of truthful dreams exist in the world, all of which it is impossible to bring forward in this place; some of which declare things directly and openly, as they happen, while others present future events in an enigmatic and parabolic way, yet in such a way that their outcome and result most certainly and ineffably follows.

## Concerning the science of the intellect or Geomancy.

### CHAPTER I.
#### That geomantic science is a true act of the intellectual soul.

[Large decorative woodcut initial Q]ALTHOUGH in the technical history of the Macrocosm, we have spoken of the property of Geomancy, and of the divination arising from it, here nevertheless we deem it not unfitting to discuss its essence, and indeed, we will openly demonstrate with sufficiently probable reasons that it is a true science of the human soul: for if we consider the origin of this science, we will certainly perceive that it is a very hidden and internal science: Whence it happens that common people, who merely tread in the footsteps of the senses, are accustomed to babble that this art is merely accidental, foolish, and empty, and possesses no virtue in itself, and indeed, it will not be surprising to those who diligently and carefully consider the matter, if sensible men, nay, even those endowed with a strong imagination, cannot grasp the reason of this arcane science, nor perceive it with spiritual eyes, since its consideration even transcends the limits of common reason. For if we attempt to give a reason for the effects in this science, that work will certainly be arduous and difficult, and a tedious and troublesome labor; The reason for this is indeed readily at hand. For who, even among common people, would not consider him foolish and vain, who would wish to inquire about the secret counsel and intention of a master from a servant executing his master's commands, and to learn and explore these things from that servant, if indeed the servant were to immediately reply thus: 'My King or Master is accustomed to command this or that; yet he does not likewise reveal or indicate the reason for the command to his executors or ministers and servants.' Thus we receive the affection of life in a manner wonderful to higher principles, while men are accustomed only to reason conjecturally from the effect about its source, vehicle, and reason, but to know or possess nothing certain: Thus also the divine mind produces wonderful effects in man and acts wonderfully, while nevertheless the obstacle of flesh and darkness prevents us from rightly knowing the reason for these actions: Therefore the mind acts upon the intellect, and the intellect patiently fulfills the acts of its king, yet the principal cause lies hidden in the center of the mind, that is, in the divine word. Thus the Master hands money to his servant, so that he may see to its transport to a certain city: yet the servant does not understand what his Master intends to do with such money, because that lies hidden

--- Page 321 ---
DE INTELLECTUAL SCIENCE, OR GEOMANCY. 39
lies hidden in the mind of the Lord: Then the intellect and reason impel the imagination to bear and carry the impressions of its King, namely the mind. Thus a servant places his master's money in a chariot or wagon, so that it may serve as a vehicle. Finally, imagination entrusts this will of the mind to the senses, so that they may draw its burdens into the visible world; And thus also horses are accustomed to draw a chariot or wagon into the destined city: Meanwhile, however, reason or imagination or the senses no more understand the intention of the mind than a servant or a wagon or horses perceive the secret and hidden will of their Lord. Nevertheless, human reason can conjecture better than imagination or the senses, just as a servant is in some way permitted to imagine and attain by conjecture the conception of his master, although he has nothing certain. From these things, therefore, it is evident that just as we cannot know God except a posteriori, so also it is not permitted to perceive or understand the mind or the reason for its actions except from their effect. Moreover, from the effect, the Artists have discovered that science to be true and admirable, inasmuch as through it, concerning unknown future, present, and even past things, they have accomplished wonderful things in a divine manner. The outcome, therefore, usually proves the perfection of a thing. But truly, if fools, by inquiring too curiously, wish to penetrate to the center of this act, that is, to the unity and point of the mind itself, they will indeed lose their labor and oil: because it exists beyond the degree of reason and intellect, to which no one can ever attain unless they shed their bodily dwelling: It is sufficient, therefore, that we know a Monk by his habit, and a thing by its effect: Thus, therefore, this sentence is divine, because it makes one divine, closest to Prophecy, because through it the mind, by its own virtue, performs that, albeit weakly, which it is otherwise accustomed to perform (but more powerfully and openly due to the multitude of superior rays united simultaneously) when united and conjoined with the divine mind: And therefore, having duly considered these things, we see that the human mind is of the same essence as the divine mind, inasmuch as it is accustomed to perform the same thing with lesser power that the latter performs with greater: For greater force produces a greater effect, and consequently, a lesser force produces a lesser one. The mind in man, therefore, by itself, without the addition of divine rays, if only it is preserved from the harms of body and flesh, and is not obscured by darkness, or affected by the enticements of the senses, can pour forth its prophetic power into a sensible effect, and perform wonders, the reason for which effect it is no more possible to render than it is possible to recognize the reason for Prophecy itself.

C H A P. II.

Why Geomancy is considered by the ignorant to be an absurd and ridiculous science.

The ignorant are accustomed to consider this science of the soul absurd and ridiculous because they believe it flows and originates mostly from points made by an accidental movement of the hand, and consequently, they say that nothing perfect or certain emanates from it: But the wise and learned, and the skilled, could respond to them in the same way, that there is nothing certain or of constant resolution in the mind of man, when deciding to execute this or that thing, or to seek this or that place on such a day, and yet what the human mind thus decides within itself, that without impediment

--- Page 322 ---
40      TREATISE I. SECTION II. PART II.
hindrance man accomplishes. Therefore, by such reasoning, even though the movement of the hand, constituting points corresponding to the disposition of the mind in its specific number and proportion, seems to do nothing in the first projection of the points, nevertheless many hidden things lie concealed beneath the multitude of points: namely, the very prediction of the soul, carried by the ethereal and elemental vehicles of the Microcosm, inasmuch as the twelve signs, seven planets, and four elements, and their virtues, are hidden under such points: For just as the mind and intellect could not descend into man without the aforementioned vehicles of the Macrocosm, so also nothing real and essential proceeds from the mind, as its origin, unless it passes through these media. This movement is therefore not accidental, inasmuch as it proceeds from the human soul, which is the complete essence of man, and acts essentially and by itself, unless it is hindered by the accidents of flesh and senses. Thus also we say that the mineral nature of lead and iron tends in its essence towards the nature of gold: but it is hindered by accidents, that is, by impure sulfur, so that it cannot reach the predetermined goal of nature. But the unlearned will reply that such impediments always occur to the body, because of the impurity of the flesh and the error of darkness. We therefore grant them this, that the more the rays of the mind are hindered in their movement by the defilements of the body, the more the effect of its action is weakened: just as we see that when a cloud is interposed between our eye and the solar rays, these rays cannot penetrate to our sight, and consequently their manifest effects are removed. So also, because of the strength of the body and flesh in the nature of darkness, the imagination is so filled with fictitious clouds of matter, that the rays of the mind, as far as the body is concerned, are hindered: Whence it happens that they cannot pass to the senses as they are. Therefore it will be necessary that the body be rectified as much as possible, refined and tempered by abstinence accepted in any way, and that the pride of the flesh be cast down, and that the scattered middle rays of the soul be drawn together to the center, and thus the whole man, both external and internal, convert himself to the nature of simplicity, and neglect and hate composition and multitude. Only then will he be best prepared for producing not accidental but essential works by the power of the act of the human mind itself.

***

CHAPTER III.

How the Geomantic man ought to dispose and prepare himself, so that the intentions of his mind may be clearly emitted, and united with the senses through reason.

Since Geomantic points are seen by the benefit of sense, and furthermore the same are compared in celestial and elemental things by the power of fantasy, and finally the hidden power itself, both of these points and also of the figures arising from them, proceeds from the validity of the intellect, both active and passive, and consequently from the mind, as from the starting point, it follows therefrom that the human body must be so regulated and governed, lest its more intellectual part be submerged or lulled to sleep by excessive commerce with the flesh, and lest the imaginative or fantastic spirit be rendered dull and unpolished. Let therefore the fantastic spirit, before this work is approached, be clean, pure, unshaken, and disturbed by cares as little as possible, so that it may be made worthy for the mind and intellect to preside over it and become known to it. For such a spirit, most apt for prophecy, receives the light of the mind's rays without any hinder-

--- Page 323 ---
DE INTELLECTUAL SCIENCE OR GEOMANCY. 41

[impedi]ment, it will receive in the mind and depict the objects of truth in a mystical way, as if in a mirror, and it will make the sense and movement of the body proceed exactly and precisely to where the effect of the mind itself tends. Therefore, since we are now sound and healthy in body, not disturbed in mind, not weighed down by food or drink, not suffering from want or poverty, and offended by no vices of lust or anger, let us enter into this arena of prophecy. Also, he who wishes to use this art should keep his spirit pure, both by tranquil and religious meditation, and by a moderate diet tempered according to nature: For this preparation is necessary for him who desires to truly foretell future events, either through Geomantic art or by any other means, inasmuch as without it, no one can become a true prophet: For he who is weak in imaginative spirit will not attain the desired end, but will judge confusedly and indiscriminately: So also, when we are filled with gluttony and wine, our imaginative spirit, as if submerged by harmful vapors, hides and depraves the glory and truth of the mind's rays, no differently than a thick cloud or earth elevated in the middle region of the air turns away the glory of the Sun from the eyes of the beholder and generates or induces a refraction of its rays. Hence, false things will appear instead of true ones, and the very portion of the cloud opposed to the Sun will seem changed into a rainbow or multicolored substance, and many phantasms will appear in the air which are not such as they appear. Hence it is reported that Amphiaraus the Prophet, as Philostratus testifies, ordered a prophet wishing to divine future events and receive the oracles of God or the mind, to abstain from food and wine for an entire day, indeed, even for three days, if it could conveniently be done. So we read that Ezra and Daniel, indeed even Moses himself, before they approached God, abstained from their wives for three days and washed their clothes; and they did all this by the command of God himself, concerning which it is read in Exodus 19 and Ezekiel 44. And so also it is necessary for him who faithfully desires to engage in this kind of divination, not to be delighted by carnal intercourse, but by spiritual union; not to be intoxicated by wine, but by the illuminating liquor of the mind; not to abound in worldly riches, but in the infinite abundance of divine intellect; not to be filled with gluttony, but with spiritual food. *In a certain old French manuscript concerning the secrets of Geomancy, I found confirmation of the above in the following words: Before you proceed to the projection of Geomantic points, I would have you understand that they are not to be counted in the projection. For if you do so, nothing good or profitable will come of it, inasmuch as this science is founded upon the soul, and therefore the number of points is in the will of the soul, and is by no means to be established according to the appetite of your senses. So therefore it is fitting for him who undertakes this work that he begin nothing unless his heart is well disposed, and he enjoys an upright and sound conscience, nor should his spirit or soul be vexed by any disturbances, and moreover, he should not even wish worse things for another than for himself: And finally, thus prepared, he should trust in God, the master of sciences, and solicit Him with prayers, that by the virtue of this science He may reveal the truth to him; Therefore, these things having been diligently performed, one must immediately proceed to the projection and disposition of the points, etc.* These are his words, in which he does not in any way disagree with our opinion, but rather, on the contrary, seems to agree exactly with it.

CHAP. IV.

That it is not sufficient for divination in Geomancy that the body and flesh be well ordered,
but that it is also furthermore necessary that the rays of the internal
soul, moving amidst the multitude, be gathered
into themselves.

„ Just as united force is accustomed to induce strength, so also, when dispersed, it produces
immense weakness. Thus we see the rays or flame of a candle illuminate a place
in wonderful ways in a narrow chamber, because the narrowness of the place compresses and contracts
the rays emitted from the flame towards each other, so that they have greater power
in illumination; But if that candle is placed in a wide and spacious place,
its light is greatly weakened and obscured, due to the dissipation of its rays in the wide
„ medium. So also we perceive one scruple of saffron to intensely dye a whole
pound of water; But truly, if the same weight is added or introduced into a hundred pounds
of water, that tincture will be pale, and not very perceptible. By similar reasoning, therefore,
the lamp of the human life-soul (whose candelabrum is the human body) if it diffuses
its rays in this or that business, indeed, in infinite external things, for example,
in lawsuits and legal affairs, in the medical art, in the care of household matters,
in sorrow and sadness over a lost thing or the death of a friend, in anger or some unexpected
adversity, in some art or science and other such things, or if it is also affected by the commerce
of concupiscence, the vice of drunkenness, the indulgence of gluttony, or other allurements of the flesh,
its strength and power in the illumination of the body will be very weak and small.

But truly, if all these rays of the soul are reduced from external affairs to the internal
economy of the Microcosm, and are withdrawn from the multitude to their center,
the force of the soul will be united, and by that reason, that body will be wonderfully illuminated,
which before was obscure and dark due to the lack of rays, and thus the prophetic power
in man will be far more effective than it was before, and consequently will elevate the whole
internal man, as it were, into the sublime part of the body and unite it with the mind,
no differently than artificial fire is accustomed to elevate and carry a molten body upwards.
However, this reduction of the expanded rays of the soul into one cannot happen without
the purification of the body, which is done in the manner alleged above. Wherefore it is necessary
above all for him who desires to claim for himself the name of a true seer in Geomancy,
that his soul convert and reflect its widely expanded and dispersed rays back into itself;
because the principal virtue of this science consists in the illumination of the soul,
inasmuch as true things are seen in its divine light, as in a mirror of truth,
and, once seen, are explained by an external intuition through points in a certain mystical
way, by the guidance of the soul attentive to this.

C A P. V.

That the act of a true Geomancer is, as it were, a movement of the mind in ecstasy, or rather a kind of rapture, in which prophecy occurs.

Just as rapture in general is called an abstraction, alienation, and illumination of the human mind, proceeding immediately from God, by which Prophecy is accomplished: so also a certain kind of rapture and ecstasy is required for divination through Geomancy, which is not called an illumination of the mind immediately springing forth from God, but rather a recollection of its expanded rays, and a gathering into a narrower place, namely into the seat of the human body itself and its own dwelling, so that through them the divining soul itself may discern simple truth more clearly: Hence, ecstasy is primarily required in this science, that is, an abstraction of the mind's rays from all external things or affairs, so that they are drawn inward into itself: For just as in great rapture the rays of the mind and soul [are drawn] upwards to the divine essence of God

CAP. VII.

Concerning many other species of divination coming to man from external sources.

Those two species of divination, which we deduced in the two preceding sections, occur to man from within; But there are also many other species of presage & prophecy which are elicited from external accidents of things by a skilled & wise man; namely, Hydromancy, Lecanomancy, Aeromancy, Pyromancy, Capnomancy, Axinomancy, Botanomancy, Cleromancy, Clidomancy, Umbilicomancy, Physiognomy, Chiromancy, Necromancy, Augury, Haruspicy, Onomancy, Arithmomancy, Nomancy, & other such things.

**CHAPTER II.**
What is Memory and how manifold is it? And the method for retaining both kinds of memory.

Before we enter the field of this art, we consider it especially necessary to know what that is about which this art is concerned, and that we may proceed methodically in this our treatise.

Memory is therefore the most faithful guardian and preserver of things received and images, or of things whose forms have been perceived by the intellect: or it is a certain habit referring to forms after some lapse of time, whose object is always the past.

And since memory is discussed here, which is common to both humans and animals, I wish the reader to understand that human memory differs from the memory of animals in this: that the latter is only sensitive, receiving only sensibles, phantasms of things, while the former is intellectual and sensitive at the same time.

Therefore, these things having been diligently observed, we think we should proceed thus to the kinds of intellectual memory, so that we may demonstrate that it is to be considered in a twofold way, namely, either as it is received in its natural disposition, whose nature...

--- Page 332 ---

by expansion, it introduces them to the rational cell, so that they may be rationally weighed there, from which they are further immediately sent to the chamber of memory, so that in its cave, with the vermiform caruncle contracting itself, they may be preserved. Medicines also contribute to memory that is diminished or unnaturally damaged, whether that occurs due to an abundance and excess of coldness and humidity, or due to an excess of heat and dryness. Indeed, imagination itself is also harmed by the predominance of these qualities beyond the laws of nature, and when harmed, it is restored by medicines and and brought back to its complete state. Physicians have treated these matters extensively. Beyond these two ways of aiding weak memory, natural philosophers and physicians have known no others, except for that unique gift sometimes granted supernaturally to the chosen, which is extraordinarily inspired in them by divine grace and splendor.

CHAPTER IV.
On the twofold action of phantasy concerning artificial memory.

Phantasy operates in two ways for the complete perfection of the art of memory, namely, either by ideas, which are properly forms separated from corporeal things, such as spirits, shadows, souls, etc., similarly Angels, about whom we will treat especially in our circular art. For we do not use the word 'idea' here in the same way as Plato, who used to take it for the mind of God, but for any thing not composed of the four elements, namely, for another simple thing conceived by imagination in the ethereal or spiritual part of the world; for example, for Angels, Demons, effigies of stars, and images of Gods or Goddesses, to whom celestial things are attributed, and which partake more of a spiritual nature than of a corporeal one; similarly for the shadows of virtues and vices conceived and fashioned in the imagination, which are also to be considered as Demons. But if the student's intellect cannot impress figures of such ideas upon the conception, he can make his choices among animals, humans, and inanimate things obvious and occurring to the senses, and conceive their images in parts of the sky instead of shadows and ideas. Or phantasy operates with images of corporeal things, which indeed, although they are perceived in a fantastic way, are not however considered as incorporeal things, but depicted by corporeal action and fashioned by imagination alone; for example, if we imagine a wolf killing a lamb, Peter on horseback devouring a very sharp sword with a hostile point, a venomous serpent with slippery embraces clinging to the shin of a certain man well known to you, etc. For the artist must consider sensible things by imagination alone and in a fantastic way, namely, those things in ph

CAP. V.

Whether memory is more conveniently expressed in a round
or square art.

Our Spherical Art is undoubtedly much more convenient, both by reason of the capacity of the figure, which is round, and consequently more useful for the work, since any place of a sphere possesses its natural division in any sphere of the world: Furthermore, any sphere also has its natural site and position without any alteration of its position: Hence the operator is certain that he always contemplates his invariable places: similarly no Planet is known to move or deviate outside its own orbit, but always enjoys its operation, act, and dominion in its own sphere: The art, therefore

52 TRACT. I. SECT. II. PORT. III. LIB. I.
thus in the fourth and fifth, so that the last reflection of the image will finally be very obscure and barely perceptible; this indeed happens because of the weakness of the refracted rays in the multiplication of reflections, so that the first reflection is stronger than the second, and the second than the third, and so on in the others: Thus we also say, that the more deeply the artisan in this art penetrates into the inner recesses of the imagination, the weaker become the effigies of its imaginary icons: And consequently, the more imperfect and deficient will be the operative virtue of the imagination. From which it follows, that the closer and more immediately the likeness of the imagination proceeds from the reality of sense, the more certain, stronger, more durable, and more efficacious it is in this art. But men of that ilk try to seek the foundation of their operation not from reality, but from a chimera, as it were, and a figment of a thing which never existed in the nature of things, as if, according to the operation of the aforesaid optics, we should believe that an image not seen in the first mirror, nor derived from truth and reality, could nevertheless be seen in the second or third mirror, which indeed is absurd and impossible: Therefore it will not be fitting to invent new palaces which never existed anywhere, because such an artist's fiction will lead his mind astray from the contemplation of truth, but let the house, or castle, or palace be real, so that, building your work upon a common place well known to your senses as a foundation, you may proceed in a more certain order: For if the foundation is removed from memory or slips away, the whole structure will perish, and suddenly vanish: Which indeed can very easily happen, if the first common place is fictitious: But in a thing obvious to the senses there is no fear of such an accident, or even, if anything of the sort perhaps happens, the place seen again will easily return to memory. Furthermore also, as was said concerning the reflections of mirrors, the further, in the multiplication of conceived things, their image is from the foundation, the weaker will be its impression in memory: Wherefore the greatest prolongation of fixation will be, first to imagine a palace, then rooms of this or that color, of a round shape, etc., afterwards to divide each of their sides into five parts, and then to fill each partition with invented figures as well, and lastly to impress the things to be retained upon them with some action: but with the palace submerged in oblivion, the rest also, namely the rooms, and their places, and images, and things to be remembered, will be entirely removed. Moreover, how weak will be that act (which holds the principal and first place in this art), by whose vivacity things ought to be preserved in memory, both inasmuch as its foundation is fictitious, and also, inasmuch as it recedes from the foundation of truth by an entire degree in fixation. Finally, the reason for this thing is also refuted by that experiment in medicine: even if a sufficiently strong medicine is administered orally to those suffering from bladder stones; nevertheless, because in its journey it gradually loses something of its property, leaving part of it to the stomach, part to the liver and blood, and part to the kidneys, it results therefrom that it is so weak when it permeates into the bladder, that it can perform little or almost nothing of its office, for the sake of which it was infused into the body: in a similar way, therefore, the act of imagination in the multiplication of one invention upon another will likewise become weaker. And therefore we conclude, that the operation of imagination should begin and proceed from real things, not from intentional (i.e., fictitious) ones, because the acts emanating from them, and hidden in them, are stronger, more certain, and closer to truth.

C H A P. VII.
Against those who place only brute animals, and those firmly, in the common places of both arts.

Indeed, we cannot consider those skilled in this art who are accustomed to impress animals, or irrational animals, upon the places of a palace or house and its rooms, even if they do so according to alphabetical order, assigning namely an ass to the first place, an ox to the second, etc. For these very things, insofar as they are brute animals, cannot explain a rational thing or act proper to man alone: Therefore, the irrationality of the image will perhaps be the cause that the artist forgets the rational subject because of the impossibility of the action attributed to the beast; for example, if I wish to impress an orator in the first place upon an ass, we must imagine an ass dressed in the manner of an orator with a book in hand and a cap on its head: Which indeed will seem entirely absurd to reason, by which man is governed; because an ass has neither clothes, nor a book, nor hands. Therefore, we consider it better and more correct that we assign rational images to the said places, since there is no action, whether bestial or human, which man cannot clearly express by his own action, whether by imitating, or by playing his own proper parts: if therefore we wish to express an ass, we can imagine that the image of a man fixed in the place jumps onto the back of the ass, or teaches the ass the art of reading, etc.

C H A P. VIII.
Against those who use empty places for retaining imaginable images.

There are also some versed in this art who fall into an even greater error, indeed, they seem to rise up against the laws of nature: because they follow a path even more difficult than those whom we mentioned previously, and use a worse method. For these very ones recede so far from the error of their predecessors that by using empty places they impress nothing at all upon them: but they place the things to be committed to memory in these bare and uncovered (places), inculcating that frequent axiom of the Philosophers: "It is done in vain by more, what can be done by fewer." But I could also infer thus, that the invention of the Tetrachord, Pentachord, Hexachord in music is futile and useless, because the entire dimension of music is found in the Monochord: And yet those who are skilled in music find it easier and fuller in a polychord than in a monochord: in a similar way therefore, we also do not deny that the art of memory can be made from empty places; yet we say that this is further from the perfection and ease of the art and more difficult for the student to apprehend. Moreover, it is also certain that there is no distinction among places, unless some figure or image, distinct by a fantastic figure, is impressed upon each of them: Hence this error of theirs will produce no small errors and confusion in this art. And therefore it will be necessary, if we wish to avoid that, that we assign distinct images to each place, lest confusion and absurdity arise in this art, since by their presence each place is distinguished from another as optimally as possible.

CHAP. IX.
*On the common place of the circular art, and on its division into proper places for the recollection of words.*

The common place of the circular art is the ethereal part of the world, namely, the celestial orbs, counting from the eighth sphere and ending in the sphere of the Moon. We have made a twofold division of it; *one, namely, by reason of place and order*, by which we first naturally divide it, according to the distinction of the Zodiac, into twelve equal parts, which astrologers have called celestial signs; *The other, indeed, by reason of time*, in which a subdivision is made: For, because the *primum mobile* completes its swift course in one natural day (namely, from east to west), therefore every hour of the day corresponds to five degrees of the Zodiac, which space is indeed half a sign. The length of a sign, moreover, delineates the movement of the Sun for the duration of one hour of the day. After completing the Zodiac or the eighth sphere, one must begin with the heaven of Saturn, and so descend through the other peripheries of the middle heaven towards the sphere of fire, as is explained in the following figure.

Again, the temporal places are twofold, since one is oriental, which indeed looks towards the eastern region of the world in the same sign, and we will imagine this place to be filled with a white theater: The other, however, is occidental, or the western portion of the sign, in which a certain black theater will be placed, about which we will speak later.

CAP. X.

*Of the description of the eastern & western theater.*

I call that a theater in which all actions of words, sentences, parts of speech, or subjects are demonstrated as in a public theater, where comedies and tragedies are performed. You will imagine one kind of such theaters to be situated at the point of the east; which is to be considered not as real or corporeal, but as if of ethereal vapor: And let that shadow of the theater be filled with likenesses of active spirits. Therefore, the first theater will have a white, luminous, and splendid color, presenting the day and diurnal actions. Wherefore it will be placed in the east, because the Sun, rising from the East, begins the day and promises clarity to the world: The second, however, will be imagined imbued with a black, dark, and obscure color: and you will imagine it placed in the West, because the Sun, being in the West, announces night and darkness soon to come. Moreover, each of these theaters will have five doors distinct from each other, and nearly equidistant, the use of which we will demonstrate later.

                    CHAPTER XI.
*Of the common place of the square art, and of its division into convenient places; similarly, of the selection and disposition of rooms for the work of this art.*

The common place of this art will be a chamber or room, whose sides are equally square or parallel. Nor will a room of this kind be fictitious or conceived by imagination alone, according to the intention of those who were accustomed to conceive palaces in their mind, because confusion would follow from it, and obscurity in the operations of fantasy overwhelming the power of action. Therefore, we deem it necessary that real rooms be chosen, and indeed such as are pleasing to the eye by their ornament, beauty of prospect, or some other thing, and that they be very well distinguished from each other. Moreover, above the door of each room let some notable story be painted, such as (for example) Hercules killing the hydra, overthrowing Cerberus, or Medea slaying her brother, or Actaeon transformed into a stag, and other such things. And let all such images of stories be depicted externally above the doors of the chambers. But the orders of the internal places, which are also called less common, and their division and subdivisions of parts, for the sake of a better method, we have reduced to the following distinction.

C A P. V.
On less principal images.

Perhaps the multitude of less principal shadows will please some less. So that this art may be more pleasing to them by excluding images, it must be known that those places can be distinguished from each other by colors in this way: The first place will be white like a meadow covered with snow, The second should be red, and have the appearance of a meadow existing before the gate of a theatre, in which a battle was fought, so that its surface, stained with blood, may exhibit a red color, The third place should be green and a certain area before the gate conspicuous with grass and green trees, The fourth should be blue, and everywhere like a valley before the gate irrigated by springs; The fifth and last should be a cave or a very dark subterranean cavern, presenting a black color. Opposite these meadows, let five columns be imagined, which likewise ought to be distinguished by shape and color; For the shape of the two outermost will be circular and round, but the middle column will have a hexagonal shape, and those which are intermediate to these will possess a square shape: They will also differ from each other in color in this way, so that their colors may have a relation to the colors of the theatre gates opposite to them, but in an opposite or inverse ratio: that is, so that white may be opposed to black, etc. You will also be able to attach rings by fantastic conception and chains to these columns, by which animals bound will signify Adverbs, Conjunctions, Prepositions & Interjections, as will be said in the sentences. And in them there will be this order: To the white column let a silver ring be imagined affixed, with such a chain also, but to the red, a copper one with a chain made from a branch; and to the bluish-grey, a lead one with a lead chain, and finally to the black, an iron ring with an iron chain likewise is to be considered affixed. Where, however, words are significant, there it is necessary that they be denoted by a more principal image or idea, and not otherwise, as will appear in the recollection of sentences.

C A P. VII.
In how many ways are significant words expressed in both arts, namely, both in the round and in the square?

[Marginal note:]
The expression of a significant word is done in three ways, namely

{ By Relation, namely, when one thing is referred to another, so that through that relation it signifies something without the explicit expression of the thing to be signified: Thus ink can signify an inkwell, blackness can signify ink, a sheath can signify a sword.
{ By Similitude: namely, when a similar thing expressed in a place indicates that to which it is similar, just as Sirens [indicate] women, Henry, a poor crowned man, [indicates] Henry, King of France, etc.
{ By Real Presence: thus an image or idea striking someone with a sword will signify the sword. This, therefore, is when the true thing in its nature and substance is expressed in some place by the action of an image or idea.

C A P. VIII.
On the Utility of Expressing Fixed Images, Which We Call Essential.

IF in the expression of these images we wish to find multiple advantages, nothing will need to be expressed in the midst of the aforesaid places except that which we have excerpted from certain histories: for example; from the life of Julius Caesar, or of some other Roman, or of Cleopatra, or of some Trojan, or of some distinguished Philosopher, or of similar ones, or from the sacred Bibles, such as the narratives of the lives of Samson, David, Moses, Maccabeus, and others. The first utility, therefore, will be the retention or memory of histories, through which you will also be able very easily to retain by memory significant words, non-significant words (namely, heard and unheard), similarly sentences, speeches, and subjects of things.

CHAPTER II.
On the recollection of significant words in the spherical art.

The places, as was said above, being distinct and described in the first theatre of Medea's story through five meadows, it is necessary to operate according to the aforesaid rule in the expression of significant words in this manner, namely, if I wish to denote the word (Book) in the first place, I will imagine Medea in a white meadow, as a subtle spirit hanging in the ether or sitting in a fiery chariot, inspecting a magic book: And such an imagination ought to be noted by a real expression in its proper place. Furthermore, let the second word be (was exalting); therefore we can imagine that spirit of Medea looking out from the top of a tower and anxiously observing whether her Father pursues her or not. Let the third word be (Joyful); which, in order to be explained, we will imagine Medea's spirit rejoicing for two reasons, namely, both because of the pleasantness of the place, and also because she found herbs serving her purpose. Let the fourth word be (knife); therefore let us persuade ourselves to imagine Medea throwing her knife, with which she murdered her brother, into the sea. Let the fifth word be (Light). In order for this to be signified, we will imagine that in the conflict of Jason with the vigilant serpent and the bulls spewing flames, an extraordinary light and a huge multitude of sparks leap forth from the cave. And thus we must proceed to the fifth western theatre, in whose obscurity we ought to contemplate Medea's essential actions, as if reflecting shadows.

CHAPTER III.
On the recollection and placement of significant words in the square art.

If the words are significant, they will be expressed either by relation, or by similitude, or by real presence: Thus I will express the signification of the word (Lion) in the first gate of the first place by relation, namely, by Samson clothed in a lion's skin, or by a real action, by Samson fighting with a lion: if the second word is (Sword), we will imagine by relation that Delilah, inflamed by the ardor of anger, breaks the scabbard of her husband which she found, or also by a real action we will imagine that, despairing, she inflicts death upon herself with a sword. But if the third word is (fly), we will imagine, either by real presence, that one of the Philistines, seeking to avoid Samson's violence and fervor, sits on a fly and flies into the air, or by relation, that he has putrid flesh corrupted everywhere by flies, or by similitude, that he flees from one place to another with wings very similar to those of a fly.

CHAPTER IV.
On the recollection of words indeed known, but either not at all, or with difficulty significant, in both arts.

by an apple, Pope Boniface by a key, Cadmus by a serpent or a tree,
David by Goliath's head, Eteocles by a divided flame, Saint Francis by
a bloody cross, Hercules by a club or a bow, Jason by the golden fleece
or infidelity, Midas by gold, or golden ass's ears, Nestor by a white
beard, Orpheus by a lyre, Prometheus by a bloody heart or a vul-

the Sun, for the Owl darkness, for the Raven blackness, for the Drepane a swallow, for the Eri-

a sharp beak, or the herb geranium, for the Swallow the roof of a house, for the Ibis a small
serpent. And thus the matter will always stand in the distinction of forms con-
ceived in the round art, constantly referring to the aforesaid exceptions.

C H A P. V.
Concerning the remembrance of known proper names.

When you wish to remember known and common proper names, it is necessary for you to
place others of the same names, who are known to you either familiarly, or from reading histories,
in places, and indeed simply with such an action, as
they commonly used to perform: For example, if I wish to remember some Ca-
rolus, I will place there a certain Carolus well known to me: who indeed, if a No-
tary, Secretary, or blacksmith he was, etc. he also in this office in that place
where he is to be placed, with the evident aid of an image, & a notable action of the same
will perform, or I will also choose someone famous in histories, such as Charle-
magne warring against infidels. Thus if I wish to remember Clement,
I will place in my common place, Pope Clement with a horn in
hand for better distinction, & thus
in other cases.

C A P. VI.
On the recollection of proper names never before heard by you.

IN this rule, alphabetical arrangements are especially required: For a beast will signify the first letter, a man the second, a dead thing the third, and a bird the fourth, and that not without an excellent action of the image, which will perform some unseemly thing with the beast, man, and bird; For example, Angels, according to the Sibyl, who are guardians, are named Heromiel, Saniel, Uriel, etc. Therefore, in the first place, I place a Hydra, which with its venom kills the principal image of the place, and upon the back of the Hydra I will imagine Eteocles burning, holding a basin in his hand, so that its water may extinguish the fire, but a swan pressing upon its head, driven by great thirst, drinks up all the water, wherefore here nothing remains but 'miel', which is very easy to remember, retaining 'Hero'; For Hydra signifies H, Eteocles E, Basin R, and Swan O. The action, moreover, will be that touching the hydra, he falls down dead. In the second place, I will place an Ape, which Adam, leading from Paradise, very often strikes with a fork

of mud, every simple movement is either straight or round: Here Orpheus will move straight and round; or the Sun will be formed in the hand, signifying movement by relation. Thirdly, if two or three adverbs or conjunctions, etc., begin a sentence, it is necessary to express them in only one place, unless the consequences are manifest and inseparable in the nature of the meaning. Fourthly, when you wish to arrange precisely and suddenly the said parts of a member in their places, you will first assign to the images actions of fictitious significant words: For example, if I place ink in the first place, and the first member is this: Form gives name and being to a thing; I will imagine the image taking ink, and after wiping it from the face of a beautiful girl, calling her Maura. C H A P. VIII.
Concerning orations and poems.

IN orations and poems, the aforementioned proposition and the same precise method are needed; but also in poems, this is most easily accomplished because of the necessity of meter.

C H A P. IX.
Concerning subjects and in how many ways a subject is understood here.

A Subject, as it is understood in this place, is a perfect action of some intention, which is expressed either by some relation, or by similitude, or at least really, in only one place: Moreover, I call a perfect action of some intention that by which the meaning of some history or wise saying, or law, or aphorism, or similar things is expressed, and perfectly explained in some place: but because in all these there is a varied mode of operation, therefore we will proceed in a certain order and methodically. Therefore, concerning the subjects of histories, it must be known that history is expressed in places in a twofold manner, namely, either generally or specially. History is expressed generally when its entire series and meaning are explained in only one place, as if I wish to express generally the entire history of the second book of Virgil's Aeneid in some place, I will imagine that the image of the place on the summit of a mountain looks from afar, by which means a huge wooden horse is introduced into the city by night, and consequently also thereafter, while the night is still dark, the city itself is lamentably set on fire on all sides. However, history is expressed specially when each of its parts is explained separately.

C H A P. X.
Concerning the method of expressing arithmetical figures in the aforesaid places.

WE have made mention of this matter in our book on Universal Arithmetic, where we also particularly proposed one or two chapters on Memorial Arithmetic, and in that way taught the method of numbering, adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing by the apt positioning of memorial figures in suitable places. Therefore, we refer you from here to that treatise of ours, so that we may briefly bring this second portion of the section to an end.

OF THE FIRST TREATISE.

BOOK I.

Concerning the Science of the vital with the intellectual soul,
that is, concerning Genethlialogy.

C H A P. I.
Concerning Astrology, and its parts.

[Large decorative woodcut initial V] The ancients enumerated four parts of Astrology, one of which they wished to be concerned with changes in the air, storms, and other things of this kind, and through it they were accustomed to foretell health, diseases, and abundance or scarcity of crops: The second deals with the beginnings of empires, principalities, republics, or cities, their changes, destructions, war, and similar other alterations of that kind. The third divides itself into three branches or species, one of which is occupied with the election of times, concerning which we wrote an entire small book in our general Treatise on Astrology; another is concerned with questions and interrogations; And the third, which is deservedly considered the chief of the other parts of Astrology, is called Genethlialogy, concerning which we principally intend to treat in this place: The fourth and last species is called *stoicheiomatike*, which consists in making characters, seals, and statues, whose marvelous effects histories of many kinds proclaim: But since diabolical art mixes itself with this (just as very often we see a good thing defiled and polluted by the abuses of the impious), we will repudiate it, and briefly gird ourselves for the inquiry and explanation of Genethlialogy.

C H A P. II.
What is Genethlialogy, and in what does its judgment consist?

[Large decorative woodcut initial G] We define Genethlialogy as that part of Astrology which teaches what goods of the soul, what goods of the body, what goods of fortune ought to befall the native, and from where those things flow, and by what signs future events concerning him are denoted. Therefore, the judgment of this Astrological part

--- Page 355 ---
DE ANIM. VITAL. CUM INTEL. SCIENT. 73
judgment or practice is divided into the investigation of goods either of the body, or of the mind, or of fortune: All these things indeed a skilled Astrologer will not hesitate to predict, from diligent observation of the celestial houses, and of the Planets possessing them, and consideration of their natures, and their mutual aspect and relation.

C H A P. III.
Concerning the Uncertainty of Common Astrologers in Finding the Lord of the Nativity.

When the practice or judgment of this science is to be dealt with, a celestial scheme or figure having first been erected in the manner which we have previously declared in our Treatise on Astrology, we deem it necessary to proceed first to the knowledge of the true Lord of the Nativity. But indeed in this work, great uncertainty of common Astrology occurs, inasmuch as in the election of the Lord of the Nativity there is no small diversity of opinions among Astrologers: For Firmicus, a man indeed skilled in this art, chooses that planet as the Lord of the Nativity which is observed to rule the sign which the Moon enters next after the nativity, with Leo and Cancer, which the two luminaries rule, excepted; for example, if the Moon at the time of nativity traverses Taurus, since it will next move into Gemini, which are the houses of Mercury, therefore Mercury will be the Lord of the Nativity. Others, however, some establish that one as the Lord of the Nativity who is stronger in the hemisphere at the point of nativity, that is, who at that time has more essential dignities in the sky. Others indeed wish that one to be the Lord of the nativity who obtains more and principal dignities in the five hylegial places, namely in the places of the Sun, Moon, the Ascendant, the Part of Fortune, and the conjunction or apposition of the luminaries immediately preceding the nativity; and so in others. Indeed, whose diverse opinions have brought forth to the world such great uncertainty of this most certain art, through the ignorance of its practitioners, that this most noble art, simple and pure in itself and by itself, and sculpted in the heavens by the finger of Almighty God, is falsely held and reputed by common people as sophistical, spurious, and deceitful: Therefore, what our opinion is concerning choosing the Lord of the Nativity, we will declare below.

C H A P. IV.
Concerning the Finding of the Part of Fortune in the Nativity

Almost all those versed in Astrology are accustomed to diligently inquire into the finding of the Part of Fortune in the art of Genethlialogy; Since this place is held in the highest regard among them, but by my Master in this art, a man certainly most excellent in Astrological and Mathematical science, Master Allen of Oxford, I was instructed to investigate the Part of Fortune in this way: The place of the Sun is to be subtracted from the place of the Moon in this way: If it happens that ☉ is in 7 gr. & 18 min. ♎, it is necessary to count all the signs from the first sign, namely from ♈, and six signs will be found, namely ♈, ♉, ♊, ♋, ♌, ♍, and 7 degrees with 18 minutes of ♎. These are to be subtracted from the place of the Moon: Let the Moon therefore be in 14 gr. & 9 min. ♑. Wherefore ☾ is distant from the beginning by nine signs, namely ♈, ♉, ♊, ♋, ♌, ♍, ♎, ♏, ♐, and 14 degrees with 9 minutes of ♑. Let them therefore be arranged in this way.

On the Genethlialogy of the Microcosm.

C H A P. I.
On the nature of the first house of the celestial schema in explaining the native's disposition.

The natural property of the first house, with its sign and the Lord of the sign, is primarily to explain a twofold disposition of the native: one is the proper constitution of his body, and the other is the natural inclination and aptitude of the soul in its manners.

C H A P. I. P A R T I.
On the native's bodily habitus and constitution.

In the exact investigation of the native's bodily likeness and his habitus, whether stout or slender, and his stature, whether short, medium, or tall, we are accustomed primarily to consider the degree of the ascending sign at birth; then we look to the nature and disposition of the Lord of the ascendant and the sign in which it is found; finally, we mix the virtue of the strongest planet of the entire sky with the others, just as a painter is accustomed to produce one different from the others in the mixture of various colors: Nor are the two luminaries to be neglected. Therefore, for the figure of the body, we look to the nature of the ascending sign, along with the dispositions of those fixed stars which, placed outside the margins of the Zodiac, rise with the same degree of the ascending sign; for example, in the following figure.

Here, however, Mars will act somewhat accidentally, inasmuch as he is found in the space of the first house: Whence, due to the malice of his nature, he threatens acute diseases: And this all the more, because he exists in Aries, his own house, and therefore will afflict the native in his illness with headaches: And this same thing must be done in all other nativities, having made or instituted an inquiry both into the nature of the sign of the angle of the sky, and that in which the Lord of the angle will remain, as well as the Lord himself: Furthermore, we must also consider the aspects, both benevolent and malevolent, of other Planets with the Lord of the first house, and according to them, judge concerning happiness or unhappiness.

The Moon in longer signs is said to indicate tallness of body, but in shorter ones, shortness.
The Sun in the west denotes height and length.
But I, omitting all these things, primarily observed the movement of the Lord of the nativity. If I found it in its Apogee, I predicted that the native would be tall and slender; if in the opposite of the Apogee, or Perigee, I foretold that he would be short or humble and low-set. But if I found it moving between those two places, I foretold a medium stature.

C A P. I. P A R S III.
Whether the native will be lean or fat.

The first half of Sagittarius, Gemini, and Scorpio disposes the native to bodily weakness, thinness or slenderness, and leanness.
Virgo, Libra, and Sagittarius attribute a good constitution, proportion, and build to the body.
The first half of Leo, Aries, and Taurus promises fatness, and the last (half) promises leanness to the native.

C A P. I. P A R S IV.
On the qualities and impediments of the soul.

Although from the foregoing we can perceive the qualities of the soul quite clearly; nevertheless, if anyone still desires a more exact inquiry into that matter, I would wish him to follow Schoner's doctrine, who wrote copiously and excellently in the seventh chapter on the qualities of the native's soul, and also expressed sufficiently the impediments of the same soul in the eighth chapter.

C A P. II.
On the Second House.

C A P. II. P A R S I.
On the fortune, or substance of the native.

For making this judgment, the second house, its sign, and the Lord of the sign must be considered; nor should the Part of Fortune and its Lord be neglected.
But as for the sign, if indeed it is good, it portends good; but if bad, the opposite of good. Therefore, a good sign promises possessions, riches, and substance, and indeed, all the more so, if a star of the first or second magnitude is found in the cusp of the second house, which has the simple property and nature either of Jupiter or of Venus, but especially of Jupiter, because it is the principal promiser of riches.
Also, the Lord of the second house, fortunately placed and receiving benevolent rays of the Planets, promises substances and treasures. But we call that position of the Lord fortunate when the Lord of the second house is constituted in some angle or a fortunate house, in which also a fortunate sign, either of the same Triplicity, or in some other way suitable to it, is found.
Also the Part of Fortune, concerning whose discovery we spoke above, is especially considered among the more skilled in Astrology, whose Lord, if found in a good place,

...found, will predict that the native will be rich: Similarly also, if the Part itself is found in a good and fortunate place, it promises much good; if in a bad place, much evil: but if in a mediocre place, its fortune will likewise be mediocre; Furthermore, a malefic Planet in a good place usually contaminates and infects it, as it were, with poison and hatred against the native; and thus it corrupts the goodness of the place. If, however, the Part of Fortune falls into the degree of the ascendant, it denotes that the native will be rich for a trivial reason: But if the Lord of the Part of Fortune is found in some misfortune, it foretells that the native will become poor from being rich due to some sudden accident.
	Note, that if Jupiter is the Lord of the place of fortune, or is found in it, or if he is the Lord of the second house and found in a good place, he promises immense riches to the native.

	**On the manner of acquiring substances or riches.**

	The celestial chart must be inspected for the place or sign in which the Lord of the second house is found: And by mixing its own nature with the nature of the sign in which it is found, that is, by investigating the manner of both rulerships, we will know how the native will acquire his wealth: Thus, if the Lord is found in the third house, he will acquire his riches from brothers, or sisters, or friendship, or journeys: If in the fourth house, he will receive them from his parent: If in the fifth, he will acquire them by the benefit of children, donations, or legacies, and so proceeding through the other houses of the celestial figure.
	Similarly, it must be known that among the Planets, Mars, Venus, and Mercury are said to have principal power in the crafts or bodily exercises: For Mars makes the native skilled in warfare, also makes pugilists and coppersmiths, founders, those who use cautery, and surgeons, etc. And similarly, he will make hunters in Aries (♈), Leo (♌), and Scorpio (♏): Venus makes musicians, also courtiers, those elevated by female favor, painters, dealers in gems or precious garments, pharmacists, perfumers, etc. Mercury makes learned mathematicians, arithmeticians, scribes, poets, merchants, those dedicated to trade, moneyers, money-changers, sculptors, etc. And yet the effects of these significators of crafts are intensified or diminished according to the configuration of them with Saturn, Jupiter, and the Sun, likewise according to the reason of the houses and signs in which they are constituted.

**F**or the number of brothers, see whether the fortunate Planets occupy these following places, namely the Midheaven angle, the place of Venus in a diurnal nativity, and of the Moon in a nocturnal one: For then their multitude is indicated; but if unfortunate Planets are found there, the contrary is shown.
	If two Planets have occupied signs of two bodies, namely Gemini (♊), Pisces (♓), Sagittarius (♐) and another has possessed a sign of one body, five brothers will be denoted as about to be born.
	Note, that masculine planets denote brothers, but feminine ones sisters: Furthermore, Oriental Planets will signify earlier ones; but Occidental ones later ones, and so forth in other matters. Here I would also like it to be observed that the more learned and profound in common Astrology take the almuten for the signification of brothers from the cusp of the third house and its lord, etc.

C H A P. IV.
*By what method Astrologers are accustomed to gather other hidden and future things of the native*
*from the observation of the remaining celestial houses.*

IN a similar manner, we must proceed with other questions and predictions pertaining to the native's life and its course; namely, if we wish to know his nature, friendships, prosperity, poverty, and other such things: Therefore, concerning the native's parents, and whether the father or mother loves the native more, or which of them will die first, namely the father or the mother, and concerning other such matters, we ought to consult the significator of the father, who by day is the Sun, and by night Saturn; similarly also the fourth house and its Lord. And at the same time, the places of the aforementioned in the figure must be carefully inspected: therefore, one must begin from the cusp of the fourth house, and thus proceed with the others. But if we wish to know the father's fertility or sterility, or the future number, quality, stature, and obedience of children, we shall first look at the fifth house and consider its Lord. Nor should the knowledge of the tenth and eleventh houses be rejected, and it should be noted that *Venus* is always the natural significator of children. And thus we believe one should proceed with the rest: To repeat all these things in this place would perhaps be tedious for both us and you, and no less useless and superfluous, since all Astrologers versed in the art of Genethlialogy have dealt extensively and copiously with the significations of particular houses: Among whom, however, I would especially commend to you the method and science of Johannes Schoner, as he, according to the common method, has discussed these matters most excellently and most suitably for simplicity in his volume on nativities.

C H A P. V.
*Concerning the secret operations of the signs and their degrees in*
*the disposition of the native.*

WHEN the predominant Planet is in a masculine degree at the time of a man's birth, this degree will be propitious to him in strength; a similar rule will also apply in the nativity of a woman, namely if the Lord or Lady is found in a feminine sign.
The degrees *Azemeni*, that is, degrees of bodily debility (because *Azemen* is a certain bodily debility) denote either deafness, or blindness, or loss of limbs, etc.
Therefore, when the ☾ [Moon symbol] is in the point of nativity in any of these signs, it announces some such defect in the native.
When the significator Planet is in luminous degrees, this will be the native's strength in the signification of good things, and it will also denote beauty, light, and form.
When it is in dark degrees, it signifies harshness, slowness, and a horrible, dark, and evil thing.
When the significator is in smoky and empty signs, it will announce an empty and horrible thing.
If it is found in well signs, it will denote that the native's beauty and appearance will be diminished and weakened.

If it is found in degrees that increase form, it will increase the native's fortune and dominion on earth, and promises many riches. And when any of these degrees has been the ascendant in a nativity, it will portend great dominion for the native and an abundance of riches.
But as for the signs themselves, when the ascendant has been a human sign, the native will be benevolent: If a bestial sign, solitary: and if it has been in fierce animals, he will love vexation and evils.

C H A P. VI.
How judgment should be made concerning a nativity through the observation of an Eclipse.

IF the Moon suffers an eclipse or defect in an angle of a person's nativity, it will bring some impediment to the native, and indeed in that limb which corresponds to that sign in which the eclipse occurs, or in the promise of the house: For example: if the eclipse has occurred in the tenth house, it will impede the native in dealings with the king: But if it is in the Angle of the East (Ascendant), it will impede the native's entire body, and especially that limb to which the ascendant sign is ascribed: such as the head, if the sign is ♈. etc. Furthermore, if it has been in the angles of revolution, that impediment will be less than in the angle of nativity:
Likewise, it will not be difficult to know the time of the announced impediment, if we observe how many hours the eclipse lasted: For if it was a solar eclipse, the hours will signify years; but if a lunar eclipse, months. But if there were [square with cross symbol] fractions of an hour, a day will be given to each of them. Then it must be seen what part out of 180 it is, which is between the degree of the ascendant and the degree of the eclipse (but we will name them 180 degrees between the degree of the East and the West). Afterwards, from that whole time which the eclipse signifies, such a part must be taken as the aforesaid part is of 180, because that will be the time from the beginning of the eclipse until the hour when the evil begins: For example: A lunar eclipse was in the first degree of Capricorn (♑), because it was the angle of the Midheaven, and it lasted for three hours: it will therefore signify that the native's reign and dignity will suffer detriment for three months: but if we wish to know when this detriment will begin, it must be seen how much space there is between the degree of the ascendant and the degree of the eclipse, and we will find that it is half of that which is between the degree of the ascendant and the degree of the descendant (West): Let us therefore take half of what the eclipse will signify, namely a month and a half, and therefore we will say that within a month and a half, after such a revolution, that impediment will befall the native. This same thing must also be done with a solar eclipse.
Furthermore, more skilled astrologers also teach that the angle nearest to any eclipse, and the figure of that angle at the point or time of nativity or revolution, must be observed, and they say that if it has been an evil sign, and the eclipse has been universal, it denotes much more evil than if it has been particular; Moreover, the aspects of planets, good or evil, increase or diminish the future evil; and this especially if they have been stationary. Likewise, observe diligently what degree ascended at the time of the lunar eclipse: For when the Sun comes into that sign and degree, then the full effect of the future event will appear. So also, as has been said in the preceding (sections), see how many hours the Sun remained in eclipse: For so many years will the effect of the matter or impediment considered in the eclipse last. And likewise, as many hours as the lunar eclipse will have, so many months will be signified.

CHAPTER VII.
Some special rules derived from the dispositions of the Planets.

IF in anyone's nativity, the Fortunes are Lords of evil houses, good men will do evil to the native. WHEN the malefics are Lords of good houses, good men will benefit the afflicted native. AND IF the malefics are Lords of malefic houses, evil men will do evil to the native.
WHEN the Fortunes aspect any * of these four parts, they will increase good, or diminish evil; but if the malefics aspect them, they will diminish good and increase evil. WHEN in a nativity the Moon aspects Jupiter, the native will be just; with Saturn, patient; with Venus, joyful; with Mercury, wise; with Mars, impatient and irascible; with the Sun, proud and indignant.
Every Lord of the Ascendant, without the participation of others, will alone rule the Ascendant, and the native will be of its nature: if it is Saturn, he will love pungent and astringent things; if Mars, bitter things and of sharp taste, etc. However, for briefly explaining the native's nature from the Lords of the nativity, Astrologers have put forth these following verses.

C H A P. VIII.
*Concerning the direction and place of the ascending promissor to the place of death or its danger.*

When the figure is erected in the usual manner, you should seek the opposition through the direction of the killing planet or the one predominating in the eighth house, or the square aspect: For example; If Saturn (♄) is in 18 degrees, 22 minutes of Cancer (♋) in the eighth house, you should seek its opposition, which is 18 degrees and 22 minutes of Capricorn (♑). Let the ascendant therefore be 24 degrees and 14 minutes of Gemini (♊). Therefore, you should seek in the tables of oblique ascension that degree of Gemini, and you will find that the equation is 51 degrees and 13 minutes. Then I find 18 degrees of Capricorn (♑). Its equation will be 79 degrees and 8 minutes. And because 79 degrees and 8 minutes is the larger number, therefore I subtract 51 degrees and 13 minutes from 79 degrees and 8 minutes in this manner;

        Grad.           Minut.
          79               8
          51              13
        —————           —————
          27              55

Therefore, I judge that such a dangerous illness or death will befall the native in the 27th year, and the fifty-fifth part of a whole year, which will be divided into 60 parts. And concerning the nature of the sign and Saturn, I say the illness will be melancholic.
Note that, according to Ptolemy, each degree signifies a year.
Observe also diligently that for any direction, the Part of Misfortune should always be taken, which has some malefic aspect. Therefore, the trine and sextile aspects are excepted.
