CHAPTER V.

*That one of the seven Angels or their leaders, closest to them in authority, has dominion over the human mind; And that several Angels keep custody of one man; Likewise, a refutation of Iamblichus's opinion attributing a single Demon to a whole man.*

There are many, I know, who will deny, indeed, and even now deny, if I am not mistaken, that every man has his own proper Angel presiding over him and directing his mind. To these we respond with a single word from the words of Joseph the Patriarch, that every man has a sacred Demon going before him: For his words are these, *Genesis 48:15. The Angel who redeems me from all evil, bless me and these boys, etc.* From which it is made manifest that Joseph himself confesses that he was preserved in his life by his sacred Demon and Angel, and redeemed from all danger and sin. Similarly, we deduce this same thing from these words of our Savior. *See that you do not despise one of these little ones. For I tell you that their Angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven. Matthew 18:10.* Hence therefore it is, that the Magi assertively say that Adam conversed in familiar intimacy with the Angel Raziel; Shem, son of Noah, with Jophiel; Abraham with Zadkiel; Jacob with Peliel; Joseph with Gabriel: From which it is clear that that Angel, of whom Joseph makes mention in the words just cited, was the Angel Gabriel: who is also said to have presided over Joshua and Daniel, and also Mary. Thus Moses conversed familiarly with Metatron; Elijah with Maltiel; Tobias with Raphael; David with Cerviel; Ezra with Uriel; Solomon with Michael; and so in other cases, as has been said before. From which it becomes most evident that not always one of those seven is accustomed to preside in his own person, but that quite often also one of his leaders administers that tutelary work by his command. Thus from the aforesaid we see that Abraham had Zadkiel or Zachariah as his Angel, prince of the Jovian star; Daniel had Gabriel, governor of the Moon; Tobias had Raphael, presiding over Mercury; Solomon had Michael, prince of the o 3 sphere

--- Page 392 ---
110 TRACT. I. SECT. II. PORT. IV. LIB. III.
Solar sphere: Whence it must be observed that to each person at their birth is given one of these princes, who presides over the mind of the born, and renders such a person admirable and fit to be able to know divine secrets and mysteries and to possess the revelation of the most holy majesty. Similarly, the other Angels also have immense and distinguished power from those leaders, by which they are accustomed to frequently endow the born with much happiness and knowledge. Hence Jophiel, as it were, the beauty of God; Raziel, the secret or mystery of God; Uriel, the fire or light of God; Peliel, as it were, the hidden thing and miracle of the Lord; Metatron, the gift of God; Meltiel, the liberation of the Lord; Phadael, the redemption of the Lord, etc. They are immediately derived from the other princes, both in power and authority. Indeed, it sometimes happens that these sacred Angels claim for themselves the name of the born person. Thus we read in Ezra the name of the Archangel Jeremiel from the Prophet Jeremiah, likewise Zachariel from Zechariah, and Uriel from Uria the Prophet, whom Joachim killed. Similarly, Samael or Samuel, Ezekiel, and Daniel are names of both Prophets and Angels, etc. Moreover, there are also several Angels who are guardians of the Microcosm, as was said before, of whom one, and the chief, regards and cares for the mind, intellect, and reason; another for life; and a third for the body's constitution and appetite. But, because this opinion of ours will seem harsh to some and more alien from the truth, we say that it is explained and proven by the words of the Prophet David, Psalm 91:10. Where he, speaking of Christ, says: "*No evil shall befall you, nor shall any plague come near your dwelling; for he shall give his angels charge over you, to keep you in all your ways; they shall bear you up in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone; you shall tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon:*" Which, according to Jerome, applies not only to Christ, but to every human being. Therefore, all humans are governed by the ministry of diverse spirits, contrary to that opinion of Iamblichus, who says that one Daemon does not merely preside over some part of us, but is present to the whole at once, leading the whole, and teaches that it is better that the body, soul, and intellect be governed by the same Daemon, adding these words: "*Do not divide it so that there is one Daemon of the body, another of the soul, and another of the intellect, for it is absurd to think that an animal is one, but the Daemon appointed over the animal is multiform, etc.*" By these words, he indeed tries to refute the arguments of Porphyry, who asserts that several Daemons preside over each person, of whom one cares for health, another for beauty, and others for a certain disposition in these matters, and moreover also states that one Daemon governs the body, one the soul, and another the mind. Therefore, taking up Porphyry's cause in this matter, I will eagerly prepare myself with the following arguments to wipe away the infamy cast upon him by Iamblichus: Firstly, if only one Daemon, and that a supernatural one, presides over the body and soul as well as the mind, then every human being, by the virtue and assistance of that Daemon, will escape fate and avoid all fatal things, and consequently neither fates nor stars will have any power over man. Yet Iamblichus himself seems to contradict himself in this, inasmuch as in one place he acknowledges that there are fates to which men are subject, and yet he says that fates are avoided by the virtue and presence of the Daemon presiding over man. So much so that if things were this way, all men indiscriminately would avoid their fates, inasmuch as they would only be participants of this one and sole Daemon and would thus be entirely free from fatal Daemons. Furthermore, he also says that it is better that the body, soul, and intellect be governed by the same Daemon, while nevertheless all those skilled in both Theology and Philosophy acknowledge such a great discrepancy and opposition between the soul and the body that it is wonderful how and by what means these two are joined to each other. Moreover, the property of Archangels, as Iamblichus himself testifies, is contrary to darkness. Hence they in no way rejoice in or are delighted by the body, which is the prison of the divine mind, but they greatly instruct and direct the mind

--- Page 393 ---
ON THE INQUIRY INTO THE NATURE OF EACH DAEMON. III

...direct, so that it may flee the body's allurements, and carefully avoid them, and constantly strive to free the mind and soul, trapped in the dark body, by the power of their perfection: Likewise, if an Archangel or Daemon were the sole and unique prince and president of both body and mind, it would follow that it would direct both the body and the mind (which can never err) towards good: But we see the body and flesh to be prone to every vice and kind of concupiscence, and therefore there can be no doubt that it is governed by some other, inferior Daemon, of a lower condition than an Archangel: who nevertheless is subject to the Archangel, as an inferior to a superior, if the middle soul constantly and faithfully adheres to the mind: By similar reasoning, if the vital soul did not have a certain Daemon distinct from the two extremes, namely, distinct from the Daemon of the mind and the Daemon of the body, it would not be so inconstant and mutable, adhering now to the mind, now to the animal soul, which is the more formal part of the corporeal composition: Furthermore, if only a single Daemon ruled the entire mass, both internal and external, it would be strange that the mind should be so alien to the soul and body, and the body likewise to the soul, and both mind and soul to the body, as we constantly perceive in humans: From these things, therefore, it is evident that there are more Daemons than just one, who have power over the whole human being. Finally, Jamblichus's last argument is no less futile than the previous ones, in which he says: "Do not divide it so that there is one Daemon of the body, another of the soul, and another of the intellect, for it is absurd for an animal to be one, but the Daemon presiding over the animal to be multiform." For I respond that it is more absurd to believe that a single animal has only one Daemon than if someone were to say that the world, which is one, has only one Daemon governing all and singular its parts. Who, moreover, doubts that in the world there are empyrean Daemons, others Olympic or ethereal, and elemental, by whom those regions of the world are governed? By similar reasoning, therefore, since the human body is composed of four elements, who will hesitate to ask whether some elemental Angel has dominion over the body? Indeed, it is rather to be believed that a particular spirit of each element has dominion over its portion of the body. As for the internal human, indeed it is impossible to believe that the ethereal ligament of life continues without the moderation and protection of an Olympic Daemon, or that fatal accidents are impressed upon man without regard to celestial spirits: In that which Jamblichus says, that one animal requires one president, and not a multiform one, we assert that both the Macrocosm and the Microcosm have a president that is both one and multiform: One, I say, they have, inasmuch as they are regarded by the supreme and one God, but multiform, inasmuch as they are governed by ministers or intelligences according to God's will: For man is therefore called Microcosm, because in his composition he participates in every region of the Macrocosm, and consequently also requires worldly Daemons and Angels of the same to govern these aforesaid portions. And now, finally, to return to Porphyry's error in the last place, in which he opines that many Daemons are present for us according to the number of our parts, and furthermore, that there are different Daemons within the body itself, some of whom he makes to care for beauty, others for health, and others to regard a certain habit in these things: I respond that it is done in vain by more, what can be done by fewer; Hence, if the Daemon presiding over the body can regard and protect all parts of the body, more Daemons are required in vain: Since, therefore, the Olympic president of the vital soul can regard and protect the beauty and health of the body sufficiently, why would more Daemons be required for such a work? Wherefore, having considered these things very well, we will perceive with spiritual eyes that there is one Daemon...

--- Page 394 ---
112 TRACT. I. SECT. II. PORT. IV. LIB. III.
one spirit of the mind, and that one royal and most principal, which we have previously proven to be an Archangel; another of the vital soul, which we have called the Olympic spirit, who is always the executor of fates; and finally a third, elemental, who regards the body, and the body's functions and appetites: but of these elsewhere more fully.

CAP. VI.

*Concerning the mind's descent into the soul and the middle spirit: where it joins to itself a portion of material life, by which its obscure dwelling may live, may move, and may flourish to its complete capacity.*

Apuleius, in his most delightful story of Cupid and Psyche, feigns Psyche, struggling upon the wings of the Zephyr wind, to have descended from the summit of a very high cliff into a most delightful valley furnished with all necessities, where, attended by invisible ministers, he relates that she received all things necessary for herself. What then should be thought concerning this descent of the supercelestial Psyche into a celestial valley, attributed to Cupid or celestial light? Indeed, it is said in Psalm 104:4: *Who walks upon the wings of the winds: Who makes your angels spirits or winds, and your ministers a flaming fire:* Is it not therefore customary, according to this very thing, also for the divine mind, the divine breath of God, the uncreated act, and the ray immediately proceeding from God, to descend upon the wings of winds or angels, and to be carried downwards, like its parent, into the middle region of the world? Thus therefore, according to those words of the aforementioned Prophet (*Who makes the clouds your chariot, who walks upon the wings of the wind, etc.*) the mind, a divine offspring, sitting upon the throne of the rational spirit or the Empyrean heaven, which is a spiritual cloud containing the glory of God, walks or passes upon the wings and pinions of the Archangel presiding over it, etc. And this also according to that passage of the Psalmist previously cited from Psalm 91:11: *He has given his angels charge over you, to keep you in all your ways; they will bear you up in their hands, lest you strike your foot, etc.* Which indeed, concerning the prince of the inner man, the Word of God, and the mind, which is the breath of God, immediately proceeding with the Word from the mouth of Jehovah, is to be understood. The mind, therefore, that divine ray or breath of God, prepared for its journey into the visible and material world, so that, having left the supernatural realms, it may traverse the realms of nature itself, both celestial and elemental, and now instructed and adorned with all the ranks of hierarchies, and fortified and attended against worldly evils and passions by the presence of the Archangel destined and joined to it, resting upon the wings of its minister, it plunges itself with a light leap downwards into the starry region, where it is received by the Olympic Angels, serving and subject to that Archangel, the mind's companion and guardian, and puts on an ethereal garment composed of a portion of the vital soul and ethereal spirit; to which, likewise, one spirit from the Planetary sphere, recognizing the Archangel of the mind as its superior and Lord, is said to preside or be placed in charge; which spirit is properly called the spirit of nativity, or the Genius of the Native, and is accustomed to have dominion over life, and actions concerning life; And by its operations, fate is commanded to be executed in every human being: Nevertheless, this spirit is subject to the leader of the mind no differently than a King to an Emperor, or a servant to his master, as is evident from the passage previously cited from Zechariah 2:3, where one Angel, as the Lord of another, commands him as a servant, saying; *Run, speak to that young man.* From which-

--- Page 395 ---
**ON THE INQUIRY INTO THE NATURE OF EACH DEMON. 113**
by which it clearly appears that it is in the power of the Archangel or the dominant and principal Angel to alter fates, and to restrain and command the fatal Angel subject to him, that he not do this or that. Likewise also the Demons of the twelve signs, who, called *avengers* by Hermes *Trismegistus*, are accustomed to assist the planetary spirits in expediting and executing nativities, have no power to resist their own Archangels, but are obedient and compliant to them, as to their principal Lords and leaders. And therefore, if the middle soul agrees with the mind, and adheres to it obediently, as to its prince, neither the stars nor their Demons have any force or power over it. Whence arises that proverb: *The wise man will rule the stars*, etc. that is, he who is governed by the mind and its leader, inasmuch as their virtues are preferred to the properties of the stars and their Demons, will avoid the actions and influences of the stars and their demons.

C A P. VII.

*On the descent of the mind with the soul and middle spirit into the lowest region of the world.*

The divine Mind, fortified by the power of the Archangel, and clothed in the garment of the vital soul, which is also guarded by its own Genius, and abounding in all ethereal virtues necessary for the preservation of life (having received, namely, *will* from the Prime Mover, *action* from the firmament or eighth sphere, *receptive power* from Saturn, *natural power* from Jupiter, *irascible power* from Mars, *vital power* from the Sun, *concupiscible power* from Venus, *phantastic power* from Mercury, and *vegetative power* from the Moon), slides downwards into the elemental region, where, protecting itself against the injury of intense cold, it puts on a fiery and airy nature, covering its former ethereal garments with a simple, and then a composite, elemental covering. All the demons there therefore, who are of the order and condition of the Archangel predominating over the mind, meet it and joyfully receive it as it sits in their ethereal vehicles, and guard it against the vexations of demons of contrary disposition. But now a question may arise here, *how these elemental Demons can be referred separately to any Demon of the seven Planets, since there are only four elements, of which the lower Demons partake?* To this doubt indeed we briefly respond, that although only four elements are enumerated, these four, however, are most conveniently referred, by reason of their natures, to the dispositions of the seven Planets, and consequently also to the demons corresponding to each of the Planets. For example: *Saturn* has a relation with earth, but *Jupiter* and *Venus* with air, *Mars* with fire, and *the Sun* with air and fire, that is, with the highest portion of air ignited by fire. *The Moon* with water, and *Mercury* with all of these and the winds. Whence it will be very easy to find what kind of elemental demon had dominion and care and power over the body of the native at birth. Which demon, however, is commanded and ruled by the mind's president, not

--- Page 396 ---
114 TRACT. I. SECT. II. PORT. IV. LIB. III.
more submerged by the multitude of matter. And in this way the internal man is
formed, and each of his three parts, derived from the three natures of the three cosmic heavens,
possesses its own Dæmon, and therefore, just as God has dominion
over Angels, and Angels over stars, and stars finally over elements,
so it also follows that the Angels of the empyrean heaven have power and authority,
both over the stars, and over the elements and their Angels.

C H A P. VIII.
*On the method of acquiring knowledge and familiarity with each sacred and*
*supercelestial Dæmon attributed to the mind,*

Iamblichus made a double treatise on Dæmons, *one, namely, sacred and*
*Deifying*, which invokes the Dæmon from higher causes, and this one indeed does
not use the exploration of each individual nativity, but more universally cultivates
and cares for the Dæmon above nature; he makes *the other artificial*, which
invokes the Dæmon from celestial circuits, and is concerned with generation,
and this one explores the nativity of each individual, etc., as has been said:
Hence, as it seems to me, he understood the first treatise to be about the good
and supercelestial Angel proper to the mind, which he elsewhere calls sacred, and the
second about the Angel or Dæmon who is called Genius, or Olympic spirit;
which Porphyry indeed greatly desired to seek or find, believing
that if someone knew the figure of nativity and the Lord of the figure, he would
find his Dæmon, through whom he would be freed from the fate of nativity.
Against whom Iamblichus, arguing, asserts that the sacred Dæmon of man is not
given by that figure of genesis, but by an older and higher principle, namely,
by the superior gods, whence he seems to recognize that the chief Dæmon of man
flows from a place higher and more eminent than the region of the stars,
and therefore it is impossible for us to arrive at true knowledge and familiarity
with this Archidæmon, or to know him by virtue of Astrology, or the science of the stars:
And Porphyry also seems to finally acknowledge this same thing after long
and assiduous studies, speaking in these words: "*It is impossible," he says, "to know the figure of nativity and*
*to know the Dæmon of nativity; because the rules of Astrology are incomprehensible and un-*
*certain.*" And we say that, even if the rules of Astrology were comprehensible and certain,
nevertheless we could not from them know, or perceive, or acquire familiarity
with the sacred Dæmon of nativity, because such a sacred Dæmon governs the stars;
so indeed, that the knowledge of the stars cannot *a priori* discover him or his nature.
By what methods, therefore, will knowledge and familiarity with this Dæmon
be acquired, since heaven and the stars themselves cannot explain his nature, name, and
property to us? Indeed, if we descend to lower things, there among the elements,
which are more imperfect than celestial things, we will not find that method:
For the impurity of the elements in human composition is the principal cause
why we are ignorant of the supreme, middle, and lowest Dæmon. What, therefore,
must be done, so that we may obtain knowledge, familiarity, presence, assistance,
and illumination from this sacred creature and our most excellent guardian?
To this question Iamblichus seems to respond thus: "*The Dæmon," he says, "is found with*
*difficulty through Astrology, but easily through divine divination:* And elsewhere: *We can find*
*our proper Dæmon not by human arts but by divine ones:* Furthermore, he also says
*that divine divination can teach the nature and effect of the stars without art; and manifest*
*each person's proper Dæmon predominating at birth.* What divination is, above

Does God usually, out of His grace, infuse a portion of the Spirit of discipline into men laboring under a lack of spirit, and swollen with the mass of an unclean body, so that they may learn the knowledge of God? The Wise Man says, *Wisdom 9:10*, that God sends His wisdom from the holy heavens, from the throne, I say, of His glory He sends it to man, so that it may be present with him in his labor, and he may know what is pleasing to Him: For it knows and understands all things: Furthermore, *Wisdom 9:17*: 'Unless You had given wisdom, and sent Your holy Spirit from on high, who among men would have known Your counsel?' Hence it is clear that the true knowledge of Astrology, and the only way to acquire friendship with one's sacred Daemon, consists in divine inspiration, by whose holy breath the ancients acquired for themselves the knowledge of every thing, indeed, even the very foundations of most holy wisdom. Therefore, we conclude this our little book with the opinion of *Iamblichus*, namely, that each person's sacred Daemon is to be known from an older and higher principle than from the stars and the figure of nativity, and that both the nature, name, and property of this Daemon, and also the most certain truth concerning the stars, can be had and recovered through divine prophecy, which proceeds and occurs solely from the mission and inflowing of the Holy Spirit into men.

CHAP. I.
*On the etymology of Physiognomy, its definition, praise*
*& utility.*

[Decorative drop cap N]Some of the ancients would have *Physiognomy* derive its name from γνώμη (gnome), that is, a sign, and φύσις (physis), that is, *nature*: Hence *Physiognomy* is called, as it were, a sign of nature, and is defined as a certain observation by which, from those signs naturally present in the body, we also denote the qualities of the soul: For, as the proverb says, *'the tools show the craftsman, and the house shows what kind of master it has.'* And although the ignorant and the common people scorn this science and are accustomed to deride it, yet among the wise it is most sacredly preserved in the secrets of Socratic and Pythagorean philosophy: And indeed, if this art is well considered by a discreet and sagacious man, it will bring him great fruit of utility; for it will teach him to safely entrust a deposit to one person, to trust another, to enter into marriage, to commit children to education, to associate with honest people, to flee from the base and obscene, not to rashly choose societies and friendships, to avoid the wickedness of criminals without any harm or danger; and finally, this Science makes those who understand and cultivate it prudent and fortunate: For as soon as we behold a person, we can through it judge concerning the disposition of that person's soul, whether for good or ill. Furthermore, *Hippocrates* also seems to assert, with *Galen* as witness, that whoever practices medicine and is ignorant of that philosophy which teaches how to give judgments about things taken from their nature (which they call *Physiognomy*), the mind of these people, wandering in darkness, grows old, wearied: and he says that such people not only do not act correctly, but are also greatly deceived: For he says, *'The mind of those who are ignorant of Physiognomy is consumed and wearied by error.'* Hence therefore the praises of Physiognomy clearly shine forth, and its utility both in health and in every


--- Page 401 ---
DE PHYSIOGNOMY IN GENERAL. 119

in every unnatural imbalance, a necessity and notable utility. But as for the inventor of this science, I find that authors vary concerning him: yet I perceive the more frequent report to be that Phylomon, the greatest Doctor and Master of Physiognomy, truly discovered its qualities and nature from the composition of man. However, we read that Physiognomy is a remarkable science, which the ancients used for a long time in the investigation of the beauty of nature in this science, whose perfection is attributed among the ancients to Phylomon, as has been said. Aristotle, Avicenna, Constantine, Palomon, Trogus, etc., also cultivated this.

C H A P. II.
That Physiognomic Science Reveals the Disposition of the Middle Soul Subject to Fatal Disposition.

Just as air enclosed in a bladder usually alters the bladder itself according to its own disposition, so indeed, that if it is vaporous and humid, it also renders the bladder itself wetter, softer, and whiter; if inflamed by heat, drier and rougher and of a yellower disposition; but if strongly inflamed, it dries it out and contracts it in a wrinkled manner, as appears in a bladder or parchment around air inflamed by fire; to such an extent that we are also accustomed from this to know the nature of the internal or contained air by the external appearance and disposition of the bladder or containing vessel; so also it is in finding the disposition of the internal human soul through its external manifestation, and in knowing the Lord of nature through the observation of his own house: For when the middle soul is fostered by a Martial genius, and draws a hot disposition to itself from it, it is observed to render the body mostly yellow in color, with black and curly hair, with a dry and thin disposition tending towards roughness; Hence, from such a bodily disposition, as from an effect, we can most easily judge concerning its internal state and indicate the nature of the soul: And therefore we will say that such a man is by nature audacious, irascible, impetuous, rapacious, and warlike, given to drunkenness and fornication: but nevertheless the practitioner is sometimes mistaken in this conjecture of his, namely, when the middle soul adheres to the mind; For this science, inasmuch as it is an indication of human nature, is powerful in those in whom the fatal Genius, of which we made mention in the preceding part of this section, has supreme dominion; that is, in whom the middle soul, neglecting the mind and its Archangel, adheres to the animal or sensitive soul: For in these, fate executes its parts and renders man prone to all celestial influences, so that by necessity those things usually happen to the human soul which the celestial bodies naturally and fatally threaten it with; inasmuch as the mind in such men either operates little, or is for the most part observed to be idle: But if the soul is obedient to the mind and firmly adheres to it, the practitioner will be deceived in his judgment; inasmuch as this soul, by the virtue of the mind and the direction of the Archangel or sacred Daemon, will emerge from fatal traces and will dominate the stars themselves. This indeed will become known from the following account concerning Hippocrates: For his disciples, when they had brought his image depicted on parchment to a certain Philosopher, named Phylomon, indeed most skilled in this art and surpassing all of his age in it, and had inquired of him concerning the nature and disposition of the image, are said to have received such a response from him after a most diligent inspection and examination of the figure, and its qualities and parts; Whom you say is represented by that image, him we declare to be a person given to luxury

--- Page 402 ---
120    TRACT. I. SECT. II. PORT. V. LIB. I.
*given to luxury and a deceiver." To whom they [replied]: "O fool, this is the figure of the best and most worthy man in the whole world, namely, that most wise Hippocrates." To which he [Phylomon replied]: "This, then, is the image of the most wise Hippocrates? Why did you ask this of me? I showed you these things according to my judgment, and I indicated what I thought about this figure." But these things having been announced to Hippocrates, he is said to have responded thus to his disciples: "Certainly Phylomon spoke the truth, nor did he omit a single aspect of certainty. Nevertheless, since I looked and considered that these shameful things were to be rejected, I established the soul as king over itself, and I withdrew it from those things, and I triumphed, my desires having been restrained and curbed." From which it is evidently clear that he alone is to be called wise who has dominion over his own soul, that is, who has so dedicated himself to the mind and to super-celestial things that he is accustomed to direct and govern celestial and natural things, and indeed even the middle soul formed from them, against the necessity of fate, or the inclination and laws of nature.*

**C A P. III.**
*On the method of judgment in this Science.*

Before we proceed to the method of judgment, it must be understood exactly how many kinds of signs of judgment there are; then, once those are known, how judgment is to be approached through them. It must therefore be known first of all that the signs of judging, according to Aristotle, are twofold, namely, either common or proper: Common ones, again, are subdivided threefold, namely, into those which judge by color, figure, and motion. But proper signs are manifested especially in certain peculiar and proper parts of the body. Therefore, these things having been considered with previous deliberation, it must be diligently noted that you should not rush knowledge, opinion, or judgment, but understand the testimonies of all; and when diverse and adverse signs are offered to you, it is always necessary to prudently incline towards the better and more probable part.

CHAP. I.
On Universal Color.

[Large decorative woodcut initial D]The more skilled in this science have said that the womb of a woman is like a pot for cooking food: Hence they say that whiteness with a livid color, and likewise a yellow color, is a sign of diminished concoction: if therefore this very diminution occurs in a creature, its nature will likewise be diminished: Therefore they warn us to shun every livid and yellow person; because such are prone to vices and luxury.
Whiteness mixed with redness, and a moderate brown color with bodily integrity in a person who possesses uprightness of stature, and a moderate head, and rarity of words, a scarcity responding only to necessity, and a moderate voice, denotes a good disposition.
They also wish a whitish color to indicate a lazy, phlegmatic, intemperate, effeminate, and incontinent and weak person.
Tawny color denotes a deceitful and multifaceted or varied and inconstant person; but it promises goodness of intellect.
Saffron color signifies in healthy individuals a hot liver, and a choleric complexion: Hence it happens that such people are untamed, irascible, luxurious, and devoted to loves or amorous because of the liver's heat, according to that saying: "The liver compels one to love."
Yellow argues a person avaricious and envious.
Honey-colored denotes an irascible, gluttonous, witty, timid person.
Fiery color in a slightly reddish body, if it persists, argues goodness of nature, aptitude, promptness in grasping disciplines, and nobility of spirit.
Red color argues complete birth.
A moderate color in whiteness and redness signifies a moderate complexion, a perfect intellect, and one devoted to virtues.

CAP. II.
_On signs derived from bodily movement._

Common signs according to a person's movement are derived from its diversity in
speed or slowness.
_Slow movement signifies a weak and sluggish person who easily suffers from_
_infirmity, or is easily overcome by passions: The reason, however, is that slowness of_
_movement denotes a weakness of the vital spirits._
_Sharp or swift movement indicates a person much concerned with worldly dignity_
_and perfection; and likewise [indicates] those who are ardent and subtle, and such who abound_
_in these vivifying spirits; indeed, those who in disposition are compared to_
_foxes, and are astute, crafty, cautious, and deceivers._
_Large and slow steps or paces denote sluggishness, and such a one who will have prosperous_
_successes in his works: just as, conversely, short [steps] indicate_
_impetuous, suspicious, troublesome people of bad will._

CAP. III.
_On the figure and stature of the body._

Common signs derived from figure are manifold; since some are considered
in defects or superfluities of nature, others in perfect and
complete bodies.
_Thus, from a deformed person, and one diminished or augmented beyond the rightness of nature's_
_laws, we are warned to beware, as if from an enemy._
_An oblong face signifies a merciful [person], a round [face] however indicates a_
_cunning and perverse person._
_People of prodigious height know little or nothing at all; but they are also im-_
_petuous, and this is all the more confirmed if they are of a lean and oblong body_
_with a stork-like neck._
_Those who walk stooped do not know much._
_Small or low stature indicates a proud [person]: From which comes that proverb:_
_"Rarely have I seen a tall wise man and a short humble man."_
_Medium and decently stout stature denotes an ingenious, prudent, and in all_
_matters expeditious [person]: For more balanced and temperate is the creature who_
_corresponds to a medium stature with blackness of eyes and hair and_
_roundness of face._

**ON PHYSIOGNOMIC SIGNS. 123**

**BOOK II. PART II.**
On specific signs.

**CH. I PART I.**
On signs taken from the head.

Proper physiognomic signs are those which pertain to some particular part of the body, or a notable action: For example: *Signs of the head, eyes, face, voice in laughter, neck and throat, shoulders, arms, hands, belly, chest, legs, knees, feet, and flesh:* some of which members are again subdivided into other, more particular signs, producing or exhibiting them: For example: The *Head* into hairs and ears; The *Face* into chin, nose, cheeks and temples; The *Eyes* into pupil, eyelids and eyebrows; The *Mouth* into teeth, tongue, lips; The *Chest* into ribs and nipples, etc. The *Hands* into fingers and nails. Therefore, to begin with the signs of the head, the shape of the head must be diligently observed, namely whether it is round, oblong, square, or triangular in its most prominent part.

A head that is round in its most prominent part signifies someone thoughtful, provident, gentle, amiable, concealing anger: And if the color of such a head is *white*, it attests to a stubborn disposition, and tenacity of memory and constant friendship, prone to anger; *If red*, it indicates a person quite amiable and of good disposition, and trustworthy in speech, but not at all concealing anger; *If dark/brown*, very modest, and kind in speech, very playful, of perfect companionship and benevolent reason.

A head that is oblong in its most prominent part denotes a person of keen intellect, doing many things thoughtlessly, impetuous, fickle, changeable, irritable, not good at keeping secrets, not naturally playful, sharp in speech, commended by reason, too profound in arranging actions: And if such a head is *white*, it will signify impetuous to anger, and naturally prodigal, *if black*, it denotes a fickle disposition, and almost no reason, etc.

A head that is square in its most prominent part indicates someone deliberate, gentle, pious, kind, not very irritable, provident, wise: but avaricious, and deceitful in speech and not seeking the favor of men: And if it is *white*, it will denote humble, but avaricious and irritable: *if black*, a more constant spirit, easily forming friendships, and preserving them for a long time, very playful, good at keeping secrets; *If red*, circumspect in useful matters, a flatterer: *If dark/brown*, better than others, modest, generous, but easily lying, perfectly keeping friendships.

A head that is triangular in its most prominent part signifies someone avaricious, cunning, artful, arrogant, ingenious, deceitful, envious, and greatly detracting from the actions of others: And if it is *white*, malicious; *If black*, a prevaricator and more prone to anger; *If red*, more proud, but liberal, *if dark/brown* signifies better than others.

A very small head denotes a person more alien from all human sense and understanding: A *medium* head denotes strong, well-sensed, magnanimous; A *very large* head denotes weak, unlettered and rude, gluttonous, slow-witted, and least wise, illiberal, of no or very little perception: An *oblique* head denotes shameless; A *short* head denotes foolish; A *long* head denotes imprudent; A head *swollen* in the anterior part, perverse; A *high* head, stubborn: *Its upper part depressed*, perverse; A *low* head indeed argues timid, and fearful, and utterly lacking all spirit.

CHAP. I. PART II.
On signs taken from hair and from body hair in various
places of the body.

In the consideration of hair, their *quantity and quality* must be observed;
which consists in color: But as for their quantity itself, we consider
the hair and the body hair of other parts either in their threefold dimension, that is, thick-
ness, or thinness, or in their discrete disposition, that is, in their rarity,
or multitude, or in the varied position of the place. Therefore, as for the threefold dimension of hair,
*thick and coarse hair signifies a rustic disposition, and a bold*
*man: thinner and softer (hair), however, (denotes) a timid person and of an easier disposition;* but more extensively on these
below.
The *thinner, fewer, and sparser the hairs are, the more they denote more subtle, cunning,*
*acute, fearful, and avaricious people, but if their substance is thinner*
*with roughness, it signifies a timid and cold person.*
*Flat hair indicates fear, and if it is flat and soft, it designates humility*
*and timidity.*
*A multitude of hairs on both arms indicates rage, or a rustic nature:*
*But a multitude of them on the chest and belly indicates a horrible and singular nature,*
*an unlettered, luxurious, and senseless person.*
*As for the position, depressed and vast hair around the ears and temples signifies*
*a curious and luxurious person; if they are few and sparse around the temples, they denote coldness and*
*weakness: If they have fallen from the crown of the head, so that it is left bare, they indicate*
*a lazy person and of little intellect: If there is a line dividing the hair in the middle of the scalp, it indicates*
*a dull-witted and luxurious person: Hair on the ribs teaches audacity and spiritedness;*
*in all parts of the body, fear and timidity, in the arms, foolishness*
*and fury, in the neck and shoulders, madness and obstinacy; in the chest and belly, a rustic*
*disposition.*
*The color of hair is considered either in general by itself, or with a more particular*
*respect; where, namely, color is compared with the quantity and shape of the hair.*
The general significations of colors in hair are these: *Gray hair in youth*
*indicates a deceitful and hot-tempered person: Black hair denotes a just person and justice: between*
*black and red (hair), a lover of peace; darkish and thin (hair), good things; yellow and thin*
*or sparse (hair), good morals.*
Particular signs of hair compared to others are of this kind.
*Black and thick and straight hair signifies a good disposition, good morals,*
*excellent eloquence, faithful companionship, but a wanton, gluttonous person: Black, thin and*
*straight*

Black and curly (hair indicates) very prone and quick to anger, gluttonous, doing everything quickly, very lustful, but not very potent or strong in lust.

Red hair, thick and straight: signifies very malicious, proud, arrogant, unclean, deceitful or fraudulent, cunning; Thin red hair, (signifies) hidden anger, and frequently thinking many tricks silently. Thin and curly red hair signifies a person suddenly breaking into anger, and nourishing anger for a long time, a flatterer, not perfectly keeping the bond of love; Thick and curly red hair indicates a proud, boastful, fickle, lying person, liberal in society, and lavishly giving many things.

Thick ash-blonde hair signifies humble people, and those deserving praise and favor; Ash-blonde and thin (hair) denotes humility, and less mendacious; Ash-blonde and curly (hair) indicates a lustful person, not greatly desiring food nor gluttonous.

Dark brown hair, and thick, and coarse, denotes a very liberal, pious, gentle person, enduring more than is otherwise customary, powerful in memory: Dark brown (hair) indicates a proud person, willingly accusing, not willingly yielding to anyone in anger, seeking many things for himself.

        C A P. I. P A R S III.
        Of signs taken from the ears.

A large ear signifies good memory, and long life, but deceitful and boasting many things; A small ear, however, denotes a humble and kind person: but, if it is very small, it indicates foolishness, likewise dullness, extravagance, a thief and malicious; A hard (ear) indicates a good disposition of the heart; A soft (ear) its contrary, and easily angered; A thin and as if circumcised (ear) denotes a fool, cunning, malicious, and a thick and large (ear) (denotes) a somewhat deaf person; A protruding (ear), (denotes) easy and prompt docility, gentleness, kindness; A pressed (ear), however, (denotes) ignorance, rudeness, A square and moderately large (ear), (denotes) very sharp in hearing; A short (ear) (denotes) foolishness; A long and narrow (ear) (denotes) an envious person.

        C A P. I. P A R S IV.
        Of signs of the temples.

Inflated temples with large main veins and full cheeks denote irascibility.

        C A P. II. P A R S I.
        Of signs of the face and forehead.

Among the signs of the face are included marks or features either of the entire face, or of its parts, such as the forehead, nose, chin, etc.

A very large face denotes a dull person; A small face (denotes) a dull person and a Gnatho (flatterer/parasite). And if a small (face) inclines towards a saffron color, it indicates a vicious and drunken person; A long (face) (denotes) a proud, impudent, flatterer, envious person; A square (face), (denotes) a wise, and constant, and of good counsel (person): A round (face), (denotes) a well-mannered, humble, simple person; A triangular (face), (denotes) a cunning person, quick to anger, and indignant; A thin (face), (denotes) provident in works, and of subtle intellect; A subtle (face), (denotes) thinking many things; An average (face) with cheeks and temples tending towards darkishness, (denotes) a true and amiable, intelligent, well-composed, and ingenious person.

A face not very beautiful rarely implies good morals; but a very joyful (face) indicates a fool.

A flat face without fear or shame denotes a bad student, contentious, injurious, but ingenious.
A fleshy face signifies a troublesome, slow, deceitful person.
Much flesh in the throat indicates a coarse nature.
A drunken face shows drunkards.
An angry face demonstrates an angry person and a hot complexion, just as a modest one (shows) a modest person.

As for the color of the face, it must be known that a pale face signifies a greedy, cunning, crafty person; a red one, a fickle, changeable or inconstant person, not easily trusting for the space of three hours, mischievous, and quickly correcting misdeeds; a white one, an effeminate, soft, cold person; a livid and Saturnine one, the worst affections of the mind, such as envy, anger, rancor, treachery.

Furthermore, concerning the signs of the forehead, we have said some things above in the first part of the first chapter; to which these things may also be added.

A narrow forehead denotes an uncouth person, a flat one a dull person, a large one a lazy person, a long one a docile person, a wrinkled one a studious and anxious person, a depressed one an effeminate person, a round one an angry person, a bulging one an insensitive person, a broad one an impudent person, a rough one an untrustworthy, cunning person, a high one a stubborn person.

CHAPTER II. PART II.
Concerning signs collected from the nose.

A very humped nose shows a very drunken, gluttonous, arrogant, lustful person, one who freely gives away his own (possessions); a straight and in the middle curved one signifies a very angry person, and one yielding to almost no one; a humped one in the middle with large nostrils denotes a very liberal person and constant in words; a large one demonstrates a person thinking many things, and easily angered; an oblong and slender one, and beaked, a strong and boastful person, and rapacious like birds: a curved, oblique, and twisted one signifies an angry person, simulating, and frequently detracting from his own (affairs), and similarly, obliquity of mind and spirit; a thick one in the middle indicates a gluttonous person, and one thinking about future things; a sharp one in the middle, a bitter, prodigal, freely giving, and very clean person.

The top of the nose, slender and thin, denotes one easily prone to anger, and a lover of discord; a thick and depressed one denounces bad morals; a full, solid, and blunt one denotes a strong and boastful person; but a long one indicates a subtle, choleric, and fickle person.

A naturally red nose indicates a subtle intellect, a light memory, one acquiring many friends, seriously inconstant; a pale one, a hard person, of inconstant memory, and constant in friendship and open in speech.

A sloping nose will give a sign of honesty of life and morals; a straight one denotes intemperance of tongue; a sharp one, facility to anger; a blunt one, softness; a hooked and aquiline one, a royal spirit and magnificence; a snub nose, immodesty, prostitution; a smaller one, fraud, rapacity; a flared one, strength of soul and robustness of body; a narrow, rounder, and obstructed one, stupidity, sluggishness, madness; a thick one, foolishness.

A flat and small nose denotes ingenuity in old people; a long one almost reaching the mouth, denotes a worthy and magnanimous person.

A nose broad in the middle and sloping in its rise, indicates many words and a liar; a subtle and thin one, an angry person.

Thick nostrils show an envious person, wide ones a luxurious person, curved ones a magnanimous, but luxurious person, perverse ones a perverse person, straight ones an intemperate tongue, open ones

C A P. II. P A R S III.
Concerning the signs of the cheeks.

Fleshy cheeks or cheekbones indicate lazy and drunken persons; but thinner ones show a sign of dishonesty, deception, [and] timidity; Fatter and full ones provide an indication of cunning, laziness, and luxury; thick and lower from the eyes have a sign of envy; round ones betray deceitful persons; excessively wide ones indicate boastfulness; thick and dense ones indicate foolish and idiotic persons; smooth and long ones [indicate] an importunate person.

C A P. II. P A R S IV.
Concerning the signs of the chin.

A round chin shows a constant person and unworthiness. A long one signifies a person frivolous in words, talkative, [and] facile.

However, the colors of the eye are of this kind.
**A white eye in a white person** argues an inconstant and deceitful person, sometimes prodigal, and sometimes avaricious; but in a **black person**, irascible, and weak from a slight cause, and not often healthy or robust: **Whitish with a little gray** argues timid and impotent; **Blue** denotes good, well-behaved, amiable, and liberal, and gladly giving of his own; **Gray-eyed with minimal keenness** [denotes] illiberal, avaricious, cunning, **purplish with dryness** irascible, **with humidity** drunkards, **Also, of gray eyes**, some are of a tan color, and of other diverse colors, **Chestnut gray eyes** are better than dry ones, **Black and sparkling** indicate dull and timid: **An eye of diverse color in the pupil, or around it**, denotes disturbance, envy, and weakness. **A black circle around the uvea with redness but not expressed redness**, indicates a flexible and good disposition and just: **Red spots in the apple of the eye** signify prone to anger: Note that, the larger the spots, the greater the vices they denote. **A black circle** argues a thief and unjust person: **Eyes like a rainbow** denote dry and furious. **Eyes red like fire** argue a very bad and obstinate person; **Red ones**, fortitude and animosity; **Gray-eyed with yellowness and greenish** [denote] a bad person. **Gray-eyed and green** [denote] bad and unfortunate, and a thief: **White in the apple or pupil** are the worst of all. **If there are reddish spots in the pupil, or like fire, and internally other pale spots mixed with other gray ones, and the circle outside the pupil is blood-red or chestnut, and the eye is clear, and moves as if angry, and also the eyelids are of this kind**, it is denoted that this person exceeds the ferocity of wild beasts, because such an eye indicates the execution of all wickedness.

Also the position and placement of the eyes produces various signs: For **prominent eyes which protrude or hang forward, and around which a swelling in the form of a circle is drawn, or which a kind of ditch like that of camps surrounds**, signify deceitful, furious, bloodthirsty, stupid: And **these, if they are more mobile**, will denote a glutton; **if petulant and bloodshot**, a drunkard; **if gray-eyed**, neither justice nor any human custom; **if more prominent, splendid, larger, pure, and moist**, they denote a person endowed with remarkable justice and upright conduct, most apt for disciplines (Such they report Socrates to have been); **if small, impudent**, stupid, luxurious, dull: **Recessed and hidden eyes, unless they are large**, are approved in no way: For such, **if they are small**, argue depravity, dissimulation, envy, treachery, and, **if they are dry**,

if they are dry, treachery; if wet, madness. Therefore, a moderate state of the eyes, between prominent and recessed, is praised, where the eyes are neither swollen nor hollow, but are of a moderate size.

Also, moisture in the eyes, whether apparent or not, sometimes produces signs: For moist eyes sometimes indicate fear, dry ones madness. From this it is clear that rigid eyes are never good: For paler, rigid eyes indicate a foolish person; larger and reddish ones indicate lustful people, those given to gluttony, and the impotent. But if such eyes are also shining, I would want you to beware of such a person, for he rejoices in the misfortunes and calamities of others.

Also, the movement of the eyes and the very manner of looking reveal many hidden signs of human nature: For mobile eyes denote a troublemaker, a suspicious person, an interruptor, a faithless person, and one more curious than stubborn, a thief; and, if the eyelids move, certainly a very powerful soul, if not outright audacious. C A P, V. P A R S III.

Concerning signs derived from the observation of the Throat and Neck.

A long and slender neck indicates a timid, foolish, weak, talkative, and ill-mannered person;
A fat and long one [indicates] spirited, boastful, stubborn [persons]; a compact one, robust, strong, and suitable for learning; a non-compact and more empty one, cunning and adulterous [persons]. An excessively fat one [indicates] irascible, and inept and unsuitable for learning, and swinish [persons]; a very short one, bold, cunning, deceptive, ingenious. A dense one not protruding in any direction [indicates] sinister, stubborn, inept [persons]. A broken neck indicates an effeminate man; leaning to the right declares adorned, prudent, and sinister [persons]; But if it leans to the left, adulterous and of no prudence [persons]; If in any other [direction], it is an indication of a most depraved spirit and mind; If in none, it indicates moderation of art and exercise: A large neck denotes a great eater.
A rough throat indicates frivolity of words, impudence of tongue, and
arrogance: If there is a knot in the throat, it signifies frivolity, depravity, audacity or spiritedness.

C A P. VI. P A R S I.

Concerning signs taken from the chest and nipples.

A large and unstructured chest signifies a robust [person]; A slender one, weak and
pusillanimous; A fleshy one, those lacking dexterity of affections.
Nipples hanging on an obese chest indicate fornicators, drunkards, and gluttons.

C A P. VI. P A R S II.

Concerning signs derived from the shoulders and arms.

Dense shoulders, a dense back, and a broad chest indicate spiritedness, a desire for good
merit, and intellect; Broad shoulders indicate good natural talent; Narrow ones
the contrary; Thin and slender and straight in an arched position [indicate] a man of uncertain faith and most wicked; Not fat but well-disposed [indicate] one dedicated to virtues; Loose ones, a sharp and
deceitful nature; Robust ones, a robust and well-mannered [person]; empty ones, an effeminate and timid [person].
A robust shoulder blade indicates a robust person: But a weak and slender one, a timid [person]:
A fleshy one indicates a lack of senses: A narrow one, foolishness: A broader one, depth of
mind: A rounder one, industry and sagacity: A gibbous and curved one, envy and
depravity.
If the forearms are so long that the hands, when lowered, reach down to the middle below
the hips, they are a sign of fortitude and happiness; But shorter ones, whose ends
meet, are an indication of malevolence and envy; Slender ones indicate
an effeminate person; Fleshy ones indicate a person lacking senses and disciplines.
Likewise, arms so long and extended that the hands can touch the knees, indicate spiritedness and nobility; Short ones, discord and ignorance, pusillanimous and
depraved [persons].
Large and strong muscles of the arms are an indication of good natural talent.
The forearms, arms, and elbows themselves ought to be well-articulated for those whom we wish to approve.

C H A P. VI P A R T III.
On signs taken from the hands, fingers & nails.

When hands are so formed with the arms that, with the body standing upright, they reach as far as the knees, they denote an able person; if they extend only to the hips, or to the middle of the thigh, they signify malevolent persons, who rejoice in the misfortunes of others; Very short hands indicate foolishness; Small, but full & strong [hands indicate] a cunning and sagacious person; Tender & softer [hands] argue an excellent disposition, & one apt for learning; Hard & large [hands indicate] a strong person & one quite suitable for learning; Narrow & slender [hands indicate] rapacity & tyranny; Smooth & subtle [hands indicate] prudence; Fat [hands] with short fingers [indicate] a miser, a threatening person & a thief; Long palms with long fingers [indicate] one well-disposed to many arts, melancholic, of good governance & prudent.
Large & short fingers argue a dull, demented person; Knotty [fingers indicate] foolishness.
Small & slender [fingers indicate] very little intellect; Oblong & slender [fingers indicate] a person of a very small & more rigid mind: He who closes & contracts his fingers is envious, impious, avaricious.
White nails suffused with redness are signs of a good disposition; very short, small & blackish [nails] indicate a wicked person; Narrow & long [nails indicate] solidity & wisdom: But if they are narrow, rather long & curved, they argue an improvident & ill-sensed person; Sharp & round [nails] denote venereal acts, & a ready person; Oblique & hooked [nails indicate] an impudent & rapacious person; Impressed & much broken [nails indicate] fools & thieves.

C H A P. VII P A R T I.
On signs taken from the hips & legs and
knees & shins.

Unarticulated & soft hips argue a timid & weak person; Very slender [hips indicate] a wicked person.
Thin legs signify lovers of women.
Knees filled with flesh denote weakness of virtue.
Thick shins argue fortitude & spiritedness; Slender [shins indicate] ignorance; Broad [shins] with broad heels [indicate] a strong body.

C H A P. VII. P A R T II.
On signs taken from the feet.

Thick & fleshy feet argue foolishness in love & an adulterer, & a lover of injury: Very fleshy [feet] indicate a difficult person & a bad disposition: Sinewy & articulated [feet] will show signs of both lineage & manners; Tender [feet] indicate a better person; Oblong [feet] are a sign of much thought: Small [feet], however, exhibit an indication of shrewdness & stubbornness; Beautiful & strong [feet] describe a pleasant person & a fornicator.
Slowly moving [feet] indicate a dull person; Quickly moving [feet], however, denote a fickle person: Large strides are a sign of sluggishness; Quick [strides] show a choleric & suspicious person.

CHAPTER I.
On the signs of a choleric man.

[Large decorative initial S] If anyone wishes to attain to a true knowledge of temperament from the inspection of the face, head, and other parts of the body, it is necessary that he first consider with diligent contemplation the color of the hairs and skin, then the stature, habit of the body, and the figure and disposition of its parts. For example, in the investigation of the bilious or choleric temperament, we are accustomed to observe these things which follow.

Therefore, in these men in whom the aforesaid signs are present, the constellation of *Mars* is said to predominantly rule: From which it is clear that a complexion of this kind partakes of a Martial nature: A Martial complexion, however, is hot, dry, and of a fiery condition.

Martial and Choleric
individuals described
previously, regarding
the qualities of their
souls/minds:

*   They greatly desire Venus (love/sex), and are dedicated to luxury by reason of their heat; but due to the presence of dryness, they accomplish little.
*   They are apt for sowing discord.
*   They are usually drunkards and heavy drinkers, and are suddenly overcome by drunkenness, in which, submerged, they are fierce and furious like lions, and indeed without any moderation.
*   They are always occupied or busy with one thing or another.
*   They are slanderers and evildoers, boastful and braggarts.
*   They easily expose themselves to danger of life for a trivial matter and one of almost no importance; and in their anger, they are like men seized by madness or frenzy.
*   They are usually governed and restrained by women, whom they vehemently love.
*   They eat little and do not sleep much.

CHAPTER I.
*What is Chiromancy? And that it is a natural science subject to fate and the stars,
whose judgment only a wise person can impede.*

[Decorative woodcut initial C] Hiromancy is called from *cheir* (hand) and *manteia* (divination), that is, from hand & science, and is defined by some as a natural science, through which, from a skilled inspection of the hands, divination concerning present, past, and future matters is customarily made: Or, it is a science, by which Artists foretell happiness or unhappiness through the lines of the hands: By which it is declared, that this science concerns matters naturally befalling man; no differently than Astrology itself and Physiognomy: It is therefore, as it were, a tablet of the nature and constitution of the born, in which the mysteries of birth are secretly sculpted and delineated, since under the characters of physiognomy and this art, formed by nature, the fates of man, both in good and in evil, are recorded, and are clearly and brightly revealed to the learned, and thus, being perceived by the wise with super-celestial acumen, they are avoided: For the wise person, as has often been repeated, will rule the stars, and much more so the signs of Physiognomy and Chiromancy that threaten evil, since these are perceived to emanate immediately from the influences of the stars: For example: if someone observes a sign in their hand, that they must end the last day of their life in the sea, and undergo death in the waves, they will be able, if they are wise, to use a twofold remedy to avoid this danger; firstly, namely, that they learn the true danger of their life from the characters of the hands, and then, once that is known, by restraining and governing their voluptuous affections of the flesh, they temper themselves from sea voyages, so that by this means they expose themselves less to that danger, which the Fates have imposed upon them according to the natural constitution of their birth. By this path, therefore, they will escape the malignity of the stars, and will be guided and guarded by the mind and by an angelic guardian of the mind.

CHAP. II.
*On some terms necessary for this art.*

OF the five fingers, the first is called the *thumb*, which is stronger and thicker than all [the others];
The *second*, which is nearest to the thumb, is called the *index finger*, because we are accustomed to use it extended when indicating something: The *third* is called, either the *middle finger*, because it is the middle of the five, or the *medical finger*, because doctors use it in infamous places: The *fourth*
is named the *ring finger*, because it is accustomed to be adorned with a gold ring, since, as the wise have willed, a very thin nerve is observed by anatomists to extend from it to the heart; and indeed Doctors say that by the virtue of a gold ring placed on this finger, the heart is restored and strengthened: The *fifth*, which is the smallest, is called by some the *auricular finger*, because we are accustomed to use it like an ear-pick in cleaning the ears.

The *Palm* is the inner flat surface of the hand, in the middle of which is situated that hollow, which is called the *Hollow of the Hand*.

The *Fist* is the hand closed and compressed with the fingers drawn in.

The *Percussion of the hand* is that part of the hand with which we are accustomed to strike things with the fist.

The *Restricted hand* or *joint* is so called, where it is joined to the arm, whence it is called restricted, because it is restricted there.

The *Mounts of the fingers* are individual protuberances, which rise from the roots of the fingers, and are attributed separately to individual Planets.

The *Natural lines of the hand* are called the more important sections, to which the remaining minor ones are referred as to principal lines.

The *Line of life* or *heart* is that which, originating beneath the protuberance of the index finger, and as it were between the thumb and the index finger, cuts the hand tending towards the restricted [part/wrist].

The *Middle natural line* is that which originates at the protuberance of the index finger, and extends across the hand, to the protuberance of the moon.

The *Table line* or *liver line*, or *stomach line* is, as it were, the triangular base of the area which the line of life and the natural line, converging into an angle, form with it: this line originates near the restricted [part/wrist] beneath the protuberance or mount of the thumb, and cutting the middle natural line, flows towards the mount of the Moon. The space encompassed by these lines is given to Mars, whence it is also called the *Triangle of Mars*.

The *Mensal line* has its root and origin beneath the auricular finger in that part where the mount of the Moon is found, and in its course seeks the index finger; And this is also called the *line of fortune*.

The *Table of the hand* is that space which, by its dimensions, forms a quadrangle.

The *Milky Way* is a certain line passing from the percussion [part] towards the received [part/wrist].

The *Martial line* is that which is accustomed to pass through a part of the mount of Venus, descending from the restricted [part/wrist] towards the angle between the index finger and the thumb.

The *Way of the Sun* is a straight line ascending from the inner root of the ring finger towards the hollow of the hand.

There are various opinions, both concerning the method of dividing the vital line, and concerning the starting point of the division: For very many begin to count from the restricted part and thus proceed towards the hepatic line: We, however, consider those to imitate nature more closely who begin from the hepatic line, or the natural middle, because at the beginning of life the heart, whose line is the vital line, and the liver, whose line is the hepatic line, concur in the composition of life and body in the embryo or fetus, and are joined to each other: And since this union occurs from the beginning of life, it undoubtedly denotes the origin of life, and consequently, from the point where the vital line forms an angle with the natural line – indeed, even if it forms no angle with the hepatic line – we believe the method of numbering the years should be commenced.
As for the division itself, various opinions are proposed concerning it, since some are accustomed to divide that line into 70 parts, others into 60, others into ten, and then those again into another ten. We, however, imitating the world and its divisions, wish to divide this vital arc into 90 parts, since the fourth part of the Zodiac (which is called Zoon from its animal disposition) is divided into the same number of degrees by astronomers: Hence we say that, if the hand is optimally disposed, then its vital line, unless hindered by curvatures, corresponds to a fourth part of a circle. From this, therefore, we can also observe that the more this proportion of the line deviates from such an arc of a circle, the shorter life it promises to the possessor, unless its curved and winding disposition prevents it, which also has its own proper and distinct meaning, as explained in the following.

The experiment is as follows.

But since human life for the most part is not of such duration, or lines of this kind are very rarely found of such perfection and such exact measure, we are accustomed to divide the arc of that line into 70 parts for the most part, if it is long enough: but if short and less proportionate, into fewer.

**PRACTICE.**

The practice and experiment of this matter is as follows: If an intersecting line, foretelling a future serious illness, or a furrow indicating sudden death, or points announcing great danger, or a single or double character of the Sun, threatening damage to one or both eyes, or a disruption and discontinuity denoting danger to life, is observed in any of the aforesaid divisions, then you can predict that that thing will happen to the native around that time of life, which that division seems to signify and denote, namely, if between 30 and 40, or 20 and 30, or 40 and 50, etc. Furthermore, we can also judge about the year, if we distribute that line into distinct and particular parts.

10 | 20 | 40 | 50 | 60 | 70 |

finger, in extreme old age.

CHAPTER VI.
Concerning the line of prosperity or the path or line of Saturn.

Although we have already made mention of this line before, inasmuch as it is that line which is projected from the restrict line towards the mounts of the planets, and especially towards the tubercle of Saturn (whence it is also called the line of Saturn by some), nevertheless, we will discuss it still more particularly.

If it ascends from the base of the palm towards the hand and is straight and continuous, and passes towards the outer part of the hand, riches and that one who is poor will become rich.
If it is full and complete, and extended to the middle of the finger, deep thoughts, and fortunate outcomes in counsels and actions.
If it is branched, riches, and a change from poverty to riches; but it is necessary that that line be intersected.

[A diagram showing a section of a palm with a vertical line labeled "linea pro sp:"]

[Marginal note on the left:]
The line of prosperity denotes, if

If one continuous line passes directly from the base of the palm to the natural line, in the first age a common life, and in the second a better one.
If it passes to the root of the ring finger and returns or reflects itself towards the little finger, prosperity and good fortune.
If it joins itself to the root of the aforesaid finger, fortune through women.

[A diagram showing a section of a palm with lines labeled "annul:" and "auric."]

CHAP. I.
Concerning the metaphysical or formal pyramid considered in itself.

[A decorative woodcut initial 'Q' containing a figure.] Since the greatest clarity of our Philosophy, both Macrocosmic
and Microcosmic, consists in the explanation of a twofold pyramid,
namely, formal and material, we have therefore not thought it foolish
or trivial to treat of them clearly, so that, these being rightly and
sufficiently understood, the Reader may arrive at a suitable demonstration
of the meaning outlined both in our Macrocosmic and Microcosmic treatise,
without any impediment to his understanding. And although we have briefly
made a word or two concerning the physical pyramid in the book on the Macrocosm,
nevertheless, because the reasons

--- Page 463 ---
DE SPECULAT. PYRAMID. SCIENT. 181

[the] essence of heaven is wider and infinitely ampler in degrees than the center or earth, as we shall more copiously relate below. We say, therefore, that the formal pyramid is nothing other than an efflux or emanation of light or splendor, tending downwards from the shining throne of God, or the radiant world of supersubstantial essence, into the substantial world: Which effluence of light we have indeed called a pyramid, inasmuch as its base is found in the higher place, while its cone seems to leap downwards all the way to the earth, because its multitude in formality is at the summit near its lucid source, while its unity (speaking in a corporeal manner) is found on earth, where there is the greatest defect of light. For truly, spiritually speaking, the fullness of form is the true unity of matter, just as its defect is the multitude of matter: Hence we say that to recede from multitude to unity is to ascend from the unity of form to its multitude, that is, from the thickness of matter, namely from the earth, to the cone of its tenuity, that is, to the throne of God. The demonstration of the formal pyramid, therefore, is as follows: When we approach a great fire, we perceive in it the greatest power and efficacy of heating: But indeed, gradually and step by step receding from it, we observe it to heat less and less, and thus always successively to lose and forfeit something of its power and act. Hence it is clear that its force decreases the more it recedes from its source into the waves of cold air.

[An illustration showing a large fire on the left. To the right, seven human figures are standing at increasing distances from the fire. Dotted lines extend from the top and bottom of the fire towards the furthest figure, forming a horizontal pyramid or cone shape. The figures are positioned within this cone.]

Thus, the matter stands similarly in the formal pyramid: For the more one approaches its source and origin, the more it is known to inform, illuminate, subtilize, purify, and bless, in a manner not very dissimilar from that which we experience in the annual motion of the Sun: For the further or more remotely the Sun recedes from our Britain, or from the Tropic of Cancer, the more we perceive ourselves to suffer a defect of heat and a decrease of light and day, so much so that if the Sun were extinguished, removed, or confined to regions of darkness and oblivion, we would believe nothing but cold would befall us: But indeed, with the Sun returning to us from the region of Capricorn, we observe the effect of light and heat to approach us more and more successively: By these things, therefore, we are taught what the formal or Metaphysical pyramid is, namely, that it is nothing other than a multitude of lucid form, progressively passing into unity, in this manner;

[Two triangular diagrams made of dots. The one on the left consists of open circles, with the base on the right and the apex on the left. The one on the right consists of solid black dots, with the base on the right and the apex on the left. Dotted lines connect the dots in the right-hand diagram.]

Nevertheless, the mystery of this pyramid has not yet been explained by this demonstration: For although we have here used the formula of geometric progression in the method of delineating our pyramid, yet the situation is different in the luminous pyramid: For its cone truly tends to expand as widely as its base: Yet light operates in the air as saffron or blood in water: For a small quantity of saffron dyes the water contained in a vessel as widely as its greatest quantity; but its small portion does not color as deeply and extensively as a larger one: So also is the situation in the air: For the slightest warmth of a place affects the entire air of the place as much as a greater, indeed, even the most intense [warmth], but that [slight warmth], being weaker, is certainly attenuated, and the smallness of its luminous substance disperses itself by subtle diffusion throughout the entire medium of the place: So also we see that a gold coin, occupying a very small space, can be reduced into leaves covering a large space, and yet those leaves do not have more value in themselves than the gold from which they were extended by the art of expansion into that amplitude. But to restrict ourselves to the former indication concerning saffron, let us take a grain of saffron and put it into a pound of water; we will indeed perceive that all that water has acquired a pale color, and yet that color will be very weak, although it will have dyed its entire medium: If, therefore, a second grain is added to it again, the brightness

C H A P. II.
*On the production of the physical or material pyramid considered in itself.*

Now after we have said a few words concerning the principles of the Metaphysical or formal pyramid, we will further turn our discourse concisely and succinctly to the Physical or passive pyramid: Therefore, Reader, I would like you to understand first of all that we have called the formal Pyramid Metaphysical for this reason: because it has its base and foundation in the supersubstantial essence, and is like a ray shining downwards from the throne of the Deity, no differently than a flame emerging from the body of wood tends upwards in a pyramidal form, or solar rays leap downwards, and straighter or sharper angles

--- Page 467 ---
DE SPECULAT. PYRAMID. SCIENT. 185

Therefore, the formal pyramid is the presence of the divine word, by whose wisdom, act, justice, and power humid nature is led from the potentiality of hyle into the actuality of waters, and is reduced into a spherical figure: And this mass of waters is called the universal spirit, or fecund Pan, son of hyle, produced by Demogorgon after the dispute, that is, the prince of darkness; which is nothing other than the universal humid nature expanded throughout the entire machine. This, therefore, is that spiritual or humid pyramid, and the universal water, which we have called the physical pyramid in many places of our Macrocosmic as well as Microcosmic Treatise: And this is reduced into the form of a material pyramid because its upper part is more subtle due to the infinite presence of light, while the lower part is thicker due to the greater or lesser absence of light. It must be known, however, that the reason why the physical or material pyramid has its base opposite to the base of the formal pyramid, seems to be this; namely, because humid nature in its origin, nature, substance, operation, and place is entirely contrary to the disposition of luminous nature: For, considering the nature of both, we see that coldness is the natural companion of humid nature, while heat is the focus of light. Furthermore, they differ in their origin, because humid nature was produced from the womb of hyle or chaos, pregnant for the second time, from potentiality to this something. But luminous nature was always in actuality, and always reserved in the supersubstantial essence itself until the creation of the world, in which also, like a son in the father, it will eternally remain, and yet in a wonderful way will always be present to mundane matter: They also differ in substance, because material spirit is in a way more or less corporeal, and consequently physical; while the substance of light is incorporeal, and as it were, a supersubstantial nature in itself: In operation also these two are entirely different, since light always acts by itself; but humid or spiritual nature always suffers (is acted upon): Finally, they differ in place, since the source of light is from the summit and apex of the heavens, while the matrix of the spirit constitutes the earth itself: Therefore, just as luminous nature, always tending downwards from the luminous source, is found to be progressively thinner, sparser, and rarer, as demonstrated above, so conversely, humid nature, emerging and rising from its thick material source or matrix, is thicker, denser, and more corpulent below (whence we have posited the base of its pyramid in the earth) But gradually and step by step, ascending upwards, it becomes progressively more slender and thinner, until it forms the cone of its pyramid there, where light has the base of its pyramid. Here, therefore, we have described the parallelogram of humid nature, and likewise finally its pyramid, by joining together the two upper extremities of the parallel lines.

will still claim for itself the name of minium (red lead): Thus therefore in the very smallest mixture of light, namely of three portions of light, with one part of spirit in the Empyrean heaven, that heaven has the name of light created on the first day. Conversely, in the portions of the teeth C. C. a contrary method is indeed observed: For three parts of cerussa (white lead) are not much changed by one part of minium (red lead); Hence the name of cerussa remains there because of the predominance of cerussa. In a similar way, also because of the scarcity of light in the lowest heaven, the spirit is little changed by the nature of the body, so that it is called corporeal, both in water, air, and fire, as well as in the earth itself. From these things therefore we conclude, that the Pyramid, both Metaphysical and Physical, are precisely mixed together in this manner, so that both the aforesaid simple hemispheres constitute a single hemisphere created from matter and form, or spirit and light: And this same thing is to be understood concerning the entire sphere or mundane orb.
